Zuko had always been fascinated by storms. He watched from windows as a child, he
wielded lightning in his hands as a teenager, and then, not long after, storms were taken from
him. A blanket of earth separating him from the sky, too thick to breach, too heavy, pushing
him down, down, down into the darkness. He couldn’t see anything down there. No one
could see him.
He turned against this dream, trying to fight it off. He knew they weren’t real. He knew it,
and he was tired, and he’d had enough. He just wanted to sleep. He could hear a voice,

distant, like it was only an echo of the original sound. You're safe now. It caught him off
guard and then he was falling, and the dream caught him in its mouth, chewing him up,
spitting him out into a familiar old cell.
Zuko's reaction was instinctive. He tried to scramble back from it, burying the heels of his
palms into his eyes. Don't look. Don't look at this. He didn’t want to be here again, but he
stepped back until he hit a damp wall, and he was trapped for as long as his mind held him
prisoner.
The cell was different. The walls were dripping gold, ignited by torches from the corridor,
and it was supposed to herald agony, that light, and Zuko waited for it to come, but nothing
happened. It smelt of something in here. It was the type of familiar that sits on the tip of your
tongue. He couldn’t name it, but it wasn’t right. It was a right thing made wrong. A good
thing corrupted with evil.
The air is electric before a storm, and it smelt like that in here but metallic.
Zuko needed to get out. He couldn’t do this again. He surged forward, stumbling and
throwing himself against the bars, desperately trying to pull on them. He opened his mouth to
scream, but no noise came. Helpless.
He was condemned to this repetition. These dreams weren’t real but the memories were, and
this was his ghost. It would haunt him until he died. Zuko would never be more than a dead
thing refusing to leave, refusing to look.
“Look.” A small voice said, layered with youth and hope and life. “It’s me, Lee.”
Zuko had to turn around because he had no control here, and before him, sitting cross-legged
in the middle of the cell, was a boy. There was a gentleness to him in the light that Zuko
hadn’t seen when they met, like he could hold butterflies in his hands without spooking them,
a gentleness Zuko had never known, never possessed. And his eyes, they were amber. Such a
strikingly familiar shade, but those weren’t Zi Se’s eyes, and the boy was taller, more filled
out, a smile on his lips, and his hair- Agni, had all of their hair looked like that? Shorn
without a touch of tenderness, black strands sticking in strange spikes. The mark of
dishonour. It should never have been given to a child.
“Lanse?” Zuko whispered, voice hoarse as he finally managed to speak.
Zi Se's brother smiled brighter, nodding eagerly. “I knew you’d recognise me. Zi Se didn’t
want to talk to you, but I dragged him over. You remember?”
“I remember.” Zuko said, eyes trailing over Lanse, trying to memorise him, as if it was really
him sat here, as if this wasn’t just a projection from deep within Zuko’s mind. He knew what
happened to Lanse. He knew he wasn’t here. He couldn’t be.
“Why am I here, Lee?” Lanse asked, and his smile became a too-wide grin, unnatural.
Zuko felt like his throat was closing up. “I don’t know.”

“Hmm,” Lanse said, getting to his feet and placing a melodramatic finger to his chin, as if
deep in thought, “you’re not ashamed of this, are you? Surely not, it wasn’t your fault.”
“It wasn’t.” Zuko agreed, remembering the child torn from his little brother’s arms,
remembering Spider’s sneer of cruelty.
“It wasn’t your fault.” Lanse said again, voice falling into a terrifying monotony.
Zuko felt his eyes beginning to water, and he shook his head. “It wasn’t.” He bit out, but he
wasn’t sure who he was trying to convince now. Leave him alone. Zuko had intervened.
That's how Zi Se came to be in his care in the first place, wasn’t it? Zuko opened his mouth,
he let his anger get the best of him as always. So temperamental in the face of injustice.
Leave him alone, and he made an emphasis out of Lanse, he shone the light on him. He made
an example of him. Leave him alone, Zuko had snarled, and in it, he said look. Look at this
boy who won’t listen. Look at this boy speaking out against you. Punish him. Punish him as I
was punished. Continue the cycle.
“There’s too many of us now, Zuko.” Lanse said, and Zuko snapped his attention back to the
little boy, to his real name. Lanse was still grinning. “You’re a walking necropolis and you
will be crushed under the weight of us all.”
“Stop it.” Zuko hissed.
“Blood is your way of putting that guilt, that shame, that fury into a physical form. There is
blood everywhere, Zuko.” Lanse giggled here, a broken, childish thing that rang through the
cell and knocked against Zuko’s bones. “You’re drowning in it.”
When the rain started, Zuko didn’t question it. They were in this cell, miles away from the
sky, and he didn’t question it because his heart was roaring so loudly in his ears that he
thought he might pass out. But then the rain felt warm, felt thick, and when he looked up,
Lanse was still grinning, droplets of red curling down his face.
“Stop it.” Zuko said, more of a beg now as he held out his hands, bewildered, only for the
rain to splash down as blood. “Stop it. Stop it.”
“You did this, Zuko.” Lanse shrugged.
Zuko's hands were drenched red, the blood falling hot and soaking his hair down, sticky and
metallic and inescapable. Zuko kept opening his mouth to shout, to beg, but the blood just
rushed in, curling over his tongue with the taste of an old nightmare. That's what it had
always been about though, right? Zuko could handle the pain, the Agni Kai, the four months,
the lightning. Survival was a knee-jerk reflex for him. He knew it intimately, knew how to
endure.
Zuko could handle the pain, but the ceaselessness, the aftermath, the bloodstains, the living...
“Stop!” He screamed, falling to his knees, slamming his eyes shut to the downpour and
letting the darkness drag him under.

Zuko jolted into consciousness, sweating and trembling, and immediately winced against the
surge of daylight that hit him, trying to push away from it and only seeing to entangle his
limbs more in the cocoon of furs he’d found himself in. His breath came out short and
shallow, heaving into his lungs like a punch as he desperately forced down the panic. It
wasn’t real. None of it had been real. He could see sunlight falling through the room’s small
window, he could smell tea.
He was okay.
Zuko shakily tried to manoeuvre himself into a sitting position, only for his entire body to
ignite with pain. His leg was throbbing, a dull sting that wasn’t nearly as bad as it had been
before, but it was more than that. He felt achy, exhausted. He felt weak.
And that was a very dangerous position to be in considering he had no idea what room this
was.
“Hey, easy.” A voice said from Zuko’s side, and he turned his bleary gaze to the man sat
there. It took him a few seconds to blink into focus, but then;
“Kanut?” He uttered, voice a hoarse croak, and the healer smiled.
“Look at that,” Kanut said, a strange tension to his voice that he tried to hide with a teasing
eye roll, “you didn’t get me confused with your uncle this time.”
Zuko exhaled sharply, his best attempt at a laugh, but even that much made pain shoot
through him and he was clutching his ribs before he even knew what happened, folding into
himself.
“Two broken ribs.” Kanut said conversationally. “I’ve treated everything else, but ribs are
tricky. There's nothing I can do for them. You just need to rest. You hear me? Rest. I'm going
to say it again to see if repetition makes things go into your thick skull. Rest-.”
“Okay, I got it.” Zuko snapped, wincing as he straightened up a bit, throwing a glare Kanut’s
way that lacked any real malice. It had been a long time since Zuko felt this nostalgia without
it being painful. There was no bittersweetness, no reality check. He was just Kanut’s patient
again.
Zuko hesitated, before tentatively letting himself relax down again, his muscles untensing
one by one, soothing some of the ache. He was okay with Kanut. He knew he was okay with
Kanut, but he had to remind himself all the same.
“How’re you feeling?” Kanut asked, handing Zuko a steaming cup of tea.
Zuko took it, melting into the warmth of it even if his hands were trembling with the effort it
took to hold this simple object. How're you feeling? Zuko’s mind flashed with images of
bloody rain, a stage and a crowd, a beach, Lanse-.
Zuko tensed up again, mind finally clicking awake and ignoring the complaints of his joints.
“Where’s Zi Se?” He demanded, reaching to kick off the furs and go look for the kid despite

the way his vision was beginning to swim.
“Hey, enough of that.” Kanut’s voice was stern as he reached forward. He was probably
going to grab Zuko’s shoulder, or slowly ease him back down like he’d done so many times
before. Zuko knew that, but he was still a little out of it and he didn’t know where Zi Se was,
and he blinked and found his arm snapping out, fingers digging into Kanut’s forearm, holding
the healer back in an iron grip.
For a moment, they both stared at Zuko’s hand, and then Zuko swallowed, gaze slipping to
meet Kanut’s. Part of him didn’t expect the anger he saw there, part of him did, the same way
he was brave enough to ask the question he did but still held Kanut back when the words
were voiced.
“Are you angry with me?” Zuko whispered, and the anger in Kanut’s eyes stilled a moment,
widening in confusion, before the healer sighed.
“Not with you.” He said tiredly, and Zuko frowned, slowly lifting each of his fingers, letting
Kanut pull away. But if Kanut wasn’t angry with him, then who could he possibly be-.
It hit Zuko with an almost endearing obviousness. Fong. He was angry with Fong. Fong, who
did all this, who made him like this, who took the boy Kanut drank tea with and ruined him.
“He’s dead now.” Zuko said, words blunt and biting, cutting him on their exit. “There’s no
one left to be angry with.”
No one but the person sitting right in front of you, Zuko thought, because that was what it
was all about, that was what the dreams were trying to tell him. The anger that should have
died with Fong, the anger that tormented him in the Fire Nation as he begged it to tell him
why, the anger burning inside right now – it all led back to him. It belonged to him as much
as it was for him.
“Is that why you killed him?” Kanut asked, and Zuko flinched like he’d been hit, unprepared
for Kanut’s suddenness, for the steely way he was staring him down. “To get rid of the
anger?”
“I-…" Zuko stuttered, before working his jaw. “No. I did it because I had to wake up every
day to a five-year-old who was terrified. I did it because I wasn’t able to tell him we were
safe because as long as that man was still breathing, we weren’t.” Zuko snarled, glaring. “I
did it for Zi Se.”
Kanut was quiet for a moment, expression pained, before sighing, sitting back a little. “Okay,
tough guy. Okay.”
And it was okay. Everything was okay now. Fong was dead and Zi Se was with Zuko and
they were with the Water Tribe and for whatever inexplicable reason they hadn’t been kicked
out yet, and they were moving on.
But Kanut didn’t believe him.

Zuko had shown up at the Western Air Temple yesterday morning, and Kanut had been
saving his stupid life ever since. Zuko had woken up for a little while just before sunset
yesterday, and Kanut could feel the bruise starting to form on his forearm as a result of that.
He'd fallen back into a fitful sleep not long after.
It was dawn the next day, and finally, the fever was starting to break.
“He going to be okay?” Hakoda asked, voice weary. He looked as exhausted as Kanut felt,
watching from the doorway, as if he was scared to come in properly. The Chief had spent the
past day working through strategy plans in a room down the corridor, pacing down here every
hour or so to check in on Zuko before leaving again, never letting himself stay long.
Kanut was sat on the floor, never far from Zuko’s side. He'd been attempting to read a book,
but the words kept swimming off the pages, his mind remembering everything he knew of
infections. Some of that knowledge he’d rather be oblivious to right about now
“I've cleaned his leg and given him a tincture.” Kanut said, clearing his throat when his voice
came out hoarse. “He'll need to change that dressing every day for a while, but we caught the
infection just in time. A day or two longer and it could have got into the bloodstream. You
heard of septicaemia? Sepsis? A fifty-fifty chance of living with that, but he’s exhausted. It'd
kill him, Chief.” Kanut was rambling now, blue eyes staring Hakoda down. “A day or two
longer and he would be dead. He would be dead.”
“Hey,” Hakoda said, frowning as he strode forward to sit with Kanut, “he’s going to get
through this. You already said he’s gotten past the worst of the fever.”
Kanut sighed, an ancient ache in his chest, a helplessness. He'd seen things he wouldn’t tell
Hakoda, knew things from medical texts he wouldn’t share, had heard things from a fevercrazed mouth he wouldn’t repeat. Zuko had a barrage of injuries, most minor or healing
despite weeks of neglect, and Kanut had spent hours treating every single one. Every cut,
every burn, every small scrape, every bruise.
“You should rest. The others are still waiting on your prognosis, and besides, you’re no good
to him half-awake.” Hakoda said, voice taking on a stern tone as he took in Kanut’s drooping
frame.
Kanut wanted to argue, but Hakoda was right, and he’d hit him where he knew it would hurt.
You're no good to him half-awake. It was perhaps the only thing Kanut would listen to right

“We’ve been here before.” He said idly, remembering a day on the Ullaakut, a lifetime ago,
him and Hakoda together looking over a broken boy and deciding to heal him instead of
throw him away. They were making that decision again. It wasn’t blind this time, or a risk. It
was a certainty, and it rallied Kanut, because for as helpless as he was in this situation, at
least he had this; the knowledge that no matter what happened to Zuko, he would always,
always be there to pick up the pieces.

It was silent for a while, before Hakoda reached forward and gently pushed some of Zuko’s
sweat-soaked hair from his face.
“So has he,” Hakoda said, “too many times.”
They went out together, walking slowly, an unspoken hesitation between the old friends. It
felt wrong leaving Zuko behind in the infirmary. He was safe here, and he was resting, and
his life wasn’t on the line like it had been yesterday, and he’d already woken up once, enough
to know he wasn’t alone, but still, it felt wrong. Hakoda felt it too, but the Chief gently took
Kanut by the elbow and stirred him away.
Kanut felt the full force of his aching joints as he walked, figuring that maybe sleeplessly
hunching over for an entire day wasn’t particularly healthy for him, and when he stepped
outside into the sunny morning air, he squinted, having to shield his eyes with his hand for a
second.
Everyone was eating breakfast, which was good, because it meant they were all together.
Mealtimes, Kanut had noticed, were some of the few occasions where all nineteen – twentyone now – members of the camp could be found in the same place. The loud atmosphere of a
dozen voices talking over a dozen more, laughter and arguing, bowls clunking and the
campfire crackling, oozed over Kanut in a nostalgic warmth. It felt like the village. It felt like

Tomkin and Nanook seemed to notice him at the same time, cutting off whatever argument
they were currently having with Sokka in favour of snapping their wide eyes to Kanut, a
question in their stare. It set off a chain reaction, and the next thing Kanut knew, he had the
eyes of the entire camp on him, a stilted silence weighing him down.
“Well?” Tomkin asked, that small question filling the space.
Kanut swallowed, before cracking a small smile. “I think Chena and Zuko are competing for
who’s been dragged to me unconscious the most times.” He looked at Chena. “Heads up, he’s
now beating you.”
It wasn’t necessarily true, not by a long shot, but it shattered the stifling tension.
“Bullshit!” Chena guffawed, affronted. “Aput, knock me out.”
Aput was already turning towards him. “With pleasure.”
“No!” Tulok yelled, quickly shoving himself between the men like he’d done so many times
before, and just like that, breakfast became enjoyable again, people talking over one another

Kanut wouldn’t joke if he wasn’t; they knew that.
Bato offered Kanut some food, and in their distraction, no one noticed the figures slipping
inside the temple.

The funny thing about Nanook was his responsibility. He prided himself on it, letting it shine

This time when Zuko woke up, his limbs didn’t feel like lead, and he could see clearly after
only a minute or so of trying to blink away the heavy hum of unconsciousness. Agni was just
rising. He could feel it. Zuko thought the comfort of that tether would never grow old, not
now he knew what it was like to have it severed.
He felt different, better. Kanut wasn’t here this time, and that was probably better too. It
should be better.
With a bitten back groan, Zuko pulled himself into a sitting position, practically collapsing
back against the cold wall after such a strain on his clearly spent body. He was lucid enough
to take in his surroundings this time, and he let his golden gaze slide lazily over the makeshift
infirmary.
It was a small room, a cosy familiarity not unlike the Ullaakut, with Kanut’s equipment
scattered about the place in an uncharacteristic messiness. There was a bucket of water in the
corner of the room, various flannels draped over its side, some of them bloodstained. Zuko
winced, turning his attention to his leg. He wasn’t an idiot. He knew the tea Kanut had given
him before, the tea he barely sipped at but still drank enough of, had been laced with

sting humming from his leg. Cautiously, he pulled away the furs, picking away his now

Zuko sighed, shaking his head a little to rid himself of the thoughts and instantly regretting it
when he was hit with a headache. He needed to see Zi Se. He was safe here, but Zuko had
been out of it for far too long, and he didn’t know if the kid was okay, or where he even was.
The thought alone was enough to send shivers over Zuko, and these ones had nothing to do
with the fever. He quickly snatched up his hastily cast aside tunic from the floor, Kanut’s
insistence of ‘rest’ echoing in his mind as he grit his teeth through the agony of pulling it

But as soon as he found the stubborn determination to try to drag himself to his feet, Zuko
heard voices, quickly sinking back and feigning innocence like he hadn’t just been about to
ignore Kanut’s orders completely. But as the voices got louder, their owners getting closer, it
became abundantly clear that it wasn’t Kanut approaching.

A conspiring whisper. A sudden laugh. A quick chastising for being so loud.
Zuko would recognise them anywhere.

Having six of them get out of breakfast to go secretly see the Prince of the Fire Nation

Finally, with minimal arguing, they made it to the infirmary, and Tomkin couldn’t tell if he

as he looked from Tomkin to Nanook and back again, before – in the infinitesimal way that
was Zuko’s – his gaze softened, and Tomkin let out all the fear that had been plaguing him.
“Zuko!” Zi Se cried, pushing from Katara and dashing to the firebender, cutting off Aang’s
spiel about the Blue Spirit. Yes, Tomkin still had several things to talk to Zuko about in
regards to the Blue Spirit, but he figured it could wait as he saw the prince’s face positively
melt at the sight of Zi Se, lighting up like the sun as he caught the kid in his arms, holding
him close.
“Didn’t Kanut say you’d hurt your ribs?” Nanook said, throwing worried glances at the way
Zi Se was pressing against Zuko’s chest. Mama-polar-bear mode, Tomkin thought with a
smile.
“Kanut is exaggerating.” Zuko grumbled, moving so Zi Se was sat nestled against his side.
“Kanut is a trained and experienced healer.” Tomkin countered, and Zuko quirked a small
smile.
“A trained and experienced healer,” he said, “who exaggerates.”
For a second, Tomkin, Nanook and Zuko stilled, holding onto each other in a silent
understanding. They were the only three there, just for a second, but it was enough.
Zuko was back.

He was really, truly back.
Tomkin couldn’t keep the grin from his face even if he wanted to.
____
“Spirits, are you three about to start braiding each other’s hair? Do you want some privacy?”
Toph asked, shattering whatever had passed between the three boys. Zuko threw a pointless
glare her way, but couldn’t bring himself to feel annoyed. He felt... light. Light in a way he
didn’t recognise, light in a way that he hadn’t in a very, very long time. He had so much to
figure out. He didn’t even know what he was doing now he’d told the warriors everything he
came here to tell them. But for now, while Kanut had handed him the excuse of ‘resting’,
while his body was still too weak to even stand properly, Zuko could just... stay.
He could stay. Agni, it felt surreal.
“You’re a spiteful gremlin, has anyone ever told you that?” Tomkin asked Toph
conversationally, sitting heavily on the floor at Zuko’s side.
“They have not. I'll add it to the list.” Toph grinned, proud of herself as she bended a lump of
rock to push herself back onto. And just like that, everyone began to settle down. Zuko had
never been able to figure out why Tomkin and Nanook made the effort to be around him, and
Toph was inexplicable by definition, so Zuko wasn’t too uncertain about their sudden
decision to sit with him, but Katara and the Avatar were a different matter entirely. The
airbender had swooped in here and hardly stopped talking until the others came in, and now
he was crossing his legs at Toph’s side, getting comfortable with a cheerful smile, and even
Katara – who’d up until now been stood rigidly in the doorway – was moving to slowly lean
against the wall in faux-relaxation, as if Zuko couldn’t see the way her hand was resting on
her waterskin.
It made Zuko uneasy. Not the sense of unease he’d grown used to these past four months, but
real unease. Dread and unease were not the same thing. He'd forgotten that.
He thought they were building up to something, he thought this was when they told him to
leave their camp, so when Katara finally spoke, Zuko flinched.
“You’re done chasing us, apparently.” She said, venom in her words. Zuko remembered all
the apologies he’d practised before coming down here, how unworthy they felt. Those words
turned thick on his tongue now, as he looked this girl in the eye and knew all the hurt he’d
caused. And all for a father who never cared and a regime that scorched the world and a fury
that couldn’t be quenched. It was all his, this mess. Every piece of it.
He knew what he had to do, and for the first time in a long time, that aligned with what he
wanted. It made it different, somehow, because within him was still the boy who thought
apologies were for honourless princes, and the boy who let them slip from his mouth in the
foggy desperation of agony, back when he thought if he made himself pathetic enough, Fong
would stop. Apologies had tied so tightly in with pain in Zuko’s life that they almost invited
it, but Zuko had once walked the tundra with a great man, and when he apologised, nothing
happened.

And this was different. It had to be different this time around. Zuko had to believe it would be
different. He was clinging to it like it was the harness keeping him to the cliff-face as he took
his first few steps out of the ravine.
“I’m sorry.” Zuko said, voice gravelly but determined, stubborn with the need to get this out.
“You have no reason to trust me, and I get that. I do. I did... terrible things. I’ve done terrible
things. But... for the stuff that happened, the stuff I put you through,” he looked between
Katara and the Avatar, “I’m sorry.”
Nanook was giving him a strange look a little like pride, and the silence of the infirmary
would have been strangling if Zuko had any more energy. As it was, he was still so tired, and
he was happy to wait. That was the best thing about having been through the worst already;
every other terrifying thing suddenly became bearable.
The Avatar spoke first, expression becoming serious, which even Zuko knew was rare, his
grey eyes hinting at an ancient wisdom.
“The last time I saw you, you saved my life.” The Avatar- Aang said. “And now, I know
about you and the Water Tribe. There's good in you, Zuko. I think...” He hesitated, before
smiling a little. “I think you’re meant to be here.”
It knocked the breath from Zuko’s lungs for a moment, that declaration. Staying had been a
surreal dream, a temporary gift. But this, this welcoming from the Avatar himself... it was too
much, too tempting, too good to be true.
Aang looked expectantly to Katara, and Zuko swallowed before doing the same, forcing
himself to stay steady under that piercing blue stare. It was familiar, at least.
“How can we trust you?” Katara asked. “You’re the Fire Prince, and you’ve tried to hurt
Aang before. How can we trust you won’t turn on us again?”
This was more like what Zuko was expecting, and there was a comfort in that. He deserved
this.
He opened his mouth to respond but was beaten to it by Toph, who had spent the
conversation sat in suspicious silence.
“It’s not my job to earn your trust on Sparky’s behalf,” she said, “but I can tell you this much;
he hasn’t lied. Not about being sorry, not about what happened in the past; he’s telling the
truth”
That made Katara narrow her eyes, and for a moment, Zuko thought she was going to argue
with the earthbender, a sudden anger filling her features as she absentmindedly touched her
necklace. But then she looked over to Aang, who looked so... hopeful, and something in her
softened.
When she turned back to Zuko, Katara looked resolved. She seemed to struggle for
something to say, awkwardly stumbling over this new terrain the same way Zuko hadn’t even
found his footing yet, before her mouth settled into a hard line.

“If your ribs start giving you trouble,” she said slowly, “I guess I could try heal them with my
waterbending.”
Zuko recognised it for what it was. This wasn’t Katara worrying about his wellbeing; this had
nothing to do with his injuries. No. This was a truce. Not a forgiveness, not a helping hand,
but a truce.
It was more than what she owed him. It was so much more and Zuko almost couldn’t look at
her because of it. This was his understanding. The people here were good, and good people
do stupid, selfless things, like offer an enemy help no matter how much it pains them because
it’s the right thing to do. It was more than what she owed him and it was something he wasn’t
a good enough person to have offered if the roles were reversed, because he wasn’t. He
wasn’t good. It was why he left the Water Tribe once, and it was why he would have to leave
them again once he was stronger.
Except...
Except the Avatar didn’t want him gone, and his friends were here, and he wanted to rest, and
staying sounded an awful lot like healing, and... and...
And it was complicated, but Zuko knew a truce for what it was.
“Thank you.” Zuko said quietly, accepting this fragile peace for however long it lasted.
The room seemed to be holding its breath in that moment, before shattering to the sound of
Tomkin sighing in relief.
“Well, that’s that!” He said, beaming at Zuko and Nanook.
“Spirits, this got dull fast.” Toph huffed, a few black bangs flicking in front of her eyes before
settling again.
“Yeah,” Aang agreed with an easy-going laugh, but Zuko didn’t miss the grateful glances he
was flicking towards Katara, “let’s do something fun. Nothing too fun though, because Zuko
has to rest.”
Zuko groaned, contemplating pulling the furs over his head. If one more person said ‘rest’ in
front of him-.
“We should play a game!” Zi Se said in excitement, looking happily up at Zuko. “I played
one earlier with The Duke.”
“The Duke?” Zuko asked in confusion
A warm smile crossed Katara’s face. “Zi Se’s made friends with another kid here called The
Duke, isn’t that right, Zi Se?”
Zi Se nodded, face lighting up in such an innocent happiness that Zuko had to lean against
the wall a little more to hold himself up.

“He knows loads of cool stories.” Zi Se said, fiddling with his necklace. He was starting to do
that whenever he got excited about something, not just when he was nervous.
“If it’s stories you want,” Nanook said, an evil glint in his eye, “then I could tell you about
the time Tomkin thought he was a firebender.”
The room filled with several immediate responses of interest and one hearty groan of despair
from Tomkin, but by then it was too late for complaints, because Nanook was already telling
a tale of the South Pole, of scorched shirts and burnt bridges, and when he tried to leave out
the part about him running through the village shirtless, Tomkin eagerly jumped in.
Retaliation here was painless, was fun, was in the eye of friends. Zuko found himself just
sitting back, a small smile on his lips as he felt Zi Se slowly fall asleep against him as he had
so many times before. They spent four months like this exactly, except now, Agni was rising
through the window, bright light flooding a room of laughter and bewilderment and questions
and safety.
Look. Look at what you have.
Look.
Choose this.

Zuko watched the sunrise from where he sat on the infirmary window’s ledge, his good leg
dangling and his other leg stretched out over the stone. It was a dizzying drop down if he fell,
but he trusted his balance, and in this moment, head leaning back and eyes lidded to Agni’s
golden touch, he was happy to just bask in the warmth. He’d fallen asleep to a nightmare and
woken up this morning with his mind insisting that he was trapped again. Not being able to
see the sky did that to him, and the confusion of sleep had only exacerbated it. It was nice
here though, on the window. Kanut had told him he needed to take it easy and Zuko knew
he’d get an earful if he was caught up and about like this; he could stand now, hobbling about

the place when necessary, but his body still felt wiped out, every strain of muscle becoming
exhausting.
But it had been a few days, and he just... he needed this.
Zuko sighed, rooting through his pocket before his fingers wrapped around a familiar weight,
pulling out his pai sho tile and holding it in his palm so that the light hit it. It was a sorry
excuse of a game piece now, after everything they’d seen together. Zuko smirked as he
imagined Uncle’s chagrin upon seeing one of his beloved white lotus pieces defaced to such
an extent, bloodied and worn and chipped, but then his smirk fell. Uncle wasn’t here. He was
at the White Lotus camp. Zuko had been too cowardly to face him.
“You’re up early.”
Zuko’s flinch wasn’t innocent at the sudden voice, head snapping to the doorway to see
Hakoda there, rubbing his blue eyes a little groggily. Zuko's heart began to race, breath
hitching in his throat.
He hadn’t seen much of the warriors these past few days. He'd been in and out of
consciousness during his fever, and after that his sleeping patterns had felt almost as warped
as they had when he first got out of Fong’s base. His body was playing catch up, and healing
was a slow, gruelling process. But for the first time in months, Zuko was being given the
space he needed. Rest. It still sounded so farfetched, food in crooked fingers ready to snatch
it back from him, yet here he was, resting, spending the days being bossed about by Kanut
anytime he pushed himself too hard. Kanut made sure no one ever bothered Zuko for too
long, herding Tomkin and Nanook out whenever they got too loud, snapping at Toph
whenever she went to punch Zuko’s arm, undoubtedly remembering what happened to him
when he caught Zuko off guard last. Zuko hated being babied, being forced to spend hours
and hours just sat here doing nothing, but there was another part of him, one he’d never let
Kanut see, that melted into it. He'd been the carer for so long. It was nice to be cared for.
Still, that usually wouldn’t be enough to make him cooperative. Zuko hated sitting still, and
these past few weeks had seen him almost as restless as he had been when he first started
looking for the Avatar. He didn’t want to be left alone with his mind. It scared him, the places
he could go there. It was why he kept quiet about his ribs for so long.
But Zuko went with it, Zuko rested, because at least it kept him away from Hakoda.
Or at least it had kept him away from Hakoda, but here the Chief was, a stern set to his
shoulders, almost like he knew Zuko had been avoiding him and wasn’t going to stand for it
any longer.
“I rise with the sun.” Zuko said sullenly, refusing to hold Hakoda’s gaze but refusing to turn
his back on him either.
Hakoda wasn’t swayed, chuckling. “I remember. You were always bothering Aput at the
crack of dawn asking what chores needed doing.”

Zuko didn’t smile at the memory, at the warmth that tried so hard to blossom in his chest, but
it was a near thing. His days on the Ullaakut had been so confusing, but looking back, he
wished he’d known how lucky he was. He would have appreciated the time more, if he’d
known it was about to be cut short. Hindsight was a wicked thing.
It was silent for a while before Hakoda sighed loudly, slowly making his way over to the
window, careful not to wake Zi Se from where the kid was sleeping beside Zuko’s bedroll.
The Chief leaned against the window ledge, turning to look at the way the sun hit the ravine.
“We need to talk.” He said simply.
Zuko’s insides twisted, fear tracing his spine, and all the warning in the world couldn’t have
stopped the way his heart thundered in his ears. He’d known this was coming. He'd tried to
set it off by avoiding Hakoda – feigning sleep when the Chief came in, even going so far as
to ask Kanut to keep people out whenever Zuko knew Hakoda was coming down the corridor

Zuko knew what would happen now. Of course he knew. It was all so simple.
Simply put; Hakoda was a good man and wouldn’t turn Zuko away when he was injured like
this, but Hakoda also had to know that Zuko wasn’t a good man. Zuko was bad and that
knowledge had echoed in the blue of Hakoda’s eyes back in the Boiling Rock. Because of

days and they were already catching his badness like a disease.
His own morality exposed like that, frowned upon like that, made Zuko remember sitting on
a beach, two hands holding blue fire, no judgement for what they were or what they’d done.
He was allowed to be angry with Azula. He was allowed to be hateful in the Fire Nation. But
he didn’t want to be. He left knowing the accountability that came with that.
The reminder made Zuko sit straighter, finally looking up to find the Chief already watching
him.
Zuko deserved this. He could handle it.
“I understand.” Zuko said, staring into deep blue eyes, wondering how he had ever looked
into them and once thought he saw his father’s cruelty echoed back.
Hakoda worked his jaw, searching for the words, before sighing, as if deciding to just get on

“You’re avoiding me.” Hakoda said in that blunt way of his, and Zuko couldn’t help how he

subtlety, but still, of all things, this was what Hakoda was starting this conversation with?
Zuko had thought there was nothing else to say, aside Hakoda telling him to return to the side

Zuko felt cornered, opting to glower back out the window like a coward.
“Listen, Zuko.” Hakoda sighed, his words losing their certainty. He didn’t know how to talk

Zuko could only stare at him, his mind working too quickly in a desperate attempt to figure

No.
He wouldn’t let himself consider the possibility of forgiveness. He wasn’t strong enough for
that hope to be crushed.
“You don’t need to pretend.” Zuko said, voice a tired rasp, eyes settling on his hands,

Hakoda frowned. “Pretend what?”
It sent a bolt of frustration through Zuko. Everything they’d been through together, and the

“You don’t need to pretend,” Zuko hissed, “that you’re okay with what I did.”
Silence, oppressive and stifling. Currents of wind darted through the ravine in whistling

head, his stomach dipped in surprise.

Hakoda's expression was open, eyebrows pinching upwards a little in the middle, blue eyes
sad. He looked guilty.
“Is that what this is about then?” Hakoda asked gently. “You think I'm angry because of what
happened in the Boiling Rock?”
Not angry, Zuko thought. Angry didn’t quite match the way Hakoda had looked at him in that
library. It was disappointment, a bit of fear, disgust. He hated him. He had to hate him.
“I saw...” Zuko trailed off, realising just how much he didn’t want to talk about this,

“And what do you think that was?” Hakoda asked, face stony, serious, waiting.
Zuko just stared at him, as if staring would reveal what was going through the Chief’s mind

Frustration won out, impatience and self-hatred simmering Zuko’s tongue.
“I can’t stay here after what I did.” He snarled, speaking slowly, like he was speaking to

Hakoda didn’t flinch, but his eyes widened ever so slightly. It went quiet again, less heavy

“Zuko.” Hakoda finally breathed, nothing more than his name, eyes fluttering shut as if he

“Zuko,” Hakoda started again, finding his voice and pinning a steady blue gaze on him, “do

He could have meant anything; there was a time Zuko and Hakoda spoke every day, sharing

Zuko suddenly couldn’t speak, but Hakoda must have seen in his eyes that he remembered,

“I said,” he continued, “that we wanted you with us, we wanted you to stay. I still stand by

Zuko shook his head, burying the butts of his palms into his eyes in frustration. Everything
was curling up in his throat and he just wanted to scream.

“Stop.” He hissed. “Stop acting like nothing’s changed.”
“It has changed.” Hakoda cut in firmly. “I know it has. You've changed.”
And yeah, that stung a bit, hearing it confirmed even if Zuko already knew there’d been a

“You’ve changed,” Hakoda said again, softer now, gently tugging Zuko’s shirt like Zi Se

Zuko wanted so suddenly to look away. The words, the stare - all of it was so heavy and he

so certain he was fine, but he knew he wasn’t. That loneliness, the terror of it, the
existentialism; he was just one boy. Just one boy unable to shoulder all that. He'd been raised

case. He wasn’t weak; he was just one boy.
So he didn’t look away. Really, when had Zuko ever been good at looking away? He looked
at Zi Se sleeping curled in on himself. He looked at the lines of Hakoda’s hands; war-worn.
He looked at the small plants burrowed into the side of the ravine, curling up towards the sun,
fragile greenery pushing aside rock to make their home somewhere they never should have
been.
“So you’re saying...” Zuko started carefully, feeling that tiny bit of hope bloom in his heart
again, daring not to squash it down this time.
“That you always have a place with us.” Hakoda said firmly, lips pulling into a warm smile.
“We want you to stay here, while you’re healing and after. Zi Se too. And Zuko,” Hakoda

The hatred that twisted into Hakoda’s tone when he spoke of Fong left no room for questions.
Usually, Zuko pulled back when Fong was brought up, but he was so stunned by everything

hardly breathe. He wanted Zuko to stay. This version of Zuko. Zuko, with blood on his hands.
Zuko, who refused to be touched. Zuko, who was bad and broken. Zuko, who took the boy
they used to care about and turned him into a killer. Hakoda was taking all of that and
looking it head on and telling it, him, to stay.
Zuko bit his cheek to keep back an embarrassing urge to cry.

“You’re not...” Zuko said quietly, desperately exhausting all possible reasons for why this
was happening. “This isn’t because you think you owe me, is it? Because of Oro and
Renmin? Because if that’s the case then-.”
“What? No.” Hakoda said, almost smirking, like the idea was ridiculous, before his face fell

Zuko had the distinct feeling he’d just snitched on himself, the distant memory of two Earth

dirt had swallowed them.
“They were the ones who brought me to Fong. I fought them in Gaoling.” Zuko said, leaving
it at that because he realised there was no way Hakoda could possibly have known about the
events that led to his disappearance. All the Chief could know was that Zuko left his sword
and wasn’t seen again until four months later. Guilt sat heavy on Zuko’s shoulders.
Hakoda’s expression darkened, like he was remembering something. “Right.” He said slowly,
narrowing his eyes. “And they beat you, did they? Completely fairly?”
Zuko realised belatedly that Hakoda was already connecting the dots, cursing himself for
bringing it up. It all felt so childish, and it should have frustrated Zuko, made him impatient,
but a part of him that he thought died in the shadows of a cell felt the sudden urge to smile a
little.
Zuko ducked his head. “Mostly fairly.”
“Zuko.”
“I really did fight them.”
“Zuko.”
Zuko sighed. He'd already dug himself this hole, and he knew Hakoda was stubborn enough
to sit here until Zuko spilled.
“They threatened you. Said they’d bury the camp if I didn’t cooperate.” Zuko mumbled,
feeling stupid for it. If he’d known what it would lead to, if he’d known Oro and Renmin
would die and he would be subjected to four months of horror, would he do it again?
All it took was for Zuko to glance up at Hakoda’s exhausted expression, at the way Zi Se
held his necklace in his sleep, for him to know he’d make the same decision, and that
terrified him, the knowledge he could go through it all again just because he couldn’t
stomach apathy.
Hakoda let out a very long sigh. “And you didn’t ask us to help because...?”
Zuko frowned, thinking the answer was obvious. “Because I didn’t want you to get hurt.”
“So let me get this straight,” Hakoda said, pinching the bridge of his nose, “in the time
between you leaving that sword and you being taken,” he hesitated here, not liking that word,

not liking the rest of the story despite this being one small part they could maybe joke about,
“you could have told us about those soldiers, but instead you left and fought them on your
own, and lost the fight not because you couldn’t defeat them, but because they threated the
camp. Is that right?”
Zuko glared moodily back at the Chief, wanting to tell him that it made sense at the time but
knowing that would just make him sound immature.
Hakoda sighed once more, rubbing a hand down his face and looking back at Zuko.
“It doesn’t matter.” Hakoda said, like he was trying to convince himself more than Zuko.
“You’re back now, safe.”
It sounded a little like an order, and Zuko felt the sudden urge to argue. He had never agreed
to staying. He still didn’t understand it. How could they just let him back like that? After
what he’d done? Who he’d become? How could Hakoda be so... so...
Unconditional.
“And if I decide to leave?” Zuko hissed petulantly. “Take Zi Se and walk away?”
Hakoda's smile flashed with mischief. “You could certainly try, but I know the difference
now between giving you the autonomy over your own choices and letting you walk yourself
into self-destruction. I didn’t before. I won’t let you do that to yourself again. Do you
honestly think you’re strong enough to unlatch Tomkin and Nanook from you if they even
thought you were going somewhere? That's very cocky, Your Highness. They're tougher than
they look.”
Zuko glared, dumfounded for a few moments, but when he spoke, he found his words had no
bite. “What happened to you respecting my choices?”
“I said I'd respect the conclusion you came to.” Hakoda shrugged innocently, “I didn’t say I'd
sit back and let you act on it.”
“So you’re holding me prisoner? Again?” Zuko asked, frustration coursing through him, but
also something else, something fond.
“Not quite.” Hakoda grinned as he folded his arms smugly. “Prince Zuko of the Fire Nation,
you are grounded.”

Hakoda was talking to Prince Zuko. This was a fact of life, one Katara was still coming to
terms with, because no matter how many days passed now with Zuko staying at their camp, it
didn’t make it any easier for her mind to come to terms with the fact that Zuko was staying at
their camp.
That was how Katara found herself in one of the hallways of the Western Air Temple, foot
tapping impatiently against the dusty floor as she tried so hard not to eavesdrop, but the door

she was stood beside led to the infirmary, which led to where Zuko was staying at their camp,
which led to where Hakoda was currently talking to Zuko.
These past few days - since Zuko regained consciousness and him and Katara shared the
closest thing to a truce that they would get - had been strangely calm. Katara never thought
Zuko’s presence would lead to her using the word calm, and that’s what made it all so
unsettling. For months, Zuko’s face was the one Katara saw when she thought of the enemy.
She thought of all the nights twisting and turning, grasping for a necklace that had been lost,
had been stolen. She thought of the nightmares, the fear in Aang’s eyes, the furrowed brow of
her brother who was trying so desperately to keep them safe. All because of this boy.
And yet, her father looked more at ease than she’d seen him in weeks, a sense of relief to him
now everyone was here and everyone was okay. Katara had spoken to Hakoda, asked for
details, hidden away to think on them, coming back each time for more, more, more of the
story that was slowly starting to make itself comfortable within her. She was okay with it.
That was what she was realising. She hated it, the contradiction, because she was still so
angry at Zuko and what he put them through, but she also saw Zi Se – who she’d dedicated
hours of her days to now, trying to coax him out of his shell – and she saw Aang’s excitement
at possibly having a new firebending teacher and she saw her father and her tribe talking and
laughing like a weight Katara hadn’t noticed before had been lifted, and she saw Zuko. Katara
didn’t visit him, because that implied that she cared and was there to keep him company, but
she was still the one who did the food, and Zuko wasn’t strong enough to join them for
mealtimes. It was the one thing he didn’t try and push his luck on with Kanut, so Katara was
the one who brought his food. Tomkin and Nanook could have done it; they’d offered
enough. But Katara... she was keeping an eye on things. Nothing more.
She wasn’t curious, because that would be childish, but she’d seen how Zi Se had been with
food that first time, and even as the days passed, Zi Se didn’t ease up, only eating when he
absolutely had to and always trying to sneak off to eat with Zuko. Usually, Katara just
brought Zuko’s food and left, sometimes throwing him a scathing comment about how the
idiot’s ribs weren’t going to heal with him lounging moodily by the window like that, but
today she’d had plans.
Plans her talkative father was currently ruining.
Katara sighed impatiently, holding the hot bowl of soup in her other hand before it became
uncomfortable, and then she walked inside the infirmary, schooling her face into something
sharp.
“Katara.” Hakoda greeted warmly. He'd been mid-way through a low chuckle, leaning
against the window ledge where Zuko was sat again, probably pulling his broken ribs all sorts
of ways they ought not be pulled.
Katara fumed. “Dad, he’s supposed to be resting.”
“You sound like Kanut.” Hakoda said, like this statement concerned him a great deal. Katara
took it with a sense of smugness; for all the healer's rough edges, she’d always loved him a
great deal, and as a healer she admired him.

“Where is he anyway?” Zuko asked, the question clearly aimed at Katara but turned towards
Hakoda. He did that a lot, Katara was noticing. Almost like he was... timid. Like he was
scared of her. No, not scared. Zuko never really seemed scared of anything these days, and
not as a point of bravery, but a point of... disinterest, if anything, like he’d seen worse. It was
frustratingly confusing.
“He’s eating with the others.” Katara said, tone a little snappier than she meant. She'd always
resented even the implication that she was being overlooked. She turned her glare to Hakoda.
“Like you should be. The food's getting cold.”
Hakoda’s face twisted into a familiar grin and Katara’s glare softened.
“Well,” he said, slapping his hands to his thighs as he pushed himself up, “I can’t argue with
that.” He turned to look at Zuko, catching the firebender’s weary gaze, expression turning to
what Katara recognised as his ‘anxiously stern’ face. Katara couldn’t help but bristle

Nanook. It was theirs. His tribe’s. Not Prince Zuko’s. But she forced it down. She was
beginning to understand that, to Hakoda, to a lot of the warriors, Zuko was theirs now.
“Think about what I said, okay?” Hakoda said, and Zuko tensed. A few moments passed
heavily and Katara was painfully aware that something was transpiring right in front of her,

Hakoda grinned again, victorious, and left the infirmary with a passing ruffle of Katara’s hair
that she immediately slapped away, but it did the trick, pulling a small smile from her.
Which left stifling, obvious, awkward silence.
It passed a few beats with Katara just stood there, moving the soup from hand to hand as she

now Toph too enjoyed his company so much, sneaking off to the infirmary whenever they

came in here, Zuko just stared at her, not quite glaring, almost waiting for something awful to
happen.
It was clear Zuko could tell something was different about today, because his gaze slipped
down to the soup, then back up to Katara, a new, almost competitive glint in his eyes that
made her want to take a step back.
She cleared her throat.
“Get down. I can try take a look at your ribs.” She said coolly, making a clear move of setting
the soup down by the bedroll and then stepping back from it. Zi Se was still asleep in the
corner of the room. Katara enjoyed the little boy’s company; he was quiet for his age, but

everything he said was so surprisingly astute that it made him a decent companion. Better
than Sokka any day, but that wasn’t really saying anything.
“What.” Zuko said bluntly, barely sparing her a moment before returning his stare to the
food, a muscle in his jaw tensing. He didn’t move.
Katara placed her hands on her hips, impatient, but she couldn’t deny the way her heart was
racing. She'd known there was something going on with Zuko and Zi Se and their food, she’d
known and that’s why she’d done this, to confirm, to try and help, but she was starting to

“I don’t have to help you, you know.” Katara snapped, and that got Zuko’s attention, his head
jerking towards her, eyes wide. “Healing is complicated and tiring and I could be wasting

grateful.”
“I am.” Zuko said suddenly, voice a hoarse whisper, like he’d shoved the words out without
fully meaning them. He cleared his throat. “Grateful I mean. It's just-.” He turned back to the
soup. “It’s just... I can’t-.”
His eyes clouded with that darkness from before, the one that made Katara want to open her

thumb. Something in Zuko, tiny and alive, softened, like he was giving up, and with that, he
stood, barely wincing when he moved despite the pain Katara knew he was in. She couldn’t
help but jump back in surprise, not knowing what he was thinking.
Which left her incapable of doing anything but staring in horror as Zuko roughly grabbed the
bowl of soup and tipped its contents out of the window.
Katara stared, mouth hanging open, and Zuko stood there for a few moments, body hunched
like he was trying to stop himself from jumping after the damn food. It was what did it for

shaking. She bit back the shout on her tongue, because Zuko was acting like the food’s very
presence had suffocated him.
This... was bigger than Katara thought.
As angry as she wanted to be, as angry as she probably should have been, she just took a
deep breath, nodding to the bedroll when Zuko’s guilty eyes reluctantly met hers. He
hesitated at first, as if he couldn’t believe she was just letting it go, before cautiously taking a
seat. Katara sat in front of him, closer than she would have liked, but she was thinking like a
healer now, a healer who had no bias, no reservations, only the urge to mend.
“Can you lift your shirt?” Katara asked, and she wanted to sound kind but it just came out
harsh, because this was all still so weird and every second with Zuko felt like she was
wobbling on a knife’s edge between pitying him and hating him.
Zuko didn’t move, expression troubled, reluctant.

“I don’t have to-.” Katara started, trying to make sense of what she knew to be fear sitting
low in his eyes, no matter how much she wanted to call it anger or hatred or anything else.
“Water healing doesn’t require... I won’t touch you.” She finally whispered, gentle, and it

For a moment she almost snapped at him for implying she wasn’t capable, but then she

She knew Fong, and she’d known, in some capacity, that Zuko’s existence with Fong

She knew what was coming, so she nodded resolutely and Zuko lifted his shirt, and she didn’t

He flinched when she popped open her waterskin. Hard. Keeping still, not getting up and

“Agni,” Zuko muttered, his tone still so horrendously forced as Chena shouted something

Katara drew back quickly, water splashing back into the waterskin and her heart suddenly
racing.

“Chena is a beloved part of our tribe and if he wants to make noise, he’s entitled to that.” She

Zuko just watched her with that strange wide-eyed yet cautious expression, both painfully

“I didn’t mean it like...” Zuko started, careful, eyeing her waterskin. Katara was scaring him,

“You know, he saved my life.”

Katara paused. She hadn’t known that.
“Probably regrets it now though.” Zuko smirked, but it turned into more of a wince as he

“Give him more credit.” She said, trying to figure out what Zuko was talking about and why

He wouldn’t regret something like that.”
Zuko narrowed his eyes, thinking, and Katara returned to her bending. The rest of the healing

Katara narrowed her eyes on Zuko, before turning back to Zi Se, brightening her smile. “The

As soon as the waterbender left, it became impossible to push the panic down. It flapped
wildly in Zuko’s chest, stuttering his breathing and making his throat tighten. He'd had to sit
there, helpless, as she waterbended. It all twisted within him; the panic, the fear, and at the
forefront, always, was anger. He was so angry with himself. Katara was one of the good
guys. If she’d truly meant to hurt him today, it would have gone against everything Zuko had
built them all up to be in his head. He'd assigned them such a strict moral code, so blunt in its
lines; good or bad. Good people didn’t take advantage of an injured boy’s trust, no matter
how much he might deserve it. And besides, Katara was Hakoda's daughter. It was ridiculous,
but the blue of her clothes, her eyes, would always relax something in Zuko. With it all, he
knew he was okay with Katara, just as he knew he was okay with Hakoda or Kanut. All of
this was just residual instincts telling him to survive, survive, survive. But he wasn’t in
survival mode anymore. He could live now, here. He could stay. Hakoda wanted him to stay.
In fact, Hakoda was leaving him little choice to do anything but stay.
But Katara had once been an enemy. He knew just how capable of hurting him she was, and
when she wasn’t an enemy, that left her as a stranger. A stranger who Zuko didn’t trust. He
didn’t want her near him, with her bending and her fake kindness, so close to touching him,
scars all revealed for her to see, but what choice had he been given?

If it weren’t for that damn soup, he might have been able to get out of the healing session, but
after he threw it away, he’d owed her. It was that simple.
The thing that scared him the most was the mindset he felt himself shift into the moment he
realised there was no escaping Katara. She honestly thought she was helping, but she’d
forced Zuko into that state of vulnerability, nowhere to escape, incapable of running. And
instinctively, without even thinking about the connotations, Zuko made himself look at Zi Se.
When Spider would bait him, when the guards would drag Zuko to Fong, he looked at Zi Se.
Whenever he thought the fear, the anger, might overwhelm him, he looked at Zi Se. Because
Zuko was the sacrifice, his ruined skin a currency to pay for Zi Se’s innocence. If they didn’t
focus on Zuko, they would focus on Zi Se. If he forgot that for even a second, forgot why he
mouthed off to Spider, forgot why he kept forcing himself to stay alive for days, weeks,
months, then Zi Se would have all that hatred and agony turned onto him.
He knew Katara had been spending time with Zi Se. He knew and it made something bitter
inside him want to grab the little boy and pull him away from her. But Katara was not Spider,
or Fong, and the Western Air Temple was not the prison cell. Zuko had been offered trust,
safety, and his automatic response was to protect himself from it.
“Zuko?” Zi Se asked quietly, and Zuko blinked, grounding himself so suddenly that a wave
of nausea hit him, meeting worried amber eyes. “What’s wrong?”
Zuko was breathing heavily, hands clutched in his hair hard enough to hurt, but Zi Se was
here with him. They'd made it. It was just a stupid fucking healing session, but Zuko felt like
he’d survived a threat to his life. Agni, what was wrong with him?
“Come here.” Zuko mumbled, and before Zi Se could even question it, Zuko had scooped
him up, holding him tightly against him. Zi Se was warm and so small, so fragile, his hair
tickling Zuko’s nose as he happily held Zuko back. He smelled of Katara’s cooking, but
beneath that, his tunic held the tell-tale memory of campfires and long walks through
woodland, and Zuko could feel Zi Se’s dagger still strapped so tightly to him – he hadn’t let it
go, not once.
Zuko was the problem here, it was obvious. None of this was a big deal. Someone touching
him wasn’t a big deal. Having food in the room and not being able to eat it straight away
wasn’t a big deal. But it was. It was and he didn’t know why he couldn’t get over it. He'd
never felt anything like the way his insides had curled when Katara put that soup down, his
mind firing question after question despite knowing he was wrong. Did she just change her
stance? Was she asking him to fight for it? Was she going to take it away?
Throwing the food out had been almost as painful as keeping it so close, but the only other
alternative would have led to him wrapping trembling hands around Katara’s neck. The
thought scared him. All of it did. He did.
He was trying so hard to do good, even if he wasn’t, but he was bad at it, and he was bad at
being bad, and he couldn’t do anything right.

Think about what I said. Zuko breathed in deep, calming. You always have a place with us. It
was the strongest of loneliness, to feel so different, so alone, in a place surrounded by people.
Zuko exhaled, meditative, like Uncle taught him. The rest we can work through together.
Small hands pushed at Zuko a little. “Too tight.” Zi Se mumbled into his neck, and Zuko
cursed, loosening his grip a little, but he really, really didn’t want to let Zi Se go. Not yet. He
was starting to calm down and he just needed a moment. It was all so stupid.
Zi Se, however, had other plans, too young to even realise what was happening, too young to
acknowledge the threat that had just been here.
“Can I go play now?” He asked, pulling back to look hopefully up at Zuko.
Zuko sighed, trying not to feel that strange ache that had begun to manifest within him. It
wasn’t like loneliness, or betrayal, but it wasn’t unlike it either.
“Let’s just stay here a little longer.” Zuko said, and a week ago, Zi Se wouldn’t have
questioned it, but now, the kid’s eyebrows furrowed and he pouted moodily.
“But I want to play now.”
Zuko stared for a moment, blindsided, before letting Zi Se go, pushing him away a little.
“I said no.” Zuko hissed, and he tried to tell himself this was no different than the tantrums Zi
Se would pull in the White Lotus camp, or on the journey here. He was just a child acting
childishly. No more. But the panic was resurfacing within Zuko, because the smarter part of
him knew this was deeper than that.
“That’s not fair!” Zi Se shouted, stomping his foot. “The Duke said he’d tell me about the
Freedom Fighters today! And I want to go check out this stream we found and-!”
Zi Se’s words carried on in an enraged rant, ricocheting around Zuko’s skull in a headache.
Just noise, all of it, a barrage to explicitly say from Zi Se’s own mouth that he didn’t need
Zuko.
“Fine!” Zuko finally snapped, rage clawing up his throat, and Zi Se flinched. “You want to
go? Then leave! See if I care!”
Zuko didn’t yell at Zi Se often, and the kid hated it every time that anger got the best of
Zuko, too familiarised with Spider’s shouts, with the way Lanse had fought when he was
taken, with the way Zuko’s voice only ever raised when he wrestled for food.
Zuko watched the kid’s face, the flush of colour, the sudden wateriness of his eyes, but where
usually guilt would stab at Zuko the moment he shouted, he now felt that ache again, curled
up with his anger that wasn’t going away.
Zi Se sniffed, before turning and running out of the room.
“Fuck.” Zuko whispered, head falling into his hands.

Zi Se was getting better every day. He played and he smiled and he ate with the others.
Akinari had said one day Zi Se would remember nothing, and he’d have no scars because
Zuko never let him get any scars, and he was leaving Zuko behind because Zuko couldn’t get
better. It made him so fucking angry, so bitter, and he hated himself for it. Was he truly so
cruel as to resent Zi Se for this? For doing exactly what Zuko wanted, what Zuko couldn’t?
For moving on? For still having some of his innocence left while Zuko’s own festered in
rage?
Zuko couldn’t get through this by himself, and he wouldn’t be allowed to get through this by
himself, but it just seemed so helpless. Some corruptions couldn’t be fixed, and Zuko’s
hatefulness was so deeply etched into his heartlines that he might as well be a lost cause.
He didn’t belong anywhere. He thought of the community within the Water Tribe, how they
flowed together like their element, the love and care they extended even to their enemies
because they refused to let this war take that from them. He thought of the strength within the
Fire Nation. No chain to be snapped by a weak link; you are strong or you are banished by
thirteen. Zuko didn’t belong to either. You had them all fooled thinking you were so good, but
you aren’t. Azula had looked so vehement. He'd never seen her yell like that. And then Ozai,
stood in the flame. You are no son of mine. Banished had a finality to it. Damnation. A
bloodline severed and a tribe that would never flow through his veins no matter how much he
begged.
Zuko's breathing was coming quicker now, the dull ease from Katara’s healing and Zi Se’s
hug being replaced with a sharp sting, and he held out his arms on his legs so that his
forearms were turned upwards, pushing the sleeves back. Marred skin, the yellowy kiss of
still-there bruises, wrists bound by memory, and veins beginning to stand a little with every
second he held his arms out. Blood. Water. Family. Dynasty.
Zuko was destined to hurt people. His lineage was one of pain. A great-grandfather who
called for war and the burning of one’s love. A grandfather who decided the worth of life. A
father who took a blazing hand to a screaming child. Zuko could try and fight it, but those
men lived within him, in his bloodstream. Sozin, Azulon, Ozai.
And Ursa, a voice whispered. Ursa, the woman who did terrible things not because they were
terrible, but because they were necessary. Though she took a man's life, she was not evil.
Was Zuko?

It's not that Sokka’s a drama queen and more so that he has an above average tendency to
lament on the miserable and imbalanced state of the universe. No, seriously; he’s friends with
the Avatar; he’s entitled to his opinions on the universe’s antics in a way most people – who
are not friends with the Avatar – aren't.
That was to say that he was grievously unprepared for the situation he’d been met with on
what was once a fine morning. He'd woken up late to a well-aimed kick from his sister, who
seemed in a worse mood than usual as she told him breakfast was going cold, and had
groggily been making his way through the temple after washing up a bit only to run directly

into a sniffling five-year-old boy. Now, don’t get him wrong, Sokka didn’t mind Zi Se, but Zi

Sokka was trying very hard not to cross onto Zuko’s territory. He stayed in his part of the Air
Temple and Zuko stayed in his little infirmary. That way, Sokka could look like he was
standing by his agreement to just give him a chance, like Suki said, while also not throwing a
blunt object at the firebender’s head when he inevitably pissed him off. Win-win.
But even Sokka couldn’t prioritise his personal grudges at the sight of Zi Se sitting crosslegged in the corridor just around the corner from the infirmary, his little hands covering his
eyes in a poor attempt to stifle the tears falling from them.

down the corridor, praying that Katara or literally anyone else who liked kids would show up,

move away from Sokka.
“Hey, it’s okay.” Sokka said soothingly, gently pulling Zi Se’s hands down and using his
thumbs to push aside more of his tears. “Wanna tell me what happened?”
Zi Se shook his head stubbornly, but didn’t pull away, and Sokka took that as a good sign.
“I just want to help, Zi Se. I can’t do that if you don’t talk to me.” Sokka said, again keeping
his voice calm. There was a lot he didn’t remember about his mother, and it twisted him up
inside with a familiar self-hatred, but this, this calmness, this patience – he knew this. He saw
it in Katara. He saw a lot of Kya in Katara. More than what was in him.
Zi Se finally looked up at him, amber eyes puffy, face all blotchy and snotty, before pulling
out his necklace and beginning to chew it.
“Zuko yelled at me.” Zi Se mumbled, and Sokka carefully schooled his face to remain
attentive. A more immature part of him wanted to latch onto this. The past few days had left
him with a feeling awfully familiar to what he felt back in Makapu Village, telling everyone
they were in danger and being met with nonchalance, their total faith in that ridiculous Aunt
Wu making them blind to a literal volcanic eruption. But Sokka had been right then.
Was he right now?
But he pushed it down, almost wanting to groan with the ugly maturity of it all. Give him a
chance, Why was it that Sokka always had to be the bigger person? Wasn’t that why he’d
trusted Zuko so quickly in the Boiling Rock anyway? He'd finally found someone he wasn’t
responsible for, someone he wasn’t charged to protect, someone on equal footing. That's why
it had all hurt so much after... after... But that... Yeah, it was definitely too early to be getting
into that.
“Yeah,” Sokka sighed, “he does that. What happened?”
Zi Se crossed his arms with a ‘humph’, clearly not intending to elaborate, and Sokka tried not
to roll his eyes. At least the tears had stopped.

“Hey,” Sokka said, poking Zi Se’s side, “what’s that face for? Very stoic of you, Lord Zi Se.”
He poked him again and this time earnt a surprised giggle that Zi Se quickly tried to hide.
“What’s this? Are you ticklish?”
“No!” Zi Se was grinning now, going to push to his feet only to be swept up in Sokka’s arms.
The kid’s loud laughter filled the corridor as Sokka tickled him, Zi Se’s own hands
desperately trying to retaliate.
“Stop!” Zi Se cried, a smile splitting his face, and Sokka finally put him down again with a
smile of his own.
“Apologies, my lord, it won’t happen again.” Sokka said with an obnoxiously formal voice,
earning another giggle from the kid.
“I’m not a lord.” Zi Se insisted with a huff, and Sokka couldn’t hide his smirk.
“You sure?” He asked, narrowing his eyes. “Could’ve fooled me with that fancy necklace.
And you’ve got that cool dagger.”
Zi Se grabbed his necklace, smile becoming smaller, warmer, but then his hand fell to where
Sokka knew he kept that dagger, and his smile disappeared entirely. Zi Se sat back down,
scrubbing an arm down his face to wipe away the last of his tears.
“The dagger was a gift,” Zi Se said quietly, “from Zuko.”
Of course it was, Sokka mentally sighed, because he couldn’t have just found the damn thing
somewhere. No, it all had to come back to the angry jerk.
“You know,” Sokka said, “it’s never okay to yell at a little kid. Zuko shouldn’t have done
that, no matter how angry he was.”
Sokka wanted to feel that familiar burn within him, the burn that hated Zuko and added any

a lot Sokka didn’t know about the Fire Nation, but in the Water Tribe, parents yelling at small

The Earth Kingdom men. Fong’s base. Sokka was taken back to a cramped storage cupboard,
the flickering orange lamp above his head throwing a torso of scars into shadow. What

I wish I could. Hakoda told Sokka what had really happened to Zuko, what had led to him
doing what he did that day. And Suki, so strong, mind made up. I won’t vilify him for what

Sokka had been very purposely ignoring all of... this. This side of things, this side that made

Zuko and Zi Se spent four months with a man so full of cruelty that it couldn’t even contain

But the thing is, Sokka’s hatred of Zuko really didn’t have very much to do with Zuko. It was

ignored it, shoved it away, insisted he hated Zuko for all these other things. I hate Zuko

Prince. I hate Zuko because everyone is letting him in but they haven’t seen him the way I

have. Excuse after excuse after excuse, and they were valid. Sokka was entitled to all of that,
all of that anger and confusion and frustration. But it wasn’t the truth, and he’d tried to
pretend it was, but it wasn’t, and with Zi Se sat here now, Sokka couldn’t pretend anymore.
The truth lay within Sokka, lay within a flawed invasion plan, lay within failure and
responsibility, lay within a chance taken, a chance thrown back in his face. A fool, his mind
hissed, you should have known better.
“Can I go play now?” Zi Se asked, and it snapped Sokka back to reality, shaken as he looked

rest of your life. You just learn to live with it, and this little boy that never should have had to
was learning to live with it.
"Interrogating the enemy, Snoozles?” Toph’s sharp voice almost made Sokka jump out of his

their new Fire Nation companions, and felt the urge now to deny any and all involvement

Instead, he smirked down at Zi Se, hauling them both to their feet. “Lord Zi Se has been most
cooperative.”
Zi Se hit his leg, smiling, before finally running off to play.

had. He gulped, focussing on his food.

It had been two days since Zuko woke up from his fever, and in that time, not once had
Tomkin and Nanook been able to shake the others in order to see him alone. Toph always
wanted to tag along, or Aang would leap over the moment they got up, and one time even
Tulok had come, which was a big deal because most of the older warriors had seemingly
made a silent agreement to wait for Zuko to come to them. Tomkin got it, he did. He
remembered the fear he’d felt right before seeing Zuko in the infirmary that first time,
wondering where they stood now, what had changed, and he’d been close to Zuko in a way
the older warriors weren’t. Well, as close they could have gotten in the month they were
given, before it was all snatched away.
But today, finally, was different. When Nanook got up after eating, hauling Tomkin – who
was still chewing, for Spirit’s sake – to his feet to go and see Zuko like they always did after
mealtimes, no one got up to join them. Tomkin had thought for a moment there that this
might be the day Sokka’s curiosity overpowered his stubbornness, but the other boy was
staring rather angrily at the charred logs of the campfire, deep in thought. He’d need a little
longer to sulk- sorry, think.
Which left Tomkin and Nanook. Alone. To go and see Zuko. In the infirmary.
Just like a day five months ago, when none of them knew any better.
They made it all the way to the temple’s entrance before their plans were ruined by a bundle
of unadulterated vengeful lemur.
“Momo!” Tomkin cried, immediately trying to grab the animal from where it had latched
onto his hair again. Nanook hadn’t hesitated to start laughing at him, being absolutely useless
and letting Tomkin struggle alone.

“You’ve made a friend, Little Tom.” Chena guffawed, and great, now the others were
laughing too, and all Tomkin could do was seethe as he pried claws away from his literal
scalp.

cretin at arm's length from him, too scared to let him go. Nanook was almost doubled over at

his face.

with Toph cackling over it like that. Tomkin fumed.

“What did you even do to make him hate you so much?” Zuko asked. He'd lifted his head

And then Nanook burst out laughing – at Tomkin’s expense, for the second time that morning

“Toph threw the rock at me first, I’d like to point out.” Tomkin said in a hurried attempt to
defend himself. “And I caught it, but it was heavier than I expected, because it was a fucking
rock, and it... happened to just... sort of... fall... and Momo was there... and...”
“And you dropped a rock on his tail.” Zuko repeated, Nanook still laughing, and Tomkin
groaned.
“You’re both awful and I hate you.”
It took a few moments before Nanook’s boisterous laughing petered down into badlycontrolled giggles, Tomkin’s moody expression lasting all the way until Nanook snorted

realised Zuko’s smile had fallen, mouth turned down, eyes tracking something with Tomkin’s
movements.
Tomkin followed the firebender’s gaze to see his sleeve had lifted, revealing an old burn scar
on his arm, long since healed, no more than an uneven sheen on otherwise unmarred skin.
Tomkin looked back up again, smile crooked as he met Zuko’s gaze. “Badass, right?” He said
quietly, and Zuko sucked in a sharp inhale, remembering exactly what Tomkin was
remembering.

“Yeah.” Zuko breathed, fingers dancing over his wrists, before his expression turned more
determined. “Yeah.”
That little moment of quiet, that moment of understanding and depth and sudden jolt into the
past, reminded Tomkin of something he’d been wanting to do for a while. He reached into his
pocket, fingers brushing against now-crumpled paper and feeling his stomach flip at the
memory. He looked up to see Nanook already staring at his pocket, having followed
Tomkin’s movement, and the other boy smiled, giving him an encouraging nod.
Tomkin turned back to Zuko and swallowed his inexplicable nerves. “I got you something.”
Zuko immediately frowned, like the prospect was bewildering, and it caused a familiar
frustration in Tomkin, frustration that some people were never given nice things without
ulterior motives, frustration that Zuko had been through so much and all Tomkin could give
him was this shitty scroll.
“What is it?” Zuko asked, cautious now, eyes narrowed, and Tomkin tried not to take it
personally, he really did.
“Well...” Tomkin started, pulling the scroll from his pocket, rolling it back and forth over his
leg anxiously. “I got it in Gaoling, when we were looking around the stalls together. I was
supposed to give it you then, but we sort of... fell out.” Both boys winced; Nanook rolled his
eyes. “So I was holding onto it, to give it you when we were talking again, but then...”
Tomkin worked his jaw, the pain in his chest stinging him, before looking directly at Zuko. “I
kept it on me every day you were gone, you know? I knew we’d see you again. I always
knew.”
Zuko stared, unblinking, unflinching, a little disbelieving, a little pained, before letting out a
shaky breath. Tomkin gave a small smile, knowing that meant Zuko was ready now, and
handed over the scroll.
The way Zuko handled it instantly took Tomkin back to that market in Gaoling, watching
curiously as this brazen firebender reached for this simple mundanity with so much
gentleness, so much care. Tomkin remembered the way his friend’s expression had opened,
vulnerable and warm, before shuttering again because someone somewhere had taught him
that this part of himself was a weakness. Zuko didn’t shutter it this time, because there was
nothing to hide. Tomkin searched for that softness, tried to find it in the way Zuko carefully
unfurled the scroll, and came up empty. He felt his heart leap into his mouth, fearing the
worst, when suddenly, Zuko’s eyes widened, taking in the words on the paper, breath
catching as he realised exactly what this was.
And there it was. The tiniest flicker in his golden eyes. A hint of a softness Tomkin had
worried was dead forever.
“This is...” Zuko whispered, voice hoarse.
“An autograph from quoted ‘the best Earth Kingdom playwright of all time.’” Tomkin
grinned. “Nan can call me an idiot all he likes, but I remembered this.”

Zuko’s eyes were a little glassy, the scroll trembling ever so slightly as he read it over and
over and over again, finally swallowing.
“When I was in that cell,” he said, and he spoke so quietly, like the words scared him, like
they were too massive to fit on his tongue and he was tearing his insides up to get them out,

not expecting this, but Zuko wasn’t finished, gripping the scroll a little tighter. “I was so far

reliving it all. “I thought I would die down there, and no one would know or... or worse. No
one would care.”
And then Zuko opened his eyes, those burning orbs trained directly on Tomkin and Nanook
with some kind of unrelenting rawness that Tomkin couldn’t name, heart thundering in his
ears.
“Thank you.” Zuko hissed, like a promise, and it was all Tomkin could do not to tackle the
prince into a hug and never ever let go.
“You’re staying, aren’t you?” Nanook asked gently, almost scared of the answer, and they

He didn’t say going back home, because it wasn’t. It never had been, not to Zuko. He might
not have told them everything he told Kanut and Hakoda, but Tomkin could figure out this
much.
“My father made it pretty clear he doesn’t want me there.” Zuko scoffed, the noise a little
wet, biting back a hollow smirk in favour of chewing at his split lip that still hadn’t quite
healed. “And Hakoda,” Zuko frowned, perplexed, “he... grounded me?”
Tomkin barked out a laugh, surprised, and the mood finally returned to normal again, where
they could just be three young boys, friends, spending time together.
“He grounded you?” Tomkin asked, smiling.
Zuko was still frowning, looking a little scandalised. “Yeah, but then he just said that I had to
stay here, that I wasn’t allowed to leave again, and that was it, which doesn’t really sound
like being grounded.”
Tomkin threw a look to Nanook, meeting his blue eyes and seeing the same thought echoed
back. I don’t want to know what the Fire Lord’s version of being grounded looks like. It was
clear what the Chief had done. Zuko wasn't actually in trouble, but he would always respond
to direct statements over implications. Now, there truly was no way Zuko would be going
anywhere, and Tomkin grinned.
“Looks like you’re stuck with us again.”
Nanook gave a faux pout. “Bummer.”

Zuko looked between them, then back at the autograph, lips creeping into a slow smile.
“I think I'll manage.”
