Sokka hadn’t wanted to go with Tomkin and Nanook because he needed to do this alone, and
because he’d still been a little blindsided by his own realisation. But he’d come to a decision
now, and he knew there was no getting out of it. Logically speaking, you can’t trust a set of
results without repeating the experiment a good few times, and technically, Sokka had only
given Zuko one chance. Call it an outlier. A spectacular, devastating outlier.
To figure out the authenticity of that, Sokka would have to face the firebender. He could
prove himself right, like with Aunt Wu, like with Jet, and feel that hollow sense of victory
when the people around him got hurt by the sharp stab of betrayal, or maybe, just maybe...
Zuko would prove him wrong.
First, Sokka needed to explain himself.
So as soon as Zuko got out of the infirmary, they would talk.

It started off with a break of laughter, echoing a little hauntingly through the temple and
reaching Zuko in the infirmary. He'd hesitated, but in the end, he’d never been able to put his
foot down when it came to Zi Se. When he poked his head out of the door, he saw them, just
at the end of the corridor, too far away to notice him. Sokka and Zi Se, laughing as the Water
Tribe boy held Zi Se close, face broken into a crooked smile. It unsettled something in Zuko,
like the way sand rushes down a dune when you make a single misstep, something a little
freeing but also jarring, a jolt in the peripheral, a shift in stance.
It started off with Tomkin and Nanook and an autograph wearied by months of being held
close. They looked directly at him and they didn’t blink, and he tried. He tried so hard. He
opened his mouth to talk about it, the great big it, but all that came out was surface level
troubles, and even that much had made them silence in horror. But still, they listened, and
they cared, and when he told them he was staying, they smiled.
It ended with him sat on a windowsill again, the infirmary a familiar empty space around him
and a pai sho tile in his hand. Agni sat comfortably in the sky now, the day continuing on
whether he liked it or not, and Zuko wasn’t at a point yet where he could say he was okay. He
didn’t feel okay, in any sense of the word. But last week, he hadn’t been able to even admit
that much. This was rest. This was staying. This was wanting and being wanted in turn.
This, he realised, in its own slow, agonising way, was healing.
Zuko smiled, turning the white lotus tile over his knuckles, and tipped his head back to bask
in the golden sunlight.

There was a tapping noise filling the infirmary. A task like this didn’t require much
concentration, but even the most focused would strain, so distracted by that insufferable,
relentless tapping. Kanut furrowed his brows, forcing himself to tune it out, forcing himself
not to rise to it as he prodded and pressed and examined, but as the seconds passed and the
tapping continued, he finally had enough.
“Cut it out.” He hissed, flicking Zuko’s head and earning a sharp jump from the firebender.
Zuko rubbed his head, glaring sullenly. “I’m not doing anything.”
And in a perfect contradiction, Zuko returned to tapping his foot against the floor. The
moment he did so, Kanut raised an eyebrow. The kid at least had the decency to flush a little
as he realised what he’d been doing, all that restless energy as he waited for Kanut’s verdict
finding some form of outlet, no matter how annoying.

stubborn asshole who didn’t listen to medical advice but then complained when his health

least it was supposed to be routine, but someone – probably Tomkin – had let it slip to Zuko

was more than a little eager to get out.

He was cut off by Zuko jumping to his feet, grinning – actually grinning – in relief as he

Kanut let him go, the two staring each other down for a second as Kanut waited to see if

Kanut was sure to nudge past Zuko when he headed for the doorway, knocking them both out

“Come on,” Kanut huffed, but his lips twisted into a wry smile, “I think you’ve been cooped

It had only been a week that Zuko was in the infirmary, and it had a window, a cool breeze,
torches he could light when it got dark, not that he ever did, and Tomkin and Nanook and the

“Yes,” Hakoda answered, wearing a similar expression, “so we can assume that’ll be at least
a dozen airships, with firebenders crawling from each. And that’s the minimum.”
Sokka felt his father’s wince. It looked grim, as they scoured battle plans and strategized,
combining their talents in a desperate attempt to think of a plan. There had to be something.
There was always something that could be done. And it killed Sokka to admit, but Zuko had

problem was with his father.
That hurt more, but Sokka was done using Zuko as a scapegoat for literally everything.
“Yep,” Sokka flashed his dad what he hoped was a convincing grin, “just two guys. Catching
up. No biggie.” What the fuck was he saying? “See you.”
Hakoda called after him but Sokka had already darted into the corridor, needing out of that
stifling room full of war and unchecked familial troubles.
It's not that he thought his dad liked Zuko more than him. For one, that was impossible even
without bloodlines. Zuko was an uncharismatic asshole with anger issues and Sokka was his
hilarious self. Add in the fact that Sokka had the biological advantage of being, you know,
Hakoda’s actual son, and it wasn’t even in question.
But Hakoda... He could do more to reassure Sokka.
No, that wasn’t right. Sokka didn’t want to be babied, and he got that what Zuko was going
through was the kind of thing that warranted attention, but still... Sokka and Katara should
have been Hakoda’s priority, no matter what. And Sokka just... didn’t feel like that right now.
Katara hadn’t said anything though, and every time she went into that infirmary, she came
back out with a small twist to her mouth, like she was trying to hide a sense of satisfaction.
Was this just Sokka? Was this like before, when he wanted everyone to see how evil Zuko
was just to realise he was overthinking it? Was he overthinking his dad now too?
Sokka wanted to bury his head in his hands and groan.
Suki, however, decided that was the perfect opportunity to jump out at him, arm around his
shoulders and knuckles digging into his skull.
“Ow!” Sokka screeched in surprise as he wrestled away. “What was that for?!”
Suki laughed loudly, only laughing louder when he turned the full force of his pout on her.
“You were sulking about something.” Suki said, like that justified grievous bodily harm. “I
could feel it all the way from the other end of the corridor. What’s up?”
Ah, a perfect opportunity for Sokka to partake in open communication and possibly find a
solution to his unsettled emotions through the love and trust of a close friend.
“Nothing.” Sokka said, shoving Suki’s shoulder.
Yeah, hard pass.

Chena didn’t like kids, and usually, in some blissful twist of fate, kids didn’t like him either.
He was big and loud and shamelessly did his best to get them to fuck off. It was a general
rule, an accepted fact of life; Chena of the Southern Water Tribe and kids did not mix. Only
four had ever defied this. The first had blinked fearlessly up at him from his own arms. The
second came in the form of Katara, stomping through the village with arms crossed
stubbornly to demand he teach her how to fight at the ripe age of eight. The third, a Fire
Prince, spitting in his face as he strangled the brat and in turn becoming the biggest pain in
Chena’s ass of the entire decade.
The fourth, an amber eyed five-year-old, currently doing a poor job of peeking over a rock to
watch Chena sharpening his machete.
“Go away.” Chena grumbled, making Zi Se jump as he realised he’d been caught, and Chena
turned his glare back down to his beloved machete, methodically running it over a whetstone.
The kid did not, in fact, go away, instead stepping out into the open defiantly, taking a few
tentative steps forward, eyes trained on Chena’s big hands. Zi Se wasn’t actually a bad kid,
from what Chena had seen. He'd thrown a few tantrums when he was separated from Zuko,
sure. And he’d fallen asleep on Chena’s chest that one time and dribbled all over him. But
after what he’d been through at such a young age, after all he’d lost, all he’d been pulled
from nation to nation with no one explaining to him why, he was a good kid. A good Fire
Nation kid. Chena almost scoffed, the humour dry in his throat.
“What’re you doing?” Zi Se asked quietly, taking another step closer.
Chena sighed, putting his machete down so he could lean his forearms on his knees and glare
fully at him. “None of your business.”
Good kid or not, Zi Se also had a gaggle of admirers, the other tribesmen coddling him,
Katara hardly ever leaving his side. He didn’t need Chena with his big mouth and scary
demeanour to add to that.
But instead of being scared off, Zi Se just frowned, entire face scrunching up in a way that
was not adorable, not even in the slightest, before he quickly began rummaging through his
tunic, pulling out a dagger. He smiled happily, offering it to Chena, not saying anything else.
What did he expect him to do with it? Chena just stared, not getting the kid’s meaning, and Zi
Se huffed impatiently, opting to waggle the dagger at Chena some more, as if he thought the
warrior hadn’t seen it.
“What do you want?” Chena finally snapped, having to restrain himself from groaning. He
didn’t have the Chief’s patience or Tulok’s kindness. Why did Zi Se have to choose to bother
him, of all people?
“What you’re doing to your sword.” Zi Se said, mumbling over words in the way children do
when they don’t yet know how to explain what they want. “Do mine.”
So demanding. Were all Fire Nation children this spoilt? Chena’s worked his jaw, stupid
question.

He rolled his eyes, picking his machete up again to show the kid who had somehow inched
closer without him noticing. “This,” he said, reluctant, “isn’t a sword. It's a machete. And
yours is a dagger.”
Zi Se frowned again, looking between the blades. “What’s the difference?”
When Aput rounded the corner sometime later, looking for his friend to see if he wanted to
spar, he paused, mind blanking. Sat on one of the rocks, face smoothed into a look of unusual
easiness, was Chena, holding Zi Se on his knee with one hand and holding his machete in the
other as he calmly explained the characteristics of the blade, how it worked, how it differed
from an Earth Kingdom dagger, as Zi Se listened intently.
Aput smiled, turning around before they noticed him. Every damn time, he thought with a
chuckle.
____
Zuko was noticing that it was impossible to be left alone for too long at the Western Air
Temple. He had been perfectly happy just sitting with Kanut, Tulok and Bato, zoning out of
their conversation and pretending he couldn’t see those infuriating looks they kept throwing
him. Concerned, observing him like he was some child. Zuko had been so relieved when he
finally accepted that, for whatever reason, the tribesmen didn’t hate him. But now he was
starting to wish they did. Hatred made sense. Hatred was what he deserved. Hatred was what
he knew how to handle. This though, this sickening coddling, this was something he didn’t
know.
But still, he had been fine just sucking it up, testing his breathing exercises now he was in the
fresh air.
And then the Avatar showed up.
“Jee, it sure is cold today.” Avatar Aang said loudly, jumping his leg from where he’d sat far
too close to Zuko, grey eyes fitfully dancing around the room. Suspicious didn’t even begin
to cover it, and Zuko couldn’t help the annoyed glare he focused on the boy. He didn’t trust
him. Didn't trust the innocence, the childishness, the forgiveness. Do you think we could have
been friends? And now, what was this? The Avatar – who insisted on being called Aang, just
Aang – had visited Zuko almost as often as Tomkin and Nanook, filling Zuko’s
uncomfortable silences with incessant chatter covering every single topic aside the ones that
needed covering. Zuko had hunted him, had captured him, had intended to drag the boy to the
Fire Lord for a fate he knew was cruel even then, but that’s not what Aang wanted to talk
about. Instead, he spoke of his pets, his friends, his travels, all with a big grin.
The kid was too pure. He'd taken every badness the world had thrown at him and instead of
internalising it and letting himself grow bitter and cold, he instead refused it, becoming a
walking ray of sunshine. And here was Zuko, wallowing in his misery, letting it consume
him, letting himself become a festering ball of rage and hatred and blood.
“Is no one else cold?” The Avatar said, voice too high-pitched. “Because I'm cold.”

He was going somewhere with this, but Zuko couldn’t tell where, and a glance to Kanut said
the healer was just as bemused as he was.
“The sun’s out.” Bato said with a wry smile and a pointed nod towards the blazing sun,
amused.
Avatar Aang turned and squinted, like he hadn’t noticed, before shrugging animatedly, not
letting it deter him.
“Well, I still think it’s cold.” He declared, before suddenly growing sheepish, turning to Zuko
with wide, hopeful eyes. “Maybe... you should light a fire.”
Oh.
“No.” Zuko said immediately, almost wincing at how harsh his voice came out. The Avatar
blinked in surprise, not expecting a negative response, let alone such a hurried one, but Zuko
wasn’t a complete idiot, despite popular belief. He knew the Avatar didn’t know firebending
yet. He knew he was the only firebender in possibly the entire world that was both close
enough to train the Avatar and willing to train the Avatar. He knew since finding out about
Sozin’s Comet that the Avatar had been training obsessively, stress gnawing away at him and
manifesting in the form of overworking.
Zuko also knew that he couldn’t be the Avatar’s firebending teacher. He knew how it looked.
He knew he looked like he was being loyal to his nation, refusing to help the kid. He knew he
looked like he was being difficult. But that wasn’t it. He wanted to help, some part of him
still desperate to be useful, because to be useful meant you got to stay.
But he couldn’t. He just couldn’t. Because fires that weren’t his own still made his insides
curl within him like the very flames they feared, and fires that were his own were an icy blue,
reflected in the shadows of a library smelling of blood. Fire had abandoned him when he
needed it most. Fire had charred his skin in a sick mockery. Fire had burned behind Spider’s
every arrival. Fire had backdropped Chan’s bulging stare. Fire had punctuated every bad
thing in Zuko’s life and it wasn’t something he could ignore, not this time. It didn’t matter if
his bending made him feel whole or if the colours above his head that night with Zi Se had
made some deep part of him feel peace, even for a moment. It didn’t matter that Azula was
out there somewhere, this same ice living within her. Three years ago, Zuko had to teach
himself not to fear fire, and it had betrayed him all over again. He couldn’t keep making the
same mistakes. He couldn’t keep reaching only for his hands to be burnt.
He wanted nothing to do with it anymore. Firebending was a necessity. Zuko did what he had
to and that was it.
Training the Avatar was out of the question.
“But,” the Avatar – Aang – frowned, almost pouting if it weren’t for the troubled twist of his
mouth, “you’re a firebender.”
Neither of them were talking about lighting a campfire, and Zuko was grateful for that. He
didn’t have the energy to watch Aang play dumb.

Zuko shifted uncomfortably, wanting to explain himself without having to lay himself bare
before the four of them, wanting to put the truth out there without having to say any of it
himself. He'd call memory a corpse, a rotting carcass, clinging to him like the smell of
something festering, but that wasn’t right. Memory was a living, vivid thing, visceral and
toxic and choking him with its presence. He couldn’t kill it. He didn’t know how to introduce
it. He couldn’t even say its name.
“He’s still in recovery, remember.” Kanut said, tone casual but with a hint of warning in his
gaze as he looked at the Avatar. It just made Zuko feel worse. Recovery was no excuse. He
didn’t need that. He didn’t need to be treated like a child.
“I’m fine.” He growled, glaring at the healer. For a few tense moments, they stared each other
down, Kanut unwilling to cave and Zuko desperate to prove his point. The silence that
surrounded them was suffocating, too warm, too clingy, hanging like the walls of a cell.
Zuko's heart felt loose in his chest, trembling with every too-controlled breath.
“Looking good, Tulok!” Suki’s sudden voice burst through with a shock of vibrance, and
Zuko startled, instinct taking over as he snapped his head to face the girl currently walking
over to them, her friendly smile oblivious to the previous uneasiness. “You’ll be an origami
pro before you know it. Aneko would be impressed.”
Zuko immediately cursed himself for looking away from Kanut, feeling an immature sense of
defeat, but the feeling quickly disappeared, his focus turning to Suki’s companion.
Sokka was with her, uncharacteristically quiet at her side, walking over with hands shoved
deep into his pockets and his eyes trained on the floor.
“You think?” Tulok asked happily, holding up the paper animal before him – it looked like
some kind of bird – as Suki crouched down to inspect it, the two delving into a quiet
conversation.
“What’re you guys talking about over here?” Sokka asked, finally noticing Aang’s strange
silence, the kid twisting his hands a little anxiously. Zuko felt a stab of guilt for upsetting
him, as ridiculous as it was, but when he braved meeting the airbender’s eyes, he was
surprised to see concern there, not disappointment. Zuko almost missed it, but he’d seen that
expression enough times lately for it to register in his mind with a crushing vividity.
“Take a guess.” Bato said, a conspiring smile thrown Zuko’s way, and it was enough of a
reprieve that Zuko’s mind went momentarily blank. I hate it as much as you do, he thought
bitterly.
“Right, well.” Sokka said, frowning a little, confused, before turning fully to Zuko. “I see
you’re out of the infirmary.”
Zuko must have looked like a cornered animal, mind racing to figure out the boy’s angle. He
hadn’t spoken to Sokka since the other teenager dragged him down here, and now he was
making small talk? Sokka didn’t hide his hatred of Zuko, letting shameless contempt
overtake his features every time they laid eyes on each other. And Zuko got it; he’d
personally let this boy down. Sokka handed him a truce and Zuko handed him a murder. I

should have known better. Sokka wasn’t the type to keep on making the same mistakes; he
was smarter than Zuko. He was smarter than a lot of people, actually. It was infuriating.
They didn’t like each other, never had. Not even when they were helping each other.
So what was he up to?
“Yes?” Zuko answered carefully, not meaning to make it a question.
“Cool.” Sokka nodded. Zuko had never seen the extroverted boy look so awkward. A few
beats passed in silence, a different kind of uncomfortable than the one with Kanut, before
Sokka sighed loudly, rubbing the back of his neck.
“Listen, can we talk?” He asked, words suddenly blunt, gaze hard, unrelenting, merciless.
“Alone.”
And Zuko was captivated, remembering the stifling pity of everyone else, even the Avatar,
who was supposed to be his nemesis. He thought of every reason he’d given these people to
hate him and every way they had ignored that. He thought of softness and how sharp it had
felt, how undeserved.
But Sokka... Sokka didn’t hide his hatred of Zuko. He took what happened to Zuko, took
scars in ragged candlelight, and didn’t translate it into an excuse for all the badness he’d
caused. Zuko didn’t know much of redemption, but he knew it was earned. He knew what he
had with the other tribesmen had simply been given, because they saw him as a wounded kid.
It was fake, hollow, pitiful.
Somehow, the person who liked him the least here had become the only point of honesty
Zuko had felt all week.
“Okay.” Zuko said quietly, relief seeping through his very bones as he got to his feet. Sokka
watched him cautiously a moment, distrust radiating from him, before nodding and walking
towards the temple, Zuko following.
____
“They’re not going to kill each other, are they?” Suki asked, breaking the silence that had
descended as her, Tulok, Kanut, Bato and Aang all watched in bewilderment when Sokka and
Zuko went inside. Sokka had been acting strange earlier. It's not like the two were incapable,
and Suki had seen people do worse to each other over lesser hatreds.
“Should someone intervene?” Tulok asked, worried now.
Bato narrowed his eyes at the temple’s entrance, deep in thought, before his lips quirked up,
as if he knew something no one else did.
“Leave them.”
Somehow, Suki wasn’t reassured.

____
Zuko counted his footsteps as he followed Sokka, hoping that the desperate flightiness in
him, the voice in his head telling him this was a trap, would be distracted long enough to just
let him get through with this. But Sokka was taking him deeper into the temple, a part he’d
never been in before, and Zuko knew hatred so he knew to have his guard up. He felt like
he’d swallowed fire, intonations branded into his throat. He didn’t know how to voice that
discomfort. He didn’t think he was supposed to.
They stopped thirty-three steps in, a simple room, plain aside two windows. Sokka sat on one
of the ledges; Zuko leaned against the doorway. Neither said anything for what seemed like a
very long time, staring each other down. Zuko felt like his skin was crawling but endured it
with the familiar sense of deserved punishment, and Sokka... Sokka just stared. Zuko
couldn’t read him, couldn’t figure him out, scanning his features in a desperate hunt for
anything. The other teenager’s hair was a little loose, dark brown strands of it falling out of
its wolf tail to frame his face, tickling his jaw, moving with his soft breaths, and his eyes were
blue. Always blue. Relentlessly, overwhelmingly blue.
“I know we’re not exactly on the best terms.” Sokka finally said, tone controlled, almost
practised, like he’d been contemplating this for a while. “But I wanted you to know that it
wasn’t... it wasn’t you.”
Zuko’s eyes widened in surprise. He'd expected raised voices and cursing, hatred and
arguing. Instead, Sokka scuffed the toe of his shoe into the floor, frowning as he searched for
the right words.
“I mean, it was you. Obviously. You being a jerk was sort of a big part of it. But it wasn’t
completely you.” Sokka took a deep breath here, crossing his arms. “I hated you because I
failed. I hated you because my plan didn’t work, because I got my dad caught, because I
needed help in the Boiling Rock – all of it. I've always been the weakest member of Team
Avatar, the non-bender. Sokka, the guy with the boomerang.” His mouth twisted into a smile
that looked more like a grimace. “My sister can move oceans and Toph invented
metalbending and Aang is the fucking Avatar, but hey, I can write a neat schedule, right?” He
scoffed. Zuko could only stare.
“When I trained on my own in Shu Jing,” Sokka continued, and Zuko got the distinct feeling
that Sokka had rehearsed this for a long time before bringing it to Zuko, now speaking with a
reverence like he needed to get the words out. “I started to think maybe I wasn’t dead-weight,
maybe I could help. After what happened up north, I really needed that.” He hesitated slightly
here, words clipping against themselves before he focussed again; a momentary stumble.
“But I think it just made me cocky, so when the Day of Black Sun failed, when I failed, it... it
wrecked me.”
It was a raw declaration to be made between enemies, and Zuko kept his mouth shut. Even if
he could find the words to speak up, he would have known to stay quiet. This was Sokka’s
moment. He was doing it for himself, not Zuko. But still, he was doing it, and that filled
Zuko with an inexplicable charge, like lightning beneath his skin.

“You were the first thing I tried to trust again, after that.” Sokka said, expression considering.
“I looked at you, and it became a strategy. I decided to trust you, to believe you’d changed, to
believe you were leaving the Fire Nation behind, and I was wrong about that too.” Zuko hid
his wince; Sokka wasn’t tiptoeing around him, wasn’t babying him. “I couldn’t plan you, and
it just reminded me that I couldn’t plan anything else either, that I was becoming a boring
repetition of failures. And to top that all off, suddenly you show up here, and my dad starts
telling me you’re so great, and the warriors from my home forgive you, and my friends act
like I’m being an asshole when I...” His tone had been bitter, words sharp and face twisted
unhappily, but as quickly as the anger had come, it vanished again, melting into something
quiet, soft. “I was the only one who knew what you were really capable of.” He whispered,
and Zuko felt like he’d been punched in the gut.
The words repeated themselves in his head, toiling and crashing against his skull like waves.
And Agni, Sokka was right, wasn’t he? This boy with his brash mouth and careful hands had
seen the worst of Zuko. He knew Zuko as the tribesmen didn’t, relentless in his hunt of the
Avatar, cruel and short-sighted. And he knew Zuko as his friends didn’t, shadowed in a
bloody library. He was the only person, the only one, to have both pieces of Zuko, to have
witnessed both and witnessed them so sharply.
Zuko had spent days, weeks, trying to convince those who trusted him that he was a monster,
trying to explain what he was to people who didn’t want to hear it, didn’t want to believe it.
But the intonations were branded into his throat, and he’d never known how to voice it. So he
lived. Lived, evil. Lived, angry. Lived, bloodstained. And they all let him because they didn’t
know better. Didn't know what he was, what he’d truly done. Hands stretched out with no
knowledge of the fire, no clue about the sharp edges ready to cut.
Sokka knew. He didn’t need to explain himself to Sokka because the other boy had seen it all
as it happened. Zuko didn’t need to desperately search for the words to explain, because
Sokka knew, he knew.
It should have terrified him. He felt like he’d looked directly at the sun.
Zuko felt exhilarated.
“No one was listening to me,” Sokka continued, oblivious to Zuko’s fascination. “And I
didn’t want to let my guard down again. I couldn’t afford to fail again. You went through
something awful, Zuko. I know that and I wouldn’t wish that on anyone.” He enunciated
every word, completely genuine, before working his jaw and jutting his chin out proudly.
“But I’m not sorry for being harsh on you. I guess what I'm trying to say is that... this isn’t an
apology for how I've behaved. I just think... maybe... we could just start again. Clean slate.”
He nodded, happy with himself, before offering a small, consolatory smile. “I'm willing to
give you another chance.”
He said it like he expected Zuko to be disappointed, like he expected someone to tell him he
was being unreasonable. Instead, Zuko felt himself coming alive, determination consuming
him. Sokka was giving him another chance. Sokka knew what he was, had taken all of that
badness and considered it with a methodical thoroughness Zuko knew he was renowned for,
and had decided to give him another chance. It meant something. It meant that even now,
some part of Zuko, some small fraction, was capable of redemption.

He'd earn it. He'd do whatever he had to. He wasn’t some beaten down animal in need of pity.
He knew he’d done horrible things, and he wanted to take responsibility for them.
Sokka was giving him the chance to do that, and he’d earn his redemption through this boy if
it killed him.
Zuko nodded resolutely, expression hardening. “Thank you.”
Sokka considered that a moment, before raising a smug eyebrow. “I still don’t like you, by
the way.”
The feeling was mutual. It was confusing, complex, but Zuko’s sudden admiration of Sokka,
his desperate determination to earn this boy’s forgiveness, lived alongside the knowledge that
they bothered each other on an inherent level. They were too different. Circumstances
notwithstanding, they never could have been friends, Zuko was certain.
“I can live with that.” Zuko said, and Sokka scoffed.
“Debatable.” He said, and Zuko had to restrain himself from rolling his eyes after everything
Sokka had just told him.
“I’m going to find Suki.” Sokka said, straightening up from the window, eyes narrowing as
he seemingly just remembered that Zuko was still blocking the doorway. “You should talk to
that kid of yours. He's been moping for days.”
Zuko moved out of the way as Sokka swanned past. “Not my kid.” He mumbled, following
the other boy.
Sokka scoffed. “Tell him that.”
Zuko knew he had to apologise to Zi Se. He never meant to yell like that. But before being
discharged from the infirmary, Zuko was helpless to do anything unless Zi Se came to him,
which he only did to stubbornly curl up for sleep at night, falling asleep instantly if only to
spite Zuko. The kid was worryingly good at holding a grudge.
Zuko would fix it today. Zi Se created a cocktail of emotions that swirled nauseatingly within
Zuko, but that was on Zuko, not Zi Se. It wasn’t his fault Zuko was so bitter, after all.
“You’re annoying, you know that?” Zuko said tiredly, no real venom behind his words, too
distracted thinking of Zi Se.
Sokka grinned like this was the best thing he’d been told all day. “Aw, you mean it?”
Zuko was not going to punch him. That would not convince Sokka to forgive him, and was
not constructive for anyone involved.
That didn’t mean the thought didn’t cross his mind.

Zuko dreamed of fire. Fire and blood and water pouring into the fractures of his mind. His
father’s eyes, ignited, hatred and fire, fire, fire, coming towards Zuko’s face, crackling with
lightning. Fire was rage, was negativity manifested into something visible. This was known.
This was taught. This was encouraged. Zuko's fire burned hottest when he was at his most
hateful, and it haunted him when he was at his most haunted. This was known. This was easy.
Zuko awoke to fire. Its orange heat curled behind his eyes and he jolted up with a start.
Before him, Zi Se lay sleeping. Zi Se, who was introduced to him through dancing firelight.
Firelight to signal the fights. Fire was violence. This was known. And to a boy like Zuko,
violence was so very easy. He wondered if these shaking hands of his, clenched into fists

beneath the moonlight, would ever be able to commit gentleness, or kindness. They didn’t
even know goodness when it held them; how could they ever hope to mimic it?
Zuko breathed fire, inhaling and exhaling only to feel the familiar stir of his chi that he once
swore would never leave him, but abandoned him the moment he needed it. Calm, he
thought, think of something calm. He was taken to an environment he never should have
known, snow crunching underfoot, shivering into a blue parka. Blue, the same shade every
time, light and warm, the very same as the fire that took everything from this land, the very
same as the fire echoing the contours of Azula’s too-young face, the very same as the fire
coating the walls of a ruined library, the very same as the fire Zuko had used to take a man’s
life. To take, to take, to take. Fire always took. It was the only element that went further than
damage; it destroyed. The difference was small but it existed, and Zuko lived on that fine
line. Fire was ruination. This was known.
This was all known, and Zuko had been raised among it, growing a tolerance to it as the years
passed. The people here weren’t so lucky. One bite and it’d kill them. It had in the past. The
Avatar had seen everyone he cared about wiped out by fire, and still, he sought it, shadowing
Zuko through his days at the Western Air Temple, eyes wide and pleading, like a naïve child
not realising fire burns for every time it’s touched. Zuko, in his own twisted way, was
protecting the kid. He was protecting Aang as much as he was protecting himself.
No one gained anything from fire.
This was known.

There were strange instances in life where one memory meets a completely separate memory,
and you’re forced to consider them as a conjoined new memory. This happens no matter how
unfathomable the combination, and it seemed to happen to Sokka on a higher rate than most.
Admittedly, nothing would ever quite beat how he felt when he walked into the library of the
Fire Nation’s most secure prison with his father who he’d just broken out only to see Iroh and
Kanut. That was... that was a whole thing, for sure. But the theory still stood. Sokka held Iroh
in one memory and Kanut in the other, but still, they’d combined, and it had been so
implausible to his mind that he’d shut down for a few confusing moments.
That was like this, because it was the first time he was really, fully stopping to take in the
scene, and he realised just how strange it was. Aang and Katara were waterbending, the
Avatar and the last southern waterbender, while Toph Beifong – runaway of the esteemed
Beifong family and inventor of metalbending – made observatory digs about their forms
despite not knowing anything about waterbending, in a desperate attempt to get a laugh out of
Prince Zuko, who sat beside her.
Sokka gave himself a moment to sigh deeply, before sitting on Toph’s other side.
“How’s he doing?” Sokka asked, giving a nod to Aang, as if he could be asking about anyone
else.
Toph blew a raspberry. “He’s fine, Snoozles. You're turning into Katara.”

“I am not.” Sokka shoved her, earning a punch in response. Zuko watched the whole

The firebender turned his gaze back to Aang, who was growing a little enthusiastic with a

He'd wondered for days now what it would be like between them, between the Avatar and the
boy who hunted him. He knew Aang would be all-forgiving as he always was, but Zuko...

call fire to his hands?
Zuko just narrowed his eyes. “He seems...” he started, voice quiet, that everlasting rasp that
had been so haunting, “stressed.”
“You would be too if you had an entire war hinging on you. I mean, the kid’s twelve. How
would you feel if you had to fight your dad at that age?” Sokka asked, scoffing to hide the

scar a little.
“Can’t say I'd like it.” He finally said.
Sokka couldn’t stop staring at him. He felt how he did in the Boiling Rock, when Zuko was

know what it all meant, all those vague sentences and timid expressions on someone
supposed to be the human embodiment of fire. But he pushed that down, cursing himself.
“Is this a seeing-person thing you two are doing right now or are you both just weird?” Toph

“Take a break, Aang.” Katara was saying, and Sokka looked over, worry making him tense

“No.” Katara said sternly, and she really could be scary sometimes. “You haven’t stopped all

Apparently, Chena had been banned from foraging since the ‘wheat incident’, leaving the job

Toph wondered what her parents would think if they saw her now, lying back in the dirt
beneath the sun, half-napping and half-listening to the conversation the Fire Prince and the
Avatar were having about the basics of firebending. The thought of her parents' inevitable
horror made her grin to herself, and she shuffled more comfortably into the dirt. What a life.
“So, what’re you gonna tell me about first?” Aang asked excitedly, hopping up and down on
his heels. “How to do big explosions? Oh, oh, what about that thing Azula does, with the
daggers? That'd be cool, or-.”
“You’re nowhere near ready for any of that.” Zuko said, unamused, and Toph snorted loudly
at the prince’s bluntness. Sparky was funny like that. He didn’t mean to be abrasive like Toph
did, but he still rubbed people up the wrong way, and then he wouldn’t get it when people got
pissy with him.
Still, Toph could feel how tense he was, more rigid than normal, which was saying something
seeing as Zuko always seemed to be expecting an attack from one of them. He'd gone like
this every time Aang brought up firebending, and it hadn’t dropped since Zuko said he
wouldn’t teach him.
That’s why Toph was here, babysitting him, to make sure Aang’s big mouth didn’t run away
from him and cause Sparky to have a nervous breakdown.
“Why don’t you just start at the beginning?” Toph suggested sagely, donating some of her
eternal wisdom to the two charity cases that were her friends. “You know, like the original
source of firebending or something. Like with earthbending, the original source is the
badgermoles. That's where I started.”
Toph remembered that cave, running away to hide from the world, being so scared when
everything started to rumble around her, so vulnerable. And suddenly, there was this big
creature in her face, sniffing and investigating, curious. They were blind too. Toph had never
felt understood before, and they taught her about her element, that earthbending was more
than just a martial art, a way of fighting; it could be her eyes, her senses, her freedom.

Which left Zuko and Toph alone, Toph smirking and Zuko undoubtedly staring off after Aang

heavy gaze.
“Can you...” Zuko started, turning to her and then to where Zi Se still stood, alone and forlorn
and so very small, deserving so much better than Zuko.
Katara's smile was small but kind. “I’ll keep an eye on him.”
“Thank you.” Zuko said earnestly.
And then they were gone.
They flew for hours and Aang didn’t stop talking for the entire journey. Zuko just stared at
the clouds, feeling the wind brush tender fingers through his hair, the sky a blue blanket
around them. It was beautiful, up here. He felt so far away, so removed. Untouchable. He

could pretend he wasn’t real up here. There were no princes in the clouds, no murderers, no
traitors, no brothers. Only air, cool and honest.
Zuko closed his eyes and let himself fade.

Eavesdropping was Bato’s forte, but observing – that was Kanut’s department, well and true.
And Kanut had been watching. He'd been watching since Zuko and Zi Se fell out a few days
ago, watching as the firebender made no moves to mend things, feigning obliviousness to Zi
Se’s obvious desire to fix this sudden rift but his inability at such a young age to do it
himself. And from watching, Kanut could tell one thing for sure. Zuko, who got so protective
of Zi Se that he’d kill a man just to tell him he was truly safe, who wouldn’t leave the little
boy’s side for so many days, who woke up from a near fatal fever and still thought only to
ask of Zi Se, did not want to fix this rift. He wanted to keep it, keep his distance, keep the kid
away. There was a sudden polarisation there, and Kanut didn’t know where it was coming
from, and Zuko wasn’t talking about it.
When Kanut’s father died and his first thought had been only that maybe his nightmares
might stop, he’d felt a shame so great that he wanted to hide. He saw that in Zuko, to a higher
degree. He was so young, but he carried so much shame in him, so burdened by an
impossible standard of honour thrust onto shoulders unable to bear it. And he internalised it,
that shame, letting it twist and snarl inside him. When he convinced himself he was rotten, it
was because Zuko thought he was evil. But that wasn’t it. The rot came from his own mind,
seeds sown from people supposed to protect him, the skin of an apple bruised and bitten into
to reveal something festering. Zuko had survived so much, but after all of it, he’d be the one
to kill himself. Kanut was sure of it.
And the worst part was that Kanut didn’t know how to help, because he saw a mirror in
Zuko, and it had taken Kanut so much time to learn to live with himself, with the seeds his
father had planted in him. He had only learnt in this last decade how to mend and care for the
orchard of his own mind; how could he possibly look Zuko in the eye and tell him what to
do?
Zuko had always been braver than Kanut. He'd known it ever since the South Pole, perhaps
even longer than that. Was it worth it? He remembered the way golden eyes had hardened.
Yes.
It wasn’t about if Kanut said the right things to Zuko. It was just a matter of trying.
He wouldn’t let him destroy himself. If Zuko didn’t get it out soon, that shame would eat him
alive.
The moment Kanut came to that conclusion, he got to his feet, placing down the book he was
reading and heading out of the infirmary to go and find the offending firebender in question.
It was only when he spoke to a rather sheepish Katara that Kanut was informed that Zuko and
Aang had gone on a field trip together, despite Hakoda grounding him and Kanut’s clear

instructions of Zuko needing to rest his leg.
He was in so much trouble when he got back.
____
Zuko was sat on the very top step of one of the beautiful tiered pyramids decorating the Sun
Warrior ruins, forearms to his knees and his head hanging between them, catching his breath.
When he’d reluctantly agreed to come with Aang, he hadn’t realised he was agreeing to what
felt like thousands of steps, his leg pulling uncomfortably every time he hauled himself
forward. And Aang was such a strange breed of oblivious, shooting ahead excitedly but then
circling back every time to check Zuko was alright.
And he was. He was fine. He just needed to rest a moment and maybe wait for his leg to stop
stinging so much. He hated how intimately he knew the pain, hated the fear stabbing the pits
of his stomach at the thought of how stupid he was being, how much it would devastate him
to have to go through that all again.
Zuko lifted his head, raking a hand through his hair and using this break as an excuse to look
over the old civilisation. From the top of this pyramid, it was beautiful, a sight of sandcoloured rocks strewn with vines beneath the golden sun. A memory of something ancient, an
old civilisation, and yet, within it, Zuko felt some familiarity. The architecture was similar to
the temples of the Fire Sages. It was a strange realisation, one that sat in his chest and
lingered.
They'd been careful getting up here, ever since Aang took one step into the ruins and almost
immediately got impaled by a spiked booby trap. There was something here, something
worth protecting even thousands of years after this civilisation’s extinction, and Zuko felt
something spark in him, stirring; curiosity.
“Zuko,” Aang said suddenly from behind Zuko, voice serious, uncharacteristically quiet, “I
thought the dragons were friends with the Sun Warriors.”
Zuko frowned, turning to face the kid, and was met with a wall a few steps away from him,
Aang stood before it, hand pressed gently to the images engraved into the stone. Zuko had
told him more about the Sun Warriors as they flew here, but now, his voice wouldn’t meet
him, sitting like a lump in his throat as he stared at the mural on the wall.
There were patterns in the stone, and amongst them was a scene of a Sun Warrior, surrounded
by fire, so much fire, dragons breathing it in snarls, angry. Rage and fire, fire and rage. Zuko
swallowed. This was known.
“Well,” he said, pushing himself unsteadily to his feet, “they had a funny way of showing it.”
Dragons were mythical creatures of Fire Nation history, but then, that wasn’t necessarily true.
The last dragon had been alive in Iroh’s lifetime; not that long ago. And while Zuko had
never seen one, they were everywhere in the Fire Nation, hiding in tapestries and portraits
and clothing and architecture. They were part of the country’s foundations, the original
masters, and they were gone because of fire’s inherent destruction. Zuko turned his face

away, the engraving suddenly making him uncomfortable, and he went to move on, move
away, but-.
“Something happened to the dragons in the last hundred years.” Aang declared, somehow
both stern and gentle. “Something you’re not telling me.”
It shouldn’t have felt like an accusation, because it hadn’t been Zuko’s doing, but still, the
sins of his ancestor’s sat heavy on his shoulders, and this was another part of their bloody
history, another part he was left in the ruins of with a thousand fingers pointing at him. Agni,
would this anger ever be sated?
Zuko took a deep breath, and he told Aang about the dragons, a tale of glory and conquering
and insatiability, all for honour and legendary firebending prowess. Aang was quiet as Zuko
spoke, head bowed, sad. Sad, because this was another part of his childhood that the Fire
Nation had reached for and mauled. That was what fire did. That was what it turned men into.
This was known.
And it felt very... telling. Aang was the epitome of good, and not just because he was the
Avatar. He was the symbol of the side Zuko had joined, the good guys. He was the one they
were all following, the one destined to save the world from this war, the one who would
defeat the epitome of badness in this world that was the Fire Nation and Ozai and burning hot
flames. But it was more, because even without all that, Aang was so incomprehensibly,
unapologetically good. He forgave. He wasn’t angry. After everything Zuko’s nation had
done, Aang still had hope for them, for him, and he made it clear every time Sokka broached
the subject that he didn’t want to kill Ozai. Aang was a pacifist and a child and he was kind
and gentle and good.
And here Zuko was, telling him about the dragons, extinct because of the badness in this
world, and he didn’t know his place in it all. Because Zuko would never kill a dragon; he
couldn’t even kill a fox-antelope, or a caribou-yak. But he wasn’t like Aang, wasn’t good.
What was left?
Fire was ruination.
This was known.

Katara didn’t say anything as she came to sit beside Zi Se. The little boy had chosen a nice
spot to set up camp; on one of the platforms facing the way Zuko and Aang took off from, a
few of the boulders naturally arranged into a small alcove overlooking the ravine. Zi Se had
watched until Appa was a mere speck in the distance, and then the little boy wordlessly
turned around, grabbing a nearby blanket – Sokka's – and some kale cookies – Aput's –
before setting them down amongst the boulders and promptly refusing to move. He'd been
there ever since, just sat, legs crossed, eyes staring up at the sky, waiting.
It felt like something Katara shouldn’t interrupt; Zi Se wanted to be alone right now. But he
was upset, and besides, Zuko had given her that look. Those golden eyes had been so

vulnerable as he turned to her, and he’d trusted her with this, with Zi Se, this boy that meant
the world to him. Her and Zuko were far from being friends, but they’d grown from just
having a precarious truce. She was starting to understand him, starting to, tentatively, figure
out how forgiving him would work, if she decided to choose that. Zi Se was their common
ground, though, and she wouldn’t let Zuko down on this.
So, she sat with Zi Se, and she didn’t say anything, just letting her shoulder brush against his
in a silent showing of comradery. They would wait together, and if Zi Se wanted to talk, then
they would talk.
The truth was, Katara knew this feeling all too well. She'd been both watcher and waiter so
many times before. Staring out at an inky sky, the cold air around her familiar, scanning the
horizon for a ship with blue sails, waiting for Hakoda to return to them. She gave that up after
only a few months, anger unsettling the waters of her fear, because how could he? How could
he leave them behind?
Sokka, though... he never gave up. He sat there, on his wall of snow, staring out at the ice
every night, tight jaw throwing shadows beneath Tui, so sure that Hakoda would come back
for them. Sokka wasn’t spiritual like Gran Gran or Aang, and he found Katara’s
waterbending silly, and he liked science, logic, things he could prove. That was just how he
was, but sometimes, when she’d watch him watch the sky like that, alone but so unmovable,
Katara thought that the reason Sokka was so grounded was because all the faith in him, every
bit of it since childhood, had been put into their father. Katara believed in Avatars and Spirits
and bending; Sokka believed in Hakoda. That was how it was, how it always had been.
“Do you think he’ll come back?” Zi Se asked suddenly, voice so impossibly quiet, like a petal
floating down the ravine, never taking his amber eyes off the horizon.
Katara knew he was asking about Zuko, but still felt her heart stumble at the question. Do
you think he’ll come back? She'd asked it Sokka one night, curled close together beneath the
furs, complaining when his cold foot touched her leg or when her hair got caught in his
mouth. He'd gone so still, and she’d felt so bad for even asking, because she knew how he
felt about this; they’d argued about it enough. But instead of the immediate attitude she
expected, the annoyed hiss of ‘obviously, it’s Dad’, Sokka just sighed, seeking out Katara’s
hand and holding tight. A little too tight to only be doing it for her.
He’ll do his best, Sokka had said, and it was the first time Katara ever realised that Sokka
knew there was a chance Hakoda might never return. It was the first time she’d ever properly
let herself consider it, too. She'd never had to. She realised how young that sounded, now she
was older, now she’d seen more of the war. But back then, Hakoda was indomitable and he
was going to come home and save the world on his way. Sokka though... he’d known from
the beginning the threat their father had walked into, he’d known that if Hakoda didn’t come
back, all of it, the responsibility of Katara, of the village, of being a warrior, fell to him.
Maybe that was part of why he sat on the walls every night, waiting, hoping, desperate.
And Katara saw Zuko in both Hakoda and Sokka. She saw him in the absence, leaving
behind a child who would sit here waiting, waiting, waiting, but she also saw him in the
memory of a boy suddenly crushed with a responsibility he was still too young to shoulder.
Sokka, face fierce, now having to take care of Katara, because kick up a fuss as she may

about her own abilities, but Kya was gone and Hakoda was gone and Gran Gran was only
getting older, and Katara had been so young, so broken. So Sokka stepped up, because no one
gave him any other choice. Sokka, shoulders broad, ready to carry them through whatever
happened next.
Katara remembered her brother brave, watchful, but as she saw Zi Se now, all she saw was a
scared little boy who deserved so much more than what he got.
“He loves you, Zi Se.” Katara said softly. “He’ll do his best.”
She wrapped an arm around the child’s shoulders, pulling him close as he held her back after
only a moment’s hesitation. Her mouth felt dry, lungs struggling to take full breaths. She
didn’t want to see her brother in Zuko, or see Zuko in her brother, because Sokka was
brilliant and kind and funny, and Zuko was... Zuko. But even when she pushed the thoughts
away, opting to just focus on Zi Se, she still felt that unsettled static in her ribcage, and she
felt her opinion of Zuko shift ever so slightly.
“Can we wait out here until they get back?” Zi Se asked, looking up at Katara then, eyes so
wide. Fire Nation, a voice inside her whispered, old and angry. But it had never been that
simple, and Kanut was right, and anger was easy, which wasn’t to say she wasn’t entitled to
it, nor that anyone would judge her for clinging to it. Katara had every right to hate these
people, but for tonight, easy routes wouldn’t cut it, and Zi Se needed her here.
It was already getting dark, the sun setting on the lip of the cliff-face like it was balanced
there, about to tumble over the rocks. This was a landscape of browns and greens, but when
Katara closed her eyes, she could have been back home. She used to tease Sokka for waiting
as he did, used to say he was being naïve, foolish, but Hakoda came back, didn’t he?
“Of course.” Katara let out a breath, a bit of tension leaving her, and she smiled down at Zi
Se. ”We’ll wait.”

“You had to pick up the glowing egg, didn’t you?”
“Shut up.” Zuko snarled, because while his days of wishing violence upon the Avatar were
over, he was currently actively considering throwing something heavy at Aang. Or at least,
that is, once he got out of this mess and was able to throw something heavy at Aang.
Because right now, they were both trapped, pressed into bars that felt too familiar, bodies
encased by whatever that thick goo was that flooded the room they’d been in. Zuko had been
lucky, freeing one of his hands in his desperation to tug the bars out of the way, but what use
was that if the rest of him was completely stuck? He was incapacitated beside the Avatar, the
stars twinkling smugly above them as the sun began to set. Zuko could barely keep his
heartrate under control, panic rushing through his veins and jolting with every sharp breath
that cut through him. He was trapped, helpless, defenceless, imprisoned. And Aang clearly
didn’t understand the gravity of the situation, because the kid was just beside him cracking
jokes, more concerned about his boredom than their survival.

This whole trip had been a mess from start to finish, from Aang setting off the booby trap to
Aang forcing Zuko to dance with him even though his leg was already hurting, and now this?
If Aang would just take things seriously, or if Zuko had just refused to come...
“You’re annoyed with me,” Aang said, voice shattering the sudden tense silence that
suffocated them, “aren’t you?”
Zuko could move his neck a little, and did his best to look at Aang. The kid’s face was
shadowed, sombre. He very suddenly looked incredibly tired, like all of his hundred years
had hit him all at once. It surprised Zuko’s anger into quieting, if only for a moment, and he
sighed. Maybe if he spoke, it would distract him from the all-encompassing terror he was
currently trying to shove aside. It was better than just sitting in silence, at least. Zuko had
learnt that with Zi Se, letting the little boy’s nonsensical words ease over him, calming him
no matter how much pain he was in.
“Not annoyed.” Zuko said honestly. “Just... frustrated. I don’t get you.”
Aang frowned then, almost offended at his own complexity. “What’s not to get?”
Zuko thought of the Avatar’s childishness, his naivety, his infallible urge to forgive.
“You’re just so...” Zuko started, struggling with the words, trying not to fidget because every
time he moved, he was reminded of his predicament. He couldn’t feel his legs. Zuko grunted.
“You seem so pure. There's so much hatred in this world, and you’re only young but you’ve
seen it first-hand. I just... How can you stand it?”
Maybe he asked because he was panicking, not thinking clearly, or maybe it was easier
because he could just stare at the stars with the excuse of being physically incapable of
meeting Aang’s wide eyes, or maybe, just maybe, he’d been wanting to know this for a long
time. The Avatar, in all his tainted innocence, was a mystery to Zuko, and had been for years.
He expected a rebuttal, Aang scoffing immaturely, because surely that was just what good
people did. They took the bad and didn’t meet it with worse. They took the pain and didn’t
feel the urge to hurt back. This was just something Zuko would never understand.
But Aang went quiet, thinking, before speaking in a voice that was at once small and large.
“I don’t know if I do stand it.” Aang said, almost ashamed. “I wobble sometimes, when I
think about the air bison, or Monk Gyatso, or how I'm never gonna see any of them ever
again.” Aang sniffled a bit, and dread filled Zuko because Agni, of course he made the kid
cry. But as quickly as he’d become upset, Aang worked his jaw, jutting out his chin as much
as he could, proud, strong. “When I feel like that though, I speak to Katara. I don’t like the
way it makes me angry, or when I get lonely, but she helps. She tells me to focus on all the
good that’s still in the world, and there’s so much of it, if you just look!” He smiled then,
perking up, before his smile turned into something a little sadder, a little more burdened. “I’m
the Avatar... so I should forgive, and not be bitter.”
Zuko thought on that, but no matter how he turned it, he couldn’t imagine anyone ever
expecting that of Aang. His whole world was torn from him, and he was left alone in the

remains, the last of his kind, and it was something Zuko would never understand, something
that warranted the uncomfortable guilt sitting within him. Aang had every right to be bitter, to
be unforgiving. It would make more sense if he was.
Still, Zuko stayed quiet, letting Aang consider his own words a few moments. Zuko almost
flinched when Aang cocked his head a little – still hindered by their current prison – and
spoke in a suddenly curious, chipper voice.
“What do you think?”
Zuko was stunned, not expecting that, blinking in surprise before thinking hard on all that
had been said. Something felt off about all of this. When Zuko had told Aang that the boy
had seen so much of the world’s hatred, he meant everything. Aang lost his people, was
forced to be the Avatar, had seen battles and loss and had responsibility after responsibility
forced onto him, and he was only twelve. It was enough to make anyone bitter, yet he just
smiled through it, but Zuko didn’t quite believe it. I’m the Avatar, so I should forgive. It was
part of his burden, Zuko realised. Aang was so desperately trying to be a good Avatar after
disappearing for a hundred years, trying to mend the damage he let happen in his absence. I
should forgive. They were the words of the Avatar, the symbol of balance, of peace. But they
were not the words of Aang.
The thing with balance though, was that it had two sides. People often forgot that. Balance
lost all its meaning without both good and bad.
“I don’t...” Zuko started, tone gentle, thinking each word through carefully. “I don’t think our
goodness is determined by our capacity for forgiveness. I think we can be angry and still be
good. They don’t have to cancel out.”
And all at once, it was like a punch to the face. I think we can be angry and still be good. His
words, his own double standard, because when he looked at Aang, this little boy who’d lost
everything, trying so desperately to force down a justified anger, it made sense. It made
perfect sense. Aang was angry and bitter and confused, and he had every right to be, and he
didn’t stop being a good person just for feeling that way.
But until now, why had applying that to himself seemed complicated? It was so simple. Zuko
was angry, and he felt anger different to how Aang did, more aggressive, louder, but it was
still anger, just as an eagle-hawk is a bird as much as a dove. And it was justified, because
Zuko went through something terrible, which meant having it live in him how it did, having it
rage and fight and rattle against his skeleton – it didn’t make him inherently bad.
Aang was looking at him with that wide, starry-eyed look he sometimes gave, cracking a
small smile. "You know, Zuko,” he said, smile growing, “I don’t care what anyone else says;
you’re pretty smart.”
Zuko huffed, before allowing the smallest of smiles back.
Which was exactly when a large man with a mean scowl appeared, dressed exactly like an
ancient, long-extinct Sun Warrior would have dressed, and everything went to shit again.

____
The Sun Warriors were alive. They were alive and living in this place thought to be ruins, a
flame at its heart burning for eternity, and Zuko and Aang were to be tested by the
firebending masters. As Zuko took his flame, he felt like his whole body was electrified.
“The flame will go out if you make it too small.” The Chief was saying, harsh gaze turning to
Aang. “Make it too big,” he looked at Zuko, “and you might lose control.”
Aang shakily took his flame, before his shoulders visibly drooped a little, relieved, like he
half expected the small fire to rage out of control.
“Oh.” He murmured, lips curling up. “It’s like a little heartbeat.”
The Chief stared at Zuko when he spoke, those fiery eyes unblinking, like he knew, knew
what Zuko’s family had mutated firebending into, knew what Zuko had himself done with his
bending, knew the blue hues of his flame, the unnatural abomination of it. Disgrace.
“Fire is life,” the Chief said firmly, “not just destruction.”
Zuko only stared; it wasn‘t what he’d expected the Chief to say. He fought off the instinctive
urge to scoff.
Fire was only destruction. There was nothing else. It had never brought anything but anguish
to the world; a weapon of violence, a translation of pain. This was known.
____
The cave of the masters was up a hill, which in turn led to a clearing heralding another set of
extremely steep stairs. Zuko knew how disrespectful it was to roll his eyes, but that didn’t
mean the exhaustion he was feeling didn’t give him the urge to. His body was weak, and he
hadn’t realised just how far from his usual health Zuko still was. Kanut was going to kill him
when he got back. Zuko had never been bludgeoned with a book before, but he couldn’t
imagine it was a very pleasant experience.
Chanting filled the clearing, indicating that it was time for Zuko and Aang to scale the stairs
and face the masters, the Sun Warriors circling fire, bowing and moving fluidly, a ritual.
Zuko felt it in his bones, each chant knocking with his racing heart, and Aang looked ready to
run away, shaking like a leaf as they started to climb, his flame flickering uncertainly. Zuko
had noticed on the walk up here that Aang was timid with his bending, scared of the flame,
and it seemed Zuko’s attempts at reassurance hadn’t done much.
Zuko wondered what the masters would be like, what they would do, if Zuko would fail. The
Chief hadn’t been subtle in his opinions. He saw Zuko and Aang as equally responsible for
the dragons’ extinction, and it made Zuko’s skin crawl. But if the worst happened, Zuko
knew they could take the masters. They had to be able to.
They were the Fire Prince and the Avatar, and Zuko had been through far too much to die
here.

____
The rocks around them began to tremble, both Zuko and Aang standing fireless and
vulnerable on the platform, staring into the mouth of a dark cave. Zuko reached for his
sword, body responding to the threat automatically, because he knew fighting, knew danger.
And then, two eyes began to glow from the cave, far too big to be human, before something
huge and blue surged forwards. Zuko didn’t have time to duck, to do anything, frozen in
place in surprise, before two creatures whirled around them, so big that each of their
movements caused a gust of wind that threatened to throw Zuko to the ground, scales dancing
beneath Agni’s light like molten gold dripping over red and blue.
Dragons.
Real. Alive. Dragons.
“These are the masters.” Zuko whispered in awe, seeing the symbols of his home, his
childhood, moving and breathing right there, barely a few steps from him.
“Still think we can take them?” Aang asked in a low voice.
Zuko elbowed him in a panic. “Shh, I never said that.”
The dragons kept moving, twirling and bending in circles, and Zuko felt so small, so aware
that if the dragons decided to kill him, he would be helpless to stop them. Still, strangely, he
didn’t feel threatened. it was a different feeling, a peace, almost, like his very core was being
pulled towards these ancient creatures.
And then Aang realised they were waiting, waiting for them to do a firebending form with
them. Them, the original masters. Each punch and twirl and step mirrored by a dragon, raw
power following them and flowing into Zuko until even his leg didn’t hurt. It should have felt
surreal, but instead, Zuko felt as he did when they first started flying here, in the clouds. He
felt numb, buoyed by something stronger, peaceful.
He wasn’t even scared when the dragons stopped in front of each of them, white teeth bared
before Zuko, golden eyes huge and all-knowing. This, he knew, was when the masters
decided their fates, and fighting didn’t even cross his mind. Violence, destruction, rage – they
were all so far away from this moment.
The blue dragon opened its mouth, fire building in the back of its throat, and Zuko was ready
for the burn, knew how it felt, closed his eyes and resigned himself to it. He heard it first.
Fire always roared when it was shot out with enough strength. Like a dragon, he thought
distantly.
But nothing burned. He felt the heat, close to his face, close but not touching, and when he
cracked his eyes open, Zuko’s breath caught in his throat.
Zuko and Aang stood in the eye of a multi-coloured storm of fire, every colour Zuko had ever
seen dancing in the flames, trickling like tributaries through the true orange, and then colours

Zuko couldn’t name, but could feel. A green that felt like the scraped knees of boyhood. A
purple that felt like shouting over a family dinner. A yellow that felt like fields. A blue that
felt like ash.
A blue that felt like ash.
A blue that felt like a hillside.
A blue that felt like a burial.
A blue that felt like a killing.
Like a cell, like the way your lungs choke when you sprint, like shattered glass, like a scar on
the palm of your hand, like Azula, like the tribesmen.
A blue that felt like home.
It blazed and screamed in his ears, this cacophony of colours, an explosion of life, like Zuko
had broken a mirror and was seeing everything from the distorted, bleeding reflection, and he
knew this, he knew what this was. He'd seen this rainbow before, in an ink-black sky, with a
different name, a different purpose.
The Aurora had been a loud declaration of life, of love and loss and the spectrum of human
emotion, good things dancing with the bad, a perfect balance. But this was fire. Fire which
meant hatred, fire which meant rage, fire which meant violence, fire which meant destruction.
But this fire... it was beautiful.
And Zuko should have been terrified, because this was the unknown, threatening to uproot
everything he’d ever believed, but instead, he wanted to reach out, to touch, to feel the fire in
his hands. For the first time in weeks, he wanted to feel it, that familiar heat, that comforting
tug of his chi. Because fire was rage, but, he realised, it was also kindness, and it was love
and hatred, life and grief, revenge and redemption. Fire was all that made them who they
were, be that good or bad. It was why he could use anger and pain to power his firebending;
because those emotions were bad, but they were also human. They made him Zuko. And with
that, he could use happiness, loyalty, determination, to power his bending, because they were
human too.
Humanity was a constant balancing act. Every living thing had an opposite. Every person had
a duality to them. Without this, the very foundations of the world fell apart.
This was a landscape of fire, and Zuko had navigated it since birth, desperately trying to
figure out his surroundings and put a name to the locations he saw. Mountains of pain,
ravines of anger, forests of love, a home on fire in the distance.
He knew. Burning was more than a weapon, or a tool, or an excuse. It was an expression, the
deepest telling of one's soul, their hopes and dreams and passions and fears, the most crude
version of their heart. And Zuko had lived through each stage of burning. He had been

snuffed out, he had been an inferno, he had been blazing for so long he’d forgotten what it
felt like to be unburnt.
He knew. He knew fire better than most people. He'd seen it at every angle. He'd seen it
thrown from cruel hands and he’d seen it held in gentle fingers. He knew the kindness of fire
just as he knew the terror of it.
He knew, for how terrifying it was, fire was one of the most beautiful things in the world.
He knew now. He understood. Fire was a weighted scale, and fire was duality, and fire was
life, energy, everything and nothing all at once. The more he felt, the more he burned.
He knew now.
The art of burning was humanity.

The ride back to the Air Temple was contemplative, and the entire time, Zuko cupped a blue
flame in the palm of his hand, right over the thin white scar that lay jagged there, holding it
steady against the wind. When he thought of Fong, the flame surged, but if he watched
carefully, thoughts of rum heists, of gap-toothed smiles, of redemption in blue eyes – these
strengthened his fire just as his anger did.
“You know, Zuko, I've been thinking.” Aang said from where he was riding on Appa’s head,
throwing a smile over his shoulder. “What you said before, about it being okay for me to be
upset about things... I didn’t think of it like that.” Aang’s expression was so raw, so genuine,
and Zuko’s flame fluttered as he watched, entranced. “But that also doesn’t change that I
don’t want to feel angry, even if I know it’s okay to be now. I meant what I said, about
Katara. Talking to people you trust helps. And we’re all friends now, so if you ever want to
talk, you can talk to us.” He beamed happily before chuckling. “Though maybe Katara
shouldn’t be your first port of call.”
Zuko was laughing before he even realised it, no hesitations, no concerns, laughing like it
was instinctive, which it wasn’t for him. But he wanted it to be.
“Thank you,” Aang continued, trying to be serious again, because he truly didn’t realise how
young he looked, “for helping me realise some things, Sifu Hotman.”
Zuko rolled his eyes at the nickname, before smiling back, a small, real thing.
“Thank you, Aang.” Zuko said, eyes landing on his steady flame. “Today meant a lot to me.”
Aang lit up like that was the best thing he’d ever been told, and maybe that was why Zuko
said what he said next, because the kid’s charm was just that irresistible, but really, he
thought he’d known this ever since they’d stood before the dragons.
“I think,” Zuko said slowly, “that I'm ready to be your firebending teacher, if you’ll still have
me.”

Aang shot into the air, backflipping with an excited cheer before landing easily back on the
air bison, grin so large it must have been painful, and Zuko didn’t fight back the smile that
curled onto his mouth. In his palm, his flame grew.
It was dark by the time they got to the temple, and everyone was in bed aside Katara and Zi
Se, who were sat beneath a blanket together, waiting. Aang immediately darted off with
Katara, talking loudly with big hand gestures, and Zuko wondered how long the secret of the
dragons would be kept if Aang had anything to say about it.
Zi Se stood a little forlornly, still holding onto the blanket which only made him look smaller
as it bundled at his feet. Zuko smiled at him, and it relaxed something in Zi Se, like he’d
expected Zuko to go straight back to ignoring him. Guilt was an uncomfortable weight sitting
on Zuko’s chest, but he didn’t try and fight it. All of that guilt and anger and shame he felt
when he looked at Zi Se pushed and pulled like tides within him, and instead of trying to
deny an ocean, Zuko merely took a few steps out of it. Focus on the good. Laughter and foxantelopes, a dagger and a necklace, a sky of fire and a riverbank. One day, Zuko would be dry
of these feelings. For now, they lived within him, and he was going to stop fighting that. He
would balance them instead. He would find the good amongst all this bad. He would let
himself feel all of it.
Because people like Zuko didn’t do things in moderation; if he was going to keep going, then
he would feel things in their entire inferno. Good and bad.
“Come on, kid.” Zuko said, reaching down and picking Zi Se up like he’d done so many
times before, using his free hand to wrap the blanket tightly around him, aware of the night’s
chill. “It’s time you went to bed.”
And while Zi Se didn’t say anything, he also didn’t argue, which was how Zuko knew they’d
be alright. Of course they would be, some part of him thought, they were Zuko and Zi Se.
That night, Zuko moved their bedrolls next to each other, setting Zi Se carefully down before
facing him, legs crossed, expression serious. He wouldn’t set a trend for ignoring these
things. He wouldn’t let apologies become rare. He would do things differently. He was going
to be better than what he knew.
“I’m sorry I shouted at you.” Zuko said, and Zi Se stared with wide, amber eyes. “That was
wrong, and you didn’t deserve that. The thing is, all of this... it’s been harder than I thought it
would be, and that’s why I didn’t speak to you for so long. But that wasn’t your fault, Zi Se,
and I want you to know that.”
Zi Se was scrunching the blanket close to his chest. It was a blue blanket, a little torn at the
edges, like it had been used a great deal. Zuko had no idea where he even got it from, but
hoped no one was missing it too much.
Finally, rather sagely, Zi Se nodded, and Zuko fought back a small smile.
“Will you forgive me?” Zuko asked, giving Zi Se a choice.

Zi Se hesitated, before nodding vigorously, and then getting to his feet, making grabby hands
at Zuko. Zuko grinned, relief swarming him like an infestation, and he wasted no time
scooping Zi Se into his arms, holding him close, a familiar weight.
“Missed you.” Zi Se mumbled into his shoulder, hair tickling his jaw, voice a little groggy; it
was significantly past his bedtime.
Zuko rubbed soothing circles into Zi Se’s back with his thumb. “I missed you too, kid.”
They fell asleep next to each other that night, Zi Se’s head on Zuko’s arm, and for a long
time, Zuko just watched Zi Se, the moonlight throwing shadows onto the boy’s face. He
wondered how he would look when he was older, how he would act, if any of this would
affect him or if it would all be a blur, and at that thought, Zuko felt a familiar selfish tug. I
hope he remembers. But instead of snapping down on it, hot shame trickling down his spine,
Zuko instead investigated it, and he found that its source was not selfishness.
I hope he remembers. I don’t want to shoulder this alone.
Fear had always been a shadow of Zuko’s. Truthfully, he was not wicked; he was a scared
boy who had done bad things. And maybe it would take him many more years to accept that
of himself, but for tonight, he had apologised, and he’d done a damned good job of it.
For tonight, he was doing okay.

Sokka went to bed late, sparring with Suki until it became too dark to justify. It was a full
moon soon, and Sokka just wanted... Well, he never really knew what he wanted, when the
moon began to grow instead of shrink, but sparring was always a welcome distraction. By the
time he stomped over to his bedroll, he was exhausted and sweaty, and could think of nothing
better than a nice, long sleep.
The universe, of course, had not forgotten their feud.
“Where the fuck is my blanket?” Sokka demanded.
Katara, conveniently, didn’t hear him.

It was getting harder and harder to ignore the rift between Sokka and Hakoda, and trust him,
Sokka was actively trying to ignore it. But each day was making it more and more apparent
that Sokka just didn’t know how to act around his dad. He couldn’t put his finger on it. Sure,
it was hard trying to go back to how they used to be, because Sokka was older and whether
he liked it or not, Hakoda had had to leave them for a very long time, and that was going to
change things. But still, everything had been fine between them for those few weeks on the
Ullaakut, and even the preparations before the Day of Black Sun had seen Sokka – while still
stressed – be pretty relaxed around Hakoda. Katara had been the one with the problem, back
then, but now, her and dad seemed better than ever, and it was Sokka who couldn’t seem to
shake this.
So what had changed?
The invasion had failed, for one, but Hakoda had made it clear that he didn’t blame Sokka for
that, that he was proud of him. And then there was the whole Zuko Situation – it had been
demoted from Catastrophe to Situation, which Sokka thought was very lenient of him – but
him and Zuko had spoken, and he’d been sure he felt no residual ill will surrounding his
father and the firebender, because he’d sorted it himself. So why were things still so strange?
Sokka hated it. Every time Hakoda tried to make conversation with him, he’d freeze up, and
he felt like he was constantly on edge, trying to prove himself, trying to show that he was
better, that he still deserved the title of son, and no one else.
Sokka wasn’t one to wake up any earlier than absolutely necessary, but that morning, as the
sun began to devour the horizon, he found himself staring at the temple’s cracked ceiling,
thoughts whirling in his mind like a snowstorm as he tried to focus on the even breathing of

the group around him, or the way the fire still crackled embers every now and then. He felt
like there was a weight sitting on his chest, only getting heavier with each day that passed,
placed there when he stood in a library and saw his father regard an enemy with fondness.
Unbudging. No matter how much he strained to lift it.
He frowned, turning in his bedroll, ignoring the chill creeping over him thanks to his lack of
blanket. Sokka could excuse overthinking, but when it started interfering with his precious
sleep, that was when he drew the line.

probably agreed on some weird early-morning bending practise. Everyone had stayed up for

complicated plot to kidnap Aang, and everyone else because they were genuinely concerned

everyone, but Aang had been practically bursting with excitement.
He told them about the firebending masters, a flame that looked like a rainbow, a deeper
meaning, and a new teacher.
If you’d told Sokka a few months ago that the Avatar he just found in some iceberg was
going to need an actual firebender as a teacher, and that teacher was going to come in the
form of Prince Zuko of the Fire Nation, then Sokka might just have dived into the polar
waters and succumbed to an icy death when he had the chance.
Now though, it... it made sense. It seemed right somehow. Sokka couldn’t put his finger on it.
He sat up with a sigh, giving up on sleep altogether, dragging a hand down his face and
beginning to untangle his hair, pulling it into its signature style.
“You’re up early.” Hakoda said, and Sokka jumped, just managing to swallow an undignified
screech. He'd been so deep in his head that he hadn’t noticed his father sat up on his own
bedroll to his left, blue eyes narrowed, analytical. Sokka felt like he’d been caught stealing.
Sokka shrugged, feigning nonchalance. “Couldn’t sleep.”
Hakoda hummed, unimpressed, and didn’t break the silence that descended, just holding

tripped Katara over yesterday, but she barely hurt herself and besides, she hit him back, so by

“Sokka,” Hakoda eventually sighed, something like concern on his features, “what’s gotten
into you lately?”

Crap, he’d been caught. Of course he’d been caught. Chief Hakoda was one of the greatest
minds in the war effort, if not the greatest. Sokka was such an idiot, thinking he could just

It wasn’t. It wasn’t normal. And he hated it.
