There was a crane-vulture circling overhead, and Zuko couldn’t stop glancing up at it. He'd
woken Aang with the dawn, because he was determined to be a good firebending teacher and
rising with Agni was one of the first things Aang ought to know. For all he’d begged Zuko to
teach him, Aang was far from a star pupil, growing bored easily, wanting to do the exciting
things despite not even having the breathing exercises down yet. Zuko couldn’t help his
patience fraying, so he’d decided to lead Aang through a meditation. This, at least, was
something the monk knew. He was still a little antsy, but once Aang finally settled, things
became peaceful, a comfortable silence between the pair as they sat in one of the temple’s
clearings.
And then Zuko had heard a shaking call from the sky, opening his eyes a fraction in curiosity,
being met with a great dark shadow swooping through the ravine.

It was just a bird. Zuko tried to go back to his meditation, fearful of looking like a hypocrite
after how much he’d scolded Aang for his lack of concentration this morning, but still, his
golden eyes could barely tear away from the creature. It wasn’t circling anything in
particular, which reassured Zuko that the crane-vulture was hunting and hadn’t found
something rotting. Iroh had told Zuko about the birds the last time they came to this temple,
when Zuko was young and scarred and stupid. He'd only been half listening to what he
thought at the time had been nonsensical blabbering, but now, the words resurfaced. The
crane-vultures are both omens of harmony and omens of death, an interesting duality. They
feed off the carcasses of other animals, and they mate for life.
He didn’t know why he was so fascinated, following the curved beak of the crane-vulture, the
crooked talons designed to rip flesh from bone. There were remains in Zuko’s body, soft skin
pulled too tight. He wondered if the bird could sense it. He wondered if it was hungry.
“Hey jerks!” An obnoxious voice sounded, and Zuko startled, glaring at Sokka as he
approached them. “Mind if I watch you two jerks do your jerkbending?”
Aang jumped up in delight, clearly bored of meditating, and Zuko felt a bolt of irritation tear
through him at Sokka’s interruption. It wasn’t jerkbending. It was an ancient and sacred
martial art. What did Sokka know?
“We’re meditating.” Aang corrected with just a touch of disdain.
“Hm,” Sokka said, unimpressed, before turning his blue eyes on Zuko, “well, why don’t you
meditate on what you’re gonna say to my dad. He's not happy that you went out yesterday.
Neither's Kanut. They want to talk to you.”
Fear. It was instinctive, written into Zuko’s very marrow, and he hated it, but tried not to
blame himself. It wasn’t his fault. Hakoda himself had been the first to tell Zuko that. It
wasn’t his fault, but it was still so frustrating. Zuko knew Hakoda wasn’t a threat, he knew
that Hakoda wanting to talk to him wasn’t the same as Ozai wanting to talk to him, but still,
his instincts were long-lasting, and they wouldn’t give in to this strange new life so easily.
Zuko swallowed. He didn’t want to speak to Hakoda, with or without that fear. He'd been
grounded by the Chief and given strict instructions involving the word ‘rest’ on multiple
occasions by Kanut, and he’d taken that and ran off to the ancient Sun Warrior civilisation of
many staircases with the Avatar. He could imagine the lecture he was in for, and it made him
want to groan loudly. Suddenly, meditating with a petulant child didn’t seem like such a bad
way to spend the morning.
“Where are they?” Zuko asked, trying not to sound suspicious, but Sokka’s blue eyes
narrowed anyway. Zuko always felt like he was being scrutinised under that observant gaze.
It was endlessly unnerving and fascinating. It blindsided him every time.
“No way.” Sokka said, folding his arms, brandishing that Agni-forsaken boomerang as he did
so. “Not happening. You're not getting out of this one.”
Zuko couldn’t help but smirk drily. “What happened to teenage comradery?”

Sokka's eyes widened as he realised Zuko was quoting him, as he realised Zuko was making
a joke, and it was strange to see Sokka caught off guard like that. It opened him up more,
made him look vulnerable instead of the usual bolshy act he put forward in front of Zuko.
Zuko was suddenly reminded of waking up in the Boiling Rock, Sokka stretching beside him,
putting his hair up, guard down and relaxed, despite everything.
Sokka frowned, scandalised that Zuko was using his own words against him. “Hey-.”
“Yeah, yeah, I'm going.” Zuko said, cutting the other boy off as he got to his feet, knowing
full well it would anger Sokka even more. Sure enough, Sokka’s eyebrows furrowed, face
flustered in frustration. Satisfaction curled warmly within Zuko, and he bit back a small
smile.
Sokka, maturely, stuck his tongue out, reluctantly walking at Zuko’s side, ensuring Zuko
actually went where he was told. Zuko rolled his eyes, but quietly admitted to himself that he
probably would have bolted if not for Sokka shadowing him to stop exactly that.
The proximity meant Sokka’s boomerang, still held lovingly in his hand, was far too close to
Zuko for his liking. He kept glancing at it, untrusting, and Sokka noticed, because he was
Sokka.
He smiled crookedly and it made Zuko blank for a moment as the boy lifted the boomerang
proudly. “Nice, right?”
“I hate that boomerang.” Zuko muttered, far from impressed.

“It also hit me in the head.” Zuko grumbled, feeling the phantom sting. They were coming

Sokka huffed. “Would you let that go already?”
“It hurt.”
“Please,” Sokka scoffed, entirely unsympathetic, “you had a helmet on.”

being so immature. He used to be a prince, and now he was bickering? But Sokka got under

He used to be rude to him, and that was when things made sense. But this here, it felt more
teasing, though still not in the way Tomkin and Nanook did it. It was frustrating.
“Sorry.” Zuko mumbled, looking at his feet, because no matter what happened, he didn’t
want to disappoint Hakoda.
This did not seem to be a fear Sokka shared with him. “He started it.”
Zuko threw the boy a betrayed glare. “I did not-.”
“Boys.” Hakoda groaned a third time, pinching the bridge of his nose. Sokka looked
incredibly smug. Zuko wanted nothing more than to make good on his threat and throttle the
boy with his own boomerang.
“Ah, parenting.” Kanut said dreamily, appearing at Hakoda’s side. “You’re doing a fantastic
job, Chief.”
“Shut up, that one’s your nephew.”
Zuko wanted to bash his head into the wall. “That’s still not funny-.”
“You make a good point.” Kanut said, cutting Zuko off in favour of giving Hakoda a sage
look that even Zuko could tell was fake. “Some nephew, ignoring me to go on a life-changing
field trip with a recently infected leg wound.”
Zuko's stomach fell sickeningly and he cringed under Kanut’s now hard gaze, knowing he
couldn’t avoid this conversation any longer.
Sokka clapped a hand to Zuko’s shoulder. “You’re on your own, bud.” He grinned, before
flouncing off.
Teenage comradery my ass, Zuko thought bitterly.

Berating Zuko always required the same level of delicacy as navigating a battlefield. Too
soft, and the boy would recognise he was being babied, and he would reel from it. Too hard,
and his instincts would kick in, screaming that he was in danger regardless of Hakoda’s
intentions. Hakoda could already see the way Zuko’s eyes had narrowed, how he’d rooted
himself to the spot where he stood before Hakoda and Kanut, how he’d subliminally turned
so the exit was directly to his side. It hurt, that Zuko still acted this way around Hakoda, after
everything they’d been through, but he knew with a stinging certainty that if Zuko didn’t act
this way, he would have died long before they met.

Hakoda wanted a world where Zuko and the other kids were safe. It was too late to ask for
them to have never known danger. It was years too late.
For now, delicacy would have to be enough, caring would have to be enough.
“Let’s sit down.” Hakoda offered, taking the first step and walking towards a quiet corner of
the room. He'd didn’t want the other warriors overhearing. They'd tease for one, as was their
nature, but it was more than that. Zuko didn’t exactly have a good history of being
reprimanded in front of an audience.
So, they sat down. Hakoda put his back to the wall, sitting as relaxed as he could, and Kanut
joined him with a scowl on his face, and when he was ready, cautious and cynical, Zuko sat
with them.
“I didn’t even want to go.” Zuko said, voice quiet, petulant as he twisted his fingers.
“But you did.” Hakoda pointed out, and Zuko winced slightly. It was strange how similar this
side of Zuko still was to the boy Hakoda had known. It wasn’t reassuring.
“I told you.” Kanut hissed, words harsh. “I told you exactly how bad your leg was, how close
you came, and this is what you do? Did you not learn anything? How can you be so
reckless?”
It wasn’t like Kanut to let the emotion bleed into his words so much, staining in their wake,
but the healer had been worried, and Zuko was special to him. They all knew it. Kanut didn’t
even try and deny it much anymore.
But still, the sudden sharpness of the conversation made Hakoda turn rigid, and he couldn’t
tear his eyes from Zuko, anxiously waiting for the boy’s reaction.
Zuko, however, seemed unfazed, guilt straining his expression, but also frustration. And it
made sense, because Hakoda knew this was how Kanut always spoke with Zuko. Sure, he
tended to refrain from such emotive outbursts, but the healer was blunt with Zuko, honest. He
didn’t baby him. He never had. Hakoda was being paranoid, but he just couldn’t stop himself.
He knew why.
The last time Hakoda had sat down to talk with Zuko, he had said something wrong, and it
led to Zuko leaving them for a very long time.
He wouldn’t mess up again. He wouldn’t lose Zuko again.
He had to do this right.
He had to do this perfectly.
“I feel fine!” Zuko insisted a little explosively. “It barely hurt while we were there, and I've
been resting it today. You're the one that discharged me.”

Kanut’s eyes flashed and Hakoda saw the exact moment Zuko regretted his words. Hakoda
needed to step in, not trusting his friend’s deadly tongue.
“We can’t change what happened.” Hakoda said placatingly, digging an elbow into Kanut’s
ribs. “But Zuko, we just want you to stop being so reckless. If this was a one-time thing, it
might be okay, but you do this all the time. What happened to that promise you made me?”
He had to be careful here; he was entering dangerous territory. “I may have broken some of
my own in the past, but you’ve always been better than me at keeping your word. Has that
changed?”
Zuko was silent, staring him down, but Hakoda knew he’d won. Honour was one thing Zuko
refused to be questioned on. He stuck to his code like he didn’t know how to breathe without
it, chasing some impossible height, a call of duty only he could hear. Hakoda had made
mistakes in his life, and he had broken promises he never meant to break, but Zuko... Zuko
had his word. There was a time when it was all Zuko had, and now, he wouldn’t let it go.
The echoes of a storm. It seemed so long ago now. I need you to promise me that from now
on, whatever you do, you’ll think things through first.
I promise.
Zuko exhaled, ducking his head so that his dark hair fell into his face. “I’m sorry,” he said,
the words soft, easily bruised, “for making you worry. It was short-sighted of me.”
Hakoda felt a warm smile grow on his face, turning to Kanut with a raised eyebrow.
Kanut seemed reluctant to let this go so easily, still glaring moodily between the pair, but he
eventually huffed under Hakoda’s gaze. “Whatever, tough guy. You can make it up to me in
some way. How about he does all my chores?”
“That’s called exploitation.” Hakoda pointed out.
Kanut shrugged. “I’m not above it.”
“Just because I’m sorry doesn’t mean I’m doing your chores.” Zuko growled, but he was
smiling a little, and this was new. This was something they never got. Zuko, brave enough to
rebuke them, comfortable enough to know nothing bad would come of it. He felt safe with
them. It eased something in Hakoda, and he couldn’t help when his own smile grew.
“Breakfast is ready!” Katara called from where her, Zi Se and the Duke were gathered around

notorious for his big portions.
Zuko, however, had gone rigid, staring at the pot above the fire like it was about to lash out at

last night, energetic and gleeful, he’d mentioned how hungry he was, rooting through the
supplies. Zuko had just gone straight to bed. Had he not eaten for an entire day?
“I’m going to wash up a bit.” Zuko said quietly, scrambling to his feet and making to flee

It was hard to incorporate much range in their diets, when they had such limited supplies and
were trying to feed so many mouths, but Hakoda was proud of how well his daughter had
managed, how she always took what the warriors hunted or foraged and managed to make

“But your food will go cold.” Hakoda said, concern coating his features. “Did you eat
yesterday?”
Zuko rolled his eyes. “Yes. It'll be fine.”
Hakoda’s concern only deepened. Through war and peace, through distance and time, there

was a terrible liar.
“You should eat, Zuko. It'll speed up your healing.” Hakoda said, and he so desperately didn’t

refused to name. Hakoda hated that he hadn’t noticed it sooner.
“Why aren’t you eating?” Kanut asked, and Zuko knew he was in trouble then, the healer's
sharp gaze narrowed on him. No one could escape Kanut when he focused on something.
“Come on, tough guy.”
Zuko looked torn, golden eyes flicking to the temple’s entrance achingly, before he sighed,
swallowing, like he was nervous, like he was scared.
“Okay.” He murmured, more to himself than them, looking slowly back to the food. “Yeah,
okay.”

There were ashes in Zuko’s mouth, sitting on his tongue and singing of the sculptures they
once were, dry and coarse, impossible to swallow, refusing to be spat out, and his stomach
ached. It ached in a way that hurt, tendrils of pain spiking into his muscle, empty. Empty.
Always empty. No matter what he ate, Zuko could never be sated. There was a crane-vulture
circling overhead, shadow still gliding over the temple, and Zuko was still a boy built of
remains. How did he explain this? This, another fracture pattern in the bones of his past that
prophesised him evil.
Zuko's collarbones dipped into his flesh like wings, and he thought of Chan.
Zuko's ribs patterned bloodstained skin, and he thought of fighting.

Zuko's fingers were crooked as they reached, and he remembered what he had done for so
little, so little in return. Scraps. Dirtied from the floor. Enough to survive on; not enough to
live on.
Katara handed him his bowl and a small loaf of bread, blue eyes never leaving him, because
as much as he had tried to bury this, he could only fit so much in his grave, and it was already
spilling over. She had seen. She had seen the way he refused to eat with the others, seen the
way he couldn’t be in the room with her with food between them, seen the way Zi Se’s eyes
shone with the honest fear of a child whenever this time of day arrived.
But Zuko said nothing, because he couldn’t escape this now. Hakoda was worried. Kanut was
onto him. Some part of Katara already knew.
Lips slick with something that tasted like blood, Zuko sat on the window ledge, separate to
the group, shaking hands warmed by the stew. He couldn’t feel a thing. How long does it take
a carcass to rot, to become inedible? How long before his mind finally stopped feeding off
this fear? A bird’s cry swallowed the temple, and the soft flesh of Zuko’s body bled with the
weight of it.
There was a crane-vulture overhead, hungry.
There was an eagle-hawk within, angry.
Zuko clutched the bread tighter, possessively, fingers digging into the rough exterior. He was
so tired, so empty, and in that absence, he had instincts. Animalistic and wild, cruel and
selfish. Instincts that had kept him alive for a very long time but would damn him here. They
whispered fight, fight and survive, survive and devour.
The bowl was empty in his hands. He couldn’t remember eating. And around him, there was
more food. Tomkin and Nanook had sat themselves close, on the floor before the window,
nearby but not pressing, and the rest of the group were littering this too-small room. It had
never felt so small before. There had never been this many people in the cell at Fong’s base.
There certainly hadn’t at the end. Many starved, and many would still be here today if Zuko
had shared.
But when he was in that mindset, when his body fell onto its instincts, it was hard enough to
share with Zi Se. Zi Se, an innocent child who was in pain. Zuko would fight for their food,
and afterwards, aching and bruised, he would hesitate. Because he was just so hungry. He
was so fucking hungry and he’d want to eat all of it because he earnt it, he was the one who
suffered for it, and because they never knew when food would come next, or if Zuko would
be too weak to win the next fight, or any of them ever again. The prospect of starving to
death was something Zuko had spent a very long time considering, and those thoughts that
had plagued him, that had terrified him, had never left.
Now, surrounded by people he trusted, who he didn’t want to hurt, was a very bad time to
realise that.
It was an even worse time for something to move out of the corner of his eye, as if reaching,
the bread still in Zuko’s grip, available to be taken, and those instincts roared to life, a fire

being fed air. He was moving before he could register it properly, and it was over before
Zuko could blink, looking to meet wide blue eyes.
Tulok's wrist was in Zuko’s hand, shoved to the side at a painful angle, and Zuko had used
the leverage to twist his body quickly, the small throwing knife in the waist of his trousers
now in his hand, the tip of the blade pressed threateningly into Tulok’s stomach.
For a second, they just stared at each other. His racing heart overpowered the sounds of the
temple, but he could feel the way eyes had turned to him, a room holding their breath. Fear
lurched uncomfortably in Zuko’s stomach, and he felt sick, terror of what he’d thought had
been about to happen, of someone taking his food, turning into horror, because this wasn’t
Chan or any of the other prisoners. This was Tulok, and they were at the Western Air Temple,
and he was safe.
“I was checking if you wanted my bread.” Tulok said softly, body entirely still like he was
scared Zuko would flee. “I’m not that hungry and it would be a waste.”
He'd been trying to give Zuko food. He'd done a nice thing, a kind thing, and Zuko had dug a
knife between his ribs hard enough to cut through his shirt, a speck of blood staining the blue.
Everyone was staring. Everyone was staring and there were entire cities of terror lining
Zuko’s skeleton, anthems of damnation, and it was already too late. He'd been about to hurt
Tulok. He'd been about to hurt Tulok just as he’d hurt Tomkin months before, and all this
time, all this sefless care asking for nothing in return, had been for nothing, because Zuko
hadn’t changed. He couldn’t change.
That horror crested within him, roiling and stormy, and Zuko knew with a sudden vehemence
that he had to get out of there.
He yanked himself away from Tulok, releasing the man, his knife disappearing into his sleeve
before someone tried to take it off him. There wasn’t enough air in here. Zuko couldn’t
breathe, lungs catching whenever they tried to take full breaths, and he could feel the way the
food he’d just eaten threatened to come back up. He practically threw his bowl onto the
window ledge, shoving to his feet and almost stumbling with his desperation.
“Zuko-?” Someone was calling his name but it was lost to the thundering of blood in his ears,
but not enough, not enough for Zuko to miss how concerned they sounded. They weren’t
angry. Agni, why couldn’t they just be fucking angry?
Like Zuko. Like this poisonous, foul beast nesting in his chest.
He barely made it outside, lurching into one of the cliff’s many alcoves where he was far
from the eyes of the others before he retched, feeling it burn his throat as he threw up, hands
grasping the rock to try and stay standing on limbs that felt far too weak . It stung on the way
up, acidic and foul as his limbs seized helplessly. Zuko could do nothing but clutch the rock,
shaking as he waited for the waves of nausea to subside. When they finally did, Zuko sucked
in a gasp of air, knees buckling with how much they trembled.
He felt disgusting, curled in on himself in the dirt, sweat sticking his dark hair to his
forehead. He couldn’t stop shaking, completely hollowed out like he was no more than a

skeleton on the cliffside, the crane-vulture no longer circling. There wasn’t anything here for
the creature. There was nothing left to consume.
He'd thought... He’d thought he was getting better. These past few days at the Air Temple,
he’d genuinely thought he was starting to heal. Fire didn’t petrify his insides when he looked
at it since going to the Sun Warriors with Aang, and Sokka had told Zuko that there was still
a chance of redemption for him, and Hakoda made it clear that Zuko was welcome here, was
wanted here. He'd thought he was getting better. He'd thought he could actually overcome the
things he’d gone through.
But this here... this was his body reminding him.
He was no better than the angry, naïve boy who had burned Tomkin all those months ago. His
first instinct was still to cause harm, and that anger had grown and raged and festered inside
him. It wasn’t subsiding. It would not be fed, nor tamed, nor appeased. All he’d done in that
library was name it for what it was, a wild creature caged behind his ribs, but what good is a
collar when the thing that bit you is still there, flesh still clinging to its beak? The eagle-hawk
within him was called rage, and it was supposed to die with Fong because he was the cause
of it, but it was still here, more vivid with each passing day as he desperately tried to push it
down, to thicken the bars of its cage, to overpower it. And he’d thought so stupidly that the
Sun Warriors had eased some of it. He'd realised that he didn’t need to rely on that anger
anymore, that there were other things, better things, good things that could fuel his bending
just as well. He'd realised he could live without this haunting, but realising you can do
something doesn’t make it a reality. He was so foolish. He was so fucking naïve. If that had
really been true, if Zuko had really been capable of good things instead of bad, then his fire
wouldn’t still be blue. Humanity fuelled firebending, and Zuko’s anger was so potent that it
made his fire burn unbearably hot, and through each day at the Western Air Temple, through
each second with people who cared about him, through each moment of his second, third,
fourth chance, Zuko’s fire remained a steady blue.
He was supposed to be getting over it. He'd thought he was getting better. Fong was dead.
Ozai was far away. There was nothing left to be angry at.
But there was an infinite insatiability within Zuko, feathers bloodstained even after all this
time, and crane-vultures were as much omens of death as they were omens of harmony. What
did it matter if Zuko was capable of good or capable of redemption? What did it matter
when, regardless, he could only sit with his anger? Two bitter, tragic enemies, damned by fate
to companion one another forever, opposed by their hatred, sealed by their wretchedness.
Breathing scratched his aching throat, and Zuko sat there for a very long time. He'd thought
he was getting better, but this was his body reminding him.
He would always be hungry.
He could never stop fighting.

Sokka had been minding his business when everything went to shit, and when everything did
go to shit like everything always did for them because they couldn’t have nice things, it did
so in a sudden, blink-and-you'll-miss-it fashion.
One moment, Sokka was sat with Suki, fending the warrior off when she made an attempt
(and it was an attempt, thanks to Sokka’s super slick reflexes) to steal his bread.

was trying to calm a wild animal, no trace of fear in his features, only concern.

There wasn’t anger in Zuko’s eyes, or aggression.

But the incomprehensible side of Zuko prevailed, and he was still suffering, and Sokka just

That crushing quiet was broken by the least likely person.
“He doesn’t like people coming near his food.” Zi Se said matter-of-factly, like this was all

“Do you know why?” Chena asked, face dark, unbearably grim.
“Chena-.”
“It’s not like the brat’s gonna tell us himself.” Chena hissed, cutting off Hakoda’s warning

“Do you know why, Zi Se?” Hakoda repeated Chena’s quiestion softly.
It felt wrong. It felt like a breach of privacy, because Zi Se was five and didn’t seem aware of
how serious this was, which meant if they asked him, he’d tell the truth, and Zuko wasn’t

he knew that if the prince had his way, he would bury these secrets inside him forever,

Zuko was taking every day at a time, when the firebender was slowly coming out of his shell.
But the display they’d all just seen was not okay.
Zuko wasn’t handling it, but he wasn’t letting anyone help him either, and Hakoda had
realised that as Sokka had.
He'd realised that, so now, he was taking matters into his own hands.
Zi Se looked uncomfortable then, not because he suspected something, but because the
memories clearly upset him. He was sat near Katara, beside The Duke, and he began to twist
his empty bowl in his small hands.
“Because when we were in the cell,” Zi Se said quietly, “the other people there, the really big
ones, they’d always try take the food off us. It was... I don’t know, it was hard to see, but I
think it was like a race, but also not? Zuko and the scary prisoner always got there first, but
then they’d fight each other, and they’d hurt each other. Some days, Zuko would get hurt
really bad, and he wouldn’t even get the food, and those days were always bad days.” Zi Se
swallowed, frowning down at his hands that were now shaking a little. “I was really hungry.”
Sokka was holding his breath, had been since the realisation of what had happened in that
cell hit him with Zi Se’s words, because he didn’t trust how he would react if he didn’t have
that uncomfortable tug of his lungs to focus on. He concentrated on that swelled emptiness,
the way his throat tightened, how his blood began to thrum in his ears, and steadily, he let the
breath out, forcing his thoughts to hit him in an orderly line instead of a stampede.
Zi Se’s revelation had been clouded by the confusion that came with witnessing the things he
did at such a young age. He didn’t yet understand what had happened, not completely, not
what Zuko had sacrificed for him. The rest of them were older though, and knew more of this
war. They knew.
Zuko and Zi Se had been starved in that cell. When food did come, they were made to fight
for it. Zi Se was too young. He couldn’t fight which meant he should have died, but Zuko
took care of him. Zuko fought, he fought prisoners undoubtedly double his age, double his
size, double his hatefulness, and after all of that, he shared his food with Zi Se.

Everyone had known that Zuko met Zi Se in Fong’s base, and because it was no place for a
child, it was a given that Zuko must have kept Zi Se alive. Sokka knew that. He'd known
since he met the firebender’s weird not-his-kid. But this was the first time he’d thought to
consider what that entailed. Zuko keeping Zi Se alive would have been an explicit, arduous
affair. Zuko was tortured by Fong, and that wasn’t even the end of that place’s torments for
him. Even food, a basic requirement, had been mutilated for him.
Zuko was coated in so many bleeding wounds that it was no longer a miracle that he was still
alive; it was a fucking phenomenon. He was stubborn and stupid and despite everything and
everyone in his life who had kicked him down, Zuko got up. He kept fighting. And Sokka
could see the way the room reacted, horror and admiration in a twisted dance, but he couldn’t
accept that. He'd sat with his dad so recently, and he’d been overwhelmed by that burning
jealousy of Zuko, that strange admiration fueling resentment, but now, it all cleared.
What Zuko went through was not admirable. It was ugly, and cruel, and Zuko was hurting.
Zuko was hurting and he didn’t know how to fix it because he didn’t have the tools to and
because everyone else was so desperate to do things on his terms. And yeah, maybe that was
better. Zuko needed people to respect his boundaries right now, to not push him, but it was
just allowing him to isolate himself and it wasn’t fucking working and Sokka felt so helpless.
It was Zuko, and he wasn’t supposed to like him, but that all felt so suddenly juvenile,
because Sokka was a nice person, dammit, and he wouldn’t let the angry jerk take that from
him. He was nice, and he solved problems, and he had never tiptoed around Zuko before, so
why would he start now?
Sokka would think of something. Him and Zuko weren’t friends and they didn’t have the
weird beginnings of fondness between them like Zuko had with Aang, Toph and Katara.
Sokka didn’t have to listen to the jerkbender’s stupid, self-destructive terms like everyone
else did. He could push a little, he could test his limits.
He had to think of a plan first, but he was tired of being helpless, tired of sitting on the
sidelines.
Finally, he was going to do something.
____
Zuko was slowly coming back to himself, holding his hand out before him to watch as the
full-body shakes gradually, gradually became a subtle tremble. The initial panic and horror of
what had happened was beginning to change too, becoming regret, humiliation, and a
familiar stab of self-hatred. Why did the warriors even bother with him? All he did was hurt
them, throwing their kindness back in their face over and over again. Tulok had only ever
been patient with Zuko, even with their tumultuous introduction. Zuko remembered the way
Tulok hadn’t been angry, only worried as Zuko fled from the temple to hide outside, like
when he was a child and used to hide in the nooks of the palace whenever Azula was being
mean. He was just so pathetic. They must be getting sick of him by now.
“I hate to say it,” a familiar voice said, tone like they were delivering bad news, “but you, my
friend, are brooding.”

“Go away.” Zuko mumbled, folding his arms over his knees, speaking the words into his
forearms petulantly.
“Nope.” Nanook said, joining in with Tomkin’s bullying, and the pair sat on either side of
Zuko. They sat close. They didn’t touch him, because they’d noticed quickly that he didn’t
like that, but they weren’t nervous of him. Tomkin's smile was lopsided and easy and
Nanook’s eyes were gentle as they took him in, and they weren’t upset.
“Is Tulok... is he okay?” Zuko asked quietly, staring at the floor. He couldn’t even look at
them. He was so pathetic. He must still look a mess, hiding away out here.
Tomkin’s smile turned a little sad. “He’s fine, Zuko. You're the one we’re worried about.”
It was worse than anger, that confirmation that this was one more thing they were letting him
get away with. Unconditional. The word swam to the surface of his memories, but no matter
how much it prevailed against him, he still didn’t understand it. Zuko was raised in a home
where love and safety were conditional by definition, and now suddenly, that was being
rewritten. He'd almost believed it once, but it had been taken away. Tomkin and Nanook, the
warriors, this safety they embraced him with – it had all been taken in a heartbeat. None of it
made sense.
“Well, don’t.” Zuko said sullenly, glaring at Tomkin. “I’m-.”
“If you say fine I might just scream in your face.” Nanook cut in, and Zuko blinked in
surprise as he took in the statement. There was a joking tilt to Nanook’s smile, but his eyes
betrayed an old frustration.
“You’re not fine, Zuko.” Nanook said, more serious now. “And you’re not talking to us,
either. You haven’t been eating with anyone because you refuse to let us help you, but when
Hakoda asked you to eat with us, you didn’t set your own boundaries. What gives?”
They knew. They knew it was about the food. How did they know it was about the food?
How had Zuko been so stupid to give it away? He didn’t want them babying him, watching
his every move whenever food was nearby. It was supposed to be his burden, he wasn’t
supposed to be bothering them any more than he had to, so how...
Tomkin looked incredibly sheepish, rubbing the back of his neck, and Zuko narrowed his
eyes.
“Zi Se told us.” Tomkin blurted, and Nanook whacked his arm. “Ow! Sorry, but he kept
glaring at me like that! What was I supposed to do?”
“Oh, I don’t know, Little Tom,” Nanook grumbled, “how about keep your big mouth shut for
once in your life?”
“Again, you’re way too young to be calling me Little Tom. Do you think it makes you look
cool? Do you feel cool, Nan? No one thinks you’re cool, do we, Zuko?”

Zuko hadn’t realised how used he was to tuning out the two boys’ bickering until he
automatically rolled his eyes, ignoring Tomkin’s attempts to drag him into the conversation.
Zi Se had told them. Zuko should have seen this coming. There was so much Zi Se had seen
that he didn’t understand, the magnitutude of which would be lost on him. It was only a
matter of time before he started talking about it, now he was comfortable with the people
here. Zi Se had no reason to keep secrets, not like Zuko did.
But Tomkin and Nanook weren’t treating Zuko any differently for it. They were still joking
around, still trying to get a laugh out of him, still treating him like their friend. It was at once
warming and horrifying. They deserved so much better than a friend like Zuko. What could
he offer them except hands that had been stained red?
He didn’t notice how quiet it had gone until Nanook bumped his shoulder, jolting Zuko from
his thoughts, looking wide-eyed at the other boy. Nanook offered him a small smile.
“We’re not gonna make you talk if you don’t want to,” he said softly, “but we’re here if you
need us. Always. Okay?”
Tomkin nodded in firm agreement, a shining smile of his own taking over his face, and the
gesture blindsided Zuko. He stared dumbly between the pair a moment, before swallowing.
“Okay.” He whispered, heart swelling. Agni, he’d missed Tomkin and Nanook when he was
in Fong’s base. He thought back to when he’d pushed his memories away, swearing himself
to apathy, how he had been determined to forget them if it meant survival.
He knew now, suddenly in this moment with a ferocity that scared him, that it wasn’t worth
it. He didn’t want to survive if he couldn’t have this. His friends made it all worth it. That's
why he’d gone with Oro and Renmin in the first place, wasn’t it? He did all of this for his
friends, and he would do it all again for his friends, and he would keep living for his friends.
Unconditional, he thought. He might not understand it, and had never been shown a love like
it before, but he thought maybe that might not stop him from giving it. The enormity of
Zuko’s experiences terrified him, so unbelievably daunting, but it was nice to entertain the
idea that maybe he could let himself be helped. It was too much for him alone to deal with,
but with his friends, could he do it? It would at least be bearable.
But Zuko couldn’t do that to them. He couldn’t corrupt them with the shadows scratching his
mind.
“Hey asshole.” Chena’s gruff voice suddenly shattered the morbid direction Zuko’s mind had
taken, and him, Tomkin and Nanook all turned to see Chena, Tulok and Aput walking over.
Tulok was in the middle, carrying a large pot with a friendly smile that shouldn’t have been
aimed Zuko’s way but was.
“Hey?” Zuko said apprehensively. Was Chena angry because of what happened with Tulok?
When Zuko had hurt Tomkin, the big warrior almost broke his arm. Still, Zuko had thought
him and Chena had made progress since then. Maybe that was naïve of him.

Chena must have seen the flicker of uncertainty on Zuko’s face, because he rolled his grey
eyes like Zuko was being stupid.
“Calm down, would you?” He said, the three of them coming to a stop not far from where the
other three were sat. “Aput made way too much of his five flavour soup.”
“And we thought you might still be hungry,” Tulok continued, throwing Chena an
exasperated look at his lacking explanation, “because of... well...”
He let the sentence peter off, guilt crossing his face, and Zuko had to force away a wince,
regret filling him at how he’d acted earlier. He was still hungry, though. He'd thrown up
everything he’d eaten, but even if he was full, Zuko couldn’t say no to food anymore, mind
still whispering that he might not eat again for a very long time, to make the most of anything
he could get his hands on.
“It’s good for the soul.” Aput said with a nod. “And I make the best five flavour soup.”
“We never should have told you that.” Chena huffed, making Aput grin cockily. Behind them,
Zi Se had appeared from the temple, approaching somewhat cautiously.
“We’ll leave it here. It's too crowded in there.” Tulok said, and it was such a transparent way
of giving Zuko an out. The whole encouter was clumsy, but unbearably kind, bleeding with
good intentions. The warriors didn’t know how to approach this new revelation of Zuko’s
time with Fong, but regardless, they wanted to help.
Zuko smiled, the tension relieving somewhat from Tulok’s shoulders.
“That would be great,” he said earnestly, “thank you.”
Tulok nodded firmly, leaving the pot on the floor, and Zuko forced down the urge to lunge
over and grab it, holding his breath when the wind turned and filled the air with the smell of
food. Zi Se had reached them now, wordlessly holding Zuko’s shoulder, and Zuko smiled at
him. They were the same height with Zuko sat on the floor like this.
“Come on, Tomkin.” Nanook said, getting to his feet. “I need to, uh... talk to Katara about
something. Yeah.”
It was a laughably terrible lie, and Tomkin jumping to his feet hurriedly made it even more
obvious, but Zuko just felt warm. He watched the five walk back inside, leaving him and Zi
Se behind, only then trusting himself to reach for the pot. Aput's five flavour soup was good;
he remembered from the South Pole.
“Want some?” Zuko asked, and Zi Se nodded eagerly.
Zuko felt rotten and shaky and empty and achingly, achingly hungry, but he also wasn’t
alone, not in a literal sense. These horrors within him were things he had to deal with by
himself, he wouldn’t burden the people he cared about, but at least he had them near him. It
reminded him of why he was doing all of this. The tribesmen cared about him, and he cared
about them, and it was illogical and stupid but it was also painstakingly obvious.

Zuko was done fighting that.
“Nice?” Zuko asked with a chuckle as Zi Se almost tipped his bowl of soup down himself in
his eagerness to drink it. The little boy grinned back at him, the gap in his teeth made clear.
“Good soup.” Zi Se said it like a solemn observation, and Zuko couldn’t help his surprised
laugh.
Zuko didn’t have much, but he had this, and if moments too could be devoured, he would
swallow this whole without looking back, feel the skin of it break against his teeth, pretty
details running down his chin, and he would keep it safe inside of him.
But Zuko hadn’t consumed enough good things to even come close to being full, and even
with this, even with kindness and support blanketing him, he was still hungry. He was
ungrateful, and lost, and terrified, and harmony is nothing against death, but the eagle-hawk
inside him was deathless.
That immortality to anger, its insatiable beg for permanence, made every good thing that tried
to enter Zuko’s life pale in comparison. Anger was never allowed to be gentle, but it lingered
in a way that came close. It lingered like fingers grazing over skin, like comebacks still
muttered weeks after the argument, like a bruise. It lingered in a secondary sense. Secondary,
because anger was always pushed aside. The world had made up its mind on anger, and it
didn’t care for those who felt its linger. Everyone is angry all the time and yet you cannot
swallow it like them. Your rage is not unique. You curse in words already invented.
You should be ashamed.

There was a spider in the top corner of the room Zuko and Zi Se were given when they were
moved out of the infirmary. It was a nice room, small but with enough windows that Zuko
didn’t feel total nausea every time he thought of how deep in the Air Temple they were.
Katara had been the one to show him here, and Zuko knew she’d taken them through a maze
of corridors, the room furthest from the others, on purpose. He also knew that if he told
Hakoda or, Agni forbid, Tomkin and Nanook about the waterbender’s spite, then they would
all have several things to say about it and Zuko would be brought closer again, like an
embrace tightening comfortingly. But Katara was doing what she had to to protect her
friends, and even though her and Zuko had made progress, he still knew she was coming to
terms with a lot of things. Zuko understood. Learning new truths takes time, but unlearning
old ones? That was an excruciating process.
But it gnawed on him, the knowledge that he was so far away from everyone in here, and
there was a spider in the top corner of the room, and night after night, Zuko watched it. It
scuttled over the walls, weaving its web, spinning around and around so meticulously, and
Zuko watched as a particularly strong gust of wind tore through the room, shredding through

the web and leaving it in knotted tatters. The spider simply continued to spin. When did it
end? When did it look back at the knots, the rips, the ruin, and accept that its web would
never be finished? It just kept going, relentless, blind. It didn’t even acknowledge the debris
of its attempts at security. It just stepped over them, stupid in its stubbornness.
This was to say that Zuko’s nightmares were getting worse.
When Zuko was younger, he had one nightmare that haunted him. It was a recurring terror,
teeth digging into his mind night after night after night. He would be in the throne room,
stood before a crowd of faceless people, and he would know, deep in his bones like rot, that
his father was stood behind him, along with Grandfather and Uncle. Their eyes bore into his
shoulder blades, a weight heavy with expectation, and someone to his side would move, pale
fingers carrying a flash of gold in dancing firelight. The crown. But just before they could
place it atop Zuko’s head, it would catch the light just right, and Zuko would see it dripping
with blood. He didn’t want it near him. He would struggle and fight to get away, but he
couldn’t move, and everyone just kept staring, and the crown came closer and closer,
dripping more and more with heavy splats that echoed around the throne room, and there was
nothing Zuko could do but submit, and then it would touch his head and... and...
And he would wake up screaming.
Mother would rush in and hold him, and he would cry himself into exhaustion, and the next
night, it would happen all over again. He couldn’t understand it, back then. He was proud of
his destiny. He knew exactly who he was meant to be. Prince of the Fire Nation. It was
before Lu Ten died, but even then, Zuko had known he was being raised with the expectation
that one day, far in the future, he might be the one to wear that crown. And it filled him with
so much pride, back then, until he closed his eyes and screamed away from it. The nightmare
plagued him for years, and the moment it became tolerable, another part of his daily routine,
Lu Ten was lost to Ba Sing Se, and Zuko’s proximity to the crown suddenly became closer by
an entire lifetime.
And then Mother was gone, and no one was there to wake him, and he was the Crown Prince.
So he did what he had to do. He grew up. He glared the nightmare down and said I want this,
you’re wrong, this is my birthright, this is an honour, you’re wrong. He manhandled so much
denial into his life, filled so much of himself with contempt at his own weakness to let even
his resting mind believe such a childish fear, that one day, the nightmare simply... went away.
No one was going to be there when he cried out. No one was going to soothe him when he
was scared. Not anymore. That was over now.
He was alone now. So Zuko learnt to survive alone.
His teenage years saw his nightmares changing. That nightmare from childhood went away,
and he hadn’t had it for years now, not even now he understood, but the nightmares
themselves had been his companion for as long as he could remember. He dreamed of his
father’s glare, Azula’s biting words, Mother’s back as she turned away into the shadows. He
saw blood spilling between too-small fingers and the knobs of a spine bending under an
unbearable weight. He felt fire and night after night he burned, and he relived every bad thing
and blue eyes watched and did nothing.

He killed.
He killed every night.
He plunged a sword into a terrified man’s chest, and he knew he deserved it, and he knew
that, despite that, he would never escape this nightmare.
They'd always been there, fear such a prominent part of Zuko’s life that it haunted him even
now he was safe. He didn’t know how to be unafraid, but he did know how to survive the
terror. He knew how to survive the terror alone. It was what he always did. Reaching out,
wanting help – it didn’t even cross his mind anymore.
The spider twisted, a string of white pulled taut behind it, and Zuko focussed on slowing his
gasped breathing. He was soaked in sweat, entire body rigid as he lay paralysed by his own
mind. Tonight, he had seen Chan. Chan, three fingers breaking, three ribs broken. Chan,
starved and barbaric. Chan, who died in Zuko’s dreams. He shouldn’t have died. Chan made
it. Not much of him was left, but his heart was still beating, which meant he made it. To the
very end, him and Zuko made it. So why had Chan stayed? You could get out. Eyes closed in
defeat. No.
Zuko bowed to the man who had hurt him, to the man who he had hurt, and then he left him
behind to a fate he had chosen but not deserved, and when Zuko jolted awake, he felt hungry.
He needed to get out of this damn room.
Zuko was on his feet before he could fully realise what he was doing. More than anything, he
wanted to go outside, wanted to see the stars and know that he was okay now, at least in some
minor sense. He wasn’t okay at all, but he could breathe fresh air, he could see the sky spread
above him, and he could know that he was at least a little bit better than when he was in that
cell.
But to get outside, he’d have to manoeuvre through the carpet of sleeping bodies that had set
up camp right in front of the temple’s exit. If he woke someone up then he’d have to tell them
why he was awake, and then he’d have to talk about the nightmares, and then he’d have to
admit what he was so scared of, what yesterday when he pressed a knife to Tulok had only
sought to prove. Zuko was the problem, and his mind was darker than the things that haunted
it, because Fong was dead and Ozai was going to be defeated, but still, Zuko lay in bed and
dreamed, and during the day, he was dangerous, untrusting, angry.
If he had to admit that all out loud, he thought it might break him.
So he stalked the labyrinthine corridors of the Air Temple, partially hoping to lose himself in
their depths, partially terrified of the thought. He was still wearing one of the shirts he’d
bought at that market, black and scratchy, cheap and nationless. It had hung from his limbs
unevenly when he first bought it, and even now, he’d been slowly putting weight back on, but
the fabric hung a little past his fingertips when he didn’t roll the sleeves, and the neck dipped
below his collarbones so he was constantly tugging it back up. It bothered him. He'd been
raised in an environment where anything shy of perfection was punished. Zuko always had to
be neat, presentable, and here he was, tiredly wandering the corridors, hair short and still

sleep-mussed, hands fisted into his shirt to keep out the bitter chill. He looked a mess. He
looked like a child.
He needed to get his shit together.
Without realising, Zuko wound up on the same corridor as the infirmary, and part of him
wanted to go inside, light a candle, silently make tea for him and Kanut because he knew the
healer would just sit with him, he wouldn’t ask questions. But Kanut didn’t sleep in here, not
unless he’d stayed up too late reading, and Zuko was just so tired.
Agni, he was exhausted.
How long could he keep doing this?
He walked past the infirmary. He kept going, and he wound up in a room he hadn’t seen
before. It was small, and seemed even smaller courtesy of the large lump of rock sat in the
centre of the room, smoothed down expertly to create a table. Everything in this temple
always seemed so haunting. Empty rooms, dusty furniture, relics of an entire culture wiped
out by the hatred of others. But this room had been well-used, and recently. The table was
completely covered in maps and papers, scattered in a way that seemed messy at first but then
revealed a chaotic order upon further inspection.
This was the Water Tribe’s strategy room, Zuko realised, and it made something
uncomfortable stir within him. Should he... Should he be here? Was he allowed? He wasn’t a
prisoner anymore, not of Hakoda and not of the Avatar. He was their ally, as strange as it was,
which meant he was allowed to know what was going on. And besides, Hakoda wouldn’t
keep it from him, would he? The Chief trusted him, right?
But still, Zuko couldn’t help but tear his eyes away, feeling guilty, like he’d snuck in and not
happened upon this all by accident. He should just leave, keep exploring, but it was so
tempting, the thought of staying, because as uncertain as it made him, the distraction had
shaken him out of his mind enough that he felt awake for the first time since he woke up. It
made him hesitate.
If he hadn’t hesitated, maybe his eyes wouldn’t have caught on the words, latching on and
suddenly unable to look away. The writing was small, note-like, and the room was
completely dark aside the moonlight shining through a small window, but still, Zuko’s mind
was entuned to this, always aware of him.
Fire Lord Ozai.
He moved as if detached from himself, stepping closer and letting his fingers brush against
the long-dry ink. There was something awful about seeing his father’s name on paper,
solidified, a nightmare making itself a living, breathing thing. He isn’t here, Zuko thought
when he felt his heart begin to thrum, he can’t hurt me.
But Father shouldn’t exist here. He shouldn’t. It wasn’t right. He didn’t get to exist here in the
home Zuko had carved out for himself, the same way Fong didn’t. Those men deserved to
live in complete darkness, far away from Zuko. Why... Why was he here?

Of course he’s here, something deep inside whispered, they are preparing for the Avatar to
kill him.
Zuko pictured Aang – childish, naïve Aang – with his tattoos glowing, pictured his father’s
hateful scowl, pictured him caught in the whirlwind of an Avatar’s rage, neck snapped or face
burnt off or lips blue from drowning, and Zuko didn’t know who he was most afraid for.
He did not want another child to face his father the way he had been forced to.
He did not want his father to die.
These two truths could not co-exist, and it was the first time he truly let himself think of it.
Zuko's thoughts were snapped abruptly away from him by a sharp cry. It carried through the
corridors the same way wind sounds like screaming when it races through windows, turning
Zuko’s stomach as he cursed and immediately began making his way back to his room.
It had been a long time since Zi Se had woken up crying like this, but Zuko had never not
been there when it happened before, and he broke into a run. It shouldn’t be a big deal, but
even when Zuko was five, he had someone there when he woke from his nightmares, and that

He wanted the anger back.
He wanted to feel that fire singe down to his fingertips as it roared up his throat. He wanted

pushing the hurt away with fists but now he was letting it surge forwards, and he felt like he
couldn’t breathe.
But anger was easy, that was the point. Zuko had leaned into its embrace for long enough
now, and he understood. Anger was not a sin in and of itself. It was not his hamartia.
It was a barrier. It was protecting Zuko until he was ready to face all this hurt.
He'd been waiting to feel ready, but he realised that that would never happen. He would never
feel ready because what he went through was awful, and he didn’t want to think about it so
acutely. If he would never feel ready, then he could either live like this forever, angry and
ashamed, or he could choose.
And Zuko had chosen. He'd chosen now.
This anger would last as long as the hurt did, and Zuko was done hating himself for that. He
had spent weeks not knowing why he could still be so angry when everything that had hurt
him was dead or gone, but he’d finally figured it out. The knife was gone but the wound was
still there, and so the bandages must remain until he could begin to slowly, slowly peel them
away, and reveal his broken body to the sun once more. A little misshapen, a little scarred in
places it never used to be, but still able to feel the warmth of a beautiful day.
And Hakoda was there, through it all. A strength at his side, holding him close, safe, because
Zuko did not have to peel his anger away alone, did not have to face all of his hurt alone. He
could rest now, and that night, he had no more nightmares. There were these people around
him who he would die for, and he...
He loved them.
And somehow, he was pretty sure they loved him too.

people. I knew that when I thought of this, and I'll know it the entire time I'm here. This isn’t
me underestimating you. It's just... It’s not your fault that you were made to respond like that,
you know? You shouldn’t have to live with it.”
“But I am living with it.” Zuko scowled, crossing his arms. “It doesn’t matter if it’s wrong or
right; it just is. And you won’t care about fairness when you do some mundane shit and I

stick a knife in your gut for it just because I can’t fucking see straight-.”
“Language.” Zi Se chirped suddenly, and Zuko broke off, looking down in surprise at the
little boy, who beamed happily. Zuko would worry later about how unperturbed Zi Se was by
the content of what Zuko had been saying, focussing only on him swearing. Right now, he
was too blindsided by how happy Zi Se looked, like he’d caught Zuko out and was now
expecting a prize. And he looked like that because they were safe here, and because now, Zi
Se’s main focus was Zuko’s bad language, was a game. Not survival, or starvation, but a
game.
Zuko smiled a little, ruffling Zi Se’s hair. “Thanks.”
When he looked back up, Sokka was watching him, and he didn’t look angry, or offended. He
looked just as relaxed as before, and Zuko made himself breathe away this sudden frustration,
made himself see clearly. Here was a boy who had seen him hateful, seen him fighting, seen
him killing. Sokka had been on the receiving end of Zuko’s rage and deceit and he had given
him another chance regardless. There was nothing Zuko could say to convince Sokka of his
badness. Sokka had already made up his mind. If this went wrong, it was because Sokka had
been naïve. Zuko had tried to warn him, and he had given Sokka no reason to trust him, and
still, Sokka was here.
The thought was strangely calming, and Zuko sighed.
“Fine, I'll... I’ll try it.” He said, and Sokka lit up. Zuko's face darkened. “But if I... if I hurt
you, you can’t hesitate. You have to defend yourself. Don't pity me and don’t trust me to snap
out of it, just defend yourself.”
He expected Sokka to deflate upon the warning, but the other boy’s smile turned menacing.
“You think I wouldn’t? I’ve been waiting for a chance to kick your ass since you showed up
at the South Pole.”
It was a joke, and it wasn’t, and either way, it was so immediately reassuring to Zuko that he
almost did something stupid, like laugh. He'd been so caught up in his confusion at Sokka
being so determined to help him that he had also forgotten what else made Sokka different
from the others. He was Zuko’s point of honesty; he stuck to his beliefs when the others were
blinded by pity, and he would continue to do so even now. It was strange. In his refusal to cut
Zuko any slack, Sokka was the only one who made Zuko feel like maybe he was still strong,
strong enough to overcome all of this. After all, Sokka wasn’t a monster. If Zuko truly was
some pathetic, beaten thing, then Sokka would treat him as such. The other boy had no filter.
He said what he saw and acted accordingly, and he treated Zuko like someone who could
handle it.
So, Zuko would handle it.
____
To Sokka’s credit, Zuko hadn’t punched him yet.
To Zuko’s credit, Sokka could tell he wanted to.

Every time Sokka moved, Zuko would flinch, golden eyes snapping to Sokka. He knew he
didn’t mean to glare, but it didn’t stop Sokka’s skin from crawling. He'd been on the
receiving end of that golden glare too many times to start relaxing under it now. But Sokka
was set on this plan. The feeling he’d had yesterday, realising what had happened to Zuko,
another pain he had suffered through silently like the insufferable jerkbender he was – it
wasn’t something Sokka ever wanted to feel again. It was the feeling he’d had watching
Katara back in the village, pulling up puddles and dropping them again like there was just
something too heavy about them, helpless and alone, and Sokka couldn’t help. It was the
feeling he got when Aang woke up in the night, terrified and restless, heading into another
day of brutal training and refusing to stop, and Sokka couldn’t help. It was the feeling that sat
heavy within him when Toph had walked away from them after Aang and Katara had argued
with her, unable to placate the situation until it went from uncomfortable to explosive, and
Sokka couldn’t help. It was the feeling he got when Azula taunted him about Suki, his mind
supplying awful image after awful imagine, and Sokka couldn’t help. It was the feeling that
consumed him when he thought of Yue, and how she...
This was something Sokka could help with, and after so long keeping Team Avatar together,
it wasn’t something he could ignore. It didn’t matter that it was Zuko, it mattered only that
there was someone in their group who needed help.
So, Sokka was helping. Clumsily, loudly, but he was helping, and Zuko hadn’t punched him
yet. Sokka tried to move smoothly as he ate, but he’d never exactly been the most... elegant.
Having to keep his gesticulations to a minimum as he spoke was a conscious effort, draining
too. It wasn’t Sokka’s fault he was such an expressive guy. It came with being such an
interesting person. Eccentric, even.
Part of his plan he hadn’t voiced to Zuko was that, Sokka theorised, if he just talked enough,
Zuko might be so annoyed by his constant distraction that he forgot the threat he saw in
Sokka. He knew it wouldn’t be that simple, that it all probably layered in Zuko’s mind like
some twisted nightmare, but he also knew that the firebender had a notoriously quick temper
and very, very little patience, and if there was one thing Sokka was good at, it was talking.
“And so we saw this rock, and I was totally not bothered by it, but Toph decided it was the
coolest thing ever because it was, and I quote, ‘shaped exactly like a bean curd puff.’ Which
is just completely inaccurate, because bean curd puffs are smooth, and also the shapes were
totally different.” Sokka swatted his hand in the air absentmindedly, needing to get his point
across of how wrong Toph was, and in turn how wronged Sokka was. “I'm telling you, this
rock was hexagonal, if anything, and bean curd puffs are just curved cylinders, you know?
Those shapes aren’t even remotely similar, but Toph was so stubborn, and the next thing I
know, she’s getting all moody with me, and do you know what she did? Guess.”
Zuko was glaring at him like he hoped a certain degree of conveyed malice might just set
Sokka on fire and blissfully shut him up, and Sokka had to bite back a smile, continuing to
feign obliviousness. Zuko was as predictable as he’d expected; his plan was working. Sokka
had been talking ever since Zuko agreed to this, about any and everything. Katara's snoring,
the healing qualities of Aang’s hugs, the waterfall Tulok found this morning, and now Toph’s
menacing assaults against Sokka’s wellbeing via the geographic landscape. Zuko was
practically fuming in his annoyance – he was exactly where Sokka wanted him.

“I don’t know.” Zuko eventually bit out, like it took a lot of effort to simply utter the words
instead of yelling them.
“She threw the rock at me.” Sokka declared, amping up his rightful indignation. “It hit my leg
right here! Look! See how big that is? It hurt too.”
He hoisted up his trouser leg to reveal where his skin was tinged a deep red and green around
his knee, pouting as he remembered the moment of impact, then looked back up to see Zuko
staring at him impatiently. The firebender was leaning against the wall, arms crossed
moodily. There was a certain nonchalance to Zuko these days, a very specific kind of
carelessness that probably came from immense trauma that made every other mundane
problem pale in comparison. Usually, it was in his attitude, and it bugged Sokka to no end,
but this morning when they sat together, Sokka could see it. The shirt he wore was a little too
big on him, black fabric bringing out the inky colour of his stupid hair that fell every which
way and the devastating gold of his eyes, and he had bundled the sleeves into his fists in his
frustration, inadvertently tugging the hem to give Sokka a view of a pale neck and the
beginning of a sharp collarbone. Sokka had obviously walked in when the prince was still
waking up, and Zuko hadn’t yet thought to correct this whole... sleep-mussed look. Sokka
remembered in the Boiling Rock when they’d woken up next to each other, how annoying
he’d found it when he had been carefully braiding back his wolf tail and all Zuko had to do
was run his fingers through his hair a few times for it to look like that. It almost made a guy
miss the angry ponytail jerk.
Then he remembered how Zuko had laughed this morning, when he hadn’t noticed Sokka and
he thought it was just him and Zi Se, how he held the kid at once gently and firmly, how
much a smile actually suited him, and when he thought of that, it was hard to find the
jerkbender annoying at all, and wasn’t that a terrifying thought? It couldn’t be good for
digestion.
Speaking of, Sokka’s plan – as usual, because he was Team Avatar’s resident genius – had
worked perfectly. Three bowls brought in, three bowls empty, zero casualties.
“I’m sure you’ll survive.” Zuko grumbled, rolling his eyes when Sokka made a dramatic
show of flicking his trouser leg back down.
Sokka winked at him. “Long enough to bring you lunch later.”
And with that, he grabbed his bowl and stood, dusting off his clothes a little before heading
towards the hallway.
“Are you telling me you just came in here to rant?” Zuko said, bewildered by Sokka’s sudden
exit.
“I came in here to execute a perfectly formulated plan.” Sokka shrugged, smugness twitching
at his lips as Zuko still stared up at him, confused. “I did that, so now I'm going.”
“But all you did was talk.” Zuko hissed.

Sokka grinned at him, blue eyes flicking to the empty bowl at Zuko’s side. “And all you did
was eat. Like I said; perfectly formulated.”
He was gone before the spluttering firebender could figure out a response.
____
A perfectly formulated plan, Zuko thought, staring after Sokka in shock. The Water Tribe boy
had been with him for only a matter of minutes, time that Zuko had been certain would drag,
and it felt like nothing at all. It wasn’t easy, not by any means, and it wouldn’t be for a very,
very long time, but it wasn’t anything like Zuko had expected. He'd sat there, rigid as the
rock around him, every sense attuned to the things that were important; the food in the room,
Zi Se, and the teenage boy before him. Nothing else mattered. The air he breathed, the wind
in the ravine, the anxiety in his chest – it all melted to nothing but a primal focus, a scathing
intensity, a readying to wound.
And Sokka had talked away, oblivious. No, not oblivious. He was completely aware of the
way Zuko was glaring at him, the way he flinched upon even the smallest of gestures from
the other boy, the way he had twisted his torso to face him and clutched his bowl so tight that
his knuckles gleamed like the bleached bones of carcasses in the morning light. Sokka was
completely aware, and he was unbothered, because he had planned for this, and he was ready
for whatever Zuko did.
It gave him more incentive to hold back. It was a twisted logic in his mind, and he hated the
thought process the moment he realised what he was doing, but knowing Sokka was actually
a threat, a boy who could handle himself against Zuko, was more steadying than if Sokka had
made himself this soft, unobtrusive thing. Zuko's mind was in survival mode the moment he
picked up his bowl to eat. If Sokka didn’t make himself a threat, then he wouldn’t be treated
as one, and Zuko would take what he knew he could. Putra was a victim of Zuko’s hunger as
much as Chan. At least Chan had beaten Zuko as much as Zuko had beaten him, but Putra
had starved in the shadows of their greater rage. Zuko hadn’t even thought twice about taking
from him, because it kept him alive.
Yesterday, Zuko had kept his cool by focussing on his meal, eating it quickly without issue. It
was only when the food was gone and he looked up to see everyone else still eating that the
awful feeling in his chest roared into a monster rather than a shadow. This time, Zuko
couldn’t even concentrate on eating. He couldn’t concentrate on anything. Sokka didn’t just
talk; his tone changed, he jumped through his sentences, he used his hands. It was like he was
constantly on three different trains of thought and was steering them away from one another
before they crashed. It was chaotic and loud and distracting, and Zuko had just assumed it
was Sokka being Sokka, and maybe it was, maybe that was the genius of this plan. All Zuko
had known was that his heart was thumping in his chest, fear becoming anger becoming
anxiety. It wasn’t a nice feeling, that restless fluttering against bunched muscles, but it also
wasn’t dangerous. The desire to hurt Sokka for his food slowly left Zuko’s mind, being
replaced with the desire to hurt Sokka if only to shut him up. The difference was that Zuko
had spent his entire life with this conversational impatience, and he knew how to control that.
He didn’t know how to control those other feelings.

So he’d controlled it, a sickening feeling in his stomach, snapping at Sokka whenever the
other boy asked him questions, and the moment he finished his food, Sokka stood and gave
him that grin, revealing that this had all been on purpose.
And Zuko was just... stunned.
Because it had worked.
Recovery had been sold to Zuko as a series of impossibilities. A dark tunnel with light at the
end. A tall mountain he didn’t know how to climb. Something terrifying, something large,
something that required strength and bravery, and Zuko was just a body of shame and anger
and fear. How did he even start?
Healing was a memory of murder. He had buried any kindness at the feet of his father years
ago and all tellings of dirt had been scrubbed from his mind, which left room for perfection,
which left a boy and his father, which left something rotting beneath the ground. Then his
father had turned around and walked away, fire in the halls of a childhood home, fire in his
eyes, which left a boy on his own, scavenging for a kindness he had buried long ago,
searching hands and desperation. It's around here somewhere. Bad things kept happening,
new shadows towering over him, but he didn’t know how to touch his skin kindly, which left
a boy without a propensity for recovery. His kindness was no more than an unmarked grave,
and it had been for a very long time.
Healing was a memory of murder, a killing of kindness, a burial without rites, which left a
boy and the dirt, and the blood in the dirt, which left his hands, which left the blood on his
hands.
Healing was a memory of murder, and a retelling of a gentler story, a promise that, this time,
nothing would be left. Unbury everything. Dirty your hands. Make maps of this landscape.
Do not forget. Do not walk away.
Zuko knew it was part of it, that unburying. He knew he could only heal if he dug his hands
into the mud and began to dig. It didn’t stop the dirt from choking him, or his nails from
cracking against the pressure.
It didn’t stop it from hurting so much.
Last night’s conversation with Hakoda left his insides bare and burning, throat raw and eyes
aching, but this... this had been easier. Not easy, just easier. He hadn’t had to hurt in order to
make this small amount of progress, and it was the tiniest thing, a single meal sat rigidly and
uncomfortably, but he hadn’t hurt anyone, and that was progress. Maybe in a few day’s time,
it would feel less uncomfortable. Maybe in a few month’s time, he could eat with his friends
again.
Maybe he could really do this.
Zuko smiled, ruffling Zi Se’s hair as he got to his feet and collected their bowls. It was a new
day. The sunlight glowed through the temple, and the sad ache in Zuko’s chest abated. It

wouldn’t go away because of one shuffle in the right direction, it might not go away for a
very long time, but it was more bearable now.
After all, Zuko wasn’t carrying it alone anymore.

The plan had been skewed with the appearance of the Fire Prince, or more specifically, with
the delivery of that critical piece of information he dropped on their little group in regards to
Ozai’s intentions for the comet. Bato had talked with Hakoda on the Ullaakut when they had
sailed here, deciding that the Air Temple would be no more than a detour, a chance to pick up
their youngest members. From there, they had agreed to meet the rest of their men at General
Iroh’s White Lotus camp, and they were going to plan further as a bigger collective.
Zuko had changed that. Their perspective had been forced to shift, because while they hadn’t
had an official plan, there had still been the outline of one, a general understanding that they
would outlast the comet so the Avatar could face the Fire Lord later. Ozai's plan to annihilate
the Earth Kingdom made that impossible. Unless they wanted a genocide on their hands, the
Avatar would have to defeat the Fire Lord before the comet.
What was originally supposed to be a detour had now become a two-week-long-and-counting
stint at the Air Temple. Zuko's injuries had provided them with an easy excuse to get a little
comfortable here, an excuse Bato had been more than happy to exploit, because he, like
Hakoda, wasn’t willing to meet back up with the Dragon of the West without at least the
groundworks of a plan for the comet. They would not leave their fate in the hands of some
retired war criminal, no matter how kind he might seem.
So here they were, still at the Air Temple, running out of time and trying to stitch together a
plan.
“So it’s agreed that we cannot take out the attack once it’s in full swing; we need to weaken
its foundations. If we hadn’t had warning beforehand, we’d be tackling the air fleet with brute
force, and we’d fail almost immediately. The Fire Lord knows that, it’s why he’s amassed
such an offensive attack.” Hakoda thought aloud from where he sat by the fire, the adults
having gathered around him, his expression serious, the kind of seriousness he only donned
when he was deep in thought.
“Assuming he’s oblivious to Zuko warning us,” Hakoda continued, “we still hold that
advantage, and he won’t have had the forethought to anticipate anything other than a head-on
collision.”
“So we take out the big guys before they even get the chance to gain heat, right?” Bato
added, following Hakoda’s train of thought with an effortlessness that came from years at
war, and even longer at each other’s side.
“Exactly.” Hakoda nodded. “Sokka ran through them with me a few days ago. Spirits know I
never wanted to be getting inside information about the Fire Nation from my son, but isn’t
that just one more reason on a mountain that we need to end this?”

It was a rhetorical question, curling with bitterness, but this was one of the things that made
Hakoda such a good chief. He insighted determination even without meaning to. Bato saw it

say the same. So few tribesmen could say the same. They were fighting for their lives, but
also for the ghosts standing in line behind them. A hundred childhoods lost to fire.
“We need to figure out a way to infiltrate Caldera City as a whole.” Hakoda said, elbows on

“She's her father’s daughter alright.”
“Whole family of dickheads.” Chena mumbled, and Aput snorted.

Tulok had found a waterfall close to the temple.
Tulok had found a waterfall close to the temple, and Tomkin had decided to make it

Zuko glanced to Nanook. Nanook glanced at Zuko.

He should have known, that something so gentle could not last. Tenderness was a thing to be

“But you said you’d fight us.” Nanook joined in on Tomkin’s whinging, and that’s when

were punctuated by roughhousing and bickering, but when they banded together, set on a
common goal, they were impossible.
Toph shrugged. “I’ll only go in if Zuko does.”
He knew he couldn’t avoid this. In a literal sense, he could. He could get up right now, stomp

mind a bloody whirlwind of determination, that this exact moment with Sokka hadn’t felt

Zuko, who was bad. Zuko, who was ugly.

Tomkin was trying desperately to smile, but it was pained, a deep sadness in his eyes. We are
human beings, he had once said, that means we have scars. But even he couldn’t justify this,

Watching Tomkin try not to get upset over it made something familiar and cool dip in his gut.
Shame.
He had once found comfort in the legibility of these scars, because they gave him something
grounding. The hurt inside of him was so big, so incomprehensible, that having physical
manifestations of it gave him some sort of validation. See, right here, you’re hurt, that’s why

He turned next to Nanook, spurred on with a gritty determination. He caught only a glimpse
of proud, blue eyes, like somehow he knew, and then a wave of water splashed directly into

Zuko spluttered in shock for a moment, before a wild grin overtook him, Toph cackling as

“You’re dead, Nan.”

“She’s also right.” Zuko pointed out, and Tomkin squawked at the betrayal.

When Zuko was a child, he used to sleep by the windows during monsoon season.

It made him want to tip back his head and laugh.
The problem had always been the enormity of this trauma. There was so much to do and
Zuko didn’t know where to start, leaving him stood in a wreckage unable to do anything but

trying to heal every single child. This was only his trauma, and he was only one boy. It was
manageable. A world within a world, one so much smaller than fear and hatred, one Zuko
was in control of because it was his.
He was going to make his world better. It was not selfish to focus on himself, and the shame
that choked him, that whispered to him that to heal was to betray his own memory, was
wrong.
In Zuko’s world, he had scars all over his body, and he could also laugh with his friends. It
was so very easy to be angry, to be hurt, but this world was going to be better. Zuko was
going to fill this life with love if it killed him. He would not be able to see for fondness and
friendship, and he would learn kindness until it no longer felt like a mother tongue that had
been ripped from his mouth. This world would be fluent in it, and things would be gentle, and
when Zuko woke every morning, he was going to take a moment. I am going to be okay, he
would say, and he would believe it.
Or even, the harder of the two lessons, I deserve to be okay.
This time around, Zuko got to be happy.

“Dude, you’re gonna get sick if you stay out here!” A voice suddenly burst through the

Sokka hadn’t forgiven him because Zuko hadn’t given him the chance to. Not once through

Sokka blinked, the rain making his dark hair plaster to his forehead, and he didn’t just take

laughing as he jumped in a puddle. He didn’t notice Sokka gawking at him. He didn’t

From where the others sheltered beneath the main camp’s overhang, Bato and Kanut watched
