Bato and Kanut, past
Bato was lucky. He was born into steady skies and a waiting village. He was blessed with a
family who loved him and gave him freedom. He was confident and happy and he made
friends easily. All of these fortunes blanketed him through his life, and he had been wrapped
so tenderly since the day of his birth that he hadn’t even noticed their weight. Not until
Kanut, a cold little boy, chattering teeth revealed in a snarl of unfriendliness. Kanut was born
into a snowstorm and his father’s absence. His family was a curse of anger, and Kanut was
quiet, sharp, and he had no one for a very long time.
Bato was lucky, but he could also be oblivious sometimes, and it took him a long time to
realise just how far the warmth of his personal fortunes had travelled into his bones, and its
subsequent absence in a boy like Kanut, who had never felt that warmth, his prickly friend
who sometimes seemed like such an enigma to Bato that he would wonder if he even knew
him at all. Bato did not often realise that this luck he had been born into was just that; luck. It
was not a given. It was not an aspect of life everyone was fortunate enough to partake in.
Every day with Kanut reminded him of that. Every tiny piece of himself he tentatively
offered Hakoda and Bato that they hoarded like the determined, curious, overprotective
children they were.

Still, discoveries stepped aside for familiarity. Careful conversation became year's worth of
friendship, and they became teenagers – taller, broader, louder. Bato supposed it made him
arrogant. Hakoda and Kanut. Kanut and Hakoda. These were two boys Bato had been joined
with, wild grins and laughter. Hakoda was a strategist. Kanut was a reader. Bato stood
between them as a diplomat and a hopeless flirt. They would bicker and roughhouse and sulk.
They all liked to fix things.
Bato had thought he knew his friends entirely, but it was a youthful arrogance, the same
arrogance that led him to believe, with the puffed chest of a teenager thinking himself a man,
that he knew himself entirely too. One day, Kanna got a new book with her latest shipment,
and both beliefs were shattered in Bato’s mind.
There was nothing about this book that separated it from the rest, though Bato wasn’t a reader
in the way Kanut was, and tended to share that sentiment with every book he came across.
Bato read to be smart, to always have an edge, but truthfully, he thought the lettering and
words were a little pointless. He liked tradition. He liked talking. He was very good at
talking.
Kanut wasn’t, and said nothing as he did his usual routine of inspecting each book Kanna had
received with an almost clinical concentration. It was a little terrifying to watch sometimes,
but Bato had long since exhausted the comedic potential of his friend’s terminal nerdiness.
That didn’t stop him trying.
“Do you think Kya was looking at me earlier?” Hakoda asked with the dejected tone of a boy
who knew full well that Kya was not, in fact, looking at him earlier. The three of them were
in his tent, Bato idly poking the burning fire he’d sat himself beside, Kanut busy with his
books and Hakoda lying gracelessly on the floor, glaring at the roof of the tent like it might
explain the mystery of girls everywhere to him.
“Do you think Kanut is going to marry his library before you work up the nerve to talk to
her?” Bato asked, matching Hakoda’s put-out tone and biting back a smile when it earnt him
a withering glare. He waited for Kanut’s scathing response, always sharper than Hakoda with
his insults, but nothing came, and Bato threw a curious glance over his shoulder to Kanut’s
little corner. Kanut was two years younger than Bato. At the time, it felt like a decade, all of
his sixteen winters stacked against Kanut’s measly fourteen. It didn’t help that Bato had shot
up in height and muscle while Kanut had remained his gangly self. Now, he sat amongst his
books, skinny with a natural inclination to hunch over himself a little, like he was trying to
look smaller than he was, though that white hair of his always gave him away, falling to his
chin. Some of the villagers thought it was a bad omen, a touch of the brutal ice they all
fought to survive, a kiss of the snowstorm Kanut had been born into and carried within him
as he grew.
Kanut was holding a book – to the surprise of absolutely no one – and was flicking through
it, brow furrowed, completely distracted, gripping the dark green cover like he might clutch it
to his chest at any moment. He hadn’t even heard Bato’s excellent joke, and Bato pouted at
the injustice. He was wasted on these two. He didn’t think much of the book; it wasn’t
exactly rare for Kanut to lose focus like this when he was reading. In fact, he made an active
point of doing so whenever he deemed Hakoda and Bato as being particularly annoying.

Bato could be oblivious sometimes, but he was also perceptive when it came to people. He
saw them as Hakoda saw maps and plans; coherent and utterly open, even when they tried
not to be. The little green book kept making an appearance, shoved deep into the pockets of
Kanut’s parka or held so close to his face as he huddled in a corner that Bato thought he
might hurt his eyes. He didn’t think much of it at first, assuming that this book must just be
interesting, and that Kanut had found his latest favourite, but he noticed that whenever he
came too close, Kanut would snap the book shut, holding it to his chest defensively.
That was unusual. One of Bato’s favourite things was watching the way Kanut relaxed when
he talked about his books, the small smile on his lips, the flicker of genuine delight in his
eyes. He would ask questions and it was one of the few things Kanut let himself indulge in.
But this, it seemed, was something the other boy was not willing to share.
Part of Bato wanted to be hurt, but mostly, he was intrigued, and he knew with Kanut that
sometimes the only thing to do was wait, to not push. It wasn’t Bato’s preferred technique,
but he could be patient when he needed to be.
It was that patience that led to Kanut’s misstep. He relaxed, he grew sloppy, and Bato didn’t
miss anything, didn’t miss the day they were messing around in the snowbanks, drawing
increasingly crude things in the soft snow and saying they resembled one another. They were
laughing, and then they were called back for food. It was an old argument by now, one they
had daily and would continue to have well into adulthood.
“I got it last time.” Bato said immediately upon hearing Kanna’s call.
“My mom doesn’t like us eating out here anyway.” Hakoda scowled, shoving Bato into the
snow. “Why can’t we just go eat with the others instead of bringing it out here? I'm always
the one who gets chewed out for it at the end of the day.”
“And we all note your worthy sacrifice.” Kanut said with a sharp grin. Despite his usually
sensible nature, this was something he agreed with Bato on. He liked eating out on the
snowbanks, not out of sight of the village lest Kanna come chasing after them, but still in
their own little corner of the world. Kanut often did anything he could to stay as far from
home for as long as possible.
“Why are you siding with him?” Hakoda cried in dismay, proceeding to try and push Kanut
into the snow right next to Bato, earning a barked laugh and a thump to the side from the
other boy, who had taken to using his smaller size to his advantage. “It’s your turn to go get it
if you’re going to insist we eat here.”
While they scuffled, a now familiar green book fell out of Kanut’s pocket. He didn’t notice.
Bato didn’t say anything.
“He’s right, Kanut. Run along now.” Bato shooed him away. “I want sea prunes.”
Hakoda perked up. “Oh! Get me some arctic hen! But don’t touch the five flavour soup; I
heard Aput’s learning to make it and I don’t trust him.”

“Don’t trust him, or don’t trust the way Kya swoons around him?” Bato asked innocently,
and this time, Hakoda shoved him so hard that he knocked his head.
“Yeah, yeah, whatever.” Kanut huffed, stomping away. “Don’t kill each other while I'm
gone.”
Hakoda immediately began an impassioned rant about the most beautiful girl in the village
who, by the way, was yet to look twice at him, and he didn’t notice a thing when Bato
surreptitiously leaned over and plucked the book from the snow.
Later, when the village was sleeping and Bato was alone, he fished the book from his pocket
and held it to the dying light of the fire in his family’s tent. He squinted, trying to make sense
of the overzealous font on the cover. It was written in white ink, bright against the dark green
background, catching orange on the flickering fire. A Study Of Expression And Identity
Across The Nations, by Yi-Ren Cheng. Bato frowned, reading the title a few times for good
measure. It was clunkier than a lot of the things he was used to reading, and his frown only
deepened as he flicked through the pages, blue eyes catching on words like orientation and
sexuality.
While these words weren’t completely foreign to Bato, they were bookish, almost formal,
rarely used in conversation, and he couldn’t help but deflate a little. He'd hoped Kanut had
been reading something interesting, like a wild fantasy novel to completely juxtapose his
stoic nature that Bato could tease him endlessly about. Instead, all Bato had was this smartaleck encyclopaedia about expression. He sighed, easing back a little more into his bedroll to
get comfortable, giving up on the prospect of finding out what was ticking behind Kanut’s
sharp blues eyes and instead reading idly. He wasn’t tired, and it offered a way to pass the
time.
He flicked to a random page and paused in surprise.
Different types of attraction, the latest chapter boasted as a bold title, and Bato frowned,
because he had always thought attraction was rather simple. Bato liked the way girls laughed,
liked the way their hands would weave, liked the way they rolled their eyes at his flirting.
Bato liked the hard set of Aput’s shoulders, liked the shamelessness of masculinity, liked the
warmth of hunting close together. This, he knew, was attraction. He had always assumed that
it was the same way Hakoda felt attraction, with his endless sonnets about Kya, and the same

his and Bato’s brutal gossip sessions. Kanut was notoriously reclusive, and Hakoda was too
besotted with Kya to notice anyone else, but it hadn’t ever made Bato doubt the certainty of
universal attraction.
He doubted it now, as he continued to read, sleep forgotten and frown returning. There were
entire pages that felt like they had dipped beneath Bato’s skin and started taking his own
blood as ink, describing specific feelings he’d never thought anything of and giving them
strange labels that felt less and less strange the more he read. According to the book, not
everyone was attracted to more than one type of person. Some people only liked girls, some
people only liked boys, and Bato liked... Well, Bato liked everyone. It was not unusual. It was
not bad. It just was.

Bato had never particularly felt like something was missing from his life, but a warm comfort

simple as he had thought it was when he woke up this morning, but he had his place in it. He

So, Bato would wait for a chance, and he would hope against hope that Kanut would keep

at the sky during these months. It was too bright, and he would hurt himself, but Bato was
stubborn and didn’t like being told he couldn’t do something. He was getting a headache.

Sokka and Zuko, present
It makes you feel like the only authentic thing here. It had been two days since Zuko, casual
and rain-soaked, had said that to him, and Sokka hadn’t been able to stop turning the words
around in his mind since. It shouldn’t have been a big deal, and that was the part that grated
on him. He just couldn’t figure it out, and that had always been the problem with Zuko, right?
Sokka solved problems, and Zuko was an enigma he couldn’t get a handle on, and what
started as curiosity in the Boiling Rock and had grown into something really fucking
annoying when Zuko joined their little group at the Western Air Temple, had now progressed
into something... else. It was a recent development. Maybe it started when they had their big
talk, when Sokka had said how he felt and Zuko – inexplicable, golden-eyed, piece of shit
Zuko – had listened. Or maybe it wasn’t that. Maybe it was the parts of Sokka’s day he
realised he was starting to look forward to a little, when he brought Zuko food and he got to
watch as it slowly, slowly got easier for the other boy, when he talked and talked and Zuko
snapped at him and they ribbed each other and it always seemed to dance a fine line between
banter and insults but never crossed it.
Zuko was funny. It was not a revelation Sokka had been expecting from their new food
arrangement. Zuko was quick-tempered and growly and he could be really horrible, had been
really horrible, but he was also trying really hard to be good, and for a while now Sokka had
felt some twisted, complicated respect for Zuko that wove around his lungs and only seemed
to tighten with each passing day he watched the firebender try so, so hard to do right by the
people around him. And Zuko was funny. Sometimes. He didn’t mean to be, and maybe that’s
why Sokka found him funny, and when Sokka told jokes, Zuko didn’t always get them,
which was fine because Sokka was a funny guy with an endless comedic arsenal, but when
Zuko did get the joke, his mouth would twitch like he was fighting back a smile, and it had
become a conscious goal of Sokka’s to bring that expression out of the other boy as much as
possible. Tomkin and Nanook could make Zuko laugh easy enough, and the adults all
brought out this specific brand of Stupid Dopey Smile from Zuko that Sokka had to look
away from, but something about the way Zuko laughed at Sokka’s jokes was different. He

was reluctant, because it was Sokka and even though they were friends (?) now there was still
that underlying rivalry and need to one-up each other at every turn, and it made that tiny
smile, those bitten back scoffs, feel earned and fleeting and Sokka was a little obsessed with
it and he didn’t know why.
Listen, Sokka wasn’t an idiot. He knew he’d liked boys for months now. He was embarrassed
about how he figured it out, something to do with a guy whose name rhymed with Bet, or
Regret – Sokka patted himself on the back for that one – but safe to say, it hadn’t been a huge
deal, more like a puzzle piece finally slotting into place after he’d spent so many years
jamming it into the wrong ends and wondering what the picture was. Since figuring that out,
a lot of things about him that he’d left to gather dust started to make sense, like how he
always used to follow Nanook about, and why he didn’t turn tail and run the moment his
instincts started to knuckle down on Jet. So yeah, Sokka liked boys, and Sokka liked girls,
but Sokka did not like Zuko. Not like that. They could hardly even figure out this weird
friendship they had going on. If Sokka hadn’t been able to think of anything to say – not a
single damn word, really? - when Zuko stood with him in the rain, if Sokka’s mind kept
drifting to that flash of collarbone and sleep-mussed laughter, if he sometimes caught himself
remembering a too-small cupboard in the Boiling Rock, then that was a purely physical thing.
He was smart and mature and could admit that he found Zuko attractive in an entirely
detached, impersonal way. He was also a teenage boy, which meant such a stupid thing could
fluster him from time to time. Shit happens. Sue him. It didn’t have to mean anything-.
“Hey, smartass, it wasn’t a difficult question.” Bato’s grating voice cut through Sokka’s spiel,
and he blinked, head snapping to the tribesman in question that had caused this whole spiral
in the first place.
“I’m thinking.” Sokka snapped, angrier than he ought to have been but he couldn’t bring
himself to feel bad, not when Bato had opened his big mouth and forced Sokka to think about
Zuko like... that.
“I literally just asked if you liked the guy,” Bato sighed, admiring his cuticles, “you don’t
need to have a breakdown over it.”
Sokka grit his teeth, glaring at the boy in question. Zuko and Aang were stood in a clearing in
front of where Bato and Sokka had sat to spectate, going through some firebending katas,
blissfully out of earshot. Sokka had been here first, by the way, but apparently, Bato didn’t
care for that, sitting himself down and immediately chatting as much shit as feasibly possible.
It had started simple, Bato asking why Sokka was watching the firebending to begin with,
and when Sokka had given some flimsy excuse about keeping an eye on things, blue stare
following the fire, Bato’s expression had taken on a dark understanding. That was the last
moment of seriousness Sokka would get from the older man, because it was clear that Bato
was bored, and a bored Bato was a very dangerous thing.
“You know, from an entirely political point of view, you are the next generation of Water
Tribe,” Bato said, feigning aloofness, though his stare held a pinpoint accuracy, “and there is
a big chance Prince Zuko will one day be Fire Lord Zuko.”
“So what, you going to marry me off?” Sokka scoffed, part of him wanting to be embarrassed
they were having this conversation, the other half too aware of how ridiculous it was to even

care.
“I was talking about the benefits of kindling a friendship between the Southern Water Tribe
and Fire Nation after the war.” Bato frowned, like he wasn't sure how Sokka had progressed
to that train of thought. The silence began to stretch. A smile crept onto Bato's face. “What
were you talking about?”
Sokka immediately flushed, and then cursed himself for flushing because it wasn’t like he’d
actually said anything bad.
“It was a joke,” Sokka hissed, tone a little too desperate, that desperation only growing when
Bato’s smile became an evil grin, “I was kidding.”
“Hey, no judgement here.” Bato said, holding up his hands, “I think that’s very forwardthinking of you. Take one for the team. Very enterprising. Hey, is that why you almost passed
out when I asked if you liked him? You know I meant platonically, right? Not that there’s any
shame with taking it another way but-.”
“Okay!” Sokka shouted, scrambling to his feet and, Spirits, drawing the attention of Aang
and Zuko with his sudden outburst. “I’m done with this conversation. I think... is that Katara
calling me? Bye, Bato.”
He stomped off to the tune of Bato’s laughter and the blood pumping in his ears.
____
Bato watched the teenager walk sulkily away with a victorious grin and a dawning realisation
that his antics had, as usual, stumbled upon something. There was potential here, and not just
potential to tease Sokka, a past-time Bato had always enjoyed, but potential for something
serious. Bato wasn’t kidding when he’d brought up the future of the Southern Water Tribe.
For all the jokes, he took his position very seriously. He was Hakoda’s Second for a reason.
He was good at people, politics, and part of that was looking to the future, planning two,
three steps ahead at all times. The truth of it was undeniable; one day, maybe sooner rather
than later, Prince Zuko might become Fire Lord Zuko. Bato trusted the relationships the
firebender had built with the tribesmen, but a friendship with Sokka, a boy his age, a boy who
would represent them when Bato and Hakoda couldn’t, would ensure the safety of the
Southern Water Tribe for a whole other generation. That was all Bato was asking, and it
seemed he might be getting a lot more than he bargained for. Besides, if that hadn’t given it
away, then Sokka openly ogling the firebender going through his forms was a bit of an
indicator.
It reminded Bato of another time, another pair of teenage boys trying to figure out who they
were, and his smile took a softer edge, gaze thoughtful as Zuko told Aang to take a breather,
the prince wiping the sweat from his face as he went to hang out with Tomkin and Nanook,
who had been sat near the cliffs this morning, dicking about with the local flora. Tomkin and
Nanook were another of Bato’s matchmaking attempts. He still had hope for them, even if
Hakoda laughed at him and Kanut grew surly whenever he found out Bato was still meddling
with other people’s personal lives. Bato had no intention of stopping, and he had a good

feeling about Sokka and Zuko. He'd be happy if he could just help them navigate a
friendship, for the sake of the tribe.
But he’d have bragging rights for the rest of his life if he could germinate something deeper,
and he couldn’t wait to rub it in Kanut’s face, especially given the healer’s weird relationship
with the fire brat.

Kanut was trying to have a peaceful day, but any chance at peace was butchered back in his
childhood, when he made the mistake of humouring the village idiots and had henceforth
been stuck with Bato and Hakoda for the next two decades, each a very specific kind of thorn
in his side, each with polar forms of ridiculousness but ridiculousness all the same.
“Kanut! How are you this fine morning?”
“Go away.” Kanut said without looking up from his book.
He'd retreated to the infirmary, an old habit, and had just settled after breakfast to do some
reading when Bato decided to torment him with his presence. Kanut’s book collection here
was limited, most of his volumes left on the Ullaakut, but wherever they went, he always
brought a handful. Usually some new ones, but also old ones, favourites of his, some that
were sentimental that he always liked to keep close. It was an ongoing trend whenever they
disembarked from the ship. His tribesmen would bring clothes, bedrolls, weapons, and Kanut
would bring his books.
“I’m being nice to you!” Bato cried in offence, pouting. “Why so growly today?”
Kanut sighed deeply, before snapping his book shut and narrowing his eyes on his childhood
friend.
“Because you’re using your scheming voice. You're up to something, and I want nothing to
do with it.” Kanut said, and the sharp twitch of Bato’s eyebrow was confirmation enough. He
should have seen this coming. Aside from strategizing, there wasn’t really much for the
tribesmen to do here at the Air Temple apart from bide their time, and a bored Bato was a
dangerous Bato. Kanut had seen it happen time and time again back on the Ullaakut, when
they would sail for weeks without making port. When he was bored, Bato began to meddle.
He was too astute when it came to people’s emotions, and while he wasn’t ever malicious, he
could often be oblivious, stumbling into fragile territory unwittingly. It was a strange
dichotomy, Bato having a level of emotional intelligence unlike anything Kanut had seen
before, but none of the delicacy to handle the things he picked up on. Kanut still remembered
the time Bato took it upon himself to sort out an argument Chena and Aput were having. It
had led to Bato accidentally revealing some things Aput had said behind Chena’s back, and
Hakoda had to physically restrain their biggest warrior from throwing Aput overboard. They
sorted it out eventually - they always did – but it had certainly been no thanks to Bato.
“Kanuttt,” Bato complained, coming to sit cross-legged in front of him, and Kanut reluctantly
put his book down entirely, glaring at the Second, “I’m being selfless here. I think I've
realised something.”

“Wow, don’t hurt yourself.”
Bato whacked Kanut’s leg half-heartedly, unperturbed. “Do you think Sokka likes Zuko?”
Kanut tilted his head then, confused and momentarily forgetting that he was supposed to be
annoyed right now. “Not really? Though they've been getting on better lately.”
“They have.” Bato agreed, grin becoming evil, and Kanut stared at him for a few moments
before his expression became serious.
“No, Bato, don’t you dare. You don’t get to just play matchmaker every time you get bored.
It'll be Hakoda and Kya all over again.”
“That was successful! They fell in love and it was all because of me!” Bato insisted, but
Kanut’s memory of that particular romance was tainted by a very traumatic courting period
which included but wasn’t limited to their other friend being a complete idiot, spurred on by
Bato while Kanut was helpless to do anything but watch.
Kanut let his head fall into his hands, a familiar helplessness returning. “You convinced
Hakoda to ignore her for a whole week, Bato.”
“So he would seem mysterious and aloof!” Bato was getting defensive now, not liking his
talents being questioned. “I won’t hear anything from you. It worked.”
Kanut sighed, “We were young and Hakoda’s our friend, which means he’s ours to bully. I
can almost appreciate that. Almost. But this is different. I will not help you drag the children
into this.”
Bato wiggled his eyebrows, “But you’re not gonna stop me?”
Kanut kicked Bato in the leg, and with a disappointed huff, Bato let it be. He wasn’t actually
a bad person, believe it or not, and aside idle teasing, he wasn’t going to force anyone into
anything, least of all invade someone’s privacy. That brand of rudeness was appointed only to
Hakoda and Kanut, lucky as they were. For everyone else, Bato would suffer just observing
from afar.
Kanut was silent for a few moments, as if ensuring that Bato had truly dropped it, before his
lips curled into a small, uncharacteristic smile.
“You know,” he said quietly, “I still have it.”
Bato perked up again curiously, “Still have what?”
“I’d almost forgotten all about it until you brought it up the other day,” Kanut said, before
getting to his feet and quickly flicking through his book collection, fingers carefully landing
on a worn green cover, “See?”
Bato stared at the book Kanut had pulled out, mind tumbling into a familiar flurry of young
hands and snow and confusion and anger and fear and understanding, a deep warmth
pervading it all, warm and safe, together, and he grinned.

“You actually kept it, you old sap.” He breathed, before making grabby hands at him.
Kanut rolled his eyes, either at the nickname or the childish antics, but gave Bato the book
and sat beside him. If someone had said to Bato when he was sixteen that one day Kanut
would feel comfortable enough to flick nostalgically through the pages of this book with him,
snickering at decades-old annotations and pointing immaturely at certain sentences, then Bato
wouldn’t have believed them, but it had been years since Kanut was that scared teenage boy,
and over time, with two friends at his side and an entire crew to fall back on, Kanut had
learned to first accept the way he was, and then learn to appreciate it, to come to love it. It
was part of him, and in Bato’s eyes, that was enough to make it beautiful, because all the
parts of Kanut came together to form just that – Kanut. Sharp, smart, sarcastic Kanut. His
best friend.

Training with Aang had gone worse than usual this morning. The kid had hinged his plans on
defeating the Fire Lord after the comet, and Zuko had arrived with the news that he couldn’t
do that, that he not only had to defeat Ozai sooner, but he had to do it when Ozai was
significantly more powerful than usual. It made Aang desperate, sloppy, always trying to rush
his training to the more explosive moves when he didn’t even have his breathing right yet,
and Zuko still resorted to anger when he was frustrated, or when he was tired, or when he
was... anything, really. He almost appreciated it now, that soft anger that had kept him alive
so long, but he shoved it down before he could ever yell at Aang. Still, the Avatar was more
astute than he let on, and always noticed, grey eyes growing so sad, and Zuko never knew
how to make him feel better.
Zuko suggested they take a breather far sooner than he normally would, the shadow of failure
weighing on him just as much as it weighed on Aang, familiar thoughts curling inside his
skull like whisps of pent-up smoke. Zuko was here to train the Avatar, that was all he could
contribute, and he was doing a shit job of it, and Aang was probably going to Katara to
complain about how slowly his bending was coming on, and Aang wouldn’t mean it as a
criticism of Zuko but Katara would take it as one, and she would tell Sokka and convince him
to let Zuko go, to stop helping him like the other boy insisted on doing every day now
without fail, and with the chief’s two children against him again, what if Hakoda finally got
tired of Zuko?
He wanted to grind the thoughts beneath his heel and leave them in the dirt, because he knew
those things wouldn’t happen, and he supposed that was progress, even if the thoughts still
existed. They didn’t exist as fear, not anymore. They existed instead almost idly, the fears of
a younger boy with a lot more pain in his chest. Even simply knowing there was no truth to
these thoughts was proof that Zuko was not that boy anymore. He wasn’t even the boy he
was a week ago, like a reptile shedding skin, something monstrous, or maybe just something
real.
Tomkin and Nanook had been sat by the cliffs all morning, laughing loudly and messing
about with something that Zuko hadn’t been able to see when he was training Aang, but as he
walked towards them, he realised there was a pile of greenery collected between the two
boys. Vines, mostly, but also large leaves the size of Zuko’s arm, an assortment of cacti that

Zuko didn’t know how the other boys had picked, and flowers he’d never seen before, with
large colourful bulbs made of thin, tendril-like petals that curled into each other, almost like
the flower was alive, and purple flowers with hairs on their stems, and then a flower that
Zuko very much did know, catching his breath in his throat as he wordlessly sat between
Tomkin and Nanook.
Scattered amongst the messy assortment, petals open like an embrace, or tiny stars in their
own right, were lotus flowers.
“What are you doing?” Zuko asked, when no one immediately felt a need to explain the
strange scene.
“We found a bunch of plants growing down the cliffs here, we think it’s because we’re near
to where the waterfall hits,” Nanook explained, grinning, “aren’t they nice?”
They were nice, so much colour and green in the Western Air Temple almost seemed strange,
and it smelled fresh, earthy, like the moment Zuko stepped out of Fong’s base to be met with
the overwhelming smell of the world around him.
“But why did you pick them?” Zuko asked, tone careful, like he was missing something
obvious here, though he was used to his friends being inexplicable, and ridiculous, and
inexplicably ridiculous, and ridiculously inexplicable. It was a talent of theirs.
Tomkin looked up at Zuko with a bright, happy expression, and Zuko didn’t actually care
why they’d picked the plants if such a stupid thing gave Tomkin so much unbridled joy.
“We’re weaving!” He declared proudly, and lifted up something that almost resembled a
small basket, no bigger than a fist, except between the tightly woven vines, Tomkin had
incorporated flowers that poked between the green in bursts of explosive colour. Practically
speaking, the basket would be useless; the flowers would bruise too quickly. But it was
pretty, and Tomkin seemed proud of himself, and Zuko looked to see Nanook creating
something similar.
“Sit down, give it a go.” Nanook said, and Zuko frowned, leaning forward to pick up some
vines. As he did, he noticed that Nanook had a white lotus in his hair, placed far too sturdily
to be there by accident, and Zuko stared a moment.
He remembered girls doing that in the Fire Nation, giggling in the summer heat, fire lilies
tucked behind ears and leaving a faint red glow on their cheek. He'd never seen a boy do it.
He wasn’t entirely sure that was allowed, but he threw a panicked look to the adults nearby,
and saw that Chena was the closest, on the side the flower was facing, and he didn’t even
seem to have noticed.
“You okay over there?” Nanook asked suddenly, eyes narrowed, and Zuko realised he was
still staring, jolting himself out of it and immediately feeling something hot and
uncomfortable crawl through his body.
“Yeah, you seem broodier than normal. And that’s saying something.” Tomkin said, and
Zuko noticed he had a chain of flowers around his neck, connected by the stems somehow.

He flicked another glance to Chena. Still nothing.
“It’s not a big deal,” Zuko said quickly, busying himself by looking at the vines in his hands,
“just training with Aang. It's not going... as well as I hoped.”
He surprised himself as always with how easy honesty was here. He wasn’t just willing to
talk his concerns through with the tribesmen; he wanted to. It made him feel better. This, he
knew, was friendship, and it felt warm and tender, something to be protected, not condemned.
“No?” Nanook asked, frowning and giving Zuko his full attention, “I thought you’d fixed his
whole fear of fire when you went to the masters?”
“It’s not so much fear anymore,” Zuko said, idly twirling a lotus stem between his fingers,
imagining how little effort it would take to produce a spark, what the flower would smell like
when it burned, if the floral scent would prevail over the smoke. He doubted it. “He just
won’t listen to me. He's too busy trying to master firebending as quickly as possible, but it
doesn’t work like that.”
Tomkin cocked his head, thinking. “Well, what about drawing from your own experiences?
Like, what would your firebending teachers do when you didn’t listen to them?”
Zuko jolted at the sudden memory, body going rigid, and he remembered shouting, demands
he couldn’t meet, orders he couldn’t follow, days ending in sweat and tears and the prickling
sting of fresh burns, and that was before he even got to Father, before that knowing gaze of
molten gold would ask him how training had gone, and Zuko always answered honestly. It
was not an easy honesty, not a willing honesty, nothing like what he had here. It was honesty
knowing there was no other option, no escape, prey backed into a corner. There was a certain
cruelty to the question every time, because Ozai knew Zuko’s failures, and would make Zuko
spell them out anyway, like an order to set fire to his own pyre knowing Zuko could do
nothing but obey.
“No,” Zuko said, too harshly, too vehemently, and Tomkin blinked in surprise, but Nanook’s
face dawned in reluctant understanding, “not like that. Not with Aang.”
Not with anyone was left unspoken.
It was quiet for a few moments, Tomkin frowning, confused, and Nanook suddenly far too
interested in the flowers before them, rooting through the pile and pulling back with a
victorious grin. He was holding one of those flowers Zuko had never seen before, the ones
that curled into themselves. This one was an impossible yellow colour, like this tiny thing had
somehow caught a drop of Agni in its petals.
“Hey, Little Tom?” Nanook’s grin grew conspiring in a way Zuko knew from experience not
to trust.
“Yeah, Nan?” Tomkin said, matching his grin, because when those two decided to scheme
together instead of against each other, they suddenly seemed able to read minds.

“Don’t you think these yellow ones go with Zuko’s whole Fire Nation look?” Nanook asked,
feigning innocence as he held the flower a little closer to Zuko, like how shopkeepers
sometimes hold samples of their wares against you to prove how good they’d look. Zuko
flinched back in alarm, but didn’t push Nanook away. He trusted the boys, and that was about
all he’d give them right now when they were grinning at him like that.
“You know what,” Tomkin said, delighted, “I think you’re right!”
Zuko did not know what was happening. All he knew was that not long ago he was teaching
the ancient and sacred art of firebending to the literal Avatar, and now he was doing a poor
job of fending off two surprisingly dogged tribesmen as they tried to put flowers in his hair.
“Stay still!” Nanook hissed when Zuko shoved him back a third time.
“What the fuck are you even-.”
Tomkin had finally had enough, sucking in a loud breath and glaring at Zuko, yellow flowers
now being wielded like a weapon.
“Prince Zuko of the Fire Nation,” he snapped, “so help me, are you going to mope about all
day because of a twelve-year-old or are you going to sit still and let us put flowers in your
hair like a man?”
This was dangerous. This was too much of a grey area, too close to a part of Zuko that was
caged behind so much more than skin and bone. He did not know if this specific thing was
allowed, only that it put things into question, and that certainly wasn’t allowed. A man could
not be questioned on these things. A prince could not be questioned on these things. And
Zuko’s last memory of what happened when you were questioned, his one and only lapse in
judgement when it came to this, was a memory that burned, one more scar to the butchery.
He didn’t want any more scars. What he had now... it was good. Soft and slow and fragile,
but it was good, he was getting better. Any sort of setback to that could break him, could send
him back to the beginning, and the thought of that terrified him. This was dangerous. This
was a needless risk.
But Nanook was grinning, and Tomkin’s eyes were bright, and around them, the sun shone on
a quiet part of the world where children laughed and fathers did not burn their sons. So much
had changed, but there would always be a part of Zuko that belonged to the boy he was that
night in Gaoling, the boy who walked himself to Oro and Renmin if it only meant he might
protect the Water Tribe, protect his friends.
He still wanted to protect them, even down to something they thought was small, effortless.
It wasn’t shame that eased through him down well-worn paths, but fear. He would have time
to be ashamed of this later, but for now, he looked again at Chena, at the rest of the warriors,
then back to Tomkin and Nanook, and sighed.
“One flower,” he grumbled, “that’s all you get.”

The overjoyed smiles made it worth it, Zuko was sure of it. It had to be worth it. Not like last
time.

Katara was making lunch, and because Sokka was the best big brother in the world and
totally not in desperate need of a distraction, he’d decided to help her, something Katara
initially took in her stride after so many weeks complaining that no one ever helped with the
cooking, and now seemed a little distraught by as his sister was forced to come to terms with
the fact that she was, ultimately, a control freak who didn’t actually want Sokka’s help. ‘It
was the principal of it’, and all that. Sokka found the whole thing hilarious, wondering how
long it would take Katara to snap and tell him to go away. He was thinking maybe by the
third moon peach he refused to cut ‘finely enough’, but Katara liked to surprise him with her
stubbornness sometimes. She might even make it to the fourth moon peach.
Narrowing his eyes at his little sister, Sokka lounged back with a sigh loud enough to annoy
Katara, leaning on his elbows and casually slicing through a moon peach. They were having
congee for lunch, and Katara was trying to make the simple meal nicer by incorporating
small chunks of fruit from where she sat opposite Sokka, cross-legged and with a pile of
expertly diced peaches beside her. Hakoda and the rest of the adults were sat nearby, talking
amongst themselves, so Sokka was careful not to be the first to break in this silent face-off
with his sister. Katara was staring at the fruit in Sokka’s hands and his pile of oversized,
mismatched pieces. Painstakingly, Sokka sliced his jawbone knife through the soft fruit
again, messily finishing his third peach. Katara's eye twitched.
It was as he was reaching for a fourth, wiping his sticky hands on his tunic in a way that
made Katara’s face scrunch in disgusted horror, that she finally snapped, the tense challenge
between them shattering with her temper.
“You’re doing it wrong on purpose!” Katara shouted, immediately drawing Hakoda’s
attention.
Sokka grew indignant then, already frustrated by the events of the day and needing an outlet.
“Am not!”
“Oh, you so are!” Katara growled angrily. “I should have known you weren’t actually going
to help me!”
“I am helping! Who cares if the fruit is different sizes? Food is food!” Sokka was on his feet
now, yelling at Katara who was more than willing to match him, getting in his face.
“Yeah, maybe to someone who eats like an animal,” she snapped, “but the rest of us are
civilised.”
“That’s enough, both of you!” Hakoda was suddenly there, looking between the siblings with
a raised eyebrow, and Sokka quickly bit back a response. “What’s going on?”
“I’m helping Katara-.”

“Sokka’s purposely ruining everything-.”
“-and she’s being an absolute princess about it, as usual.”
“Oh, you’d know a lot about royalty, wouldn’t you?”
“The fuck’s that supposed to mean?”
“Hey!” Hakoda raised his voice a little to be heard over the vicious back-and-forth. Sokka
could see Tulok smiling to Chena about something as the other warriors watched, and that
certainly didn’t do anything for Sokka’s growing anger.
“Katara, we all appreciate how much work you put into the cooking, but it’s not bad to accept
help every now and then, even if that help is different to how you normally do things,”
Hakoda said, in his calm voice that always seemed to fix everything. At least when they were
together to hear it. “And Sokka,” Hakoda raised a trying-not-to-be-amused eyebrow there,
“it’s nice that you’re helping your sister, but this is her area of expertise. It’s respectful to

Sokka and Katara, both feeling appropriately berated, threw a bashful look to each other.
Sokka raised a shoulder in a small shrug. Katara rolled her eyes, but her lips pulled up a little,
and just like that, Sokka knew they’d moved on from what happened, and he nudged her as

needling his sister on purpose before – but stopped when Hakoda grabbed his arm.
“Dad?”
“Is everything okay, son?” Hakoda asked, frowning, looking a little too close at Sokka and
making him squirm. Spirits, Sokka was glad Bato had disappeared. The other man would be

Back in Sokka’s Pre-Suki days, he saw Chena as the perfect ideal for a warrior, which

Kanut had been watching. He'd been watching since Zuko and Zi Se fell out, since Zuko went

wanted to add to that, but now, watching each change in Zuko as he slowly opened the book,
he wished he’d said something sooner.
Kanut knew a lot about shame, knew the language of it, how it felt to trace those letters with
young hands, knew still how they felt beneath the callouses of older, wiser hands. Kanut also
knew a lot about Zuko. He knew that almost all of the prince’s emotions boiled down to the
same two things; anger and shame. It was a hereditary weight, carried so dutifully for so long
that the body disfigured itself around it, unable to walk without the load. There needed to be
healing, recovery, time. These were things no one had given Zuko for years, but he was with
the Water Tribe now, and they cared about him. Here, he could take what he needed.
And Kanut was so proud of him, because he could see Zuko improving. When it came to

he even thought it was him, and he was it, and it had festered at the hands of his father in a

He hoped not, for Zuko’s sake.
Because Kanut had read this book a dozen times, and he knew the Fire Nation were not

Zuko imagined he was watching a play. Not a feverish nightmare in which he stood on a
stage before an audience, but simply an idle daydream, nothing harmful about it, nothing
dangerous. In the dream, he got to be a part of the crowd, faceless, so painfully dull and
normal and mundane that his face blended into a hundred others to become a collective, not
an individual.
He slipped deeper inside the Western Air Temple after his conversation with Kanut and Bato,
feigning going to his room where every day now Sokka had brought him food, but instead,
Zuko travelled deeper, navigating corridors he was learning to recognise until he walked
outside to a clearing hidden in the alcoves of the cliff. Appa was here, taking advantage of the
shade and the quiet, never too far from Aang but allowing himself some well-earned peace.
The creature grumbled in greeting to Zuko, but didn’t even lift his head, non-plussed by his
arrival, and it soothed something that had been racing inside Zuko ever since Tomkin had
tucked a flower into his hair, ever since he held a green book in his hands that spoke of
dishonour.
It wasn’t the topic itself that scared Zuko, not anymore, and that’s what unsettled him the
most. He was terrified, because he had looked at this book, realised what it meant that Kanut
and Bato had such a thing, discussed such a thing so casually, and Zuko looked at the facts.
Fact; not everywhere was like the Fire Nation. Fact; not every father was like his father. Fact;
this was okay amongst the Water Tribe. Fact; Ozai had been wrong about everything else.
That was the part that terrified Zuko, because he took all of those facts, and he’d looked at
that book in his hands, remembered the pain in his leg from the scar he got when he was
eleven, remembered his newest scar on the very same leg given to him by Fong, and with the

context of every other awful thing that had happened to him since he was that confused
eleven-year-old boy, the only thought he could conjure was; is this truly such a bad thing?
Zuko had seen bad now, had seen evil, and a boy who kissed another boy in the fire lily fields
couldn’t match it.
The moment he let the thoughts sit on the surface of his mind, Zuko was engulfed by such a
great wave of shame, of disgust at himself, that it was all he could do to shove the book back
to Kanut before Zuko bolted, needing to be alone.
Zuko imagined he was watching a play. He saw a boy on a stage with two swords in his
hands, the set pushed messily together into a mimicry of a library, and the boy dropped one of
his swords suddenly, the metal thudding soundlessly to the floor. Zuko knew every line, every
cue. He had the ending memorised. He knew someone was about to die. He knew it would be
horrible and bloody and that killing was wrong. He knew also that this particular killing had
been right. There never was a more bloodstained word than justice.
Next act. The boy stood with someone his own age, wearing Fire Nation armour that clanged
with his inexperience, the only other teenager on the ship. A second killing, though really his
was the first, delivered by a different blade but the same hands. This was wrong. This was
also right. This was war. Zuko remembered confessions uttered in the heat of fever. You
always thought it was anger that would damn you, that patronymic fury that snarls in your
chest. It is not. Your fatal flaw has always been shame.
Which brought the next act and eyes like honey and the words redemption comes with the
price of regret but you don’t regret and you’re ashamed of me and I burned for you and I'm
sorry and I'm sorry and I'm sorry.
This was the part he needed to remember, needed to watch over and over again until he
finally stopped trying to question it. Zuko was a fragmented pattern of bad things forced
together to make something human, a series of mistakes that started with his father’s fist and
ended with a blade separated from its other half. He wanted to think this was like that, that
this part of him was something he could learn to forgive like everything else. Ozai's abuse,
the Agni Kai, Lee’s death, General Fong – these were all things Zuko had misunderstood, all
things he was having to learn all over again, placing blame on the right people, knowing that
not everything was his fault, not every awful thing had been deserved. But there was always a
dark secret to each of them. For all of his shame, these were also things Zuko regretted, and
that created more shame, but it also gave him a propensity for healing. There was a part of
Zuko that, if he could, would go back to every fumble in front of Ozai and correct himself,
would sit silently in that war meeting, would do whatever it took to stop Tulok from taking
Lee’s life, would let Fong live. Some regrets would right wrongs, others would wrong rights,
each a rewrite of the original script to create a new story where Zuko was different at the cost
of some other sacrifice. In this story, he got to be the perfect son at the expense of the rest of
the world.
That was the shame of his regret, and it ate at him, but it was almost timid against the other
shame. This shame. Mizu with his crooked grin. Lee with his flushed cheeks. Zuko had been
a curse to both of them, and while he regretted aspects of Lee, this was one angle he could

not bring himself to regret. If he could rewrite the script, he would still let himself stare. If he
was back in those fire lily fields, he would do it all over again.
Can you heal from something if you can’t even regret it? Do you deserve to?
With Zi Se, Zuko learnt to look at his shame and find its source instead of immediately
pushing it down. Avoidance was the easy option. Automatically assuming everything was his
fault, that enough self-hatred might purge this latest wrong, was the easy option. But for this,
Zuko wasn’t willing to budge. He couldn’t regret it, and it made him sick. He made himself
sick. Sick that he kept indulging in the first place. Sick that, when he did, he wasn’t even
sorry. He just mumbled the words around numb lips like a recitation. I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm
sorry.
It never changed anything.
It felt like Zuko’s world had ended over and over again for years. Each awful thing that
happened created a new world, a new stage, a new Zuko standing front and centre, but it was
a lie, wasn’t it? How many times can one actor play a new role? How many times can you
piece yourself back together until all of the original pieces are gone? How many times can
you look at debris and call it by another name? How long until it’s all just dust, and you can’t
cover it? What do you do then? How do you live with yourself?
The answer: you don’t.
You become child of the wreckage, creature of the carcass, blood still dripping from your
maw. It will never dry.
This was all he had.
This was all he knew.
This was all he knew.
Teaching of the homeland. Lessons of the father.
“Why do we have to make things so complicated?” Zuko whispered, turning to Appa’s big
brown eyes that had been watching him for a while now. Zuko was sat close to the creature,
staring off at the sandy cliffs around him, and Appa had allowed him silence while he
thought.
“Of all the evil in the world...” Zuko trailed off, not brave enough to voice the words. Of all
the evil in the world, and we chose this. It was wrong, and Zuko wasn’t blind enough to
Ozai’s whims to deny it was wrong anymore, and he knew the Water Tribe thought it was
wrong, thought it was barbaric, but this was one fight Zuko wouldn’t have. He needed, for
once, to have been right about something, even if that something was evil. The thought of
Mizu, of what might have happened to him, would tear him apart otherwise. The thought of
another agony Zuko suffered undeservingly and at such a young age would buckle him. This
time, he might not be able to get back up. He needed this, in a cruel way. He needed a
destruction he recognised.

“Did you purposely sit out here to make my life difficult?” Kanut asked, and Zuko jumped so
hard he was certain his heart had leapt into his mouth for a second there, whirling around to
see the healer stood in the entrance to the temple, a little sweaty, like he’d been trawling the
corridors for a while now looking for Zuko. Shit, Zuko thought, with the distinct sinking
feeling of someone who had been caught.
“I wanted somewhere quiet,” Zuko admitted, turning his back on Kanut to return his glare to
the cliffs. He listened as Kanut approached, sitting to Zuko’s side, a safe distance between
them. Appa continued to watch, uninterested.
It was silent between them for a bit. Zuko had assumed Kanut was out here to find out why
he was skipping lunch. There was no way Kanut could actually know what Zuko was
thinking, what had rattled him so much when he saw that book, and Zuko viciously shoved
down any paranoia that tried to convince him of the contrary. Kanut was scarily observant
when it came to Zuko, but he wasn’t a mind reader, and this was one secret Zuko kept so
close it was seared into his skin.
Finally, Kanut took a deep breath, like he was preparing for something difficult. Neither
looked at each other, always at a quiet understanding, and that didn’t change when Kanut
began to talk, even if Zuko immediately tensed at his words.
“I’m going to say some things,” Kanut spoke quietly but purposefully, “and I need you to just
listen for a bit. I'm not very good at this whole talking crap, but it needs to be said. So just.
Don’t be a smartass for a bit and let me get through this, okay?”
Zuko’s hands clenched into fists, anxiety thrumming through his blood, but he nodded,
“Okay.”
“When I was about your age,” Kanut said, and Zuko was immediately bowled over by the
fact that Kanut was about to open up about something entirely willingly, but he stuck to his
agreement to keep quiet, listening close, “I watched all the other kids in the village change.
Suddenly, the world stopped and started with who liked who, and I was so smug about it for a
long time, thought I was better than all of them because I didn’t like anyone, but as time went
on,” Kanut frowned here, fists clenching like Zuko’s had, “it got lonely. I had Hakoda and
Bato, but they could always have others in other ways, and I just... couldn’t. It was like the
way I loved was wrong, and I hated myself. I was embarrassed and ashamed and angry and I
hated myself.”
Zuko held his breath, because this wasn’t about him missing lunch. This was about the book,
and for a moment, blind panic took over him, mind racing to try and figure out what he’d
done to give himself away to Kanut, but he pushed that terror aside for later, because he’d
latched onto Kanut’s words and couldn’t let go. It was like the way I loved was wrong. Every
single muscle in Zuko’s body was rigid, vulnerable, everything he’d been so scared of only a
few moments ago, but he couldn’t move, couldn’t save himself. He was completely at the
mercy of Kanut’s words.
“At that point, I read mostly academic things,” Kanut continued, a nostalgic mist in his gaze,
staring without seeing, “medical books, when Kanna started teaching me. Shit like that. But I
started to pick up other books. Storybooks. No matter what I read, I couldn’t find anything.”

Zuko knew he’d agreed to listen, but he couldn’t help the timid question from leaving his
mouth. “What were you looking for?”
Kanut exhaled, a sad sound, but an old sadness, a memory more than an emotion.
"I have read about love a thousand times over in a thousand different stories,” he said
carefully, “and it never looks like me.”
It gutted Zuko. He thought of plays and childhood and how he put himself in the shoes of the
villain or the protagonist and recreated the action scenes with Azula and recited his favourite
lines while he got dressed but never, ever saw himself as the lover. This soft, gentle given that
so many strived for, this beautiful thing a thousand different playwrights spoke of, and it was
never written for Zuko, because Zuko’s love was wrong, was smaller, was lesser.
“And seeing that, or rather not seeing it, really hurt, and I didn’t think to blame anyone else
but me, so all of that confusion and shame and hate – I internalised it, because that’s how it
was in my family. You felt things, and you let them rot you from the inside.” Kanut said, and
Zuko didn’t know what to do, didn’t even know how to look at this man that he respected so
much, because how could he care about Kanut when he suddenly looked just like him?
They'd always been similar, always had an understanding, but Kanut’s inability to voice such
things had made it easy to simply avoid acknowledging it altogether.
But sat here, they were two sides of one pai sho tile, a white lotus cracked and faded but still
there, after everything, and Zuko knew he couldn’t afford another freefall, knew this was one
fight he wouldn’t have, but he found himself hanging desperately onto Kanut’s words,
waiting for him to just tell him what to do.
Kanut looked directly at Zuko then, a sudden intensity to his stare. “I found one book, one
book, that spoke about a love I recognised, and it’s stupid because the whole point of that
damn book is to talk about that shit, but I just... I just held it and everything went still.
Because it meant I wasn’t alone. It meant I wasn’t broken.” Kanut smiled a little, softly, selfdeprecatingly. “That’s the one me and Bato were looking at. Asshole likes to tease me about
it now just because he found it all so easy, back in the day.”
Zuko watched. Kanut's smile faded back to something serious. “It doesn’t have to be easy,”
Kanut said, “but everyone deserves to know that they’re not alone. Not about this. Not ever.
There's not a single person out there who can care about someone the same way twice. The
stupidest thing humanity ever did was try to make sense of something like love, to put it into
neat little boxes and label anyone who didn’t fit as other.” Kanut sighed, shaking his head,
“It’s at once this great, all-encompassing thing that defines us, and also the most simple thing
in the world. You can love friends, or pets, or a girl, or a boy, and you can love each one in
crazy, contradicting ways, and you will still never be able to love in a way that is scarier than
what the world will throw at you, so why bother being scared of it?”
Zuko thought of Mizu and then Ozai, thought of fire lilies and then fire, the smell of
cinnamon and then smoke, soft lips and burnt skin. The world had thrown fire at Zuko and he
had convinced himself that Mizu was the scariest part of it. What would life be if he wasn’t
terrified of this part of himself? He imagined it would be terrifying in its own right, but no
more than normal. He imagined a freedom so immense it was dizzying, liberating.

He squeezed his eyes shut, forcing the thoughts away. He was walking into another fight,
finding a rock to push uphill for eternity, and he couldn’t do it, not with everything else going
on.
“Why are you telling me all this?” Zuko forced out through grit teeth.
Kanut had the nerve to shrug, loose-limbed and casual like he hadn’t just shoved Zuko’s
world off its axis.
“Dunno,” he said, and now he was definitely smirking at Zuko, “needed to vent. You're a
fantastic listener.”
Zuko contemplated telling Kanut to eat shit, but that would be an admission that Kanut’s
words resonated with him. He had to believe that this was the truth, that the usually stonefaced healer was simply feeling chatty today. It was an easy enough excuse to fall back on,
even if Zuko didn’t believe it, and he forced some of the tension from his muscles.
“Well,” he grumbled, “you’re a lot better at this talking crap than you said you were. Why
don’t you do it more?”
Turn it around, Zuko thought, keep the attention off yourself.
“Honestly?” Kanut asked, suddenly growing serious, and Zuko blanked, curiosity and
concern pushing to the front of his mind. He nodded, leaning in a little when Kanut lowered
his voice; “I am terrified of becoming like Bato.”
Zuko blinked, staring at the healer, before shoving the man so hard he fell into the dirt. Kanut
laughed in surprise, and his laughter only followed Zuko as he scrambled to his feet and
stomped inside the temple.
He needed to think.

Naturally, the staff of an airship was significantly lacking in numbers compared to that of a
palace, and meant certain luxuries were sacrificed. One such sacrifice was that of Azula’s
personal servants. She usually had three women who tended to her, one to do her hair, one to
do her clothes and armour, one to do her makeup, each trained to the upmost standards in
each compartment, not a stray hair or a buckle left loose or a smudge out of place, but on the
airship, it was only one woman, the woman who usually did Azula’s makeup. Yuna, of
course, was an adept servant – they didn’t let just anyone serve the blood of Agni – but today,
she was doing Azula’s hair wrong.
“Sharpen it,” Azula ordered, staring at her reflection in the mirror. Everything else was
perfect. Everything else was perfect except this, her hairstyle too soft around the edges. Yuna
hadn’t done anything differently today – Azula knew, because she watched, always watched
those hands coming too close to her face, moving too quickly in her blind spots – but
something just wasn’t right.
She looked too soft around the edges, and with the way she was filling into herself more
lately, Azula almost looked like...

Suddenly, Yuna was too close.
“Get out,” Azula growled, shoving the woman’s hands away. “I’ll do it myself if you insist on
being incompetent.”
Yuna had been Azula’s servant for years. She didn’t meet her eye, she didn’t say anything,
she simply did as she was told, and left Azula alone.
The silence of solitude always seemed so much heavier than the sort of silence that settled in
larger spaces. The silence of sitting at Father’s side, for instance, had a different weight to it.
There was tension there, a dozen invisible threads holding everyone in place like one of
Zuzu’s ridiculous plays. This silence here though, between Azula and her reflection, was
heavy, as if waiting for something.
Azula didn’t care, never gave it enough time to reveal itself to her. She saw her reflection
without seeing, ignoring the soft edges, the familiar eyes.
She fixed her hair, and just like that, Azula was perfect. It wasn’t a difficult standard to
maintain and had only gotten more natural with time. Time and practise and her brother’s
instance of making it easy for her. Her weak, foolish brother.
Azula cursed quietly. She was not supposed to think about him.
Trust is for fools, Father had always said, and Zuko was the biggest fool of all of them. Fools
make fools and Azula would not be made a fool of. His pretty promises were fickle, childish
things. Apologies on a beach, blue fire in hands dancing dangerously close to touching, a
softness, an openness that Azula knew Zuko couldn’t have faked for the life of him.
He said they could be better. He said he was sorry for leaving her. He said they didn’t have to
be terrible.
He said a lot of things, and then, Zuko had done what Zuko did best.
Zuko left.
Azula scoffed. Her brother would pay for his treachery towards the Fire Nation, towards their
father, towards her. She'd make sure of it. She was better than him, after all.
Azula smoothed down the cuff at her left wrist, securing the button there for the third time
since dressing, and then caught herself in the motion of it, pulling her hand away before it
became a nervous habit. Azula did not have nervous habits. Azula was not nervous.
She turned her back on the mirror.
Perfect.

“So, it’s decided then.”

The mood was sombre in the strategy room, all of the adults gathered around the spread of
papers and maps Hakoda had accumulated in his time at the Air Temple, countless nights
tiring over a plan, even if it was just the barebones of one. Anything that meant the Water
Tribe didn’t have to rely entirely on whatever General Iroh had thought up.
“It’s the best we can get with the information we have,” Bato said honestly, blue eyes
focussed on Hakoda like he knew the doubt he felt crawling beneath his skin.
Kanut shrugged. “I’ll be glad of it. This place is nice and all but we’ve spent too long here.
Everyone's getting restless, even the kids.”
“And the comet’s getting closer,” Chena grumbled, arms crossed. “We have two months left.
We need to reunite with the other men.”
Hakoda nodded. He knew all this, he’d arranged all this, scheming alone and with Bato and
oftentimes with Sokka, going over their lists again and again. They knew what the Fire Lord
was planning, they knew who to target, but Iroh understood Fire Nation military movements,
had insight on his brother that even Zuko lacked, and besides, Kanut and Chena were right.
They'd spent more time at the Air Temple than they intended to and leaving the rest of their
tribe in the camp of a Fire Nation General – traitor or not – left everyone feeling
uncomfortable. Restless.
In two day's time, they would have been here for exactly two weeks. That was the day they
intended to leave. The Ullaakut was docked a short walk away from the temple and had more
than enough room for everyone, including Chit Sang’s group who had, tentatively, agreed to
come with them to the Earth Kingdom.
From the directions Iroh had given them, Hakoda and Tulok had concurred that they were
looking at a week at sea, and that was with the wind on their side. Time had finally caught up
to them, and with it, the war.
Stress, Hakoda could handle. Doubt was par for the course of being chief. Fear, too, was an
emotion he knew intimately.
But this reprieve at the Western Air Temple was something Hakoda hadn’t known since
joining the war effort. Even their stop at the South Pole couldn’t match the dread Hakoda felt
now, because it was too brief, only a handful of days of comfort before the men were off
again. This dread came from security, safety, a routine of getting up and talking with his men
and eating his daughter’s cooking and watching the bending. There was no blood here and
everyone, Hakoda included, had become complacent.
They had two days to pack up. Then, the war returned to the Southern Water Tribe warriors.

The sun stood fitfully behind whisps of clouds, shimmering through the humidity that hung
in the air since the latest showers, and the inhabitants of the temple stood with it, restless as
the day around them. The air was thick and warm and smelled earthy; there would be rain
again soon. Potentially before they left.

Because that was what had everyone so on edge. The plan had been laid out. Their break at
the Western Air Temple was over. They had two days.
Sokka was just as restless as everyone else. They'd all known they were leaving sooner or
later but giving a definitive deadline to it made everything seem so much more real, so much
closer. For the first time since they left the South Pole, Team Avatar had a steady adult
influence watching over things, stable enough to relax into. For Sokka, it was the first time
since Hakoda and the other warriors left. He'd had Gran-Gran, sure, but he’d insisted on
shouldering the detritus of his father’s responsibilities alone, isolating himself because he was
a warrior and the last man in the village. He could hardly remember what it felt like to just
breathe, to know his sister’s safety and now the safety of Aang and Toph wasn’t in his young,
shaky hands.
But Sokka was also a realist, possibly bordering on pessimist, and he’d known this was
temporary. He hadn’t let himself become too comfortable, because that was a luxury they
were never offered. It was the burden of being the Avatar’s companion, and the awareness of
that was the burden of the plan guy.
So Sokka was restless, and a little bummed-out, but he was handling it fine, reluctantly
resigned to moving on from comfort once again. Admittedly, he had a squirming, panicked
flutter of dread sitting in his stomach like it owned the place, but that was a feeling he was
more than familiar with, a feeling he woke with and travelled with and slept with every day
with Team Avatar, a feeling that had shadowed him ever since he was a boy expecting each
day to be the day a Fire Nation cruiser appeared on the skyline, here to raid their village just
once more. It was never the last time. He knew that. He didn’t care how cynical the thought
was, and he had been right. The raid that took his mother was supposed to be the last one, and
then there was Zuko.
Zuko, who was currently in one of the temple’s clearings, training alone with his sword,
swishing it about and twisting on nimble feet, because of course Zuko could use a sword.
Why wouldn’t he be able to? Sokka wasn’t sure whether to be in awe of the other boy or kick
him.
For a moment, Sokka let himself watch. His mind buzzed with questions. Zuko wielded a
curved, single-edged sword, but Sokka knew all too well that it came as a pair, the second
still in his father’s possession. Could Zuko really wield both? He knew the rumours of the
Blue Spirit being a master of the dual blades, but Sokka’s training with Piandao had been
thorough; he knew how difficult that would be. Even having enough dominance in both
hands to hold the blades firmly would prove a challenge, let alone learning to move both, to
focus on both at once. Sokka had taken to swords; Piandao had been impressed with him and
he was improving every day, but he knew dual blades were one thing he would never be able
to handle. He was too clumsy, for one, and couldn’t pinpoint his focus like that. But Zuko
could, and not at a novice level either. He was good. It was clear in the fluidity of his
motions, the way he moved complimenting every swipe of the blade, kicking up dust in the
clearing, an intense focus to his burning gaze, and that was with his body still clearly causing
him pain when he twisted certain ways or too harshly, if the hissed winces he intermittently
let slip were anything to go by. Kanut was going to be furious if he saw.

And of course, there was the unfamiliarity of only using one blade of two.
If Zuko had used both blades in the Boiling Rock, how much quicker would Fong have died?
Would it have even been a fair fight?
Sokka shuddered, that restless unease flickering in his stomach, because at no point had it left
his mind that Zuko was a threat. Zuko, royal firebender and master of the dual blades, a boy
so much stronger than Sokka who looked four months of horror in the eye and stabbed it
between the ribs, enough of him still alive to tell the story. Zuko, violent and sharp in his
actions even now, training alone at the Western Air Temple, the black fabric of his shirt

Sokka knew what Zuko was. Sokka knew what he had done. It didn’t scare him anymore.
Instead, Sokka ate with the other boy, and reluctantly found him hilarious, and found himself

As he watched Zuko training, Sokka’s mind buzzed with questions, and only one prevailed.
“Is Zuko okay?” Sokka asked, nodding at the firebender in question. “He seems pretty

Tomkin and Nanook looked over to their friend from where the three of them were sat

The moment they stepped into the woodland, Zuko shifted. It was a subtle change. The prince
already moved with such an infuriating elegance, even when injured, pushing through any
pain and still holding his head up, shoulders back. Regal. But as they left the temple behind,
Zuko’s elegance became... smoother. Each step purposeful, moving with the woodland and
not breaking a single twig underfoot, his good ear always slightly turned towards the thickest
parts of the brush, and he walked in front of Sokka. At first, Sokka thought it was an
arrogance thing, the prince thinking he could hunt better than someone raised in the South
Pole, because of course he’d think that; he was Fire Nation. But after some time passed in
silence with just the sound of the trees around them, Sokka noticed that Zuko’s movements
seemed to be almost covering Sokka’s. He wasn’t as broad as Sokka, but he had a control of

himself that was mesmerising to watch, and he made it so his body was always shielding
Sokka whenever a noise crackled through the woodland.

know – ought to have made Sokka grow indignant, or embarrassed that the prince clearly

Sokka and Zuko didn’t hate each other anymore. They had an agreement at mealtimes, and

him that if it collapsed, not even an earthbender would be able to sense his body from the
