pictured the sound of it, how it would feel as the dirt filled his throat and lungs until he
wasn’t even allowed the dignity of choking on it. He escaped. He knew he had. But for a
moment, he hadn’t. He was right back there, and the earth was crumbling around him.
“The rocks are all pretty small, there’s just a lot of them,” Sokka said suddenly. “Zuko, if you
hit it with enough fire power, I think we should be able to smash through.”
He turned to Zuko expectantly, that same calm from earlier in his blue gaze, and Zuko
blinked, looking again at the rubble. Sokka was right; the debris was mostly lightweight,
stacked together in a colossal pile. Zuko could get through.
He nodded once and handed Zi Se to Nanook. The little boy looked like he wanted to argue,
but went willingly, and Zuko stepped forward.
It was a basic firebending kata, one that prioritised sheer force over control. Force and control
had always been elements Zuko was stronger in, and where once he would have sought the
familiar rage inside him to power such a direct hit, he instead pulled on the panic he was
feeling, the desire to protect his friends, the swirl of emotions living inside him and creating
Zuko.
Blue fire shot from his hands and slammed into the rubble hard enough to shake the corridor.
Immediately, Zuko turned his back to the explosion, feeling stray rocks smack against him in
ways that would leave bruises if they ever got out of this. Still, Zuko tried to make himself as
broad as possible, focusing on Zi Se but trying to take the brunt of the force for all of them.

When the dust settled, there was sunlight at the end of the corridor, and Sokka whooped
victoriously, Tomkin clapping a hand to Zuko’s shoulder and Nanook carefully handing Zi Se
back to him.
“Never thought I'd be so grateful for firebending,” Tomkin said, making a sound like he was
dragging every ounce of air from his lungs just to sigh dramatically in relief right by Zuko’s
ear.
But Zuko didn’t care, still blinking at the scattered rocks in surprise.
He did it.
There was something so strangely cathartic about that, about being the one to get them out. In
Fong’s base, he’d kept him and Zi Se alive, but he gave up actively trying to escape after only
a few weeks. The only end to his imprisonment had been a seemingly inevitable death. It had
played out in his mind a hundred times. Zi Se would go first, and with him, Zuko’s last shred
of will. After that, it would be easy. Fong would take him, or perhaps Chan, or even Spider.
Zuko would stop fighting. He would die quietly, pathetically, without preamble or rites or
even anything to alert anyone that he had passed. It would not move the earth or change the
tides. One moment he would be there, a dead-live thing. And the next he would be gone,
dead entirely.
Tovah, cold and forceful in a way he’d needed at a time when he shrunk away from soft
things, was what got them out. Luck and Tovah, and they were pulled from the earth almost
unwillingly. Zuko would never forgive himself for that; he’d given up on himself, he’d given
up on Zi Se. But this here, this quick explosion and burst of sunlight, was warming.
He did it. He got them out.
“Come on!” Nanook shouted, and they were running again, bursting out into the blinding day
to be met with chaos. The sudden swell of noise hit Zuko like a downpour, shouts and
explosions and more and more of the temple falling away; soon there would be nothing left.
But over the noise and the darting bodies, Zuko’s eyes locked on Fire Nation reds and four
stationed airships.
He froze in the entrance to the temple, staring out at the battle before him. The Water Tribe
seemed evenly matched with the soldiers that had ambushed them, and no one had gone
down yet, not even the kids who were putting up a fight of their own in a barrage of earth,
water and air. The Fire Nation had found the Avatar, or they’d followed Zuko, or something
had gone wrong – he didn’t know. All he knew, like always, was that trouble had found him,
and with each flash of fire that came too close to a tribesmen’s skin, Zuko knew he had to
fight.
It wasn’t a shadow of instincts anymore. What he’d felt for Sokka’s grazed knee paled in
comparison to this. This had teeth and claws that Zuko had never had the privilege of dulling,
sinking deep into the flesh of him where the blood poured heaviest, and he heaved with it,
snarled with it.

Tulok and Kanut stood separate from the fight, Tulok’s chest rising and falling rapidly like he
was just having a moment to collect himself, and Zuko knew Kanut stayed out of combat. He
was looking directly at Zuko, a warning in his eyes, but Zuko instead looked over to Tulok,
and made a decision.
“Tulok!” he shouted to be heard over the fighting, leaping over tattered bedrolls and sprinting
over to the startled tribesman. “Take Zi Se. I can help the others. Keep him safe.”
“What? But-!” Zuko was already handing Zi Se over, the little boy’s alarm smothering itself
when amber eyes met gold. Tulok also looked like he wanted to argue, but held his tongue
and held Zi Se in turn.
“I always come back, remember?” Zuko said quietly, pressing his forehead to Zi Se’s. For a
moment, there was no battle. It was just them two and a cacophony muffled by some
invisible force that left nothingness and the warmth of Zi Se’s skin on his, the subtle pulse
jumping against him, the smell of moon peaches that Katara insisted on indulging the kid
with.
Zi Se nodded against Zuko, swallowing a sob. “Okay.”
Zuko dragged his burning stare to Tulok and was met with only acceptance.
“I’ll protect him with my life.” He spoke like he knew the weight of that promise. “I'll keep
him safe.”
No, you won’t, Zuko wanted to growl, not like I can.
“I trust you,” he said instead, against every screaming shadow that begged him not to.
And then Zuko turned, and the fight fell around him in stunning clarity, a mess of every
element and cries of determination and pain and blades clanging together, and amongst all
that movement, Zuko saw a figure stood completely still, watching him with eyes the same
gold as his and fire the same blue as his and blood the same tormented as his.
He stared back at her, and it must have only lasted a moment for the shock to fizzle out and
the immediate danger to settle in, but it dragged on like three years bitten out of their time
together.
Azula.
Azula, and there was a question on the tip of his tongue.
Azula.
Good or bad?
____
Azula had made a slight miscalculation on Ember Island. Zuko had returned home entirely
passive. He did not care to challenge Azula both in conversation and for her rightful spot as

heir to the throne. He was stepping back, and under that new light, they were able to find the
barebones of common ground, far-fetched as it might have seemed to Azula a few months
ago. She knew her brother as young and foolishly gentle, and then she knew him banished,
and then he was a death sentence sealed in an Earth Kingdom general’s correspondence.
But for those few days he was home after she picked him up from the Boiling Rock, it was
something new. Something not unlike their brittle alliance of childhood but not entirely like it
either. It had made Azula think, naively, that perhaps her brother could be useful to her after
all. He was strong-willed and skilled in combat, and he was now the second wielder of the
blue flame in their generation, but most of all, he cared for Azula. He did not see a monster;
he saw his little sister. He looked at her with a rawness so intense it was frustrating, because
he should fear her; this stupid trust of his was what kept getting him into trouble to begin
with. But that was just Zuko. It always had been. No one in the world had figured out how to
stamp it out, not even Father. Zuko cared about her and that was more useful than any of his
other skills. He could have been a strong ally that was hers, not Father’s, and she could have
used him while simultaneously keeping an eye on him, just so the idiot didn’t get himself
dragged from home again where he couldn’t be wielded.
So, she’d tried something new. Real truths scattered into their conversations, moments of
vulnerability she’d never allowed anyone else, scraps of that gentleness Zuko had always
clung to, and for a moment on a beach, he held them softly. He said he was sorry. He cared
about her even now, at the end of it all.
Here was her miscalculation, because Azula had believed him.
She didn’t think he lied simply because he wasn’t smart enough to trick Azula, but he had
changed his priorities so easily. It was like Mother all over again, because as natural as it was
to dismiss that woman altogether, Azula knew her mother had cared for her; in fact the
knowledge of that gave Azula some sick satisfaction. She just hadn’t cared enough.
Azula’s skin itched where it brushed her sleeve and she held a familiar golden gaze over the
battle. She had underestimated Zuko once in her entire life and had paid for it. Now, he was
here with the Avatar. He'd said he couldn’t allow Father’s attack, and naturally, Azula
assumed he was leaving to warn the Earth Kingdom, but it seemed her brother had a bigger
treachery in mind.
Had Father known? Azula knew Zuko had gone to the throne room to face their father one
last time; had he said something then? Why hadn’t Father warned her?
She knew why.
Azula had not stopped Zuko that night.
Father found out.
Azula must remain perfect. She was not allowed miscalculations. She would not make the
same mistake twice.

Her face twisted into a snarling smile, and she called fire to her hands in a familiar rush of
burning blue.
“Hello, brother,” she said, smile becoming all teeth as she walked forwards, her soldiers
automatically turning their own fights away to let her pass. Azula picked her way through the
debris easily, catching the wide blue eyes of the waterbending girl who was currently making
quick work of some of Azula’s best soldiers. For a moment, Azula thought the peasant might
attack her, but the Fire Nation soldiers pushed back and, with one desperately understanding
look Zuko’s way, the waterbender returned to her own fight.
What could the Water Tribe possibly understand about any of this? Azula sneered as her
brother settled into a loose defensive stance, eyes narrowed on her. He would lose this fight,
but he knew that, so what was his plan here?
Of course, her brother had never been known for his plans. Azula had always teased that it
would be the death of him. She hadn’t imagined it would be at her own hands like this.
“What are you doing here?” Zuko asked dumbly.
Azula rolled her eyes. “Do you think the war stopped just because you ran away? Father still
wants the Avatar, and I will be the one to capture him.”
Something pained flickered in Zuko’s eyes, like he saw a familiarity in Azula, and briefly,
she wondered where she misspoke. Her tone had been level, perhaps a little determined near
the end, but not enough for her oblivious brother to notice, right? Had it been determination,
or was she fooling herself to hide that there was a note of desperation here? She had to
capture the Avatar. She needed a victory so that Father might ignore her small failure.
If it weren’t for Zuko, she wouldn’t even have to worry about this. Years of perfection
wobbling, and for what? For him?
Azula wanted him to burn.

“You’re not going to say anything?” the smiling girl pouted.

quickly so we can go home.”
The smiling girl’s pout deepened a moment, before she clapped her hands together, grinning

Chena whipped his machete around when he sensed movement, the girl just jumping back

Zuko was cantankerous enough on his own, but now, there was two of them.

hastily applied war paint smeared onto his father’s sleeve. He thought about the men growing
smaller in the distance until the icy horizon stole them from his view. He thought about two
long years and a boy’s inception in the wake of his father’s absence. Sokka had relaxed at the
Western Air Temple, had thought he could finally share some of the responsibility that had
shaped him to the very skeleton, but it wasn’t meant to be, and this time, he wasn’t angry. He
was just... sad, and scared, and brave enough to let these things show when he hugged his
father.
Hakoda held him so tightly, like he knew he wasn’t fragile, and Sokka melted into the
embrace, reminding himself against the burning sensation in his eyes that this wasn’t the end.
There would be more time, more hugs. They would be okay.
“I’m so proud of you, son,” Hakoda whispered.
Sokka sniffed. “Thanks, Dad.”

Zuko looked away as the chief said goodbye to his children, quietly checking on Zi Se
instead. He knew it wasn’t his place to intervene, and even looking at the familiarity with
which the family was torn apart was difficult.

Tomkin, however, didn’t seem to have any such reservations, and was speaking before
Hakoda had even properly released Sokka.
“Wait, who’s going with who?” he said suddenly.
Katara frowned, teary eyes blinking in confusion. “Aren’t we keeping the same groups?”
“Exactly,” Tomkin said. “I’m not entirely sure which group me and Nanook are in. Hey! We
should start our own group!”
“Absolutely not,” Nanook said immediately.
“Why not? We'd be so cool. We could have a fun name like they do too.” Tomkin’s face
twisted as he began to think a little too hard than what was really necessary. “Team Nan-kin?
No, that’s not good at all. Team Tom-Nook? Oh, I like that one!”
“Only because your name comes first,” Nanook scowled.
Tomkin pinched his cheek. “Don’t be jealous, partner.”
“Tomkin and Nanook can come with us again,” Aang said, somehow managing a small smile
despite the explosions rattling one of the last remnants of his culture.
Hakoda looked to the two boys. “I’d feel better knowing you were all together.”
“It would be our honour, chief,” Nanook said seriously, before his eyes found Zuko’s. He
smirked, ruffling Zuko’s hair, and Zuko quickly smacked him away. “Besides, I'm not letting
this one out of my sight again, and the Avatar needs his firebending teacher.”
Everything paused a moment, Zuko’s thoughts going quiet, because he’d known they were
saying goodbye, known they were splitting up, but he’d been so busy scowling at the thought
of Tomkin and Nanook changing groups that he hadn’t even considered their motive, or
where he stood in it all.
Zuko was supposed to go with the Avatar’s group.
He was being left behind.
No. No, that wasn’t fair. He knew it wasn’t fair, could see it in every line of Hakoda’s pained
expression. We looked for you. You have to know we looked for you.
Zuko was joining the Avatar properly. They wanted him. No, they expected him.
And this time, he was doing it without the Water Tribe’s support.

even say anything.”

“Whatever,” Zuko agreed quietly, and he knew they’d said all they needed to, that sudden

not looking at him but squeezing a little.

Flashes of pain and memory, so often the same thing. Zuko swallowed an acrid taste in his
mouth and shrugged Kanut off him, glaring at the ground.
Still, he said; “Okay.”

the tunnel, Chit Sang’s group talking amongst themselves behind them, the youngest kids

trying to help Toph’s earthbending when it seemed they were finally running out of time.
They needed to leave.
But Hakoda was right there, and Zuko was alone now, and the only time they’d really said
goodbye was in the Boiling Rock, moments before the bloodshed, a compensation for what
they never got in Gaoling.
This wasn’t like that. There were two steps between them. Each space, a chasm. Each space,
infinitesimal. The chief smiled.
“Here,” he said, unstrapping the sword from his back. “I’ve held onto this for long enough.”
The Dao was beautiful and glistened like someone had cleaned and sharpened it regularly in
the months he’d been separated from it, and Zuko’s stomach turned. Good or bad, he
thought, good or bad good or bad good or-.

This took the or from the sentence. This shifted the grammar, altered the structure, changed
the meaning altogether.
Good and bad.
Despite his smile, Hakoda’s stare was unwavering, and Zuko knew the chief was finally
forcing him to this conclusion that should have been so simple in theory. The Air Temple had
been a reprieve, a healing period, but now, they stepped into the real world again.
Zuko wasn’t allowed the easy route anymore.
“Thank you,” Zuko said, and that said it all as he reached out for his sword, a perfect match
for the one in his scabbard, one a warning and a last act of loyalty, of compassion, the other a

handle. The weight shouldn’t feel so familiar when he had done everything to cut up this side
of himself.

there to repeat myself. You will have bad days. You will get better in spite of them.”

he wanted to believe Hakoda, wanted to be able to do this. When Hakoda walked towards the
tunnel, Zuko watched him go a moment, heart thumping heavily in his chest, before he turned
to Tomkin’s warm smile and Nanook’s attempts to haul the other boy back into Appa’s saddle
before he fell off the side. You're not alone. He'd say it until it meant something.
Toph was going to use the rubble to earthbend a shield around the bison. It couldn’t last, but
it would get them out of Azula’s firing range and into the open air, and after that, they would
be okay. It wouldn’t take them longer than a week to get to the White Lotus camp, and they
would all be reunited again.
One week.
Zuko steeled himself, holding Zi Se tighter and giving him a reassuring smile, before walking
towards the mismatched group of children.

weeks hunting the Avatar, and now Zuko was sat on his bison with a five-year-old peering at
everything with wide eyes. It was all he could do to shake his head at the ridiculousness of it
all, like if he jostled his thoughts enough, he might wake up and find himself back on the
Erlong, the sounds of music night drifting up through his open window. Sokka caught his
expression and wiggled his eyebrows knowingly, and Zuko contemplated kicking him.

“Yip yip!” Aang called. The bison lifted into the sky and Toph yanked down the earth wall,
quickly reforming it into a shield around Appa’s face as they pushed out into the open air.
Sound hit them all at once, deafening explosions and the particular whistle fire made when
hurling towards you. Zuko crouched as best he could, his sword still in his hand as he
scanned the temple below. He spotted Azula quickly, her fists blazing blue as she watched
him leave with furious eyes.
Next, he saw a familiar form, tall and moody like she’d rather be anywhere else. He'd known
the moment Sokka deduced that Aput had been chi-blocked that Ty Lee was here, which
meant Mai wasn’t far behind. He met her tawny gaze now, flicking a glance to the knife in
her hand.
She could hit them from here. Zuko knew she could, and with pinpoint, fatal accuracy. For
the few moments before Appa shot off completely, Zuko and Mai stared each other down. He
wasn’t sure if he was willing her to try something, to show her true loyalty, or urging her to
stand down, but slowly, so subtle it was nearly imperceivable, Mai lowered the blade.
He breathed out in relief and a certain sadness. Something to miss, despite it all.
“So,” Tomkin said, and Zuko turned to see him staring with a knowing grin, “who was that?”

There seemed to be a concept amongst the people here, forced upon them by a war living
within Zuko’s bloodstream, that home was not a place but a feeling, like the cold coming in
from a harsh breeze or the bubble of laughter in your chest. It was not about brick or wood or
tarp, but people, family, whatever meaning given to the word. They found earth in the souls
of each other and it was there they planted roots, not on some plot of land, and even scattered
across the world, that home stood firm and tall.
Zuko felt himself building, learning to accommodate new things, bringing down the hammer.
He wondered what home was to him. An echoing palace. Dead portraits. Anger at the dinner
table. Fire. He would build something better and full of love, but he couldn’t demolish his old
house. One day, he hoped it would be no more than a relic, a memory, something that didn’t
hold living people anymore, but if he tried to burn it down or take his hammer and smash the
windows, he knew it would still stand firm and tall, his hands now burnt, the glass slicing
skin. His home fought back, and had done since before he came along, and would do so long
after, this war sitting in their family tracing back ten decades, three generations.
He would be picking his home from his fingernails all his life.

It had been one day and one night since they left the Western Air Temple and Zuko had a
headache.
It had been building since Appa first burst into the sky and they fled from Azula’s attack, like
the smallest grain of gravel had inched itself under his skull; miniscule, bearable, but present
nonetheless, a pressure that became pebble-sized after hours of flying and planning and
talking, endless talking, until finally, it started to get dark and they were forced to make
camp.
Zuko had been snappy, he knew he had. He stalked the perimeter of their camp so many
times he thought he might tread a path into the grass, and each time he tried to sit with the
others, to settle, he’d grow restless again with an urge to check just once more that they were
safe here. He thought someone might have followed them, or would at least be tracking them

down, or perhaps there were locals here that wouldn’t be friendly, or wild animals. His mind
tortured him with endless images of their little group, his little group, the ones Hakoda had
left him with to protect, being torn apart by blades and teeth. He had to just... check. Just
once more. It was hard enough when it was just Zi Se under his charge, but now there were
eight of them to look out for. Seven, really, when he was lucid enough to acknowledge that
Sokka could share some of the burden, and four if he followed that logic with Tomkin,
Nanook and Suki. Still, four people to keep alive, to protect when the danger wasn’t limited
to a small cell. The world was so cruel and full of horrors. How was anybody supposed to
save anyone?
He'd sat down by the fire in the end and ignored the looks Nanook was throwing him. His
headache was pounding now, like the stone wanted to break back through his skull, and Zuko
felt aware of every part of himself, felt the coarse material of his black clothes dragging
against his skin, felt the bright light of the fire catching his eyes even when he squinted them
closed, felt each bark of laughter and sudden swell of chatter. It was all too much, too loud,
too soon and yet why was it happening now? He'd never had anything like this in the White
Lotus camp and he’d been fine getting to the Air Temple with Zi Se, but he guessed he was
distracted then, too far into survival mode to see the wood for the trees. The temple itself had
been the opposite; a recurring reminder of safety, certainty, a warm place free of danger for
him to get his strength back.
He thought he’d gotten his strength back, or was at least on the right track, but one step into
the real world and he felt like everything in him was shutting down. He almost found himself
craving the darkness and solitude of the cell in Fong’s base. He knew his place there, knew
the pain was coming and didn’t need to worry over pointless uncertainties.
So Zuko went to bed early, and ignored the confused looks it earnt him, and snapped when
Tomkin tried to catch up to him.
He just... needed to be alone. Until the headache went away. Until it wasn’t all so... much.
It had been one day and one night since they left the Western Air Temple. The dawn was
breaking outside – Zuko could feel it – and the headache had become a layer of stone coating
every crevice of his skull until he was weighed down with it. Moving sent sharp stabs of pain
behind his eyes and through his temples, and while he’d closed the tent tight last night, light
was beginning to crawl beneath the tarp like the beginning flickers of a fire, and it burned.
He needed to get up, but instead, Zuko pulled his blanket over his head and turned away.
Exhaustion sat in his bones, in his mind, like stone. He imagined the cell, where all he had to
ask of himself was to survive the day, and his stomach turned from the longing it brought
him.

They were making good time with Appa, to the point Nanook expected they’d arrive at the
White Lotus camp days before the others and would be sat twiddling their thumbs with
nothing to do. How did anyone do anything without a flying bison? It was revolutionary.

So when Zuko didn’t get up for his dawn meditation and practise with Aang, Nanook wasn’t
so much in a hurry as he was concerned. The firebender had been acting strange the night
before, skittish, irritable in a way that surpassed his terrible social skills into the realm of a
genuine problem. Sokka had noticed too, and the boys decided quickly amongst themselves
that they should stay at their camp longer than originally scheduled today. They could leave

Katara was making breakfast when Nanook decided he’d given Zuko enough space, and with

“Zuko?” Nanook said gently.
Zuko’s voice was a muffled rasp when he spoke, weak, more of a growl than words. “Get

“You... You are killing me,” he finally huffed, throwing his arms in the air and turning on his
heel to leave the tent. “Finish your stupid broth and meet us outside or I will drag you.”
Zuko shook his head at the odd behaviour and needless threat, mostly because he wasn’t
actually sure Sokka could drag him, and finished his broth quietly. It eased a lot of the
restlessness with its warmth, filling the ache inside, but something was still indisputably off
and Zuko just couldn’t shake it. It was similar to the sadness he’d felt with Hakoda that night
after his outburst, finally shrugging off the armour of anger to reveal the hurt he’d been
hiding all along. That sadness had sat with him ever since, never abating, a weight that
wouldn’t allow him to take full breaths, but this was different. The same source, but a restless
bite to it, a panic beneath the skin.
He'd barely brushed the surface of the problem with Sokka. I'm adjusting. That was it, really,
but there was just so much more. Always more, with Zuko. More issues, more burdens, more,
more, more. He was sick of himself, how weren’t the other’s bored of this yet? Constantly

waiting for the day he’d reach that miraculous label of better and never quite making it. And
he didn’t want to talk about. He did. He needed to. He didn’t. His friends wanted him to.
He wanted to talk about a lot of things, if just to put words to feelings and hear the tune of
them. He wanted to talk about how familiar this sadness was, and how most days that
familiarity suffocated him, convinced him he would never know anything else, but some
days... some days it was a comfort. He wanted to say that there was a part of him that loved
it, that when he noticed it creeping in again, one of the first things he felt was relief, and
wasn’t that just awful? He wanted to say there had been birds in his chest, caged behind his
ribs, for years now. It did not start with Fong, a single creature in a menagerie. His friends
weren’t the ones who memorised every feather, every sound of distress, every wing-flutter on
marrow. His friends weren’t the ones who offered seeds from trembling hands, slowly
coaxing this trauma forward into something he could name and make his own. They weren’t.
He was. He had preened and petted these birds within him ever since the first had cracked its
shell. This one was rage and this one was shame and this one was the back of his father’s
hand, and the others didn’t understand why anyone would nurture such a horrific thing. They
didn’t understand. They didn’t understand that badness can often feel like a friend. That
goodness can often feel like grief.
If he spoke them, if he let them out, his friends would snatch these birds from the sky and
beat them to death, and they would call it salvation. It was not salvation. In the worst times,
the times his friends were nowhere to be seen, these crooked creatures had stayed with him.
They were the only things to know him entirely, to have seen each awful thing through his
eyes. They were the very language he used to make sense of what happened. What was he
without them? Hollow. Speechless.
It did not negate the fact that the birds were devouring him, peck, peck, pecking away at his
insides, needing more the bigger they got, and Zuko only had so much to give. His entire
body was dedicated to them, to this memory, to this pain that he was both forced to carry and
willingly housed. If he continued to keep them caged, they would eat him alive.
The others thought letting them go would be something Zuko welcomed.
They didn’t understand.

Dad was gone. Dad was gone again. It shouldn’t have sat so messily in Katara’s chest; she’d
had two years to familiarise herself with the shape of her father’s absence. But this... having
him back just to lose him again, to the war again, to the Fire Nation again – it was worse,
somehow.
Zuko was struggling too. She highly doubted it was because of what she was struggling with,
though there was enough crossover that it still made her feel weird, but still, despite his
broody, calcitrant demeanour that didn’t indicate distress in the honest way she was used to,
she knew he was struggling, if only because of the shifty looks Nanook threw him or the way
Tomkin had gone quiet. Even Sokka had taken on that observant shine in his eyes he got
when he was trying to solve something. The firebender was snappier than normal, more like
his old self than ever, and when he wasn’t pacing the camp, golden eyes darting, almost

hungry for a threat, he was in his tent hiding from the world. They'd made camp yesterday
and hadn’t left even as the sun climbed into the afternoon, and Zuko hadn’t emerged for
Aang’s ridiculously early firebending training.
Katara thought she might find some mean satisfaction from Zuko’s discomfort. The Fire
Nation had taken her father from her again, but here, their prince was suffering. In a sense,
the very cause of her turmoil was sat a few paces away with his own turmoil. Maybe in a
different situation, she’d relish in that, even though it was wrong, even though Aang would
be disappointed in her.
But she knew Zuko, knew the scars on his body and his own rebellion against Ozai. Zuko
was not the enemy. He wasn’t even bad. Sure, he was annoying and would always be a
firebender, but him and Katara had found common ground. Her skin didn’t crawl when they
interacted anymore. Her heart didn’t thrum with instinctive terror. He was part of their team
now. She would put herself before him if it spared him more pain.
Was it friendship she felt for him? No, maybe not quite yet. He felt almost like another
brother figure for her to bully and fume and fuss over, never doing what she said and always
glowering at her. Entirely different from Sokka’s brand of annoying but annoying all the
same. Like Toph. The thought made a small smile tug at Katara’s cheeks.
At the very least, she knew Zuko’s current struggles didn’t please her. She wanted to help
him, but this wasn’t a physical ailment. Not that she knew of. Zuko had been through so
much, and he hardly gave himself the chance to just sit with it. It was bound to catch up with
him sooner or later, and it seemed having the security of the adults removed was the final
straw.
Not dissimilar to what Katara was feeling, despite the oceans between their traumas.
Just as Katara was lost in thought, combing the same section of Zi Se’s hair over and over as
the little boy sat quietly in her lap, Zuko emerged from his tent, squinting up at the sun and
holding an empty bowl. Sokka had been in there not long ago, chasing out Tomkin and
Nanook who seemed to be sitting sentry by their friend. Tomkin had been more than a little
frustrated to find out Katara was, in fact, not currently waterbending with Aang and in need
of targets, but Nanook didn’t even look surprised.
Now, the two of them were sat with Katara, Suki and Zi Se, chatting amongst themselves.
Sokka had gone to fetch Aang and Toph from their earthbending, and their reticent firebender
was stalking forwards.
Zi Se leapt out of Katara’s lap with a grin. He was getting much better at giving Zuko his
space, but this had been a particularly long period and the child was starting to nag. Katara
had thought the least she could do to help was distract the boy, even if it wasn’t much. She
felt very suddenly useless as she watched Zi Se run to Zuko, looking up at him with starry
eyes and grabbing his hand.
Zuko paused, kneeling in front of Zi Se and saying something to him that Katara couldn’t
hear, turning the little boy’s face every which way, smoothing down the fabric at his
shoulders, expression pinched. He looked almost like he was checking Zi Se for injuries, not

satisfied until his ministrations came up empty, a flicker of relief on his face as he stood
again, ruffling Zi Se’s hair.
The worst part was that Zi Se didn’t look remotely surprised by it.
“Hey, Zuko,” Nanook said as the pair came and sat with them. “We’re leaving as soon as
Sokka comes back with the others, that okay?”
Zuko glared at him. “Why wouldn’t it be?”
“Just checking,” Nanook smiled, unperturbed.
Suki jumped to her feet suddenly, stretching out her arms and giving a crooked grin to the
group.
“I’ll go take your tent down,” she chirped, hands on her hips.
“I can do it,” Zuko said, staring at her like she’d sprouted another head.
“Cool! But I want to, so tough shit.”
“Language!” Zi Se called from where he was trying to climb onto Zuko’s back, earning a
giggle from Suki as she jogged away. Zuko’s glare did look significantly less menacing with
a five-year-old attempting to scale him.
That didn’t make it unmenacing, and Zuko landed each of them with a murderous look.
“Why are you treating me differently?” he snarled. Zi Se paused, amber eyes wide and
blinking over Zuko’s shoulder, slowly sliding to his feet again. “I’m not weak. I apologise for
not pulling my weight today, but that doesn’t mean you have to do it for me. I don’t want
your fucking pity.”
Zi Se said nothing. Again, there was no surprise on his face, just careful inactivity that
seemed so unnatural on someone so young.
“It’s not pity to want to help a friend, Zuko,” Nanook said tentatively, expression troubled. A
conversation they’d had before, no doubt.
Zuko opened his mouth, but Tomkin interrupted.
“Do not say you don’t need our help,” he snapped, unusually serious. “I need Nanook’s help
all the time, and he needs mine even if he likes to act all stoic. Do you think that makes us
weak? That's just how this works,” his old smile melted into his words then, “so suck it up.”
Katara sat there, useless and silent, every word she knew evading her. She didn’t know what
to say. She didn’t know what her dad would say. She wanted to help so desperately that it was
like a pull in her chest, but she couldn’t. She didn’t know how. Even with Tomkin and
Nanook’s attempts, Zuko still looked furious, that near-animalistic glint in his eyes like
everything was dangerous.

Sokka was back not long later. Aang and Toph were tired from earthbending and Suki
returned with a bundle of tarp that she attached to Appa without comment, despite the glaring
she was currently on the receiving end of. They packed away and took to the air, the group
chatting and teasing like normal, but through it, Zuko was silent and troubled, and Katara sat
opposite him, barely a pace away, and said nothing, consumed by her own troubles, an ocean
between them.

Firebending with Aang had been hit and miss from the start, the Avatar too busy trying to
master a whole element as quickly as possible, Zuko too quick to anger, fear of fire being
slowly unlearned by both of them all the while, Tomkin’s words from the Air Temple still
echoing in Zuko’s head about drawing from his own experiences. He'd reeled from the
concept for obvious reasons, but he’d thought harder about it, remembering his other tutors.
Uncle had always been kind, patient. It had frustrated Zuko, but Aang would respond well to
some of his methods. Piandao also, despite not being a bender, had been a good teacher. Not
all of Zuko’s experiences were awful.
He'd wanted to start introducing those teachings into the Avatar’s training. He'd wanted to be
a good teacher, better than what he had known, someone who was helping the good guys,
who was useful.
But it had been two days and one night since they left the Western Air Temple and Zuko was
faring no better than yesterday. Every noise was as loud as an explosion, every touch felt like
it was burning him, too close, too much, stifling. He heard twigs snapping where there were
none, footsteps when no one moved, saw shadows swooping and earth rumbling underfoot,
about to burst forth and envelope his wrists, leaving him bound and helpless to the agony that
followed. He existed here, on this grassy flatland where they had made camp, but in his head,
he was with Fong. Always. A rot in his body too deep to merely be cut out. He was surviving
again. Protecting again.
It made him snappier with Aang, jumpier with his bending, out of control. He forced himself
through it on principal, despite the now familiar headache growing behind his eyes. He'd
missed training completely yesterday, and that was unforgiveable. It didn’t matter if his limbs
were too heavy, if his heart wouldn’t stop racing, if he couldn’t even keep his gaze on Aang
because he swore he saw something out of the corner of his eye. It was infuriating, and it was
made worse by the fact there was a considerable part of him that knew he was wrong, knew
there was no threat here, but he had to check anyway for the smaller part of him convinced
there was, and how the fuck did he explain that? He sounded like he was losing it. Maybe he
was.
Zuko shot out a furious blast of blue flame as he finished the kata him and Aang were
working through, earning a yelp from the younger boy who was stood a little too close to the
fire. A malicious part of Zuko felt satisfied by it; that's what Aang got for being in his space.
As soon as the thought burned his mind, it blistered and ached, making him reel from it.
Agni, what the fuck was wrong with him? Was that how it started, violence as some sort of
revenge, slowly becoming the only language you were fluent in?
Is that how it started with his father? Is that what was happening here?

Nausea hit Zuko like a fist to the face and he keeled over, barely landing on one knee before
he toppled to the ground entirely, hands scrabbling at the dirt and hating the way it felt
beneath his nails.
“Zuko!” Aang called, and he was there again.
“Don’t touch me,” Zuko spat out, not knowing what he’d do if someone touched him right
now. It was bad enough being seen like this, heaving in each breath and swallowing bile, his
father’s cruelty so familiar in his mind’s eye. He'd always looked like him. He always would.
In fact, it was likely to worsen as he aged, growing into his father’s features, his father’s
violence.
No. No, he had a choice here. He was stopping the cycle. He was changing. He was healing.
Fuck, what part of the last two days had even been close to healing?
“That’s enough for today,” Zuko said, voice weak as he pushed to his feet, wobbling but
managing to just stay standing. “I’m going to my tent.”
Aang said something, a barrage of concern, but Zuko’s ears were ringing and he was just
lucky he made it to the dark nothingness of his tent without anyone else accosting him. He
collapsed onto his blankets, burying himself beneath them and squeezing his eyes shut tight,
breathing past the headache, past the nausea, past the spinning calamity of what felt like
inevitable horror. You will have bad days, Hakoda had said, you will get better in spite of
them. Zuko repeated it over and over, using the memory of Hakoda’s voice to drown out the
memory of his father.
It worked slowly. He didn’t know how long it took him to marginally calm down, feeling less
like he was going to be sick and more like he was so exhausted he might sleep for a week.
Agni, he felt so pathetic. It wasn’t so bad yesterday when he could hide it out in his tent, but
even then, the others had met him with that insufferable pity.
This time though, Aang had seen it. He would tell everyone because he’d think he was being
helpful, and they would pity him even more. Poor little Zuko, always so troubled, always
hurt, always falling behind.
Again, he longed for his old rage, the way it consumed all of him and left no room for
questions. He didn’t care that it was a lie, a shield for the hurt that toiled beneath, forced to
the surface by hands too gentle to have anything to do with Zuko. He didn’t care if his anger
was ugly and unsustainable, because at least it was dignified. This sadness, this moping, this
exhaustion – there was no dignity here, no fight. It was everything he’d kept bitten back for
years suddenly exposed to the open air for anyone to see and know he wasn’t okay. At least
the anger scared away uncertain eyes. This was just pathetic, and that only made him hate
himself more, which only made him curl into bed more, suddenly incapable of doing so much
as getting up. Something so fucking simple. He was acting like a child. Worse than a child.
This was not loud or immature. It was nothing at all. A complete revocation of humanity. It
disgusted him, and the more it disgusted him, the less capable he was to do anything about it.

The tent opened suddenly, Zuko instinctively shrinking from it, dread lodged in his throat as
he waited for the suffocation of pity, but instead, the darkness returned quickly.
“Zuko?” Zi Se asked in a small voice, and Zuko choked out a breath of relief.
It hurt to move, but he lifted his head, just making Zi Se out in the darkness, and wasn’t that
familiar? It eased something in him. Whether having Zi Se nearby or its similarity to the cell,
he didn’t know, didn’t think he wanted to know, but he beckoned the boy forward. It took
some manoeuvring, but soon, Zi Se was tucked happily against Zuko’s chest and he was

the world.
“Are you okay?” Zi Se whispered. His hands were cold as he traced Zuko’s jaw, his scar,
mapping him because once that was all they knew of each other between flickers of terrifying

“I will be,” Zuko said, taking Zi Se’s hands in his and warming them gently, feeling more in
control than he had all day. “It’s just... things feel heavy sometimes. This is a heavy day. Does
that make sense?”
It shouldn’t. It did. Zuko wasn’t surprised when Zi Se nodded, inky hair tickling his chin.
“Sorry I've not spent much time with you,” Zuko said, finally relaxing into the edges of sleep.
Zi Se pushed his face into the hollow of Zuko’s throat, his own tiredness catching up to him.
It wouldn’t hurt if they had a quick nap, and Zuko had at least done some firebending with
Aang today. He hadn’t been completely useless.
“S’okay,” Zi Se mumbled without hesitation, and was asleep just as quickly. Zuko allowed a
small smile.
He dozed lightly, jerking awake every now and then from even the quietest noises of the

But suddenly, a deafening crash sounded from outside, the ground beneath Zuko rumbling

surging forwards and pushing past the explosion of sunlight that tried to blind him.
Not far in the distance, Zuko saw a pillar of earth shooting from the ground, Aang’s control
of it quickly wobbling with his panic, realising he’d bitten off more than he could chew as the
colossal rock began tipping towards him.
“Aang!” Toph shouted. She was too far away. She was calling him by his name.

Zuko felt the roil of earth. He heard the way it rumbled. He remembered how it felt.
He was the closest to where the pair were training, something he noticed with a quick glance
to the campfire where everyone else was only just getting to their feet in horror. Zuko put Zi
Se down roughly and took off running.
If he’d been quicker with Fong, it would have done nothing. The interrogation room was
barely three paces in any direction. If he evaded the earth, it would simply pull back for
another bite. He'd be dragged to his knees. Someone else’s blood would already be staining
the floor. His would join and drip over his back, his legs, his ankles, soaking the soles of
cheap shoes, the bite of earth cutting his skin. He used to be able to feel the dirt sinking into
him, contaminating him, forever calloused into his skin, never quite healing right. They never
would, those manacles on his wrists for a lifetime.
Zuko shoved Aang out of the way, the both of them tumbling just as the tower of earth fell
heavily right where Aang had been standing, enough to bury him, a cell ceiling collapsing on

For a moment, they lay on the floor like that, cut off from the others by the debris. Aang

beginning to beat in time with his racing heart as he inhaled warm, dusty air. He was out in

“Wow Zuko, thank you so much!” Aang’s grin was strained as he hopped to his feet. “That

Zuko stayed on the floor, one hand fisting the earth like he had earlier. It at once grounded

“What,” Zuko hissed, “the fuck is wrong with you?”
Aang blinked, smile dropping and hurt flashing over his face, already fragile from such a

“Do you think this is a game?” Zuko continued, unable to stop, voice a cruel growl. “Bending

“Aang, what’s going on?” Katara asked gently, a note of horror in her voice as she watched

Zuko's anger, that sudden swell that had felt so soothing, so invigorating, melted away at

So he did what any coward would do. He walked away.

“Hey, wait up!” Sokka called, jogging to catch up to Zuko. Zuko's shoulders hunched, like if

“What happened back there? Aang looked like you just insulted his entire bloodline,” Sokka

between them, and Zuko was too guilty to avoid this.

Of course it had to be Sokka who caught him. Sokka, who he was trying so hard to prove
himself to.
“Just leave it. Ask him if you’re so curious,” Zuko growled, more bite to his words than he

Zuko had done something horrible, to the surprise of no one.

The other boy returned to Zuko’s space with a vengeance, a little shorter but broader than

thought were harmless insults, not when his competence was consistently questioned. He

He felt satisfaction curl in his gut, Sokka’s chest heaving with his rage, eyes a burning fury,

Zuko curled up on his bedroll, hugging himself so tight it made it a little hard to breathe. The

dry, petrified laugh. What terrible timing.

Sokka couldn’t remember the last time he was so angry as he stormed over to a collection of
rocks, determined to find somewhere to hide for a bit while he got everything back under
some sort of control. He couldn’t let the kids see him like this, or Nanook with his impossible
perception, or Katara, who would worry. He'd talk to her about this later, but right now, he
needed to figure out what he was feeling.
Fuck, how had things gone so wrong so quickly? And why had Sokka risen to it? He knew
Zuko was baiting him, knew it in the vicious glint of those golden eyes that wanted to be
punished for what he did to Aang, so why did Sokka play along like that? Spirits, he’d
thought he was going to hit Zuko, and it scared him. Sokka wasn’t a quiet person, and when
things upset him, he tended to be expressive about it, but despite all that, he was actually very
controlled. He had to be, when he was left as the only man in their village. He had to be
strong. He had to control exactly which emotions Katara saw so that she wouldn’t be
stressed. Sure, he wasn’t always successful, and he let her in more as they got older, but that
instinct was still there.
It had felt like Zuko was ripping it out of him, every feeling playing out in startling colour on
Sokka’s face without his permission.
He'd wanted to help Zuko. He was angry that Zuko had upset Aang, but he knew it was much
more complicated than that, and he knew Zuko was currently responding marginally better to
Sokka’s no-nonsense attitude than he was Tomkin and Nanook’s pity. Sokka scoffed as he
crouched behind a rock – he was not hiding – and raked a hand down his face. Spirits, he’d
thought he was the best man for the job, had even felt a jolt of glee from it, from knowing he
could help Zuko in ways the others couldn’t.

But he’d underestimated Zuko, had let himself forget that the other boy wasn’t some
wounded animal and was in fact a force to be reckoned with, an equal. Sokka couldn’t tell if
he was more annoyed with Zuko and his blatantly self-destructive tendencies, or himself.
Who was he kidding? He was definitely more annoyed with himself.
“Stupid,” he muttered, tugging on his hair a little to ground him. “Stupid.”
“Room for one more?” a voice suddenly sounded, and Sokka jumped so hard he whacked his
head on the rock.
“Katara!” he whined, rubbing his head as his sister came to sit next to him, smirking evilly
and entirely devoid of pity.
“Why are you hiding behind a rock and mumbling to yourself?” she asked once she’d settled
comfortably beside him, crossing her legs so that her knee pushed into his thigh a little. Any
other day and he’d shove her for taking up too much space, but he leaned into the touch now,
huffing as all the fight left him.
“Zuko’s an asshole,” Sokka said sullenly.
Katara hummed. “That does seem to be the general consensus today.”
“Aang’s still upset?”
“Yeah,” Katara frowned sadly, “he’s back to training like there’s no tomorrow. I'm worried
about him.”
“You’re always worried about him,” Sokka mumbled, earning an elbow to the side.
“I can’t get through to him,” Katara sighed, ignoring the casual abuse as Sokka rubbed his
surely bruised ribs. “Guessing you didn’t have any luck with Zuko either?”
“I wanted to punch him.”
Katara laughed, shaking her head, before her smile slipped from her face as she took in
something from Sokka’s expression.
“Oh, wow,” she said. “You’re being serious.”
“I didn’t,” Sokka clarified, troubled. “But still. It got too close. He wanted me to.”
“He’s punishing himself,” Katara summarised, and Sokka hummed in agreement.
“You know that’s not your fault, right?” she asked, nudging him much more gently than
before. “We can only do so much, especially when neither of them are being cooperative.”
She huffed a little, frustrated. Sokka knew the feeling.

“I just... It was going really well with him, and now I just feel useless, like I have to watch as
someone hurts and do nothing to help,” Sokka admitted quietly. It wasn’t rare for him to be
so open with Katara, but admitting a weakness like this was hard for Sokka to do with
anyone, and he couldn’t help but tense up, a voice in his head begging him to swallow back
the words, tell some dumb joke, lighten the mood.
Katara held his hand and gave it a squeeze.
“I know how you feel,” she said, and that was it. No advice. No condescension. No mockery.
Just the simple validation of acknowledgement.
It did more for Sokka than he thought it would, and he squeezed her hand back.
____
Zuko didn’t join them around the campfire that night, and Katara hadn’t expected him to.
She'd been keeping an eye on his tent ever since her and Sokka eventually emerged from the
rocks her brother had hidden himself in, but Zuko had stayed inside all day, only leaving a
few minutes ago. No one else had noticed him quietly sneak out, vanishing into the shadows
of the very rock pile Sokka had found solace in. There was a certain humour Katara could
find in the boys’ identical stupidity.
Subtly, Katara gave an excuse and got up, slipping away to find Zuko. No one suspected
anything, and she released a small breath of relief.
The rocks were mismatched and dangerous beneath Yue’s light, and Katara stumbled more
than once trying to navigate them towards the mop of inky hair she saw ahead of her. Zuko
heard her coming, which she supposed was probably a good thing given how frayed his
nerves seemed lately. She didn’t particularly fancy getting fried tonight.
“Getting some air?” she asked when that sceptical golden glare landed on her.
Zuko just grunted an affirmation, and Katara rolled her eyes.
She sat next to him, giving him room but close enough that it was clear she wanted to talk,
and looked out at the grassland before them. Under the darkness like this, the grass fluttered
in the wind like waves in an ocean. It was beautiful, hypnotising if you stared too long. For a
while, it was quiet between them as Katara waited for Zuko to relax a bit. When it became
clear that he wouldn’t, Katara sighed.
“We want to help you, Zuko,” she said, and he somehow went more rigid, a sneer pulling at
his features. Katara continued quickly. “But I don’t think any of us truly know how. I think
my dad did, and some of the others, but we... we don’t, and I’m sorry.”
Zuko looked at her then, like he thought that was it, like he thought they were abandoning
him.
Katara's expression hardened with determination. “But you have to let us try. We’ll make
mistakes, and you’ll make mistakes, but unless you’ve given up, we haven’t either. We're all

getting through this war, Zuko. I mean it.” She searched his eyes like if she stared hard
enough he’d have no choice but to hear her and hear her well, tone a little desperate. “I’m not
leaving anyone else behind. I'll drag you if I have to.”
Zuko let out a surprised laugh, a little wet with a relief he didn’t even seem aware of, too far
into his desire to see them hate him. Well, screw that. Katara meant what she said, and her
own panic dissolved with Zuko’s shy smile as she realised she’d said something right.
“I...” Zuko started, frowning and ducking his head. “I’m sorry, about... well about all of it.
The past two days, what happened with Aang, Sokka... Agni, I've made a mess of things.”
“Yep,” Katara said, smirking. “And you better apologise to both of them.”
“I will,” Zuko said vehemently, and Katara knew he already intended to apologise long
before she got here. In fact, she felt she knew Zuko a lot better than she ever realised. He was
so similar to her. A few months ago, the thought would have kept her up at night. Now, it felt
a little bit hilarious.
“Do you know why you acted like that today?” she asked carefully. For a second, Zuko’s
expression shuttered, before opening up again slowly, vulnerable and full of self-loathing.
“I guess I just wanted everyone to go away,” he explained. “It’s all been so loud, all the
noises and lights all of a sudden after being still so long. I got overwhelmed and the
moment... the moment I realised I wanted you all gone... it was like I suddenly needed to
prove to you all that I'm... I’m bad news. I'm a waste of time. I can’t-.”
“Can I hold your hand?” Katara asked suddenly. Zuko's stunned expression was priceless.
He thought over her request for a few long moments, before presenting a scarred hand to her.
“Just don’t... don’t touch my wrist,” he said, and Katara nodded, carefully interlocking their
fingers. Zuko's hand was rough and calloused, raised scars pushing against Katara’s soft
palm, and his nails were dirty and brittle. Holding him like that, even such a tiny part of him,
Katara felt a surge of protectiveness, like while his hand was shielded in hers, he was safe.
Just like she did with her brother earlier, she gave Zuko a grounding squeeze. He looked
disproportionately surprised by how comforting he seemed to find it.
“I’ve found it hard too,” Katara said. “I’m so... I’m so angry that we’ve been split up again,
and I can’t stop thinking about my mom, and I worry myself. There’s so much anger in me. I
don’t like it. I don’t have anywhere to put it, not until the Fire Nation comes to justice. I hate
that part of me, hate that the people who hurt me so badly still have such a hold on me, that
they can make me... make me bad too, if that makes sense?”
Zuko nodded.
“I don’t know what makes a good person, Zuko,” Katara continued. “I know Aang is good. I
know my brother and Toph are good. But if you asked me what made them good, I couldn’t
give you a set list. I just know Sokka makes me laugh. Aang keeps me honest. Toph,” she

chuckled here, shaking her head. “Toph keeps me on my toes, at the very least. None of us
gets to dictate the boundaries of what’s good and what’s bad, but I think... I think trying to be
good? Wanting to be good? I think that’s a pretty big part of it.”
Zuko was quiet for a long time. Katara didn’t push him, worrying at her lip as she wondered
if she’d said the right thing, if she’d misread the situation, misread him.
When Zuko eventually spoke, his voice was the softest Katara had ever heard it, liable to be
trampled by anything she chose to say to him, completely vulnerable to her.
“You think I'm good?” he asked.
The answer came quicker than Katara expected.
She smiled. “Yeah, I think so.”
It went quiet again, comfortable this time, and Katara let her gaze unfocus, watching the
grass twirl and dance in the breeze, and the late hour began to pull her eyelids down, relaxed
in the company of a firebender she had once cursed.
She blinked awake when she felt Zuko give her hand a shy squeeze, and couldn’t bite back
her smile.

Gradually, things got easier and they fell into a routine. Zuko's paranoia haunted him, as
consistent a shadow as any, defined by the person it was bound to and just as hard to kill, but
he learned to live with it as more of a companion than a problem. He would patrol their
camps each morning and night, listening out for any noise or possible disturbance, but now, it
was almost comforting; a routine.
It seemed illogical to have such a thing – they’d only been travelling a few days together –
but somehow, all of their unique experiences out in the war came together in a generally fluid
way. Tomkin and Nanook knew of battle, of soldiers and supplies. Suki knew of leadership
and teamwork. Sokka knew of strategy and navigating. Zuko knew of discipline, travelling,
protecting. Between the five of them, they silently managed the youngers of their group.
Katara contributed far too much to be written off as simply someone under their charge, but
she was still just fourteen, and Aang and Toph were younger still, and of course there was Zi
Se.
Zuko had never had a group of peers before. He’d felt similarly when he first started relaxing
around Tomkin and Nanook, but that had been a trio, where this was a group. A real group of
something getting oddly close to friends. It was so different to being around the adults.
Katara was right; none of them here truly knew what they were doing. The comfort of
knowing there was some older, stronger being around to protect them and fix things was lost,

but in its stead came a comradery that Zuko hadn’t anticipated. They all had so much in
common, children of this war in each of their individual ways, and for how much they still
didn’t know, if there was one thing they all shared, it was their stubborn will to try in spite of
it all.
“Your hair’s getting long now, Zuko,” Suki pointed out one afternoon. They'd been flying on
Appa all day, the group of them tired and stressed from being sat still so long while flying
through Fire Nation territory, and had set up camp near a stream. It was a luxury after days of
travel, and Zuko relished in the feel of the cool water darting past his ankles, leaning down to
cup handfuls of it and wash his face of sweat and grime.
Suki wasn’t far from him, dipping her water flask into the current, a curious glint in her eyes
as she watched him. Zuko frowned, threading wet fingers through his hair. It brushed his
shoulders now, likely long enough to pull back if he wanted to, and still a little uneven from
Fong’s rough treatment. He knew if he traced his scalp, he’d feel scars, jagged little bumps.
He could still remember the feel of blood clotting and scabbing in his hair, flaking off with
each movement. It had been one of the lesser things to make him feel disgusting in that cell,
but it hadn’t been pleasant.
He ran his hands through his hair again with more water, imagined washing it all off him, and
he grunted an acknowledgement at Suki.
She scoffed, rolling her eyes. “I mean it. This new look actually suits you. Very roguish.”
“Broody,” Tomkin added unhelpfully from where he was sat looking blissed out on the bank,
Nanook braiding his hair back into its wolf tail with gentle hands. His head was ducked, but
Zuko knew Nanook was trying not to laugh.
“I don’t think either of those things are compliments,” Zuko grumbled, crossing his arms and
glaring at the three of them.
“Zuko, dude, buddy.” Sokka appeared from where he’d been washing his frankly disgusting
tunic, now leaving it to drip around his neck, shirtless as he clapped a hand to Zuko’s
shoulder. “If a girl calls you roguish, it’s a compliment.”
Zuko was hyperaware of Sokka’s hand on him, the warmth of his fingers, the way they
dipped into his skin, but where before the contact might have made him panic, now it just felt
like his mind wanted only for him to acknowledge it, to shiver and know it was there but not
feel threatened by it.
He frowned at Sokka, before frowning at Suki, pulling at his hair a little, curious as to how a
mark of dishonour, a mark that had signalled the end of a life for Zuko, could now be seen in
any way positively.
“Thanks?”
Suki snorted. “Don’t mention it, hot stuff.”

Suki had an affinity for odd nicknames. For some reason, this seemed to bother Sokka more
than anyone. Hot stuff was one of her favourites, which Zuko thought made sense. He was a
firebender, after all. It really didn’t warrant the spluttering and indignance Sokka met it with,
stomping over to Suki and kicking water at her while she cackled.
Nanook was smirking again, which was never good. Zuko huffed and began walking back to
camp.
Things with Sokka were awkward. Their argument happened two days ago, and in the
meantime, Sokka seemed determined to ignore it. It wasn’t that he was acting normally,
because he wasn’t; even Zuko could feel the tension in each of their encounters. But it was
like Sokka had more important things to worry about, too focused on getting them all to the
White Lotus camp in one piece to worry about Zuko and his stupid problems. Zuko got it, he
did, but it was making it difficult to apologise when he felt so dismissed.
Or maybe that was just an excuse. Katara kept throwing Zuko knowing, disappointed looks
whenever he let another opportunity to talk slide, like she knew he was grasping at excuses
not to address the situation.
He’d apologised to Aang the very next day after shouting at him, and it had been so easy, so
painless, like the Avatar hadn’t even considered holding a grudge, and there was both relief
and hurt in that, like Zuko was grateful for such easy forgiveness but felt he was being
punished double as a result of it.
But Sokka? What could Zuko say to Sokka, who always saw too much of him? Sokka, who
had been the only one to push back when Zuko pushed first? Sokka, who might not forgive
so easily?
At least existing in limbo like this was undetermined. It wasn’t often Zuko let himself be a
coward.
Returning to camp made him wince, because this had been another thing they’d all been
avoiding.
Katara was in a foul mood today. It had been building ever since they left the Air Temple,
and Zuko couldn’t help but think about what she’d said to him during their talk, about how
much anger she kept in her, and how hard it was to have Hakoda taken from them again.
Zuko knew a lot about anger, had given everything to begin letting it go, fingers cramped and
aching from holding on so tight so long. Katara had helped him. If he could, Zuko would help
her.
But she was downright terrifying when she was annoyed about something, and she seemed to
be showing her anger by getting annoyed at just about everything, and they were all just
trying to stay out of her way as much as possible. It was easy for Zuko to slink back into the
camp, sitting quietly beside Zi Se around the fire, watching Katara fume and mutter beneath
her breath as she made dinner, Aang sharing a look with him that seemed an awful lot like
they were in the stocks together.

Zuko just hoped Sokka stayed by the stream a little longer. No one angered Katara quite like
her brother.

“You know,” Nanook said quietly, lost to the rhythm of separating and braiding hair, and
Tomkin’s was so soft, pliant beneath his fingers. “Your hair’s getting long now too.”
Tomkin hummed, barely listening. He always got like this when someone did his hair.
“Not really had a chance to cut it, I guess,” he said, shrugging a little. Nanook tugged a little
harshly to reprimand him for moving, and Tomkin elbowed his leg.
He supposed that was fair. They'd been away from the village for years now, but this year had
been particularly hard on them. It felt like the war had once been this great, awful creature on
the horizon, snarling at them, batting away their advances, nightmare worthy and terrifying
yet somehow... too great to be realised.
But this year, it lunged, breathing down their necks. They'd taken the Fire Prince prisoner.
They met the Avatar. Neither ended how Nanook would have anticipated. It all shouted of a
proximity he felt distinctly too young for, which was stupid. He was twenty. He ought to be
able to figure this out.
Once, when they were kids, Tomkin had felt so much younger than Nanook that he’d pushed
him in the snow to get him to stop following him around, thinking himself important and
much cooler than he was. Now, he’d watched his friend mature right alongside him. It was
both an honour and a tragedy to witness.
“I could cut it for you?” Nanook offered, coming to the end of the braid but finding himself
lingering, the pads of his fingers just brushing the nape of Tomkin’s neck.
“What? You worried it makes me look roguish too?” Tomkin jumped up when he felt Nanook
tie his hair off, turning to face him with a grin. “You getting jealous?”
For a bizarre moment, Nanook didn’t know what he meant, stuttering over a response.
Tomkin cackled at him, ruffling his hair before beginning to walk back to their camp.
“Don’t worry, Nan,” he called over his shoulder, “I’ll leave some of the girls for you.”
He was still smiling. Always smiling. Nanook let him go.
“Wait up!” Sokka called, and whatever strange emotion was trying to fight its way past
Nanook’s ribs was beaten down by a wave of dread.
He joined the others in the walk back to camp and sighed. “Try not to antagonise your sister,
Sokka. We all have bad days.”
“I didn’t antagonise her!” Sokka spluttered, offended. “She started it.”

Suki laughed, and Tomkin got Sokka in a headlock to grind his knuckles into his hair,
ignoring the boy’s cry of indignance. Nanook smiled to himself, already preparing to mediate
the inevitable argument between the siblings.

Sokka and Katara were arguing.
Well, more accurately, Katara was arguing with pretty much everyone, but her brother was
not only her current target but her most frequent one. She'd woken up in a bad mood and the
rest of their little group had seemingly decided to make it their mission to frustrate her in one
way or another, from Aang shouting a cheerful greeting in her face within moments of her
waking up, to Tomkin and Nanook bickering all through breakfast, to Toph trying to wipe her
dirty hands on Katara when she told her to wash them. Even Suki, who usually kept out of
Katara’s way, was enraging her with every boisterous laugh she gave to inadvertently
encourage whatever behaviour Katara was actively berating. It was a miracle they survived
such a long journey on Appa together without Katara pushing someone off. That someone
likely being Sokka.
When Katara got like this, even her brother’s breathing was enough to set her off, something
which he was currently doing entirely too close to her ear.
“Sokka,” she said slowly, trying not to lose it, “do you have to sit so close to me?”
He was oblivious of her growing rage, instead huffing. Loudly. In her ear.
“Why is it even a big deal if we’re down two carrots?” he mumbled, rolling his eyes.
They'd set up a good camp, and most of their spirits were high from being able to wash even
slightly in the nearby stream, but Katara had to make dinner, and their supplies had been
dwindling for days now. Every time she made a meal, she took stock of what they had left so
she could make a mental list for what they needed. Inevitably, they would need to resupply in
a town. A Fire Nation town. It promised to be a nightmare, seeing as the only members of the
group that could pass as Fire Nation were either a five-year-old boy or the very recognisable
prince of the nation, who had kept himself suspiciously out of Katara’s wrath all day.
“Ugh! This was so much easier with Dad,” Katara snarled, emptying the burlap sacks in her
frustration, uncaring for how their food scattered to the ground. Sokka squawked, instantly
grabbing the more easily soiled food and throwing her a glare.
“What is with you? It's just a couple carrots. What’s Dad got to do with it?”
"Everything!” she yelled, aggressively taking the food out of Sokka’s hands and shoving it
back into the burlap sacks, giving up on the carrots and the entire endeavour of resupplying.
She was so angry her hands were shaking, had been all morning, since she woke up with the
dream of a man known more for his absence than his personhood still fresh in her mind.
She'd dreamt of her father being killed, a world away from home, lying in his own blood,
skin bubbled and completely unrecognisable with burns, but for his blue eyes staring
lifelessly up at a smoky sky. And she couldn’t help him, because he was gone. He was gone

again. He was always gone again... and Katara... She was always so angry, and when she got
like this, she wanted her mother, more than anything. And that made her angry, angrier,
because Kya wasn’t here and Hakoda wasn’t here and it was all because of those ashmaking
monsters and Katara was expected to move above it, to be better, to forgive. Anger is easy.
Why couldn’t some days just be easy?
She'd learnt a lot about anger these past few weeks. She'd befriended a firebender, a prince,
when she once thought she could never so much as like anyone from the Fire Nation. She
knew she could move past this rage, but today, it was all-consuming, and she was staring
down a tsunami, a little girl left behind without a mother, without a father, without a mentor
to guide her hands. When she felt like this, she couldn’t even recognise the water.
So she couldn’t be angry at the Fire Nation as a whole anymore, so what? There were still
targets for her rage.
Fire Lord Ozai, for one.
For another, the men who killed her mother.
She pictured killing them sometimes, returning the death back to them, a fair exchange,
pulling at the water in their blood until they danced to their own death march, necrotising
their cells one by one. She could do it. She wasn’t that helpless child anymore that could do
nothing but find the carnage after the fact.
The thought scared her. She hadn’t thought herself violent, not in the way that particular
vision made her feel. It made her feel sick, so she pushed it down, all of it, the thoughts, the
dreams, the anger, and redirected it at stupid, mundane things.
Like the fact someone was definitely eating the carrots without telling her.

Zuko had taken the carrots.
He hadn’t even thought much about it. Katara had mentioned a few days ago that their
supplies were dwindling, and the thought had sent such a tangible bolt of paranoia through
Zuko that he hadn’t even listened to the rest of the conversation, focusing only on the fact the
food might run out. He'd known, logically, that they would simply get more, hence the
conversation to begin with, and it wasn’t like they were completely out, nor would they ever
be, because Katara always kept on top of it, but taking a few bits and pieces here and there
just felt like the smart thing to do.
Which meant, awkwardly, the carrots currently at the receiving end of Katara’s ire were
hidden in Zuko’s pillowcase, as well as some tofu, a few strips of seal jerky, and Tomkin’s
water flask that he ‘lost’ yesterday. Zuko had his own water flask. Even he wasn’t entirely
sure what possessed him to stash it when he found it unattended, the only voice of reason
asking him why he wouldn’t take it, still whispering about starvation, about not knowing
where the next meal came from, about a life of so little means and such large want that even a
water flask would have seemed like salvation.

He wasn’t about to admit to his mistake, though. Not today, at least. He truly hadn’t thought
enough about it to realise how it would disrupt the group, nor was he paranoid enough
anymore that he thought keeping the carrots in his pillowcase was a matter of survival. He
was safe now, he was fed and sheltered and befriended, it just sometimes took his instincts a
moment to trip and correct step before returning to the path.
But today, Katara was livid with just about everyone and everything, and Zuko was not about
to put himself in the firing line, thank you very much.

tread on his little sister’s toes, and that caused an inexplicable fondness in Zuko’s chest as he

“I already told you,” Katara snapped, shoving a finger to her brother’s chest, “you’re going to

“And I told you that it’d be quicker if we all just load our own once we’re done, why are you

It also seemed like Zi Se’s last straw, because the next thing Zuko knew, the kid was crying.
