louder Katara got – Nanook responding with even, unbothered quips – the louder Zi Se got,
almost like he was matching her.
Zuko moved him to his lap, holding his face in his hands and frowning.
“Hey, hey, you’re okay,” he shushed, wiping the tears even as they kept coming. “What’s
wrong? What happened?”
Zi Se wailed, burying his face against Zuko again, little fists grabbing at his shirt. He
seemed... frustrated, more than genuinely distraught, but Zuko didn’t know why, knew only
that it correlated with the incessant bickering.
He glared at Katara as he rubbed circles into Zi Se’s back. “You’re upsetting him.”
“Me?!” she shrieked, and Zi Se cried louder. The noise grated on Zuko’s nerves in a distinctly
unsettling way, that shadow in his mind whispering that Zi Se was in pain, something was
wrong, Zuko had missed something, fix it, fix it, fix it. He felt like he was in the cell again.
He felt like he was back at the Air Temple with Hakoda, ignoring the child between them
while he cried and cried and cried.
“How long until we land?” he asked, desperately wrestling the panic out of his voice. If the
way Sokka looked at him properly for the first time since their argument was anything to go
by, Zuko failed magnificently.
“We’re almost there,” Aang said, voice soothing. Zuko chose to believe he was talking like
that for Zi Se’s sake.
There was nothing Zuko could do in the meantime but hold Zi Se and mutter reassurances,
praying to whatever spirit was listening that the boy would be quiet. Zuko's heart was
thundering against his ribs by the time they blessedly began to descend, and he was aware
that he was getting a few distasteful looks for Zi Se’s crying, but he didn’t care. He couldn’t
think. He just needed the noise to stop.
Still holding Zi Se tight, Zuko hopped off Appa before the bison had even fully landed,
throwing one last murderous glare to everyone.
“I’m going ahead, try not to kill each other in the meantime.”
With that, he stomped away, feeling slightly mellowed by the fact Katara had looked guilty.
Zi Se at least stopped crying so loudly as Zuko put some distance between them and the
group, but the tears were relentless, hiccupped into his shoulder, and there was definitely snot
on Zuko’s neck that he was trying very hard not to think about.
The forest they were in was sparse, the sunlight jumping through in fitful waves, tracing long
shadows on the dirt that crunched underfoot while the trees danced around it in the breeze.
Above them, Zuko could see the rooves of a town, chimneys puffing up smoke into the sky,

distant chatter and the smell of street food in the air. It was a distinctly Fire Nation smell,
spices and grilled meat, and Zuko’s stomach rumbled, but he stopped just before the treeline,
placing Zi Se on a boulder even when the kid tried diligently to hold on to any part of him he
could find.
“Stop it,” Zuko said firmly, wrenching his hand from his shirt as gently as he could given Zi
Se’s surprisingly strong grip. “Tell me what’s wrong.”
He crouched in front of him so that they were eye level, and with the time to calm down and
enough space from the others, Zi Se was more willing to talk, face red and amber eyes
watery.
“Everyone’s shouting,” he sniffled, rubbing at his cheek. “It’s too much like before. I don’t
like it.”
Before. Zuko didn’t know if he meant Spider or his father. Perhaps both. Likely both. Zuko
knew better than anyone how bad memories tended to lap over each other, until it seemed
like his father’s eyes were the ones staring him down in that cell, until he felt Fong’s touch in
the halls of the palace, each ghost a friend of the next.
“I get it,” Zuko said softly, holding Zi Se’s hand and giving it a squeeze, “but you should talk
to me next time. I'll always get you out, Zi Se. I promise.”
“Promise,” Zi Se repeated in a whisper, before nodding resolutely, offering a wobbly smile.
Zuko grinned back at him, relieved. “Come on, I'll get you something from town.”
“Like what?!” Zi Se perked up instantly, jumping to his feet with his hand still in Zuko’s. The
group had a collected pool of money, but Zuko had his own that he stuffed in his boot.
Another secret he kept for no other reason than just in case.
“Whatever you want,” Zuko said, lifting his obnoxiously big hood up and over his face.
“Unless it’s more than four coppers.”
They passed the morning easily. The town wasn’t large by any means, but the market was
busy on such a clear day, stall after stall selling food and clothes and trinkets, the noises of
people shouting greetings or bartering with one another punctuating the underlying crackle of
food sizzling in pans or on grills, firebending a casual, unobtrusive tool. Zuko had been in a
Fire Nation town not long ago, when he travelled with Zi Se to the Western Air Temple,
stopping to buy clothes, shedding their colours. Zuko hadn’t had time to appreciate the town
then, but he allowed a fondness now, a nostalgia. He remembered seeing street performers
with his mother, remembered Azula’s childish awe at the different masks, remembered
gorging himself on fire flakes.
By the time Tomkin and Nanook found them, Zi Se was giggling in delight while a
stallholder showed him how the arms of a little metal trinket danced in the wind. Zuko
bought it without a word, head down, but Zi Se smiled up at him with enough brightness to
rival Agni.

“There you are!” Tomkin grinned, Nanook giving a jovial little wave from his side. They
were both wearing Fire Nation reds and the sight was so jarring that Zuko could only stare a
moment, shocked to total stillness.
Tomkin just grabbed his elbow and steered him away from the stall.
“We stole some things off a few clothes lines,” Nanook offered when they were out of
earshot.
Zuko yanked his arm back from Tomkin, grumbling. “You look weird.”
“Always so charming,” Tomkin sighed, before focusing on Zi Se. “What you got there, little
man?”
Zi Se proudly held up the trinket, grin gap-toothed and so young that Zuko couldn’t help but
smile, and Tomkin positively lit up. The pair walked ahead as Zi Se explained the trinket in
an overly serious tone to an overly enthused Tomkin, leaving Zuko and Nanook to walk
together.
“How’s Katara?” Zuko braved.
Nanook laughed. “She mellowed out a bit after she upset Zi Se. She says it was Sokka’s fault
but it’s obvious she feels bad. Try not to hold it against her.”
“I wouldn’t,” Zuko scoffed, because for him to hold something like that against someone
would be ironic to say the least.
The familiar smell of fire flakes hit Zuko, and he paused to watch a stallholder shake a bowl
of them with a range of eye-watering spices.
“What on earth is that?” Tomkin hissed, holding his nose like even the smell was
overwhelming.
“Fire flakes,” Zuko said, before giving Tomkin a knowing look. “I doubt you could handle
them.”
Tomkin reacted immediately, gasping before his expression resolved into something
stubborn, determined. Nanook shook his head with a laugh, but bought them each a bag.
Zi Se was delighted with them, happily snacking, his face every so often scrunching at the
heat, and Zuko barely even flinched, always having a higher tolerance for such flavours than
most.
“It doesn’t even look nice,” Nanook despaired as he held one of the crispy snacks in front of
his face.
Tomkin tapped one of his own against Nanook’s piece in a mocking cheers. “We go down
together.”
“Together,” Nanook nodded, and popped it in his mouth in time with Tomkin.

Nanook took it better than Tomkin, at the very least, which was to say that while his
expression immediately flushed and twisted in horror, coughing and spluttering while he
scrambled for his water flask, he didn’t find himself bent half over, practically falling to the
floor in a show of distress that felt distinctly overdramatic.
Zi Se couldn’t stop laughing as he watched the boys, and his unadulterated joy combined
with the idiocy of his friends was too much for Zuko. He laughed shyly at first, trying to bite
it back, but when Tomkin started grasping at Nanook’s leg like he was dying, Zuko couldn’t
help himself, hands covering his mouth to keep back boisterous barks of laughter.
“What the fuck,” Nanook wheezed hoarsely.
Zi Se could barely talk through his giggles. “Language!”
“Tui and La, take me,” Tomkin begged, tears in his eyes. “It’s getting worse. How is it getting
worse? Stop laughing at us and help-.”
“You’re making a scene,” Zuko managed to say, yanking Tomkin to his feet and laughing
harder when the other boy all but collapsed into him.
Zuko pushed him off, unclipping his water flask. “Here, have some water.”
Nanook seemed mostly recovered, looking only a little traumatised as he blinked at their
surroundings like he had no memory of getting here, but Tomkin decided to empty the entire
flask into his mouth, uncaring for how he spilled it everywhere.
“Calm down, you idiot,” Nanook hissed, because now people were really looking. “It goes
away after a while. That's... How is that legal? How are you giving that to a five-year-old? Zi
Se, spit it out!”
Zi Se grinned up at him and arrogantly ate another fire flake, making Nanook gasp in horror.
Zuko just shrugged. “We like spice in the Fire Nation. These aren’t even the strongest ones
I've had.”
“You’re so scary, dude,” Tomkin spluttered, forehead pressed into Nanook’s shoulder, the
picture of a defeated man.
“We’ve got everything we need, we should head back!” a new voice called, and they turned
to see Sokka approaching them. Zuko couldn’t help but laugh again at the miserable way
Tomkin groaned, not even lifting his head from Nanook’s shoulder. Sokka seemed startled,
pausing in front of them and watching Zuko with wide eyes. Zuko's laughter faded quickly,
something anxious replacing it, a heaviness to the words unspoken between him and Sokka.
He almost hoped the other boy would say something, but he simply shook himself out of his
daze, grinning at Tomkin and throwing some teasing comments his way. Zuko wasn’t
listening, and said nothing for the entire walk back to camp, letting their conversations wash
over him.

He wondered how much longer they could ignore this. By the way Nanook nudged him, he
knew it wouldn’t be long.
____
Maybe it was upsetting Zi Se, or the calming, repetitive motions that came with resupplying,
no matter how unfamiliar the town or how itchy the red clothes felt on her skin, but Katara
felt herself stepping away from her anger, at least enough to look at it directly. She felt awful
for how she’d been behaving, but that was almost a motivator. She wanted to feel awful. She
wanted it to be so bad that everyone saw it, everyone felt it. Sometimes, it felt like no one
else was angry for what they’d suffered, which she knew was unfair; who was she to
invalidate how her tribe chose to respond to their collective trauma? Part of her felt that if she
was angry enough, awful enough, then they’d all be forced to tackle it instead of moving on.
Part of her didn’t want to move on. She carried Kanut’s wisdom with her every day, repeating
it like a mantra; sometimes, breaking the cycle can feel like surrendering to what happened,
but it isn’t. It's just how we move on, and how we make ourselves better than the ones who
hurt us. But it was one thing to hear the words spoken, to know they were true, and it was
another thing to convince the little girl inside of Katara who found her mother’s corpse.
Children are not logical, are not bound to the laws of wisdom, and it was a child that Katara
was soothing, and that child was angry.
“Mind if I join you?” Suki’s voice sounded, and Katara blinked, realising she’d been stood at
the vegetable stand, staring at a box of tomatoes in a way that had the stallholder eyeing her
unhappily. She smiled in apology, quickly buying the vegetables she was after.
“Of course,” she said to Suki, moving on to the next stall. Suki clasped her hands behind her
back as she walked, posture relaxed.
It was a little awkward. Katara had been hopeful that another girl in the group would be a
relief, given how disappointing Toph was in that department, but Suki always seemed so...
cool. She was older than Katara, and had dated Sokka, which inherently made their dynamic
quite strange, and Katara didn’t know how to talk to her, and Suki never seemed very
interested in Katara, so they just... hadn’t hung out together alone. Ever.
The thought was jarring, and Katara felt even more awkward than before, wincing as she
thought about how miserable she’d been for days now. Spirits, Suki must find her so
annoying.
“You know,” Suki said, a small smile on her face as she glanced at Katara from the side, “you
can talk to me about what’s bothering you. I won’t tell Sokka. Girl code.”
Katara raised an eyebrow. “Girl code?”
“Yeah!” Suki beamed, nudging Katara a little. “The boys are great and all, and your brother
will always mean the world to me, but sometimes, you need someone who... gets it, you
know? It's probably what I miss most about the Kyoshi Warriors. It sounds silly, but just
being able to talk to my girls about anything and nothing, even if it was just so Aneko could
tell me I was being dumb – it's invaluable.”

Katara had always been starved of girl talk, and to be offered it by a girl who was older and
so infinitely cooler in Katara’s eyes sent a thrill through her. She felt silly for it, but couldn’t
help the shy smile she gave Suki.
“It’s not exactly like anything’s happened,” she said quietly, hesitantly. “I just have good days
and bad days. I don’t know what’s triggered it. Leaving the adults, being in the Fire Nation - I
don’t know, I just can’t stop thinking about it all. The raids, the war, everything they’ve taken
from us, my... my mother.”
Suki frowned sympathetically. Katara didn’t know anything for sure, but she knew Suki was
an orphan, and something would have had to happen to cause that.
“It’s why I struggled so much with Zuko for a long time,” Katara continued, contemplative as
they began making their way back to camp. “It was easy to be angry with him, like he was a
convenient personification of everything I'd ever fought against, but I don’t hate him
anymore. Maybe that’s my problem. I don’t have anywhere to put the anger anymore so it
just... it sits and festers and I hate who I become because of it. I want to... I want to kill the
men who took my mother from me, and what does that make me? A murderer, just like them.
Just as bad as them. What would Aang say?”
“Would you talk to him about it?” Suki asked.
“Aang?” Katara frowned.
“Zuko,” Suki clarified. “You don’t have to, obviously. Just because you’ve forgiven him
doesn’t make it any more his place to speak on these things, and he doesn’t stop being the
prince just because we like him now, but if you could speak to him as just Zuko... as the boy
who went through what he did... I think it could be more helpful than you’d realise.”
The way Suki spoke gave her the impression that she knew something Katara didn’t, but it
was a curious point to make, and instead of dismissing it like she would have done even a
few days ago, Katara thought about it. If there was anyone in their group who’d even come
close to showing anger like Katara, it was Zuko. Past their nationalities and cultures, they
were achingly similar people, and after everything Zuko had been through, Katara had never
quite figured out how he could move on.
They didn’t talk for the rest of the walk, Suki happy to let Katara contemplate her words,
Katara lost in thought as she came to a decision.
____
Zi Se was clingy for the rest of the day, which meant the only time Zuko found himself alone
with Sokka, both being sent to get water from the stream for Katara to start cooking, also
meant the kid followed them. Zuko wasn’t too bothered by it; perhaps Zi Se would mellow
Sokka a little for what promised to be an uncomfortable conversation.
It was silent at first. Zi Se sat on a rock, jabbing a stick into the water, flicking little pebbles
up from the surface, while Zuko and Sokka filled their flasks. Sokka wouldn’t even look at
him, seeing no need for pleasantries now it was just them.

Zuko cleared his throat. “Can we talk?”
Sokka looked up, alarmed, before narrowing his eyes, standing straight and folding his arms.
“Shoot,” he said, raising an eyebrow. He was still touchy from arguing with Katara so much,
and Zuko immediately regretted choosing now of all times to apologise, but he couldn’t let it
drag on another day. He wasn’t built to tiptoe around things like this, always too brash,
always too curt.
“I’m sorry for what happened the other day,” Zuko said, sounding more confident than he
felt, posture rigidly militaristic. “I was out of line and you were right; I was lashing out at
you. I wanted you to rise to it.”
“But why?” Sokka snapped, frustrated. “Why bait me like that? I just wanted to help.”
“You’re always fine, Sokka,” Zuko growled, losing his calm far too quickly as he always did.
“I’m always a mess, always angry, always fucking things up, and you’re always fine. It's hard
being helped by someone like that. I just... I wanted you to be angry too for once.”
“Language,” Zi Se mumbled, like he was trying very hard not to be noticed but couldn’t help
himself. It was so suddenly endearing that Zuko exhaled sharply, smiling a little at the boy.
For some reason, this made Sokka snap, and he stepped forward, jabbing an angry finger to
Zuko’s chest.
“You’re such a jerk,” he hissed. “You’re a jerk and you brought your cute kid here to be
jerkish and I'm sick of being surrounded by jerks. I'm not fine.” He laughed here, a sudden,
hysterical sound. “In fact, I've not felt fine in ages, but people like you and Katara are so busy
agonising over everything to realise that, and it’s a jerky thing to do!”
Zuko blinked, startled by the outburst and not entirely sure what was being said past the
overuse of the word jerk. Sokka's finger was still jabbed into his chest, right over his heart,
and Zuko couldn’t help but glance down at his arm. That feeling from before returned, of
needing to acknowledge the touch, but Sokka mistook it for Zuko being uncomfortable,
quickly pulling his hand back. Even now, he was trying to help him.
I'm not fine. Zuko felt so guilty, because he hadn’t meant to imply otherwise. He knew Sokka
struggled, had wanted to get a rise out of him in order to prove it, but he feared he’d only
isolated Sokka further. The other boy refused to let the others see him like this, always
needing to be mature, in control, fine, but he was showing Zuko, letting it out willingly this
time, and despite being yelled at, Zuko felt a little touched to be trusted with it all the same.
“You told me you would help me,” Zuko said softly, wrapping his fingers around Sokka’s
forearm, reconnecting the touch Sokka had broken. “And you’ve done that. You're still doing
that. You said it didn’t mean you were underestimating me or seeing me as weak; you help
me and you don’t pity me. So let me do the same. Let me help you. Let me carry some of it. I
know why you have to be strong for the others, but from now on, don’t do that with me.
Don't be fine if you’re not.”

Sokka's eyes were wide pools of impossible blue, his skin warm where Zuko touched it, a
tether, a plea. Let me help you. Let us help each other.
“Okay,” Sokka breathed, before swallowing, voice coming out stronger. “Fuck, okay.”
Zuko allowed a small, pleased smile, letting go of Sokka’s arm with a firm nod.
“Language!” Zi Se chimed in, and both boys flinched out of the moment, Sokka laughing at
the little boy watching them closely from the bank.
“So,” Zuko said carefully, “we’re good?”
Sokka rolled his eyes. “Yeah, jerk, we’re good. Come on, let’s head back.”
Zi Se ran ahead happily, and Sokka fell into step beside Zuko, and blessedly, the
awkwardness from the past few days was gone, replaced with something comforting, known,
easy.
“Maybe Katara will be in a better mood,” Zuko said, expecting Sokka to tease, or roll his
eyes at his sister’s behaviour. Instead, he sighed.
“I think I know what’s going on with her,” he said, sounding troubled.
Zuko had suspected that what was bothering Katara was more than just random moodiness
the past few days, but seeing it confirmed in Sokka’s concerned expression made his heart
sink. Sokka was quiet a few moments, trying to find the words, unaccustomed to sharing his
burden, and Zuko waited, enraptured, hanging off any minute change, desperate to do for
Sokka what he’d been able to do for Zuko.
“Our mom...” Sokka started, voice soft, lined with an old grief. “She was killed in a raid
when we were kids, and Katara was the one who found her. She's never been able to get over
it, and sometimes, it gets the better of her. She won’t talk to me about it either, not really. I
guess I didn’t help myself. I just... didn’t talk about Mom for a really long time, and I think
Katara decided that meant I didn’t care, or at least that I didn’t love her like she did.”
Zuko was silent. Tomkin had been the one to tell him about the fate of Hakoda’s wife, Kya,
but hearing it from Sokka was haunting. He'd only been a child, and Katara had been younger
still, their mother stolen from them by raids, Zuko’s own grandfather giving the order. It
made Zuko feel sick. He knew what it was to lose a mother, but to know she had been killed,
to find the body? It was an unrealised horror, one he’d never had to know.
How could Katara stand to look at him? How was a few bad moods every now and then the
worst of her behaviour?
But this wasn’t about him. He thought his words over carefully, recollecting all he knew of
Katara and all he knew of Sokka, finding it easy to paint a picture of what had happened.
“You loved your mother,” Zuko said quietly. “I can tell. People grieve in strange ways.
There's no right way of doing it. People like Katara,” people like me, “can take things too far,
get too angry, make every emotion louder to validate it. That isn’t always a bad thing. Anger

isn’t always a bad thing. People like you and Aang could stand to feel it more, I think.
Refusing yourself the space to grieve isn’t the same as not caring in the first place. It just
means you’re holding off the inevitable.”
Sokka was staring again, eyes a little watery.
“When’d you get so wise, huh?” he sniffed, looking away.
Zuko scoffed, before his face fell, eyes landing on a spot in the distance, unfocusing a little.
“It’s not the same,” he started, swallowing the urge to stamp the words down, “but when I
was in that cell, I detached myself from the pain too. I had a responsibility to keep Zi Se
alive. That was the only thing that mattered. If I spent even a moment thinking about all I'd
lost, all I was still losing, I'd shatter, and then who would be there for him? So I just packed it
all away for months and months, and now, it’s all coming out, something new each day, and
it’s messy and awful... but it gets better. It was gonna happen sooner or later.”
He looked over at the other boy with something like awe. “To live like that for so many
years, prioritising the others over yourself, prioritising your sister, and still having the energy
to make them smile every day - I can’t even imagine what that’s like. You're stronger than
me.”
“Don’t be stupid,” Sokka muttered weakly, head ducked, fists clenched. He stopped walking,
not wanting the camp to see him, and Zuko stopped too, watching, understanding.
“I mean it, Sokka,” he urged, frowning. “Growing up, you were told that getting angry was a
sign of weakness, while I was told it was a strength. Neither are right. Anger just is, and we
all need to find a balance with it. What you’re doing now, acting fine all the time, that’s not
finding a balance. It's not sustainable.”
He knew he was probably pushing too far too soon, so he stopped talking despite the sudden
rush of things he wanted to say, because he knew these feelings, had suffered the hard way to
come to these conclusions, and he realised suddenly that not only did he want to help Sokka,
but he could. He could provide something here. If all he’d suffered simply made him more
equipped for this single conversation with a boy so much better than him, then perhaps it
might have been even a little bit worth it.
But the conversation was delicate, and Sokka would be reeling from it regardless, unused to
voicing what was bothering him. Zuko needed to be careful, tactical. Blind honesty wasn’t
enough.
Still, he couldn’t help but say one last thing. Sokka wouldn’t look at him, and likely wouldn’t
respond, but Zuko needed him to listen.
He spoke on a breath, the words gentle yet urgent, firm.
“She was your mother too.”

Zuko left Sokka, returning to camp alone. For the first time since Zuko had known him,
Sokka missed a meal, and Zuko was saved from having to lie for him when he retreated with
Zi Se to eat, still uncomfortable with eating in such a large group. Katara threw him glances
periodically, but Zuko couldn’t tell if she was holding herself back from asking about Sokka
or apologising for what happened with Zi Se earlier.
Eventually, Sokka returned, and he did so with a wide grin and two dead rabbits, expertly
excusing his absence and distracting everyone with the promise of fresh meat. No one even
questioned it. Zuko wondered how often he’d done that, and meant what he’d said before;
Sokka was one of the strongest people Zuko knew.
____
“Zuko, can I talk to you?” Katara asked quietly when everyone started drifting off to their
tents for the night. She hadn’t had any more arguments with anyone, but the tense, moody
atmosphere of the past few days persisted, making dinner an awkward affair that even
Tomkin, Aang and Toph struggled to fill with their usual noise.
If all went well with their itinerary, they were due to arrive at the White Lotus camp in the
next three days. Katara wanted to fix this before then.
Zuko had the distinct look of someone being caught doing something he shouldn’t, halfway
to his own tent before Katara had stopped him, shoulders hunching when she did.
The only ones still awake were Sokka, Suki and Nanook, and if Katara spoke quietly, they
wouldn’t overhear anything, but still, this conversation felt too large to have out in the open
like this, stood up and casual.
“Is everything okay?” Zuko said carefully, and Katara huffed at being regarded like a
dangerous animal that might lunge at him.
She turned to walk up a slight hill next to their camp. “Follow me.”
He hesitated, but followed. Katara smoothed out the blue folds of her robe as she sat at the
top of the hill, having dressed back into it the moment they returned from town, unlike some
of the others still wearing Fire Nation reds and browns. It was illogical – the new clothes had
been clean and blended them in more – but Katara had needed her familiar blues, had needed
that oppressive red away from her. It was a strange thing to be of importance, but for the first
time as he settled uneasily beside her, Katara wondered if Zuko’s black clothes had been
more of a conscious decision than she’d given him credit for.
She'd been unsure about Suki’s idea to talk to Zuko about this of all things, but she couldn’t
shake the feeling that Suki knew something, something about Zuko, something Katara didn’t
know, and for whatever reason, the other girl thought it was relevant.
Katara decided to be clever about this, and kept her expression calm, confident, her voice
even.

“There’s something you’re not telling me,” she said, staring out at the grass around them, the
stars in the inky sky. It was the exact same as when they’d sat together the other day, hand in
hand, when she’d first admitted to this anger.
Zuko was tense beside her, before sighing in defeat. “This is about the carrots, isn’t it?”
“What?” Katara spluttered, thrown, snapping her head to face him and immediately
forgetting her decision to be cool about this. “Carrots? What do you-?” Her expression
darkened as she connected the dots, gasping in offence. “You! You've been taking them!”
Zuko blinked at her. “Is that... not what you were going to say?”
“No, it very much wasn’t! Oh, I am so cross with you,” she grumbled, crossing her arms and
glaring out at the horizon. Focus, she berated herself. She could yell at him about the carrots
any day. She had to focus.
“We will be talking about that later,” she threatened, turning her glare on him sharply, before
softening again, sighing. “But that’s not what I wanted to talk about. I wanted to tell you...
about my mother.”
Here it was. She was really doing this.
“Sokka told me,” Zuko said quietly, and Katara once again looked at him in surprise. “I’m so
sorry for your loss, Katara.”
They were practised words, required words, formal. She'd heard it a thousand times before,
and while there was a new satisfaction to hearing it from someone who bore the eyes of the
men who committed the act, it still wasn’t what Katara wanted. She didn’t want pity from this
boy, or guilt. She wanted change.
Katara huffed. So Sokka told him, huh? That was... interesting, given that Sokka barely even
talked about Mom with Katara. She didn’t know if she was relieved or bitter.
“No offence, but I wasn’t going to say anything to you about it,” Katara said, picking at a
loose thread on her robe, the blue unspooling in her fingers. “But Suki seemed to think you
might know something about this, and at this point, I'm desperate enough to try. I don’t want
to be angry anymore, Zuko.”
His eyes widened a little in recognition, previous confusion leaving him for something
determined, and he nodded, offering her to continue. Katara quite liked this quiet side of
Zuko. He didn’t sugarcoat things, and didn’t stray from silences most people would find
awkward. It forced her to gather her thoughts, to address the situation head on.
“The men who killed my mother,” she said slowly, breathing through her mouth as she
remembered the acrid smell of ash coating the back of her throat, mixing with blood, “they
were part of a set group of raiders, and they got away unharmed, and I can’t help but think
that they’re still out there. They're just... alive, while my mother is dead, and as a child there
was nothing I could do against them. I was weak and I couldn’t waterbend, but now? I could

kill them. I could actually kill them. There's nothing stopping me from getting on Appa and
hunting every last one of them down. And why shouldn’t I? Why shouldn’t I?”
She'd started crying, quiet and frustrated, biting out each word on a snarl, and through it all,
Zuko said nothing, only watching her. He took his time to collect his thoughts, and Katara
appreciated that, appreciated the time to just breathe and think and be angry.
“I could probably help you find those men, if you wanted,” he finally said, and Katara stared
at him in shock, something cold and awful tracing her spine. Dread. Hope, maybe.
“You... You’re not trying to talk me out of it? You don’t think it’s wrong?” Katara asked
almost desperately, eyes wide as she watched the firebender’s contemplative expression. He
seemed... resigned. There was recognition in his eyes, like he’d been here before, and Katara
suddenly felt so distinctly seen that it sent a bolt of panic through her.
He watched her as she watched him, and spoke lowly. “I think that when you have suffered as
greatly as you have, it’s your choice how you decide to act on it. Killing those men... It will
make things worse in a lot of ways, but it will also correct something, will put something to
bed that’s been up for far too long. It's your choice, Katara, but know I will help you in
whatever you choose, without judgement.”
Katara was stunned, mouth open like an idiot.
“Why are you saying this?” she whispered, words barely audible.
Zuko seemed to war with himself for a moment, shoulders hunching, hands gripping his
knees tightly, before he sighed, breaking eye contact with her to stare at the dirt.
“I killed General Fong,” he said, so simply, so tonelessly. “Sokka, Suki and the adults all
knew, but I guess they never told you guys. But I did. I killed him.”
Some part of Katara thought she already knew this, knew how odd it was that the man
seemed to just disappear from everyone’s narrative despite all he’d done, left to rot in prison
when Katara knew that wouldn’t be good enough for any of them after what he’d put Zuko
through, but to hear it confirmed out loud, to know a man she knew and had spoken with was
now dead and rotting because of the boy right beside her – it was shocking.
And it was liberating. Katara knew only a fraction of the torture Zuko had suffered, but
thinking on it sent the righteous part of her mind into uproar even before she’d forgiven him.
Zuko hadn’t deserved that. No one did. He would live with it forever. In comparison, a
capital punishment felt like the bare minimum.
Katara suddenly knew unquestioningly that Zuko meant what he said; if Katara went through
with this, he wouldn’t judge her. He understood. He'd been where she was and he’d taken the
darker path regardless of what the blood would do to his hands.
Katara stopped crying, expression becoming fierce, blue eyes unblinking as she stared at the
sky.

“Do you regret it?” she asked calmly.
Zuko was undaunted beside her. “No.”
____
Sokka didn’t know what to think. He'd been staring at the roof of his tent for hours now,
going round and round about his conversation with Zuko. She was your mother too. Funny,
how only five words could punch six years of expert avoidance out of Sokka and leave him
scrambling in the wake of his mother’s death all over again, ten again and terrified. Zuko had
said he wanted to help him, had said he was strong, had said he deserved to be angry and no
one... no one had ever spoken to him like that before, let alone someone like Zuko, whose
strength was so impossible to ignore it was almost laughable. Sokka was no one next to him,
yet the way Zuko looked at him... he almost thought...
No, he was being stupid. Suki had been teasing him for days, insisting that there was
something going on with him and Zuko, which yes, there was, because they were friends
now, thank you very much. Buddies. Bros. Who talked about things they didn’t tell anyone
else and shared glancing touches that made Sokka worry he was on fire.
Spirits, he liked Zuko.
He liked liked Zuko, with his stupid, roguish hair and his muscles and his gentle way of
handling Zi Se and his stupid sense of humour and his sheer, stubborn will to keep going.
How could Sokka ever talk to Bato again? This was the worst thing to happen ever, until
Zuko had looked Sokka in the eye and told him he thought Sokka was stronger than him.
Sokka couldn’t sleep, he was so giddy. Zuko was right. Not about the strength thing, but what
he’d said about Sokka’s mom. He'd packed his feelings about her into a tiny box in order to
keep things running at home, to keep Katara as his top priority, and never let himself feel any
of it, and now it was festering inside of him and it wasn’t fair. He wasn’t about to start crying
and blubbering in front of the rest of the group at any given point of the day, but maybe...
maybe he could ease up a bit, now Katara was older and they weren’t in the village.
He'd lost his mother too. He'd been a child too. The thought made something sharp twist in
his chest, and for once, he let it sting.
He was awake until sunrise, thinking, trying to remember his mother’s face, the curve of her
smile, the smell of her parka, the way she used to laugh at Dad’s terrible jokes, the time she
took them penguin sledding, the way it felt to be told she was dead, had been murdered, and
knowing there wasn’t a single thing he could do. Death couldn’t be unwritten. It wasn’t an
easy lesson for a ten-year-old, but he’d been so busy wondering at the horror Katara had
witnessed at only eight to realise his own youth. At the time, he was a big brother before he
was ten, and that was all-encompassing, but out here, with Suki and Tomkin and Nanook,
with Zuko, they were equals and he could have this.
Katara came in when he was just tucking Boomerang into his sheath, about to head outside
for breakfast.

“Morning,” Sokka said, frowning even as he smiled at her, unsure why she was here. If it was
just to yell at him again, well, Sokka was not in the mood-.
“The men who killed Mom,” Katara said briskly, and wasn’t that a quick way of crashing any
train of thought Sokka could have possibly had? “I’m going to find them and I'm going to kill
them.”
Sokka blinked at her for a few agonisingly long seconds.
“You... what?!” he hissed, finding his voice even if the words came out strangled. He was
sure he’d misheard, or perhaps was having a really fucked up dream, or maybe Katara was
sick. He placed a hand to her forehead to check, but she swatted him away.
“I mean it,” she snapped, resolute. “I’m going to kill them. You can’t stop me.”
“Uh. Yes, I can. What is happening right now?”
She... was being serious. Tui and La, she was being serious. His fourteen-year-old sister
wanted to commit premeditated murder.
And with that, she gave him a firm nod and turned around, like there was nothing else to be
said or done. Sokka stood there spluttering for a few moments, staring at where she’d stood,
before surging forwards and stomping after her.
“Katara!” he shouted. “There’s so much wrong with that! You don’t even know who did it,
for starters, and if you did, how would you find them? And where is this even coming from?”
Katara whirled around to face him, expression still so determined, eyes stormy.
“I’m tired of knowing they’re out there, living, enjoying life, while Mom is dead,” Katara
hissed, voice cracking a little. She looked so young and so old at once, and Sokka didn’t
know what to do with it. “They don’t get to have that. They don’t deserve it. And as for
finding them, Zuko said he can-.”
“Wait, Zuko?” Sokka hissed. He felt something like betrayal crawling up his throat, choking
him, stealing all the air. Around the fire, the rest of their group were awake and watching, all
of them confused save one, who met Sokka’s gaze and held it.
Katara, his baby sister, wanted to hunt down and kill the men who murdered their mother,
wanted to willingly, consciously bloody her hands when Sokka had lost so much sleep hiding
the worst of the war from her on their travels, and Zuko was handing her the tools to do it,
had told her it was okay.
“What’s going on?” Aaag asked timidly. Spirits, what would Aang say? At least he would try
and talk Katara out of it while Sokka dealt with Zuko. He shamelessly threw his sister at the
Avatar’s mercy.
“Katara has decided to go on a mission to kill the men who murdered our mother in the
raids,” he spat, and Aang gasped, those wide, grey eyes turning to Katara, who held her head
up proudly even as she trembled beneath the group's judgement.

Toph let out a low whistle. “Damn.”
“Katara...” Nanook started gently, placatingly, like he was approaching a wounded animal.
“You can’t talk me out of it!” Katara snapped, before turning on her heel and rushing to her
tent. Aang followed her quickly. Toph gave them a few moments before the sound of an
argument could be heard past the tent’s material, and she got up with a sigh.
It left the five older members of the group and a very nervous Zi Se. Suki looked shocked,
still staring at Katara’s tent, and Tomkin’s head was down, fingers tapping erratically on his
leg. He knew better than most the pain of the raids, what it had cost them, what it was still
costing them.
Nanook was watching Sokka watch Zuko, blue eyes flicking between the boys, Zuko’s hard
stare, Sokka’s growing fury.
“Guys-.”
“How could you do this?” Sokka growled before Nanook could try and placate him. Zuko
remained expressionless. “She’s fourteen. She wants to kill someone and you humoured her.”
“I’m going to check on Appa with Zi Se,” Tomkin said suddenly, pushing himself to his feet
and offering his hand to the little boy. Zi Se hesitated, waiting for Zuko’s nod of approval,
before leaving with Tomkin, and past his rage, Sokka was grateful for that. This wasn’t an
easy conversation for Tomkin and it wasn’t something Zi Se should hear, regardless of all
he’d seen.
Zuko started speaking the moment they were out of earshot.
“She deserves to have a choice in this,” he said calmly. “I didn’t encourage her nor did I
discourage her. I just made it clear that if she chose to go through with it, I could help.”
“I thought... I thought you got it,” Sokka whispered, shaking his head. “I thought you
understood but you just... you... you of all people should know why this is such a bad idea.
She'll be haunted by it for life.”
“Me of all people?” Zuko asked, voice getting an agitated edge to it as he walked closer to
get into Sokka’s space, glaring at him. “That’s exactly why I'm not judging her. I would do it
all again if I had to, and I had to. It isn’t a choice, not in the way you think. I couldn’t live
knowing he was alive out there, and Katara... She’ll never be able to heal properly knowing
those men are living unpunished.”
“And that’s what this is? Punishment?” Sokka snapped. “So what, you just decide who
deserves to die and then you murder them? That's not justice, it’s tyranny, but I guess that’s
something else you of all people can understand. You're your father’s son after all-.”
"Sokka!” Nanook yelled, but Sokka barely heard him as Zuko lunged forward, grabbing him
by the collar until their faces were only inches apart.
“I,” Zuko growled, golden eyes blazing with anger, with horror, “am nothing like my father.”

“You’re a murderer,” Sokka breathed, those scarred hands that had touched him so gently
yesterday now careless in their strength. “And now you want to make a murderer of my little
sister.”
There was a knot in his throat, tight and suffocating, and he wanted to cry, to swear, but he
held that golden gaze. Slowly, Zuko let him go, collecting himself.
“She’s seen too much of this war for you to be treating her as some naïve child,” he said, and
he almost sounded sorry. “She knows the severity of this. She knows the consequences. This
is her grief, Sokka.”
“What about my grief?!” Sokka yelled.
It was too much, voice breaking and the tears finally falling. Every memory of his mother
that Sokka had painstakingly dragged to the surface last night now flooded him,
overwhelming him completely with the agony they brought. She was everywhere, in
everything, and those men were still taking things from Sokka even after all these years,
wanted to kill the part of his sister that was kind, humane, empathetic.
Zuko’s eyes widened, like he’d been missing something and finally had it put before him in
plain terms. He looked guilty, eyes flickering over Sokka as his tears fell quietly.
“Let’s give them a moment,” Suki said gently, and Sokka saw her and Nanook leave from the
corner of his eye.
Zuko made to step forward, hesitating, movements awkward, unsure in a way he rarely was,
and Sokka wanted his hands on him again, something violent, something tender. Anything to
distract him from the sadness he was choking on, a grief so massive he couldn’t even
comprehend it in its entirety.
“Sokka...” Zuko said softly, and that was what did it, Sokka’s feet carrying him until he was
throwing himself at the other boy, hugging him tight like he might be able to tether them
both, fists gripping the fabric of Zuko’s shirt and Zuko... Zuko held him back. Jittery at first,
coordinating them into a position that felt less like Sokka was trapping him in place, before
those strong arms became firm around Sokka’s torso, fingers tracing soothing patterns against
his back.
Those hands had killed, could summon fire and push it into Sokka’s skin, but here, they were
comforting, safe, and Sokka let himself break beneath them.
“I’m sorry,” Zuko kept saying, whispered against Sokka’s hair. “I’m sorry, I'm sorry, I'm
sorry.”
____
Katara had to tune Aang out as he tried to reason with her. She wouldn’t be dissuaded. She
wouldn’t. She had to do this. It was the right thing to do, whether Aang agreed or not. That
day when they all got on Appa for another gruelling leg of travelling, Katara ignored
everyone and sat beside her brother, at the end of the saddle in their own little pocket of

privacy. Sokka looked harrowed, somehow so much more exhausted than when he’d woken
up.
Despite everything, Katara hoped he wouldn’t be angry with her now he’d had time to come
to terms with her decision. She loved her brother, and the thought of disappointing him was
unbearable. Say something, she wanted to plead into the silence between them. Tell me you
understand.
“Do you remember when we were little and we both got sick at the same time?” Sokka asked
suddenly, voice soft, reminiscent.
Katara blinked. “No?”
“You were really young,” Sokka said, staring at his hands. “No older than four. We were sick
for days, curled up in bed together, completely miserable. Kanut would make us this one tea
that was absolutely disgusting, and the whole time, Mom was there. She barely left us, even
when Kanut said she’d get sick too. You weren’t sleeping well and it was making you fussy,
so she’d sing to us. Every night.”
Katara’s throat was tight as she listened, eyes watery, a small smile on her face as she tried
desperately to remember. For years, it had felt like all she had of her mother was what she
could remember, that forgetting something was equivalent to losing her all over again, but
Sokka was older and remembered more, and for the first time, he was sharing it with her. If
forgetting was like Mom dying again, then being given new memories was like life being
breathed into her, even if only for a fleeting, beautiful moment.
“Did she get sick in the end?” she asked gently, almost scared of spooking Sokka.
He cracked a grin, finally meeting her eyes. “The very next week.”
It was a long ride on Appa, and Sokka and Katara talked. They shared what they could
remember of Mom and they addressed how Dad leaving them behind had changed things,
casting a wedge between them as Sokka forced himself to take all the responsibility alone,
without Katara. Sokka explained how desperate he was to make Dad proud and that, initially,
he’d felt like Zuko was replacing him in Dad’s eyes, and how they’d resolved it. Katara
explained her anger, how much it scared her, how desperate she was for somewhere to put it.
He berated her for not talking to him sooner and she berated him for his hypocrisy, and they
decided to be more honest with each other in the future. No more secrets. Upon that, Sokka
told Katara about Fong, about watching him die, watching Zuko kill him, and for a moment,
they both looked at the firebender sat ahead of them and the little boy safe at his side.
Through it all, even when they lost their temper or became upset, the conversation was
gentle, and they apologised over and over again, Katara gripping her brother’s hand tightly in
hers.
Eventually, Sokka sighed.
“Well?” he said, defeated. “Will you kill him?”

He wasn’t fighting her on it anymore. There was a finality to it.
“I don’t know,” Katara said honestly.
Later, she found Zuko again, sitting with him at the edge of their newest camp, and he asked
her the same question, a hesitance to him that he hadn’t had the day before. Katara turned it
back on him.
“If there had been another way,” she said carefully, “would you have taken it?”
She knew he’d understand what she was asking.
Zuko’s expression became distant, sad, and Katara knew he was back in that room. He would
always be in that room, sword in hand, body at his feet.
“In a heartbeat,” Zuko whispered.
There was a lot left unsaid. If Zuko could have healed any other way, he would have. This
group, their friends – they were Katara’s other way. If Zuko had someone, he might have
been saved from the darkness he was forced into, but nobody had known how to help him.
He was alone there, alone in that cell, alone in that room. Katara wasn’t alone, and she knew
in that moment with startling clarity that she could kill the men who took her mother from
her, and her brother would still love her, Zuko would understand her, Aang would forgive her.
They would all move on eventually and Kya would finally, finally be avenged.
But that wasn’t who Katara was. It wasn’t who she had to be. For that, she was both grateful
and angry. She always would be. This anger was her mother’s memory just as much as the
love.
“I’ve made my decision,” Katara said.
Zuko looked at her like he already knew.
____
Katara wouldn’t kill those men. The relief of her choice swept wordlessly through the group,
Aang’s happy smile reignited on his face, and they fell back into their routine, passing the
days training and travelling. They would arrive at the White Lotus camp soon, but the few
days separated from the adults felt mammoth, like everything had changed in their short time
apart. Things had certainly changed with Sokka. He looked more content, confident in his
interactions with Katara in a way that seemed different than before, and Zuko’s dynamic with
him had shifted. It was a subtle thing, but it was there, the other boy now seeking him out,
sitting next to him when he could, offering casual touch, and Zuko liked it, liked knowing he
was safe to the other boy, liked knowing he was helping Sokka just as he did for him. It felt
like his correct place in the group. A fighter. Someone who protects. It was what kept him
sane in that cell, and he knew Zi Se did more for him than Zuko could ever have returned. He
remembered Uncle’s words. Martyrdom and self-destruction are two very different things.
Zuko could tell himself what he liked, but he knew the truth – he killed Fong for no one but
himself. Zi Se had just been an excuse.

Seeing Katara, someone so similar to him, walk away from a fate Zuko hadn’t been able to
escape left him feeling torn. There was a sense of satisfaction, like if he couldn’t save himself
then at the very least he’d been able to save Katara, like perhaps it wasn’t always supposed to
end this way. But it had. It had ended that way for Zuko and there was a grief to that. Zuko
lost a piece of himself to his rage that Katara hadn’t. He would always be a little bitter at the
world for it.
It was all so complicated, but here he was at the end of it all, and this, what he had with this
group, was good. It was nice. Having a group of people was nice. Having a routine was nice.
Katara’s laughter ringing through the morning when she found two carrots outside her tent
was nice. Hugging Sokka was nice.
Perhaps there was nothing else to it.
