It had been Zuko’s idea. It made sense at the time, sat beside Sokka and deciding where to
stop next on their route, the words leaving Zuko’s mouth on the basis of logic before he could
even contemplate what it would mean, and now Appa was touching down on the soft sands

of Ember Island, and Zuko was back in the only place that had ever felt close to a real home
to him.
He’d done well to keep Azula from his thoughts since her appearance at the Air Temple. It
wouldn’t do either of them any good to agonise over it. He could hear her in his head. So
emotional, Zu Zu. Always creating problems that aren’t even there.
But she was here, on this island. Not in person, but in the crash of the waves, the smell of
salt, the creaking beams of the house. Unignorable. His little sister in a thousand bleeding
splinters.
Conflating that with that appearance of the Avatar’s group, of Zi Se, of Tomkin and Nanook,
was jarring, to say the least. Toph was already throwing seaweed at Katara, sat near the dune
Zuko had sat with Mai when they first realised the extent of his injured leg. The campfire sat
cold and charred beneath the sun where Zuko and Azula had shared their blue fire
It all felt... ghostly. Something had lived and died here, but hadn’t moved on. Zuko didn’t
know how to talk about it, so he followed the others silently as they made their way into the
house.
“Which room was yours, Zuko?” Suki asked once they reached the wooden porch, peering
into the open corridors wondrously.
“End of the hall,” Zuko said. “On the right.”
“And which room was Ozai’s? You know, so we can decontaminate it. Maybe light some
sage.” Tomkin elbowed Nanook with a snicker, causing the other boy to roll his eyes. Still,
Zuko decided to just give everyone a quick tour. In the end, the others decided to set up camp
in the courtyard, no one wanting to voice their discomfort at sleeping somewhere Zuko’s
family had.
He wasn’t offended. Even he felt wrongfooted here. There was a tension in the group,
everyone at once existing in the anticipation before a question was asked, and Zuko knew it
was only a matter of time, so he hid in his room, the only one to sleep in the actual house, and
unpacked some things for the single night Sokka had permitted them to rest here.
They gave him some space, thankfully, but he’d have to resurface eventually.
____
The sun beamed down on them overhead as Aang chased Zi Se across the beach, kicking up
water from the shallows and cackling loudly at the delighted squeal the little boy let out upon
being grabbed beneath the armpits and lifted into the air, a boost of airbending sending them
much higher than normal.
“Again! Again!” Zi Se demanded the moment his bare feet returned to the wet sand.
“Sure thing, Zi Se!” Aang said, smiling. “We can play whatever you want.”

And they did. Aang knew the others found it a little tiring constantly humouring Zi Se’s
childish side, but Aang didn’t mind it one bit. Fun and play were integral to a happy life, at
any age. Monk Gyatso had always said so, and no one really played with Aang anymore. It
was always war talk, war talk, war talk, and he was sick of it. It was so depressing.
Zi Se’s latest game of tag was much more interesting, albeit different than how Aang had
played before.
“Tag!” Zi Se yelled, out of breath from chasing Aang while the airbender zipped and hopped
around, grin victorious.
Aang beamed back at the little boy, before exaggeratingly falling back into the sand. “Oh no!
You caught me!”
“You’re dead now, you have to go stand over there,” Zi Se said matter-of-factly, pointing over
at the little rock pile he’d gathered in preparation for the game.
Aang tilted his head, confused. “I thought that was a base camp?”
“No,” Zi Se huffed. “It’s where you go when you’re dead. I caught you so you’re dead.”
“Dead seems a little...” Aang struggled for a word that wouldn’t dismiss Zi Se’s game.
“Extreme? How about we just make that be the loser camp? I'm the loser ‘cause you caught
me, so I’m stuck there while you tell everyone you won-!”
“No!” Zi Se said, surprisingly frustrated. “I caught you so you’re dead.”
For a moment, they stared at each other, the younger boy growing increasingly frustrated,
like he wanted to express something but didn’t have the words, and Aang growing
increasingly uncomfortable. He didn’t want to humour this, not even for the sake of Zi Se’s
fun. He didn’t want to play at dying. He didn’t want it to be something Zi Se knew, let alone
be so adamant about. He wished none of them had to know it. I caught you so you’re dead.
Zi Se had a brother, once. Sokka had told them, and they each quietly held the truth of it in
every exchange they had with the boy, but only Zuko and Zi Se knew what really happened
the day Lanse was killed. How did a five-year-old even make sense of death? Aang was twice
Zi Se’s age and still couldn't quite wrap his mind around the concept of all his old friends
being gone.
Aang wished he knew what to say to Zi Se, some Avatar wisdom, or maybe just comfort from
someone older, but he felt so painfully young in that moment, clueless and searching and
grieving in spite of it all.
“I don’t think I want to play this game anymore,” Aang said quietly.
Zi Se looked confused, then sad, and kicked at the sand indignantly before stomping off,
sulking. Aang let him go, not knowing what else to do.
____

Most of the rooms in the beach house were open, either by having entire walls that looked out
onto the courtyard or large windows with thrown open shutters. The kitchen was no different,
a soft sea breeze perpetually dancing between the pots and pans hanging from exposed
beams, oil lamps flickering as the sun began to set. It was a relatively big kitchen, with thin
shoji panels pushed aside to reveal the courtyard where Katara had decided they would eat,
but compared to a palace, Zuko had always found the Ember Island house... cosy. He decided
not to voice that thought, for fear of ridicule from his friends. They'd been set up in the
kitchen for a while now, laughing as they cooked, excited at the prospect of so many utensils
at their disposal, as well as a lot of food and spices in the cupboards that weren’t at risk of
going bad. Katara was in such a good mood she was even letting people help her. Willingly.
Suki was cutting vegetables with Sokka, Katara herself was mixing something that smelled
amazing in a large pot, Tomkin and Nanook were on the courtyard steps preparing tea for
everyone, and Toph was sat on a counter, kicking her feet back and forth, apparently having
been benched upon immediately setting something on fire. Zuko had joined her nervously,
not knowing how to help without inevitably getting in the way.
The overwhelming smell of food made Zuko’s stomach twist longingly, and with it, that
familiar stab of violence. He was better on the sidelines, he decided. Things had been going
well lately; he didn’t want to push it.
“Hey guys!” Aang chirped, entering from the corridor with a grin. “Whatcha making?”
Zi Se ran in ahead of the airbender, making straight for Zuko and wordlessly tugging at his
trouser leg. Zuko frowned, picking the little boy up and holding him on his hip, gold eyes
searching amber. Zi Se wasn’t nearly as clingy as he used to be, and generally only wanted
Zuko to pick him up like this when he was upset about something.
Zi Se’s expression was frustrated, but he didn’t say anything in response to Zuko’s
questioning look, only scowling before hiding his face in the crook of Zuko’s neck. Zuko
looked over to Aang, hoping the airbender had some sort of explanation, but he was chatting
away to Katara excitedly. Almost too excitedly, like he was pointedly avoiding looking
Zuko’s way.
Zuko narrowed his eyes, but was stopped from saying anything when Katara announced that
the food was ready and to help carry bowls out.
“Can you believe we’re gonna be at the White Lotus camp in only two days?” Katara asked
the group with a smile as she joined them on the steps, settling back with her bowl. “I know
it’s not been long, but I miss having the others with us.”
“I just hope they haven’t run into any trouble on the way,” Sokka sighed, already halfway
through his portion. “Or caused any.”
Zuko thought of Chena’s ineffable ability to start a fight, and smirked. Sokka, who was sat
next to him, offering a firm barrier between Zuko, Zi Se and the rest of the group, looked
ecstatic at the admission of amusement, making Zuko bite back his smile on principal.

“Please, they’ll be fine,” Tomkin said, flapping a hand in the air. “They might have even
beaten us. The Spirits know Bato would bet on something like that, and Aput has a nasty
competitive streak when it suits him.”
Everyone laughed, rolling their eyes and sharing knowing smiles, sated by warm food and
good company. There was a dark voice in Zuko’s mind that wanted to pull him back from this
moment and make him dissect it, wonder at what he would have done if he’d known of this
back then, but he pushed it away. He wanted to just exist here.
The mood was sobered by the most unlikely person. Aang had been quiet since they’d come
outside, and Zuko still didn’t know what had caused Zi Se’s odd sulking, though the little boy
had clearly moved on if the way he was trying to sneak away some of Nanook’s food while
he wasn’t looking was anything to go by.
When Aang spoke now, his voice was quiet, thoughtful, and beneath it all, he sounded
scared.
“I can’t believe we’ll have to fight the Fire Lord soon.”
Zuko felt his food turn ash-like in his mouth, forcing it down with a dry swallow. Flashes of
his father’s face, always framed in fire or lightning, flickered through his mind. He had
existed here, at the beach house. There were memories here. A looming shadow in the
corridors. A master bedroom Zuko and Azula were not allowed to enter. Their mother’s
muted smiles.
Sozin's Comet was coming. Time was running out. It would be the fight of their lives, and for
Zuko, who had fought for every day of his life, a bone-deep tiredness overwhelmed him.
“It doesn’t feel real,” Tomkin concurred, staring into his teacup. “Like, the Fire Lord himself
doesn’t even feel real. He doesn’t feel like one man.”
There were several murmured agreements, and Zuko realised, dumbly, that he was the only
person here who’d met Ozai. Everyone seemed to realise it at the same time as him, because
Tomkin blinked, head snapping in Zuko’s direction.
“I mean, obviously he’s real,” Tomkin spluttered. “I just mean-.”
“I know what you mean,” Zuko said cooly.
Aang was staring at him, and spoke before Tomkin could dig himself a hole.
“When the comet comes,” the Avatar said, words oddly careful, “do you think... is there a
way we can defeat him without fighting him?”
A chorus of ‘huh’ and ‘what’s sounded from the group, blindsided by the question, and Zuko
found himself staring right back at the Avatar, uniter of nations, bringer of peace, twelveyear-old boy.
“You’re kidding, right?” Zuko hissed.

Aang shook his head. “I just think... He doesn’t know us, he hates us, I get that, but you’re
his son-.”
“The fuck’s that got to do with anything?”
“Don’t swear at him,” Katara berated quietly, but even that felt more knee-jerk than like she
was actually annoyed with Zuko, her blue eyes boring into Aang in frustration and confusion.
Nanook tried a more gentle approach. “Aang, I don’t think Zuko can change his father’s mind
on this.”
Zuko was too baffled by the sudden conversation to even be upset. Why on earth would they
think Zuko could just talk to Ozai? It was laughable. In fact, he felt that hysterical need to
laugh bubbling in his chest, too tight, off-kilter. How could the Avatar be so clueless?
“So, just to be clear,” Zuko asked, letting out a dry huff of laughter, “you want me to... speak
out against my father? Tell him what he’s doing is wrong? Appeal to his humanity? And you,
what, think that because I'm his son, he has to listen to me?”
And Aang, stupid, young Aang, hesitated before giving a hopeful nod.
Zuko couldn’t help it; he laughed freely then, shaking his head, clutching his stomach with
one hand, his free hand reaching for his face, digging into his scar. They didn’t know. Hakoda
had never told them. It was... sweet, in a sense. Hakoda had kept this for Zuko to share if and
when he wanted to, even when the chief owed him nothing, but it never stopped hurting.
Each time Zuko had to declare his father’s lack of love for him, it felt like being burned all
over again.
Ozai had left him to rot in an Earth Kingdom cell. Ozai had only been proud when Zuko
killed Fong. Ozai banished him, burned him, mutilated him, and Aang didn’t even want to
fight him, to fight the one man in all the nations who indisputably deserved punishment.
Zuko’s father died the day of the lightning strike, crackling revelation jumping from his
hands into Zuko’s, ricocheting around the throne room before finding home in his father’s
empty chest. The world ended that day, and opened up into a new world, one where Zuko
might live softly. It didn’t matter what happened next in this war, or how Aang would defeat
Ozai, or how the man would die. It mattered only that they won. Zuko was grieving a man
still breathing. It was more courtesy than Ozai had ever granted Zuko in return.
“Zuko?” Sokka placed a nervous hand to Zuko’s shoulder when his laughter petered off, and
Zuko shrugged him away. He couldn’t be touched right now.
“He won’t change his mind,” Zuko said drily, staring at his hand now in his lap, fingers
curling, crooked in places from being broken and rebroken too many times. “Not about this.
Not about anything. I'm the last person who could convince him.”
Aang still had that stupid sparkle in his eye, and even Katara looked considering.
“But-.”

“But nothing!” Zuko snapped, finally addressing the group as a whole. “I tried to change his
mind about something three years ago, and this,” he gestured at his face, “is where it got me.
Why do you think something this substantial would be any different?”
Silence. Eyes watching him, unblinking. Breaths held. It felt good to say it, to snap teeth in
warning, but Zuko wanted to retreat all the same. This was one more thing to surrender.
“What do you mean by that?” Nanook finally asked, voice hushed.
Zuko suddenly remembered the South Pole, the burn-turned-scar on Tomkin’s arm, and
remembered that Tomkin and Nanook knew something the others could only guess at –
Zuko's scar was personal. It was no accident. They'd respected him enough since that
incident to let it go, to not pry, to trust him to come to them when he was ready, but they’d
never... they’d never figured it out. It made sense, but Zuko always felt so known by them
that such a fundamental part of him still being a mystery just seemed impossible.
Dread kept a matching vigil on both their faces now.
All the fight left Zuko on an exhale, and he ducked his head, unable to handle the ferocity of
so much attention on a wound that would always be raw.
“It doesn’t matter now-.”
“It does,” Tomkin said vehemently, blue eyes wide.
The others nodded in agreement.
Eventually, Zuko sighed.
“My first war meeting...” he said, tongue thick in his mouth. “I was thirteen, and one of the
generals suggested sending a division of new recruits into battle as a diversion. He intended
for their slaughter to benefit the bulk of the army.”
Katara gasped. “That’s terrible.”
A morbid smile twisted at Zuko’s mouth. Once, he’d tried to defend the action, tried to find
the logic in his father’s cruelty, tried to find his own fault through it all. Not anymore. Katara
was right. It was terrible, the whole bloody saga. He wouldn’t waste any more days
defending Ozai.
“I argued it,” Zuko said simply, golden eyes tracing the scars littering his hands and arms.
“But me speaking out was taken as an act of disrespect, so I was challenged to an Agni Kai.”
“A fire duel?” Aang asked, head tipping to the side, birdlike. “I thought you had to be sixteen
or older for those?”
Zuko scoffed. “That’s technically the law, yes.”
His words settled over the group like ash, each expression pulled into a troubled, nervous
frown.

“I’d spoken out against the general who suggested the plan,” Zuko continued, “but it was my
father’s war room – the slight was to him, not the general, so it was him who I wound up
facing on the Agni Kai grounds.”
Each time he blinked, he was back there, the sun heavy on his bare back, the prayer shawl
falling from his shoulders, a million hungry eyes and not a single voice to defend him.
“Your father...” Nanook said slowly, anger dripping into his voice. “Your father tried to duel
you when you were thirteen?”
Zuko hummed in confirmation. “I refused to fight him. Begged him to forgive me. Prostrated
myself. He said I was only furthering my own dishonour, and that he needed to teach me a
lesson.” Zuko worked his jaw, clenching his fists, and grit out the next words. “So he held my
face and burned me.”
Aang’s hands flew to his mouth, Katara letting out a horrified gasp, and Tomkin had tears in
his eyes, lips parted. The others watched him with quiet, contemplative looks of realisation.
Even Toph, whose mouth was twisted down, looked troubled. Zi Se leaned his weight against
Zuko. He knew he probably shouldn’t discuss something like this in front of the little boy, but
he’d never intended to talk about this today in the first place. He made a mental note to have
a long talk with Zi Se later, to reassure him that he was okay, that they were both safe now,
just like he promised.
Even if Zuko would return to war with the comet. Even if he would leave Zi Se behind once
more.
“The burn I could handle,” Zuko said quietly, words he’d never voiced before. “The pain, the
scarring, the punishment – none of it was new from him. But he... he banished me. He said I
couldn’t return home unless I restored my honour by finding the Avatar.” Aang flinched. "At
the time, no one thought it could be done. For three years, no one thought it could be done.
He never once hoped for my return, I know that now, but I wanted so badly to come home...
and then suddenly, you appeared.”
He gave Aang a wry smile, small, weak against the weight of his words, but genuine. The
Avatar looked harrowed by his story, grey eyes filled with tears.
“That’s why you were hunting me?” he asked quietly.
Zuko nodded, before swallowing, clearing his throat awkwardly and setting his bowl down.
“It doesn’t matter now. It's done. I’m sorry...” He looked around at the assortment of halffinished dinners. “Sorry, let’s finish eating. I didn’t mean to-.”
Sokka grabbed Zuko’s arm just as he reached to tug at his own hair anxiously, careful not to
hold too tight but keeping his touch firm, grounding, slowly pulling his arm down to rest
between them.
“Thank you for telling us,” Sokka said gently.

Zuko’s entire face flooded with heat.
“Yeah,” he said, like an idiot.
“We’ll kill him,” Nanook said suddenly, gaze fierce, tone an unmoving growl. “The Fire Lord
will pay for what he’s done to everyone. Whatever it takes, we'll win.”
The intensity of his words stunned Zuko to silence, such a brash statement from a boy usually
so contained, so intentional. Zuko could hear Nanook’s anger, his grief, and knew it wasn’t
just for the war he had been forced into so young, for everything and everyone he’d lost to it,
but for Zuko too. Zuko, his friend, against all odds.
Shy grins broke out, tentative hope. Zuko held Nanook’s stare, swallowing the lump in his
throat as he pictured his father dead in his own throne room, and nodded.
“Fire Lord Ozai is no match for Team Avatar!” Tomkin cheered, pumping his fist in the air,
though the confidence was lost a little to the way he’d clearly been trying not to cry only
moments before, nose running. Nanook bumped his shoulder with an eye roll, at once teasing
and supportive. Zuko couldn’t help but smile then. He felt so completely like he was part of
something, something big, something greater than all of them.
Change, finally, was coming. They would herald the new dawn. Peace – hard-earned, gentle
peace – would finally rest in their hands.
“We’ll win,” Aang agreed, the only one not matching their smiles, gaze on the floor, “but I
can’t kill the Fire Lord.”
“Sure you can, Twinkletoes,” Toph said, her grin all teeth. “We’re still training you up. No
student of mine will embarrass me in front of the Fire Nation.”
“And you’ll have us to help you,” Katara said, soft and determined in turn. “You don’t have
to defeat him alone.”
Aang looked troubled. “That’s not my point. I know we can defeat him, but I won’t kill him.”
Oddly, it was Zi Se who Aang’s gaze landed on when he looked up. The little boy was
frowning, not nearly disturbed enough by the subject matter as he should have been, but
confused all the same. Aang stared at him for a few moments, before shaking his head.
“Sorry, I'm tired,” he said, faking a yawn. “I’m gonna go to bed early.”
“The sun hasn’t even set yet,” Sokka pointed out, but Aang was already making his way over
to his tent. They all watched him duck inside and pull the flaps down firmly behind him,
throwing confused glances to each other like anyone might have an explanation for the
Avatar’s odd behaviour.
“What does he mean, he won’t kill him?” Tomkin hissed quietly, earning an elbow from
Nanook.
“Maybe he’s just got cold feet?” Suki suggested.

“I think it’s best we just leave him be for now,” Katara said, clearly worried. “He’s been
training so hard, it makes sense he’s tired.”
The others agreed and began packing away their dishes, but Zuko continued staring at Aang’s
tent, a strange knot of dread settling in his stomach. He couldn’t shake the feeling that they
were missing something.
____
Everyone split up after dinner, the benders doing some light training in the dusk, Suki
running through her own katas, and Sokka taking Zi Se back to the beach to play. It left Zuko,
Tomkin and Nanook in the kitchen to wash up, and they settled into an easy routine of
Nanook washing, Zuko drying, and Tomkin putting everything back in content silence, only
speaking to ask Zuko where certain things went. Still, Nanook could feel a tension in the air,
a conversation waiting to be had, and by the time he started running out of dishes to
methodically scrub past the point of cleanliness, he felt like he was choking the words back.
It took his hand knocking into Zuko’s for him to finally speak.
“I wish we’d known sooner,” he blurted out, guilt in every letter, both for his selfishness to
say such a thing, and for his friend’s perpetual suffering in silence. “It could... I wouldn’t
have been so hard on you, at the beginning.”
Tomkin looked over at Nanook, bewildered, but decided to let the conversation play out for
now. Zuko didn’t look up from where he was delicately wiping a plate with a cloth, using his
firebending to warm it.
Eventually, he said, “I deserved it.”
“You were scared.”
“So were you.”
Those golden eyes never stopped being so piercing. For a moment, they just stared at each
other.
“That day in the village, with the fire,” Tomkin said carefully, making them both turn to him
as he traced his fingers over the scar on his arm. “You told Hakoda, didn’t you?”
Zuko almost looked like he was going to reach for Tomkin then, eyes wide and wanting, like
even just touching the scar might confirm something, or reassure him, or scare him away
entirely. It was always hard to tell with the prince.
He ducked his head. “I did. It's why he changed his mind about me, I think. I didn’t really get
it at the time. I think I do now.”
Because the concept of the chief deciding to spare Zuko simply because he saw a boy who
was hurting and wanted to help was so foreign to the firebender that it had taken him months
to come to terms with it, just as he’d needed his father to abandon him to torture in an Earth
Kingdom prison before he even considered letting him go. It was devastating, the shackles of

Zuko’s devotion, how much he was willing to let the people he loved hurt him, never once
questioning if they even loved him back, and so often they hadn’t.
So often, Prince Zuko of the Fire Nation had devoted himself to undeserving causes and
suffered gladly for them.
Nanook was helpless in this war. He didn’t have the horror of a destiny, like Zuko and Aang.
He wasn’t a prodigy, like Katara and Toph. If not for the definitions of those that loved him,
Nanook would be another faceless soldier, sent forward into battle, but he was loved, and it
made him known. It made him matter.
He wanted Zuko to know he mattered too. He couldn’t save him from what he’d suffered, but
he could comfort him now.
Nanook dropped the handful of chopsticks he’d been washing and turned to face Zuko,
overly-serious and making the firebender blink at him in surprise, tipping his head to the side
a little like he was about to ask a question.
Before he got the chance, Nanook was hugging him, not so tight as to spook the other boy,
but holding him close, tucking his chin over his shoulder and scowling at the blinding grin
Tomkin sent his way.
“Is this really necessary-?”
“Group hug!” Tomkin announced, before throwing himself onto both of them, knocking into
Nanook’s ribs.
It was too warm and Nanook’s hair was caught in someone’s armpit and Zuko looked like he
might set all three of them on fire with how red his face had gone, but it was perfect, and
before he realised it, Nanook was laughing. It never took much to set Tomkin off, and with
them both laughing and hugging him, Zuko couldn’t fight back a small, disgruntled huff.
Nanook took it as a victory. There weren’t many in this war, but this, undoubtedly, would
always be theirs to claim.
____
Staying in the holiday estate of the Fire Lord on the night of a full moon was disconcerting,
to say the least. Sokka felt it like a constant itch, the wrongness of it, but beggars couldn’t be
choosers, and they hadn’t stayed somewhere with actual shelter in too long.
Part of Sokka had wanted that kind of stability even in the bowels of war. It had been months
since the Siege of the North; this was hardly Sokka’s first full moon to reckon with, but still,
he sat sleeplessly for each of them, gazing up into those beautiful white moonbeams and
imagining them as locks of hair playing between his fingers, a ghost of breath, lips cold in
distance.
Yue was dead. Three words. Simple, in the grand scheme of a war waging a hundred years,
but the thing about someone dying was that they never stopped being dead, and each day, she

was more dead than the last. Sokka didn’t know how to handle that. Time was supposed to
heal, but he was terrified of forgetting Yue like he’d begun to forget his mother. One day,
maybe years from now, maybe not long at all, she would start to blur at the edges, and he’d
forget the girl of moonlight who taught him what it meant to hold love in one hand and duty
in the other.
He saw her in Zuko. It was a thought he would have reeled from even a single full moon ago,
but now, he sighed into it. Two royals, inheritors of nations, honour-bound and selfsacrificing. Two children in a world where gentleness could not exist, who had been made to
suffer more than their years.
If Yue had known anger as Zuko had, would she still be here?
If Zuko had known softness as Yue had, would he have been saved?
The irony of Sokka’s appeal to first Yue and now Zuko was not lost on him. It felt at once
laughable and like a stinging betrayal to Yue’s memory. Zuko was not his nation, was not his
father, even if Sokka had spat that horrid insult at the other boy only yesterday – and how
shitty did that make him feel now upon Zuko’s latest revelation? – but he still had a
responsibility to those things. Yue’s death swam amongst it all, blood in an ever-flowing
river.
Sokka sat on the sand dunes watching the sunset, deep in thought, pulling up the spikey grass
beside him. He’d played with Zi Se for a little bit, but the boy was quieter than usual,
exhausted from the long day, and had gone to bed pretty quickly, which Sokka was grateful
for. He always took full moons to himself. Katara knew to leave him alone, and Aang tended
to become reclusive for his own reasons. Even Toph had started to approach these nights with
as much tact as she was capable of, which admittedly wasn’t much, but the thought was nice.
“I don't know what to do, Yue," Sokka admitted with a huff. “I think you’d like him. It's
weird, picturing it. You’re always so soft and he’s... not, but still, I think you’d be one of
those pairs that just work, you know? I know he’d like you. I even think... I think him being
around would have helped me understand you better, and you being here would help me
understand him better. Is that awful?”
The moon was, as always, silent. He could almost imagine Yue sat next to him, quietly
watching him talk himself into a hole he couldn’t climb out of, giggling behind her hand
when he ultimately threw her a helpless look.
“I like him,” Sokka whispered, barely a breath. “I really, actually like him. Ugh!” He buried
his head in his hands, because really? Prince Zuko, of all people? He couldn’t make it work
with Suki – beautiful, amazing Suki – so his stupid heart landed on a firebender?
And what was he supposed to do now? Should he do something?
In the past, Sokka had always acted before he could even come to terms with his feelings.
Falling for someone was very much a fall; clumsy and awkward and unintentional. With both
Yue and Suki, logic had come much later, and only then had he given the situation pause.

With Zuko, it had been the complete opposite. Sokka had hated the other boy, and every step
towards fondness had been hard-earned and intentional. He wasn’t used to painstakingly
coming to the realisation that he liked someone and then acting on it. He felt... wrongfooted.
“Mind if I join?”
Sokka let out an undignified squawk at Suki’s sudden voice, and she laughed shamelessly at
him.
“Spirits, are you trying to kill me?” Sokka hissed, clutching his chest dramatically.
Suki cackled. “What happened to those warrior instincts, huh?”
"I think you got them all when we split up,” he said, before pausing awkwardly. Sure, him
and Suki were never properly dating, and they’d ended amicably all the same, and were good
friends now to the point the lack of awkwardness was a little astounding, but outright joking
about it when it had only been a few weeks felt... insensitive.
Suki, easy-going as ever, just continued smiling as she took a seat next to him, before looking
up and sighing.
“Full moon, huh?” she asked.
“Yup.” He knew what she was really asking, but couldn’t meet her eye.
It was quiet for a bit, peaceful even, but peace was never a constant in Sokka’s life à la the
ongoing war the universe had waged with him since birth, and he should have known not to
lower his guard.
Suki snickered. “Well, you sure know how to pick ’em.”
“What’s that supposed to mean?” Sokka asked, throwing a bewildered look her way.
“It means,” Suki said, “your first girlfriend turned into the moon, and now, you have a crush
on probably the biggest trauma magnet in the world condensed into teenage boy form.”
And listen, Sokka knew Suki had been onto him these past few days, with her stupid
nicknames for Zuko just to rile Sokka up and her childish expressions whenever Sokka so
much as looked at Zuko, but outright saying it was too far. Sokka still had some dignity,
thank you. Some. A tiny bit. Negligible.
“Hey!” he hissed, snapping his head over his shoulder to check no one was nearby. “Keep
your voice down! And I have no idea what you’re talking about.”
Suki giggled. Giggled. “Sure you don’t, hot shot.”
Sokka groaned into his hands. There was a certain relief to knowing he wouldn’t have to
attempt confessing all his weird, complicated emotions towards the firebender to Suki
anytime soon, but she always pulled the truth out of him and laid it bare whether he was
ready for it or not, and now was no different.

He also felt that niggling awkwardness from earlier, and peeked up at her with a frown.
“Do you... Do you think it’s too soon?” he asked. “Are you annoyed?”
Suki's smile softened. “Too soon after us?”
Sokka nodded.
“Nah," she said, like it was easy. “I think we both knew what we had was finished long
before we talked about it. I had fun, and I'll always like you, Sokka, but that means I want
what’s best for you, just like you want what’s best for me. We can’t be that for each other. I'm
glad we realised that sooner rather than later. And you have to admit,” green eyes flashed
with mischief, “this is probably the funniest possible outcome.”
Sokka groaned again, shoving Suki into the sand as she began to cackle in earnest, but he
couldn’t bite back a pleased grin, eventually laughing with her.
“Thanks, Sooks,” he said once they’d calmed a little.
Suki elbowed him. “Don’t mention it. Spar?”
It was becoming a tradition of theirs to spar through a full moon until Sokka collapsed from
exhaustion and didn’t have the energy to think too hard.
He took the offer instantly.
____
Zuko couldn’t sleep. He ought to have passed out the moment he fell back against his
expensive bed after growing so accustomed to sleeping in the dirt, but he was left staring at
the ceiling, listening to the distant waves as he twisted his pai sho tile around and around his
fingers.
He couldn’t focus on any one thing. His mind jumped from Fong to Ozai to Iroh to Azula like
he was forever going to be beholden to those in his life that represented the most pain. Zi Se
slept soundly beside him, curled into himself on the mattress, practically buried beneath the
blankets and looking soft, safe, entirely exhausted from playing on the beach for so long.
Zuko periodically pushed his dark hair from his face.
His memories of Azula in this house saw her at a similar age, small and bright-eyed, quick as
a whip even then, but salvagable. Sometimes as children they’d stay up so late playing that
they’d sleep in the same bed, too scared to sneak across the corridor and risk waking their
parents up, and she’d kick him and push him for supposedly crossing the invisible line
cutting between them, but when she slept, she’d always shuffle gradually closer to him. Zuko
wondered if she still would, if there was a part of her subconscious that still leaned towards
her big brother.
He doubted it. Blue fire and gold eyes. Two killers. Two children.

Zuko pushed himself up with a start, unable to stay in his room anymore with these memorysoaked walls closing in. Just like all those nights ago, he ventured out onto the beach for
some fresh air, and just like all those nights ago, he was surprised to find he wasn’t alone. He
bumped into Suki, covered in sweat and her hair in disarray.
“Zuko!” she greeted, somewhat out of breath. “I was just going in. We've been sparring for
hours, I think I'm gonna pass out.”
“We?” Zuko asked, looking down the beach, only then noticing Sokka sat on the dunes, chin
on his knees, staring up at the moon. It was full tonight. Not a cloud in sight.
Suki followed his gaze and gave him an oddly knowing smile. "You should join him. It
doesn’t do him good to think too much on nights like this.”
Zuko frowned, not knowing what she meant by that, but Suki was already making her way up
to the house. He walked over to Sokka, avoiding surprised blue eyes blinking up at him as he
took a seat.
“Hi,” Zuko said lamely.
“Hi,” Sokka said. His sounded more like a question.
Zuko leaned back on his palms. “I couldn’t sleep. Why are you out here so late?”
That seemed to put Sokka a little more at ease, and the other boy sighed tiredly,
contemplating his answer, finally shrugging.
“Couldn't sleep either, I guess.”
“Suki said the two of you have been sparring for a while,” Zuko said. “You aren’t tired? It's
important to rest after intense physical exertion-.”
“It’s not that,” Sokka huffed, a small smile playing at his lips, before it fell into something
sad. He turned to face Zuko. Agni, those eyes. Zuko felt pinned in place.
“I never told you about Yue, did I?” Sokka asked.
Zuko shook his head.
“I figure if we’re trading tragic backstories today,” Sokka laughed bitterly, turning back to
look at the moon. Zuko tried not to show how confused he was.
“She was the princess of the Northern Water Tribe,” he said, voice soft, so soft, liable to
bruise. “I only knew her for a few days, but it felt like more. She just got me, you know? But
she was the princess, and her duty would always come first. How much do you know about
the Siege of the North?”
Zuko knew he’d been rotting in a cell for it, but somehow, he thought a comment like that
wouldn’t be appropriate here. He frowned, thinking back. He'd heard bits and pieces from the
soldiers in Fong’s base, snarled insults from Spider, and had heard of it further in the White

Lotus camp. Red moon. No moon. Tui. He knew Zhao had attacked the Northern Water Tribe
and had attempted to kill the Moon Spirit. He knew the Avatar had been possessed by the
Ocean Spirit in vengeance and had killed Zhao as well as most of his fleet. He knew it was
one of the worst Fire Nation defeats in the history of the war.
He hadn’t heard of a princess. He told Sokka everything but that.
Sokka nodded solemnly. “That’s the basic gist of it, but Yue... She restored the Moon Spirit
by sacrificing her life in its place. It wasn’t even a question for her; there was no scenario
where she didn’t give the entirety of herself for her people. And now, she’s up there.”
Sokka nodded up at the moon that somehow seemed so much brighter than before, like it was
watching them.
Zuko was speechless for a moment, just staring at the glowing white. He knew what it meant
to hear the call of duty and leave everything you loved for it, to be honour-bound to a people
without knowing if they’d even value your sacrifice. Zuko thought of a princess staring out at
a land of ice. He thought about the 41st division being marched into fire. Somehow, he felt as
though he knew Yue, and knew also that he would never get to.
“I’m sorry,” Zuko said quietly. “That’s... rough.”
Sokka snorted at what Zuko immediately realised came across as a catastrophic
understatement, cursing himself, but his bashfulness just made Sokka smile wider, and Zuko
would take it if it stopped that sad, wounded look in the other boy’s eyes.
“What can I say, I have a habit of surrounding myself with reckless, self-sacrificing idiots.”
Sokka shook his head. “You’re all going to send me to an early grave.”
Zuko couldn’t help but feel pleased at the jab, at even an indirect admission that Sokka
viewed him as one of his group, responsible for Zuko as Zuko felt responsible for Sokka.
Suddenly, the other boy groaned, stretching out his arms.
“Spirits, but I sparred too long with Suki,” Sokka said, wincing. “I feel like all of my muscles
have turned to jelly.”
Zuko cocked his head, considering. “Going in the water might help.”
“It’ll be freezing.”
“I can keep you warm,” Zuko said. It would be good practise for regulating his chi.
Sokka's reaction was very strange, flushing so quickly and obviously that Zuko was able to
see it even in the dim moonlight, then spluttering for a few long moments like Zuko had said
something entirely untoward. Zuko just frowned at him, wondering if the other boy was
alright.
“Uh, sure!” Sokka said, sparing him from worry. “Yeah, sure, that’s. Yep! Okay!”

He got up quickly, brushing sand from his trousers before rolling them up to his knees. Zuko
copied him. They both looked ridiculous as they headed down the beach to the gentle tide,
throwing off their shirts as they went. Zuko didn’t even think twice about it. Not with Sokka,
who’d seen it all before under much worse circumstances.
Sokka was right; the water was freezing. Zuko instantly puffed out a wave of heat the
moment the water lapped over his ankles, and Sokka jumped into the warmth instantly,
yelping when they stepped in deeper.
“Technically,” Zuko forced through grit teeth, "cold water immersion is recommended after
intense exercise. I used to have ice baths when I’d had long days of training.”
“Of course you did,” Sokka grumbled, arms crossed tightly. “I’m gonna be honest, I'm not
feeling the benefits yet.”
“You need to go deeper,” Zuko said, before deciding to just suck it up, diving forward,
uncaring of his clothes. The shock of cold almost made him gasp under the water, but the
moment it washed over his head, he began to climatise, and surfaced with a buzz, flicking his
hair out and grinning over at Sokka, who was kind of just... staring.
“I am not doing that,” the other finally spluttered.
Zuko raised an eyebrow, before lunging forward and grabbing Sokka by his middle, shoving
him over. The water rushed over both of them, barely giving Zuko time to suck in a breath
before they went under and knocked into the sand bed, arms scrabbling against Zuko as he let
go and they both surfaced with a gasp.
“You asshole!” Sokka cried out, quickly crossing his arms over his chest again to preserve
some warmth, but he was grinning, his hair coming out of its tie to frame his face, and Zuko
couldn’t help but laugh.
“You wouldn’t have done it otherwise,” he pointed out.
Sokka huffed, rolling his eyes.
The water was up to their ribs now, and Sokka was stood much closer than Zuko had
anticipated, making no move to distance himself from the bubble of heat Zuko kept up
around him. He didn’t think the proximity bothered the other boy. He'd always been so...
engimatic. So comfortable in his own skin, so confident in the space he took up, while Zuko
shrunk beneath the attention, staring at the water lapping against his scarred chest. He could
feel Sokka’s eyes roving over him, refamiliarising himself with what he’d seen in the Boiling
Rock. Zuko had been bitter then, defensive, angry. Now, he felt... grounded.
He felt safe with Sokka’s eyes on him. He didn’t know what to do with that.
Zuko flinched suddenly when a cool hand grazed his stomach, snapping his gaze up to see
Sokka watching his own fingers trace a deep scar there. He didn’t look judgemental, or
disgusted, or any of the things Zuko feared most. Only... considering. Like all things, this was
something Sokka wanted to understand.

It was a silent question, one Zuko didn’t have to answer if he didn’t want to, but the enormity
of what Zuko went through often meant the details got missed. He was the only one carrying
each individual scar. No one else had to know the exact circumstances of all of them. How
could he expect them to? There were so many. But each had been its own experience, each its
own memory he would be cursed to forever, and the silent offer to share some of that, to give
these memories to hands that were touching him gently...
“He used different blades,” Zuko said, voice choked, hoarse. Sokka nodded, urging him to
continue. "He’d... He’d leave these scratches a lot of the time. Deep enough to hurt, not deep
enough to scar, to taunt me, I think. But these... He’d cut back the skin... Peel it, in these
small sections.” Zuko indicated a few other scars on his chest, one on his shoulder. There
were more on his back. Sokka took a moment, brow furrowed, pained, before moving on, the
graze of his fingers hitching Zuko’s breath and sending his heart racing at the suggestion of
sensation.
Sokka paused on Zuko’s sternum, where jagged flesh lay in a pink-white-red mess.
“Fire,” Zuko husked, barely whispering the next words. “He thought it was funny.”
A muscle in Sokka’s jaw twitched at that, anguish on Zuko’s behalf, and it was... nice. He
couldn’t take this pain from Zuko, but he could hold his hands against it and condemn it.
They went like that until Zuko felt somehow dizzy and steady at once, calloused fingers
tracing every scar they could find, brushing against his own fingertips to feel the bend of
poorly healed bones, dancing fearlessly over burns, walking the precipice of lacerations.
Undaunted, in the face of all Zuko was, until finally, like a river flowing to sea, Sokka’s hand
reached up to hold Zuko’s face, right over his scar. Zuko felt like he was in a trance as he
watched the other boy, fetterless from the singing nerves that had known only agony for
months, and was entirely at Sokka’s mercy now, clueless to what he was thinking, knowing
only that he... he trusted him with it.
He didn’t know when they’d stepped so close, didn’t know who had moved, knew only that
his chest was brushing Sokka’s, and he was a little taller than the other boy but Sokka was a
vision against the waves. In that moment, Zuko knew perfectly how the moon pushed and
pulled the tide, because without thought, without even realising, Zuko found himself drawn
to Sokka, leaning into him, the grip Sokka had on his face becoming firmer, but not to push
him away. His fingers carded through his hair, resting at the back of his head and pulling him
in until their noses brushed, until they were sharing air and Zuko could have sworn mere
moments ago they were separated, but now it was impossible to tell where each of them
started and ended, contained so wholly in each other, in this moment.
And then Sokka leaned closer still, a ghost of breath on Zuko’s mouth before lips pressed to
his, so tenderly, so briefly, that he almost wondered if he’d imagined it, this thing they had
created, impossibly fragile, and reality snapped back around Zuko all at once.
Sokka had kissed him.
Zuko was pressed entirely against him. His... His hand was on his hip-. When did he even-?

Agni, what had he done?
The fear that struck Zuko was unknowable in its vastness, the indisputable feeling that he’d
done something wrong, something unforgivable, and punishment the likes of which he could
no longer stomach would be inevitable. It always was.
Terrified, Zuko pushed away, shoving Sokka hard by the shoulders and causing the other boy
to stumble back, yelping as he fell into the water with a loud, inelegant splash.
“I need to go,” Zuko said, the words coming out snappish, strained. He turned around before
he could see Sokka get to his feet, fleeing towards the beach and barely thinking to grab his
shirt before he was racing towards the house, breaths coming to him in panicked pants.
He dried himself as he walked, steam billowing from him, and snuck through the house like a
child out of place trying desperately not to get caught. Zi Se hadn’t even stirred in his
absence, and it reassured something in him, like maybe Zuko could pretend none of that had
happened, like maybe, maybe, just once, no one would find out what he’d done.
So he forced himself to bed, slammed his eyes shut, and choked back dreams of another boy,
honey eyes and cinnamon tea, and scars no one had ever touched gently.
____
Unsurprisingly, he didn’t get any sleep, high strung like a prey animal with its foot in a trap,
waiting for the hunter to wake up and kill him. Forcing himself to brave breakfast was an
arduous thing. No matter how many times Zuko walked himself into his own damnation, it
never got easier.
He wondered if Sokka had told everyone. He wondered if they’d even still be here.
Whatever he’d feared, it didn't match the chaos of the courtyard when he sheepishly stepped
through the kitchen shoji. Zuko was usually the first to rise, but no one could sleep through
Katara’s panicked shouting, and it made it easy to quickly decipher what was wrong.
Aang wasn’t in his tent.
A hasty search of the island gave them one conclusion.
The Avatar had vanished.
