Currently, Sokka was very stressed. It could be argued that he was always somewhat stressed.
Indeed, if stress had its own metric, Sokka’s constant state would probably rest near a
middling mark even on a good day, and right now, he could safely place himself far towards
the highest extreme. He might even be exceeding the capacity of quantifiable measurement.
Stress enough to exhaust the magnificent skill of his beloved mathematics.
And listen, he really was stressed about Aang disappearing. The comet was so close now, and
without the Avatar, they had no hope of defeating the Fire Lord, and what if Aang was in

trouble? Captured? Hurt? Really, that was very, very stressful.
But Aang had a habit of disappearing sometimes. Sure, this time felt different – there were no
signs of a fight, his body wasn’t left behind while he journeyed on some Spirit World
shenanigans, and Aang would never normally leave Appa behind – but after months of
travelling with the flighty kid, Sokka had gotten used to a more laid back mindset. He trusted
Aang. He wasn’t the immature little boy Sokka had seen fall from the iceberg. Aang knew
what his responsibility was and he knew he had to face it. He would face it, somehow, some
way, even if he mysteriously wasn’t here days before the comet for some inexplicable reason.
See, Sokka was very stressed. An appropriate amount of stressed.
But he was, well, inappropriately amount of stressed about something else too.
Like the fact he’d spent all night horrified by what had happened with Zuko on the beach
yesterday, and hadn’t had a chance this morning to really pull himself together about it given
the everything happening this morning, and now, Zuko was on the steps leading down into
the courtyard, looking all sleep-mussed and soft with his dishevelled hair and loose day
clothes, even though his golden eyes held a sharp alertness, and he refused to look at Sokka.
They had kissed.
No. Correction. Sokka had kissed Zuko and had gotten himself shoved into the water for it.
Which was probably the most humiliating rejection he’d ever received in his life and he
wanted to die, thank you for asking.
Sokka was no stranger to being rejected, but if he was being honest, with hindsight and a lot
of swallowing his pride, he could admit that they were always predictable rejections. Girls
he’d never met before and immediately approached too intensely, too soon, or been all out
rude to in his attempt to impress with his oh so macho demeanour, or casual flirting that
simply never bloomed into anything else.
It made sense, even if it had been embarrassing and stung a little at the time. But this...
Zuko... Sokka had thought...
Zuko was different. He wasn’t a passing fancy or all-intense infatuation. Sokka had hated him
for so long, and when Zuko joined their group, it had taken time to like Zuko. A conscious
effort. A friendship forged on purpose. Liking Zuko had come so gradually, so carefully,
fragile as glass shards underfoot, that he had hardly noticed it at all until it was too late.
That intention to their dynamic made Zuko so different to any crush Sokka had stumbled
upon before, because every part of Zuko that Sokka had gradually come to like, he’d noticed
slowly, he’d searched for it, he’d lured it out of the firebender even when he’d have rather
kept it locked away. No one else saw Zuko the way Sokka did – he’d even admitted it. The
only authentic thing here. Sokka was Zuko’s honesty when everyone else had been blinded
by pity, his accountability when he wanted to hide from the worst of his memories, and a
hand held to pull him out of them. They were equals. Fighters. Leaders. But when it was just
the two of them and they didn’t have to be anything grander than that, they were learning to
just be... boys. Scared. Lost. Hurt.

Zuko had trusted Sokka with so much, but somewhere along the line, Sokka had
reciprocated. Push and pull. Fire and water. Immovable object and unstoppable force. Helmet
and boomerang.
But Sokka took it too far. Zuko was an inferno of stubborn grit and indomitable survival,
smart and silly and scarred in fits and starts. A killer. A firebender. A boy with fingers broken
a dozen times over and hands gentle enough that Sokka imagined a bird cradled in those
calloused palms. A steepled cage. Not a feather unsettled. He had once thought Zuko
belonged entirely to his temper, but he was wrong back then. The boy who hunted Fong
down and killed him was also the thirteen-year-old who burned for a division of soldiers he
did not and would never know. It was that gentleness to Zuko that defined him, and even after
all the violence he had seen and delivered and suffered, it was that gentleness that tried still to
claw out of him. Sokka saw it with Zi Se, with Zuko’s clumsy friendships, and he’d received
it too. Gentle touches, soft words, glowing eyes.
Prince Zuko of the Fire Nation had consumed him in his inferno. How could he not kiss him?
He'd looked otherworldly in the moonlight, with the waves around his hips, and he’d let
Sokka touch every scar, each with a story no one else had heard before, and Sokka had...
He’d wanted to keep them. Keep him. Keep every agony and memory and swallow it down
so Zuko never had to deal with it alone ever again. How could he not kiss him?
And he’d thought, for a moment there, a perfect, infinitesimal, breath of a moment, that Zuko
had kissed him back. Lips a little rough on his. The taste of smoke. A sure hand on his hip
that Sokka was sure would burn into the skin and leave the imprint of clever fingers
forevermore with how much that touch seemed to ricochet through his entire being, pulling
him closer, pulling him in.
When Zuko had recoiled back, there had been an amalgamation of horror in his expression. A
thousand things Sokka couldn’t understand. A strange terror. Most of all, Sokka remembered
the disgust. He couldn’t make that part of Zuko beautiful, couldn’t decorate it or pretend not
to have seen. The truth was unavoidable. In the moment before he pushed Sokka back and
ran away, Zuko had been disgusted.
And now Aang was missing. And Zuko was awake, slowly descending into the courtyard like
he thought someone might snap at him, and Sokka wanted nothing more than to hide.
----The Avatar was missing and Zuko felt restless with it, skin itching, fingers twitching. He was
supposed to protect this group, to keep them safe, keep them close, and he’d lost the Avatar?
The comet was in a matter of days, and no one knew when Aang would be back, or if he even
would be back, and when had he even gone missing? Last night, when Zuko had been...?
What if that was the reason they lost the Avatar, lost the war? Did that not confirm every
hissed threat his father had lashed him with? That this... mistake inside of him could cause
entire nations to fall if he let himself indulge? Hadn't he indulged? For just a moment, hadn’t
he kissed Sokka back? Hadn't he liked it? Why the fuck was everyone staring at him?
“Why are you all staring at me?” Zuko snapped.

“Well, no offense, but aren’t you sort of the expert on tracking Aang?” Katara said, tone
hopeful. “If anyone can find him, it would be you.”
“That was a long time ago,” Zuko said, suddenly needing to have said it, even though Katara
didn’t look angry, just sick with worry. Spirits, Zuko needed to focus. Aang was missing.
That was more important than anything else. The Avatar wasn’t anywhere on Ember Island
and this wasn’t like any other time he’d vanished. If Zuko could help track him down, even
just a little, that would be enough.
“If we keep travelling to the White Lotus camp,” Tomkin said carefully, “then won’t Aang
know to meet us there?”
“But what if he’s in trouble? We can’t just leave here without him!” Katara insisted.
“But we haven’t got any idea of where he’s gone,” Nanook pointed out, trying for calmness
as the group got more and more agitated. “We can’t just track him when we have no direction
to even follow.”
“No, we can’t,” Zuko said quietly. “But I know someone who can. If she’s where I hope she
is, it won’t even take us far off course; she can usually be found in a bar on the coast of the
Mo Ce Sea.”
“That wouldn’t take more than a day,” Suki concurred. “Right, Sokka?”
Sokka, instinctively, looked over at Zuko to discuss his plan, before his eyes widened, and he
quickly looked away again.
“Yeah! Definitely doable!” he said, voice strained. Zuko felt like someone was grabbing his
insides and twisting.
They packed up quickly after that. It wasn’t much of a decision. Between continuing to the
White Lotus camp or ensuring Aang was okay, the group’s determination was wordless. It
was more than the loyalty of alliance – Zuko felt it too. In the past few days, it felt like the
eight of them had closed ranks around one another, not wanting to stray too far, always
watching someone else’s back. A group no longer just in technicality, forced together when
the adults had to take a different route that day, but a team.
As he joined his friends in Appa’s saddle, he imagined being cast out of the group. Banished.
An entire livelihood up in flames because of his wrongdoing. Again and again. Always the
same. Always wrong. Like something was rotten in his very core, and no matter how hard he
tried, it would always seep out of him, dripping poison from violent hands or spewing it from
an angry tongue, or this, a low, quiet desire, the stalking predator of longing. A skipped
heartbeat. A brush of lips. A natural disaster.
He shook his head of the thoughts, refusing to let himself be distracted by them. No one
knew. No one could find out.
And with that, Prince Zuko set off to find the Avatar.

----It was a tense flight to the Earth Kingdom. Nanook had expected a day of nerves, soothing
the kids when their anxiety peaked, doling out calm reassurances, remaining steadfast in his
own belief that everything would be fine, even if deep down, he wasn’t so sure.
What he hadn’t accounted for, however, was whatever had occurred between Sokka and
Zuko.
Sokka was restless, spending some hours overly chatty and other hours deep in thought,
shrunk into himself, and outright refusing to so much as look in Zuko’s direction. And Zuko,
sat as far from Sokka on the saddle as he could get, had been snappy to say the least, prickly
whenever anyone turned any amount of attention towards him, like a guilty child who knew
he had been caught doing something wrong, a flash of prey-like terror in each glance. First,
Nanook assumed they’d simply fallen out, but when he’d tried his luck with the historically
more rational of the pair, Sokka had gone bright red and stuttered out some ridiculous
insistence that everything was fine.
It was a relief to finally land in the Earth Kingdom. Zuko took the lead to show them the way,
and everyone else scattered somewhat, grateful for some room after a long day clustered
together on Appa. They'd usually make camp around now, the sun having set before they
even touched down, but it had been a wordless decision to keep going. They didn’t have time
to lose. They needed to find Aang.
Nanook was desperately wracking his brain for what the others would do in this situation,
wanting to be that for these kids. Hakoda’s wisdom, Bato’s sharpness, Chena’s bravery,
Kanut’s skill, Tulok’s kindness, Aput’s resolve – their responsibility was his now. A leader by
proxy. A whole tribe in the push and pull of him and Tomkin, and they were making it work.
They had to.
But Nanook couldn’t figure this hiccup out. It nagged at him, like he could see something and
he was missing it.
He'd wound up walking with Tomkin and Toph, the earthbender unusually quiet, even though
Tomkin kept talking nonsense like nothing was wrong. In fact, Nanook was certain Tomkin
hadn’t noticed anything odd between Sokka and Zuko.
“I mean, I’m all for a guy going off mid-job – sometimes you need to take a day for yourself,
you know?” Tomkin was saying, in a voice that implied he genuinely thought he was
spouting some great wisdom. “But when we’ve got days before the comet? It's like really,
dude? You’re doing this now? And I've never been the Avatar either, so the time I ditched the
crew during a two day stand-off with a Fire Nation cruiser so I could sneak to shore and buy
emergency dumplings isn’t even that comparable.”
“Or at all comparable,” Toph snorted. “Like not even a little bit, slightly comparable,
actually-.”
“Do you think something’s up with Sokka and Zuko?” Nanook interrupted, not even
pretending to have been paying attention to the conversation.

“What makes you say that?” Tomkin asked, throwing a bewildered look Nanook’s way as
their walk began to turn from grassy knolls to the start of a forest, the trees creaking in the
nighttime breeze. At their head, Zuko stomped on, undaunted.
“Oh, for sure,” Toph said, making both boys snap their attention to her. “What? Their
heartbeats keep going all over the place, it’s obvious something’s wrong.”
“Maybe they’re stressed about Aang?” Tomkin suggested, frowning.
Toph shrugged. “Maybe. One way to find out.”
“Hey,” Nanook said, suddenly urgent, “what are you going to-?”
“Hey, Snoozles!” Toph yelled. Ahead of them, Sokka jumped, along with Katara and Suki
beside him, and even Zuko and Zi Se up ahead turned around in confusion, making Sokka
look visibly more horrified.
Nanook paled. “Wait, Toph, hold on-.”
Toph did not hold on. “What’s up with you and Prickly today? You're both acting weird.”
Zuko stumbled on seemingly nothing, before immediately spinning to face the front again,
walking onwards with a vengeance, while Sokka spluttered under the attention of everyone
else. Zi Se, curiously, threw one last concerned look Zuko’s way before coming to walk with
them.
“Me? Zuko? Haha! What?” Sokka squeaked, each word coming out more and more forced,
as if he was shoving them from behind his teeth. “We are completely fine. Not weird at all,
super normal. Why would you even- Ha!”
It was almost impressive watching Sokka laugh without smiling even a little bit. In fact,
Nanook thought the other boy had stopped breathing entirely.
“Well, that was a weird reaction,” Tomkin said, unimpressed, before looking at Nanook.
“What’s going on?”
Nanook shrugged and made an I-dunno noise, watching as Sokka quickly tried to sweep
Katara and Suki’s attention away in some loud story. Zuko was walking quite far from the
main group now, alone, shoulders up in a rigid line. Nanook pictured him breaking into a run
and fleeing. A vanishing act twice done.
He couldn’t bear the thought. He had to fix this, somehow.
“I thought they’d been getting on better lately?” Nanook asked, frustrated. “If anything, I
thought they were close now. They spend so much time just the two of them, and in some
ways, Zuko lets Sokka closer than he even lets us. Even Bato’s been making those jokes, so
why-?”
He stopped speaking with all the sudden severity of an axe coming down. Then, a long
silence. A tree creaking before crashing to the ground all at once. The only way you could

read the lines within it speaking of its history. Because Nanook suddenly remembered a
beach. Gaoling. Hakoda's tent. A conversation only they knew. An argument that never got
cleared up, but drowned beneath four months of blood.
I don’t think Zuko likes girls. I don’t have a problem with that. I think, however, that he does.
Oh.
Oh, shit.
----Zuko wanted to hide. He knew what it was for the ground to yawn open with sharp teeth and
swallow you whole, knew what it was to be consumed like that, so far from the surface that
the sun could stretch golden fingers to try and reach and only ever come back with dirt
beneath fingernails. He'd disappeared for so long. The perpetual disorientation of waking up
too early and needing a moment to get your bearings. Dizzy with loss, with absence. Starving
on it. Four entire months lost to that void, that lack of feeling punctuated only by such
immense pain that it whited out any colour he might have remembered.
There comes a point in agony where a person no longer has a response for it. The body loses
its language – no screams, no cries, no moans, no begs, no curses. In its place is just some
long, animal wheeze. Not yet a death rattle. Something else. Something unnameable. Zuko
heard it now like a low hum no one else knew to notice. It backdropped everything, and he
hated how it made him wonder. He'd suffered so terribly for so long, and after everything,
why torture himself about this? He'd long since lost his nation’s favour. He'd given up on his
father and the non-existent love he’d craved from him. He knew better what it was to be
honourless than prince. So why did this matter? Why did he so desperately need to be right
about this being wrong?
He'd felt so real with Sokka’s hands on him. For the first time since Gaoling, he’d felt like
someone had dragged him back down to the ground onto feet that were finally able to carry
him. He'd felt strong, brave. And maybe if he was a little braver, he’d throw caution to the
wind and grab this with both hands, because he didn’t care anymore for consequence. This
old terror... It was just that. Old. The scars of a younger boy he no longer recognised. The
taste of cinnamon in tea.
Some days, he couldn’t even remember what Mizu had looked like.
“How much farther?” Katara asked, coming quietly to walk beside Zuko. Zuko didn’t look at
her.
“Not long,” he said. “There’s a bar a little deeper in the forest. There's a bounty hunter there.”
Katara looked troubled. “I don’t think we can afford a bounty hunter.”
“Probably not, but my uncle can. Once we’ve found Aang, we’ll go to the White Lotus camp
like we originally planned, pay June, meet up with the tribesmen and the other forces
gathered there, and get ready for Sozin’s Comet.”

Katara was quiet a few moments, before sighing, voice soft, oddly docile.
“You make it sound so easy,” she whispered. “I’m... I’m scared, Zuko. I don’t think things are
going to go our way this time.”
Zuko looked at her then, taking in her expression. She looked exhausted, stress pulling at her
mouth, and her usually fierce eyes were dulled in the face of her anxiety. Again, Zuko felt a
stab of guilt for letting his thoughts get away from the problem at hand.
“We’re going to find him, Katara,” he reassured, a little too blunt, a little too harsh.
“It’s not that I’m worried about,” Katara said mournfully. “I trust Aang. I believe in him more
than anything. I know that when the time comes, he’ll pull through. But... I’m so scared of
what this battle will take from him. I've been thinking about last night, before he disappeared.
He was so determined not to kill Ozai, and none of us listened to him-.”
“Because it’s a ridiculous suggestion-.”
“Is it?” Katara asked, some of her usual fierceness returning as she stared imploringly at
Zuko. “Is it ridiculous for the Avatar, the symbol of balance and peace, to find a path to
victory that isn’t... isn’t violent, isn’t bloodstained? Is that so bad? Aang has lost so much –
his people, his culture – but if he could do this one thing... And if anyone could figure it out,
wouldn’t it be him? Why couldn’t we have just listened to him? Helped him?”
Zuko had been aware of the others gossiping and throwing knowing looks to one another
when it came to Katara and Aang. It was apparent even to Zuko that the pair had... something
going on. He'd known that Aang trailed after Katara like a lovesick puppy and he’d known
that Katara got all flustered and snappy whenever someone implied something between them,
but he’d never seen this side of it. Katara had gone from withdrawn and frightened to
passionate and determined in a matter of sentences, and it was because of Aang, of the belief
she had in him, the trust, the respect. Of course she loved him – everyone in the group
seemed to feel that for one another, even if Zuko was incredibly unaccustomed to such
displays – but it was different here, deeper. Aang and Katara represented everything the other
strived to be and filled each gap the other may have stumbled on.
Balance.
Unity.
Unsure what else to do in the face of Katara’s wide, searching gaze, Zuko reached over,
carefully squeezing her arm.
“He’s going to be okay,” he said quietly. “We’re going to find him. We won’t let him do this
alone. None of us are doing this alone. You guys taught me that, remember?”
Blue eyes became watery and Zuko panicked a moment, before Katara reached for his arm
too, almost a strange form of the Water Tribe handshake, and squeezed just as tightly. Her
smile was wobbly, small, but real, and there was that determination she was so known for.

“Thanks, Zuko,” she said.
He gave her a small smile back. “No problem.”
“You know,” Katara said, reaching to wipe her face a little with a sniff and a little laugh, “you
should talk to Sokka.”
Zuko's smile dropped. “What did he say to you?”
“Nothing.” Katara raised an eyebrow. “I don’t know what happened, but I can tell that
whatever it is, it’s between just you two. So don’t go wasting time hiding again. We need to
all be together as best we can when the comet comes. Whatever happened, whatever you’re
scared of, we... we can be bigger than it. We'll beat it together just like everything else.”
Zuko just stared at her a moment, before ducking his head, swallowing. He could only give
her a jerky nod, and thankfully, she didn’t push him for more than that.
----The bar Zuko took them to seemed so laughably at odds with the prince’s stiff, regal
demeanour that Sokka almost braved talking to him again just to tease the firebender on what
on earth he must have been getting up to in his free time at sea. The place was seedy, lit
dimly by candles and crowded with drunkards, various fights taking place in different
corners, glasses shattering, alcohol sloshing on the bar’s wooden walls. And there, right in
the centre of it all and evading her own bar fight with little effort, was the bounty hunter that
had attacked them with her weird, paralysing animal-tracker-rat-thing back when they were
staying with the nuns at the Abbey.
She raised a sharp eyebrow when she spotted their approach, zeroing in on Zuko.
“Oh great, it’s Prince Pouty,” she said. Sokka would normally have found that hilarious.
“Where’s your creepy grandpa?”
“I’m not travelling with him anymore,” Zuko said, lip already beginning to curl. “And he’s
my uncle.”
Nanook tried to interject before some sort of fight broke out. “Uh, miss? We need your help
finding the Avatar.”
She kept her unimpressed stare on Zuko. “You’re still on that?”
“This time is different.”
“That’s what they all say,” the woman huffed before finishing her drink and getting to her
feet. “Come on, Nyla’s outside.”
They found out quickly that Nyla was a shirshu, the only animal that could track someone’s
scent anywhere in the world, and the woman, June, had no delicacy when telling them that
not only was Aang somehow not anywhere in the world right now, not dead or alive – gone,
but that she also charged just for that little consultation, and wanted her payment now.

And Sokka had just been gearing up to join Nanook on what was becoming a pretty
impassioned row when he paused, noticing Zi Se off to the side of the group, tears in his eyes
and lip wobbling. Naturally, Zuko had spotted him too, and was just making his way towards
the kid when Zi Se bolted into the woods.
“Shit!” Zuko yelled, taking off after him.
Sokka moved without thinking, shouting back at the others. "You guys stay here and deal
with her!”
The forest was dark and eerie, shadows creeping around the moonlight that threw everything
into a ghostly silver, but Zuko wasn’t trying to be quiet, and it was easy to follow the
firebender’s crashing sprint.
“Zuko!” Sokka called. “Slow down!”
“I can’t see him!” Zuko sounded terrified, words coming out strangled, and suddenly, all
Sokka’s embarrassment and confusion and hurt fell away to the simple foundation of their
dynamic, the basis that began their truce – a want to help the other, to share burdens they’d
only ever carried alone before.
Sokka forced himself to still suddenly, listening instead of running blindly, and heard a
choked sob to his right. He stalked through the shrubbery as quietly and quickly as he could,
and there, knees tucked to his chest and hands in his hair beneath a large tree whose trunk
seemed to curl around him in an attempt at comfort, was Zi Se. He looked so small like that.
“Hey, buddy,” Sokka said carefully, taking a few steps closer when the kid didn’t run off
again. “Mind if I sit here?”
It took a moment before, timidly, a fist wiping at distraught amber eyes, Zi Se looked up at
him and nodded. Sokka sat close, wrapping an arm around the kid’s shoulders, both in
comfort and to make sure he could grab him if he tried to make a break for it again. Seriously,
what was in the air today? Were people just actively trying to stress him out? When this war
was over, Sokka was taking a long vacation.
“You scared Zuko half to death, Zi Se, what was that?” Sokka asked. “Can I call him over?
Preferably before he sets the forest on fire?”
Zi Se let out a shaky laugh, before nodding.
“Zuko! Over here!” Sokka called. Normally, the immediacy of the following branch-snapping
and loud footsteps headed their way would have been funny, but Sokka was trying not to be
intimately aware that him and Zuko were about to be as close and alone as they’d been all
day, with only a crying five-year-old as a buffer. Again, Sokka would like to reiterate: postwar, long vacation, spa retreat non-negotiable.
Zuko appeared before them ruffled and wide-eyed and so impossibly human, and Sokka’s
heart ached with the knowledge that he had touched, and he had burned, and he could not
have this. He had to accept that. He had to make that okay. He didn’t think he was strong

enough, brave enough, to let this vulnerability get trampled, and that alone was a humiliating
realisation. Sokka was usually so stubborn, so dogged in his pursuit of what he wanted, but
this... scared him. It felt bigger, realer, more painful than anything he’d felt before, and when
Zuko had thrown it back at him so meanly last night... Sokka couldn’t do that again.
“Are you okay?” Zuko asked, voice so soft as he came to kneel in front of Zi Se. So close.
“What was that? What's wrong?”
Zi Se let Zuko assess him with frantic hands, lip wobbling, before he let out a sob.
“I told him he was dead,” the little boy cried. “Yesterday, when we were playing, I said he
lost so he was dead, and he said he didn’t like it and I got mad, and now he’s gone. He's
gone! Not dead, or alive, but-... but gone! I don’t want him to be gone like we were. Lanse
never came back-!”
Zuko pulled Zi Se into a hug, the little boy’s head tucking familiarly under his chin as Zi Se
let himself sob against Zuko, and for a moment, when he forgot Sokka could see him, Zuko
looked stricken. Sokka himself had felt his stomach drop when Zi Se had mentioned Lanse,
and being gone, and what that meant to a five-year-old who still couldn’t comprehend losing
four months in a prison buried beneath the earth. Had Zi Se ever had a single normal
experience of absence? Every person who had ever left him had left him for good, except
Zuko, and even though Sokka didn’t quite know what he was talking about with Aang, it
sounded like the pair had had some sort of... disagreement, that happened to be pretty topical
to what Aang had blown up about last night. Had Zi Se been blaming himself all day? Did he
think that Aang was gone forever now, and the last thing Zi Se did was upset him?
“Aang’s coming back, Zi Se,” Sokka said, voice quiet but firm, not an ounce of doubt to him.
Zi Se turned a little in Zuko’s arms until he was sitting on the firebender’s lap, still tucked
beneath his chin but able to blink wet eyes Sokka’s way.
“He’s the Avatar,” Sokka continued. “He’s the coolest guy there is, and very soon, we're all
gonna help him end this whole war, and no one’s ever gonna be gone the way you two were
ever again.”
Zuko flinched.
“Why did he leave?” Zi Se asked. “Why did he have to go away if we’re all gonna win
together?”
Sokka chewed over his words a moment, feeling something raw and insecure trying to claw
its way out. He flicked a glance to Zuko and saw the firebender already staring at him, but
those golden eyes were no more than a flash of wonder before they immediately dropped
upon being noticed, and Sokka worked his jaw, a little spiteful.
“Sometimes,” he said coolly, “people insist on doing things alone even if they have help.
Aang thinks he needs to shoulder all of the world’s pain by himself, otherwise he feels like
he’s failed, but that’s silly, isn’t it?”
“That is silly,” Zi Se said. Zuko was glaring at the floor.

“So how does this sound?” Sokka gave the kid a bright grin, a mask he knew well. “When we
find Aang, and when the war is over, we’ll both give him a very stern, very boring lecture on
shared responsibility and saviour complexes, and we’ll make him do all the chores for a week
to apologise for making us worry.”
Zi Se let out a giggle then, a sound that instantly sanded down Zuko’s edges. “You can’t
make the Avatar do our chores.”
“Oh, I can and I will! I'll have him washing socks, and let me tell you, I wouldn’t wish
Chena’s socks on my worst enemy.”
Zi Se laughed properly, a full, loud thing, and Sokka’s smile came easier.
“Feel better?” Zuko asked, wiping the rest of the tears from the kid’s face and giving his hair
a gentle ruffle. It would never cease to amaze Sokka how natural Zuko took to Zi Se, the
softness that came so readily to his hands when they held the little boy like he was the most
precious thing in the world. Sokka forced himself to look away, suddenly unable to watch,
pretending to observe the forest around them.
“Alright, why don’t you head back to the others?” Zuko said when Zi Se nodded, pointing
through the trees. “See that light there? We're not far from the bar. You go ahead for me and
shout when you’re with them. We won’t be far behind.”
“Promise?”
“Promise.”
Sokka jerked his gaze back up, blue eyes widening with some nauseating mix of horror and
hope that he immediately hated himself for. He didn’t think it was even possible to be
rejected more plainly than how Zuko had pushed him away, so why was he still holding his
breath on this? Why did his heart begin to pound so heavily in his chest as Zi Se got to his
feet and walked back to the others, calling when he found them, that he was worried he
wouldn’t hear anything Zuko said over the rush of blood in his ears?
But as he watched Zuko, he saw the other boy pull himself together in real time, any softness
he reserved for Zi Se, that specific openness he reserved only for Sokka, closing off and
hardening to something indifferent. Awkward, but not in the way Sokka had become
endeared by.
Hope drowned in his chest beneath a fresh flood of mortification.
Zuko cleared his throat. “Listen, about last night-.”
“Can we just forget about it?” Sokka cut in, forcing the words to sound chipper, nonchalant,
and landing closer to strained. He just... couldn’t hear it said out loud. “I get it, man. It's fine.
It's not a big deal, so let’s just... move on?”
Zuko blinked at Sokka for a very long minute, like his words completely blindsided him, and
didn’t that just add salt to the wound? Spirits, had Zuko spent all day thinking of ways to let

Sokka down easy? Did he really think Sokka was this pathetic? Was Sokka this pathetic?
“Okay,” Zuko eventually said. He sounded so... small. Sokka almost asked what was up with
him – that was still normal, right? They could still be that for each other? – but Zuko just got
quickly to his feet. “Yeah, okay. Sure. Let's forget about it.”
And with that, he stomped off, leaving Sokka behind.
----“What do you mean, she’s coming with us to the White Lotus camp?”
Nanook dragged a hand down his face. “I mean just that. She's insisting we owe her at least
three silver pieces and she’ll just track us down regardless until we pay up.”
“But all she did was get her weird pet to sniff Aang’s glider and tell us he doesn’t exist!”
Tomkin stressed. “Which is the only reason we’re even going to the White Lotus camp
without Aang, that’s not helpful! That's the opposite of helpful!”
“Business is business,” June said, raising a saccharine shoulder, seemingly amused by the
group’s indignation, before pointing to Zuko as he emerged from the treeline. “And I know
His Highness and his uncle are good for it. So, when do we leave?”
Tomkin continued arguing, backed by an incensed Katara and extremely vocal Toph, which
was somewhat laughable, seeing as Toph generally had little idea about expenses and was
likely arguing for the sake of arguing, but Nanook’s attention was distracted watching Zuko
and Sokka return to the group. Zi Se seemed much more at ease after whatever that little
moment was, clearly having spoken it out with someone, and Nanook had hoped the boys
spending a little longer in the woods meant they had talked and finally sorted out this strange
rift between them, but as he watched them return, he knew that wasn’t the case. There was a
distance between them, both in the intentional physical gap they kept and also the stiffness
both of them held. Sokka looked somewhat stoic, like he’d made a decision and was
determined to see it through, but Zuko looked... not upset, because the prince never looked
upset the way most people did, never any tears or fragility, but something was definitely
wrong. His scowl was twisted with anxiety and guilt, and golden eyes immediately searched
for Tomkin and Nanook.
He held Nanook’s stare when he caught it, and Nanook tipped his head slightly, a silent
question. Zuko seemed to debate something rather fiercely for a bit, before steeling himself.
"Appa has flown all day, and we haven’t lost as much time as we thought we might,” he said
decisively. “I think we should set up camp for the night.”
“I agree,” Sokka said, not looking at Zuko. “If Appa gets enough rest, we could make it to the
camp as early as tomorrow evening. There's not much else we can do for Aang now. He'll
either meet us at the camp... or we’ll see him on the battlefield.”
The mood sombred quickly, but no one had any qualms with the plan. Nanook wished he had
some great wisdom to impart on the group, or a rousing one-liner to bring spirits up, but he

was just as lost as the rest of them.
He thought, though, if he was right about this, then he might at least be able to help Zuko.
They set a small camp up in a clearing they found in the woods, their tents around a small
fire, and Suki was handing some snacks out. At least June hadn’t tried to camp with them,
instead hinting that she’d lifted something of theirs and would use it to track them, leaving
with an ominous see you tomorrow. Katara was still seething, loudly, about the woman’s
cheek. Nanook was just worried the bounty hunter intended to sell on information about
where they were going.
He'd planned to wait for everyone to settle a little more before trying to talk to Zuko, and was
absolutely blindsided to notice the firebender making his way over before he even got the
chance. Nanook dug an elbow into Tomkin’s side, despairing when the other boy only looked
up with a complaint on his tongue that morphed into a clueless smile when he saw Zuko
coming over, like he wasn’t aware of anything going on around him at all ever. Nanook really
didn’t know what he’d expected.
“Can I sit here?” Zuko asked, pointing to the log Tomkin had proudly yanked over,
dramatically showing off his biceps once he’d positioned it by the fire. Nanook hadn’t had
the heart to bring up the fact the log was sodden and half-rotted.
“Course you can, buddy!” Tomkin chirped. They were on the opposite side of the fire from
everyone but Zi Se, who had of course come to sit wherever Zuko did, and with the
conversation getting louder on that side, Toph randomly beginning to applaud something
before being forcibly stopped by Suki, this was about as private as they could get without
walking off on a midnight stroll. Now was Nanook’s chance.
“You okay?” he asked, gaze searching. “I can tell something’s been bothering you.”
Zuko hunched his shoulders, frowning. “It’s nothing.”
“Clearly not if it’s bothering you,” Tomkin pointed out, throwing some tree nuts in his mouth
and only managing to catch half. Nanook pulled a face at his lack of seriousness, turning a
little to cut him off. Tomkin made a garbled ‘hey!’ noise around half-chewed food.
“Do you want to talk about it?” Nanook suggested. “Doesn’t matter if you don’t think it’s a
big deal. Tomkin complains about literally everything ever, so you’ll never have him beat for
mundane whinging.”
“Hey!” said louder, food fully chewed. Tomkin grabbed Nanook’s arm, trying to pull him
back so he could get back into the conversation, and when that didn’t work, he resolved for
stubbornly hooking his chin over Nanook’s shoulder, his front pressed entirely into Nanook’s
side.
“Get off, you’re heavy,” Nanook hissed, but didn’t actually make much effort to push him
away.

Their behaviour had tempted a small smile from Zuko, his rigidness falling somewhat, and
Nanook gave him a reassuring smile in return. Finally, the prince sighed, twisting his hands
in his lap, refusing to look up.
“I... need advice. Romantic advice.”
It was silent for a few moments. Nanook prayed to Tui and La and every other spirit he knew
to please, please make Tomkin realise the fragility of this conversation and not run his big
mouth, but Nanook’s prayers very often went unheard when it came to the other boy.
“Holy shit, it’s finally happening,” Tomkin whispered, before grinning, grabbing Nanook's
arm and proceeding to squeal like a child. “It’s happening, Nan!”
“Shut up, moron!” Nanook hissed, as quietly as he could, as if there was even a slight chance
that Zuko couldn’t hear them. “What do you need advice about, Zuko? We can get rid of
Tomkin if he’s being unhelpful.”
“Excuse you, I am an expert at dating.”
“Expert at getting rejected at every port you’ve been to, more like.”
“At least I wear my heart on my sleeve, Mister ‘I sneak off every couple weeks to spend a
night with someone and never give my best friend any details on it’.” Tomkin huffed. “It's
okay if you want to admit you just have no experience, Nan, I won’t judge.” He held up a
solemn hand, as if swearing a vow.
Nanook cuffed him over the head. “I don’t tell you because you would run your mouth and
tell the entire crew, you liability. Zuko, please continue.”
Zuko looked like he had been thoroughly convinced not to continue, but he either trusted
them enough not to snitch – or trusted Nanook’s ability to shut Tomkin up if he tried – or he
was desperate enough to take his chances, because he cleared his throat, speaking quietly. He
made it look like he was just trying to keep the words from reaching where Zi Se sat playing
with his trinket from the market at their feet, but Nanook suspected he was more paranoid
about the others hearing.
“So,” he said, abundantly awkward, “there’s this... person... And I thought they liked me, but
now I’m not so sure, and I...couldn’t be with them even if they did. So I should just forget
about it, right? It's stupid.”
“It’s not stupid,” Nanook said carefully. “Do you like them back?”
“It can’t happen-.”
“But do you?”
Zuko looked like an animal in a trap, eyes so wide, so scared, and Nanook felt his heart break
a little. He didn’t need any more answer than that.
“And you think they like you back, did they say something?”

A deep red flush suddenly filled Zuko’s cheeks, and he looked all around before leaning
closer to Tomkin and Nanook, who at this point were both hanging on every word.
“They, uh, kissed me,” Zuko said.
“Let’s fucking go!” Tomkin yelled, and immediately got shoved to the floor by Nanook and
kicked in the shin by Zuko, topped off with a stern glare from Zi Se.
“Language,” the little boy said, tone extremely disappointed. Nanook had to bite back a laugh
at Tomkin’s dazed expression.
“It’s not how it sounds,” Zuko was quick to minimise it, still blushing fiercely. “We... They
were completely off with me after that, and now... I don’t know. Nothing can come of it
anyway, so it shouldn’t matter, but I wish I knew what they were thinking. How can they
just... switch up like that? Did they not even want to try and make it work?”
Nanook had a big speech planned, about how frightening it could be to reveal your feelings,
how it was safer and tidier to just keep them locked inside, and that Zuko’s mystery crush –

Azula would never normally have doubted her father’s battle plans, and even if she had, she
never would have dared sneak into his chambers to quickly read over the finalisations for the
day Sozin’s Comet arrived, but things were different now. She hated that Zuko had seen it so
clearly, had wrapped his fingers around still smarting skin and demanded of her tell me again
how nothing has changed, but on this one topic, he had been correct. Azula would call it a
lucky guess, refusing to give his intelligence the benefit of the doubt.
She had been right to snoop. Father was planning on separating from her to destroy the Earth
Kingdom by himself, leaving her behind to watch over the Fire Nation in his absence. An
important job, no doubt, but burning everything to the ground had been suggested by her
first. She had done everything right for years, and now, he was casting her aside like... like
Zuko.
She felt the rejection like claws around her throat, stifling, not yet strangling, more so the
threat of injury if she made even one more small mistake. She had been raised this way, that
silent threat hanging over her. A mother with fitful eyes who never hugged her. A father too
quick to anger. Azula learnt perfection before most children even learnt to walk, but these
past few weeks, everything around her felt like it was slipping. A landslide she could not will
into stillness. Her carefully manufactured control beginning to rattle with the force of an
outside storm that would, sooner or later, break.
And what would be left when it broke? It would take everything with it. She would have
nothing left. Mother, Zuko, Uncle, Lu Ten – they had all left her behind. All she had was
Father, and now, it seemed, even he had exhausted his use of her.
It was the middle of the night, but Azula found herself in the palace’s main corridor, looking
up at the royal portraits. It was an odd tradition she had come by, when sleep evaded her as it
so often did now. It did not bode well. She was beginning to get bags beneath her eyes. A
small imperfection in the smudge of that darkness. Unacceptable. A hairline crack. But if she
slept, she imagined assassins in her room, a knife to her throat, Father’s glowing eyes and
heartless call to action before the knife cut and all she knew was blood.
Azula was not frightened. Azula was perfect. She could handle all this.
Still, she stared up at Azulon’s portrait and thought of blue flames reflected in eyes the same
shade as hers, holding a fear she could not accommodate. A brother she never wanted.
He was the last to abandon her. She would never forgive him.
But alone entirely in the palace, without allies and facing a destiny larger than what fourteenyear-old hands could hold, Azula wondered distantly where Zuko was, and how he would
meet his end when they crossed paths again.
No one else was allowed to kill him. That, at least, Azula had always been certain of.

The warriors of the Southern Water Tribe were long accustomed to spending extended
periods of time aboard the Ullaakut, sailing various oceans between various ports, sometimes
spending months at a time with nothing but the endless water and one another’s inevitably
stifling company around them. The week or so that it would take them to reach the White
Lotus camp was, in comparison, practically nothing to the more seasoned sailors on board.
With hindsight, however, Kanut should have been prepared for the restlessness and boredom
that would very quickly arise in their latest and historically youngest crewmember – The
Duke.
The Duke’s first day at sea had seen the eight-year-old wonderous and excitable. He was
quick to let everyone know that it was not his first time sailing, but it was hard to tell for his
awe at every little thing. The second day was similar enough, with that excitement translating
to curiosity, wanting to know how any and everything worked. It was a very peaceful time in
Kanut’s memory, when The Duke had been utterly content doing knots with Hakoda for
hours at a time
As always, Kanut's peace was not to last. The Duke quickly grew bored, and it seemed to
finally hit the little boy that he was, in fact, stuck on this boat for the foreseeable future, and
apparently, to a child, a week was a very, very long time. He grew restless, irritable, his
curiosity suddenly too vast for the tribesmen to keep up with and thus invading each room
like a bad smell.
None of this should have affected Kanut. He was more than happy to do his jobs, check in
with the others, and read his books quietly in his infirmary, as he spent years doing before
everything got so strange. There was absolutely no earthly reason for The Duke to be in his
space, going through his things. Hakoda's pitiful attempt to coral the child somewhere else
had been a colossal failure, and the chief had since sent Kanut a shit-eating grin and
wandered off to go and pretend to be important elsewhere, leaving Kanut once again alone
with the ship’s newest menace. The Duke had sat himself on the floor now, pulling drawers
out of Kanut’s cabinet and inspecting each one’s contents with a laughable seriousness, in
that it would be laughable if this was happening in another room and to literally anyone else.
At the very least, The Duke had finally paused his ceaseless, asinine questions, and Kanut

attempted, as he had valiantly been trying to do even with the ongoing distraction, to
continue reading and pretending as if the boy wasn’t there. He probably should have
wondered what had caught The Duke’s interest so thoroughly. Really, anything that could
make the little boy go quiet for even a few moments consecutively should have at least
worried Kanut enough that he paid some attention.
He blamed that oversight on his frayed nerves, but really, he had no excuse for only noticing
the literal fucking bone saw by the time it was already in the kid’s hands, the blade alone the
size of The Duke’s torso but dwarfed by the sheer elation in the little boy’s grin.
Kanut's book dropped to the floor with the speed in which he sat up straight in the infirmary
cot, eyes wide and hands automatically rising, as if calming a wild animal, or surrendering.
“Hey, kid,” he tried calmly, “you should really put that down.”
It was an excellent blade, strong enough to amputate, a beautiful ivory handle – one of
Kanut’s favourites out of his trusty surgical set that he always kept sharpened for
emergencies. The blade seemed to wink at him in the afternoon sun coming in from the
window, held cluelessly in soft, young hands. Spirits, Hakoda would kill him if he saw The
Duke with a bone saw.
“What? Why?” The Duke asked, immediately indignant and, if anything, holding the blade
tighter like he thought Kanut might snatch it off him. “I like this one, it looks super cool! Can
I keep it?”
“No, you absolutely can’t,” Kanut said, strangled. “Put it down.”
This, apparently, was not the right thing to say. The only warning Kanut got was The Duke’s
face pinching up in frustration at being told no, and then the telltale twist of his position
before the little boy darted out of the infirmary at a full sprint, bone saw still very much in
hand.
Kanut jumped to his feet in horror. “Duke!”
“It’s The Duke!” the kid yelled from the hallway as he made a break for it. “And this is
mine!”
----Chena didn’t like the Fire Nation trio. He didn’t like having them on the Ullaakut. He didn’t

at least that had felt like somewhat neutral territory. Things were different on the Ullaakut,
confined to such a small space, and it made Chena antsy. He knew for a fact that at least one
of the trio was a firebender – Chit Sang, an incredibly large man with cropped hair and a dim,
unintelligent stare. He didn’t seem to be overly smart or observant, none of the trio did,
happy to spend their days within their own circle and not bothering with the tribesmen, but he

Fire Nation takes everything they want from the whole fucking world, and one firebender

Chena didn’t know what to say. It was quiet between them for a few moments but for the

“He’s eight-years-old,” Aput hissed, glaring at the firebender. “Why would it be normal for
him to have a saw?”
Chena scratched at his chin. “I dunno, it’s always good to start ‘em young.”
“Can you guys shut up and help?” Kanut snarled, eyes on the kid who looked like he was
seriously considering his escape options, grip pointedly tight on what Chena recognised as
Kanut’s bone saw. The blade glinted in the sun, wickedly sharp. Discomfort tugged at Chena,
the severity of the situation beginning to realise itself.

“The chief's gonna kill you for giving him a weapon,” Chena pointed out, and the healer
whirled on him, eyes widening.
“I did not fucking give it to him!”
Aput snorted. “Tell Hakoda that if the kid hurts himself. Hey, The Duke?” he raised his voice
a little for the boy to hear. “You wanna come give us that saw? It's dangerous, you shouldn’t
be playing with it.”
“Do you really think telling an eight-year-old boy that the cool weapon he found is
dangerous will convince him to give it up?” Chena grumbled, and sure enough, The Duke
seemed to have refocused his attention on the saw, eyes sparkling.
Aput glared at Chena. “Well, what’s your genius idea, wise guy?”
“Oi!” Chena yelled, turning to the little kid, who jumped at the sudden volume. “Give us it
back or I’ll throw you overboard!”
Aput groaned into his hands. Kanut looked at Chena like he’d grown a second head. The Fire
Nation trio, generally, looked very confused by everything going on. And The Duke seemed
even more resolved to stay far, far away from the adults, pointing the blade out at them as he
backed away towards the bowsprit.
Well, Chena thought, shit.
----“We’re coming into the Mo Ce Sea. We wasted almost all of yesterday in irons, but the wind
direction turned in the night, putting us in a better position to sail with the north wind.” Tulok
illustrated their position on the large map spread over Hakoda’s desk, brow furrowed.
“Assuming we keep this speed, we should arrive at the camp in the next three or four days.
We've made better time than we thought we would, even with yesterday’s setback.”
“That’s good,” Hakoda said. “Thank you, Tulok. It’s a relief to know we’ll be seeing all the
men again soon.”
“It is.” Tulok nodded with an indulgent smile, eyes trailing down the map to look longingly at
the South Pole. “Hanta ought to have letters from my sister, it’ll be nice to know how Miki is
doing.”
Hanta was one of the men waiting for them at the White Lotus camp and Tulok’s brother-inlaw, father of the baby everyone but Bato had been able to meet when they travelled south
with the Fire Prince a few months ago. He tried not to be bitter – Tui and La knew he
couldn’t beat Hanta’s own bitterness when he found out Miki’s uncle had met her before her
own father had, getting Tulok in a headlock when they last reunited at Chameleon Bay – but
a baby was a wondrous thing, and it meant a lot for their tribe.
Besides, “Hanta still owes me money,” Bato huffed, crossing his arms.

Tulok rolled his eyes. “Would you stop saying that? Hanta hates gambling, and even if he had
agreed to that stupid bet, which he didn’t, that was with Aput.”
“It was not!” Bato gasped. “He’s lying to you, Tulok. He’s getting in your head, don’t let
him.”
Tulok looked remarkably unimpressed.
Hakoda chuckled, clapping a hand to Bato’s shoulder. “I think Bato is just confused. You
know, what is Aput’s is not yours... yet.”
Bato shoved his friend off him. “I have no idea what you mean,” he hissed, hating how
flustered he suddenly sounded. Hakoda guffawed, head tipped back with it, and Tulok
laughed along with him, even if he looked a little confused – thank the Spirits. Bato did not
need anything being said to Aput, and Tulok was one of the man’s closest friends. Not that
there was anything to be said to Aput, of course. Just Hakoda and Kanut’s stupid running
joke that had absolutely no basis.
“Why don’t we get back to our work? Right, chief?” Bato stressed, glaring at Hakoda, who
was trying and failing to pull himself together. Bato cleared his throat and forced the
conversation forward. “Where are we at with strategy ideas? I know there’s not much we can
do until we get to the camp and see what our numbers are looking like and what kind of
benders the Dragon of the West might have been able to recruit, but I think Hakoda was right
about a visible victory.”
“Will it not be enough just to defeat the Fire Lord?” Tulok asked, the seriousness of such a
task sucking the last of the humour from the room. Bato only felt a little bad for it; after all,
this was something they needed to keep discussing for as long as they still had time to plan.
“The defeat of Fire Lord Ozai will be, in itself, massively symbolic,” Hakoda concurred with
a firm nod, “but that is the Avatar’s fight. I have faith in him, but he’ll need our help. If we
can weaken the Fire Nation at her very foundations – invade their streets, take over their
strongholds, neutralise their main points of defence – then it lessens the load put on the
Avatar and puts us in a better position if he... fails.”
“Which he won’t,” Tulok said, overly optimistic.
Bato didn’t say anything, but he and Hakoda shared a loaded glance, both far too strategic
and far too war weary. Truth be told, neither of them liked the idea of the battle hinging on a
twelve-year-old, Avatar or not, and when they were all gathered at the White Lotus camp
with a better idea of their resources and numbers, Bato knew Hakoda would start preparing
countermeasures, but for now, it didn’t do well to dissuade the men. Believing in the Avatar
was to believe in something bigger than all of them, a grand, Spirits-blessed miracle, and for
some of them, who had only known fire and agony and war, the only thing they could believe
in now was miracles.
Hakoda steeled himself, giving Tulok a rallying grin. “We will not fail. The Avatar has us to
help him just as much as we have him to help us. We've fought this whole war as a tribe, and
we will win it that way, and I don’t know any warriors braver or more worthy.” Blue eyes

landed heavily on both Bato and Tulok, as if seeing all of their doubts and refusing to be
dissuaded by them. “It will be an honour to fight with you all, one last time.”
Tulok gave the chief a wobbly smile in response, nodding in determination. Hakoda had
always been good like this, inspiring the warriors with no more than the sheer authenticity of
his faith in them, and normally, Bato would build off of it, catch morale in the wave of the
chief’s words and let it swell around them until everyone was laughing and cheering and
made brave by it all, but movement on the deck caught his eye, and he turned to look out of
the window taking up a large portion of the cabin’s far wall.
He snorted. “What was it you were saying about not knowing any warriors more worthy than
us?”
Hakoda frowned, both him and Tulok coming to the window to see what Bato was talking
about.
“You’ve got to be kidding me,” Hakoda said.
Tulok looked very suddenly despairing. “Why does this keep happening?”
Down on the deck, Bato watched as Aput, Chena and Kanut, all with varying expressions of
panic on their faces, tried to convince The Duke to get away from the bowsprit, the little boy
wielding a large blade with a ferocious expression as he made to clamber up onto the wooden
pole, much to the yells of horror from the tribesmen. Hakoda didn’t wait around to see if the
kid would fall overboard, immediately running from the room, followed by Tulok.
Bato shook his head, cursing beneath his breath, before joining his friends outside.
----Seeing a scared little boy push himself back onto the bowsprit while the ocean churned
mercilessly far below was a disturbingly familiar sight for Hakoda, and he had to agree with
Tulok’s sentiment, because there was no way this was a common enough occurrence to have
happened to him twice in one year. He steeled himself as soon as he was on the deck, forcing
a calm demeanour and striding forward. The Fire Nation trio – Chit Sang, Yuna and Yasu –
were stood to the side by the ship railing, watching the proceedings with mixed looks of
concern and confusion. Hakoda gave them a stern nod that he hoped conveyed I-am-incharge-and-have-this-under-control.
“What’s going on?” he hissed as soon as he reached his men, coming to stand between Kanut
and Chena. “Why does he have a bone saw? Kanut?”
The healer kept his eyes on where The Duke clung to the bowsprit, remarkably sure-footed
for an eight-year-old – Hakoda had to remind himself the boy had spent years living in the
trees with his Freedom Fighters – but his tone was accusing enough that Hakoda knew he’d
rather be turning a poisonous glare his way.
“He was going through my things,” Kanut snarled. “Remember, like he was when you
ditched me with him? I told you to get him out of the infirmary!”

“Oh, this is my fault?” Hakoda hissed.
“Well, you could have prevented it!”
“Chief, what do we do?” Aput asked. “He just moves further away every time we try and get
closer.”
Hakoda frowned. “Have you tried talking him down?”
He was met with a guilty silence that he presumed meant that someone, probably Chena, had
tried talking The Duke down and had likely made everything significantly worse as a result.
Hakoda sighed.
“Okay,” he said. “Everyone back off, he’s probably scared because he’s being cornered by all
of us. Let me try and talk to him alone.”
No one seemed eager to argue, grown warriors practically fleeing in the face of a child’s
tantrum, Kanut in particular immediately stomping off to the infirmary while muttering
something unseemly beneath his breath, and then, it was just Hakoda meeting The Duke’s
surly glare. There was something to be said, he thought, about his biggest concern the last
time this happened being the flammability of the sails, attached to the bowsprit by the
forestays. He was no more in danger of the Ullaakut being sank now than he had been then,
not that he knew it at the time, staring down a firebender and seeing only destruction in
young hands. They'd been so frightened of each other.
But patience went a long way, Hakoda knew, and compassion. He gave The Duke a soft
smile, relaxing his posture.
“Do you want to tell me why you’re upset, kid?” he asked.
The Duke glared at him, clutching the bone saw to his chest. “I’m not upset! This is mine! I
got it first! The Freedom Fighters let me play with sharp things all the time!”
As a parent, Hakoda had several thoughts about the group of armed children that had called
themselves the Freedom Fighters, but giving that lecture now was probably ill-timed, so he
swallowed it back and kept his expression understanding.
“I see,” he said. “It’s probably frustrating you now that the rules are different here, is that
right?”
The Duke looked considering for a moment, like he hadn’t expected Hakoda to actually try
and understand his point of view. He narrowed his eyes.
“I don’t like being condescended,” the little kid said, the big word clumsy on his tongue, like
he’d heard it said only a handful of times and had never actually repeated it himself until
now. It was a little bit adorable, and reminded Hakoda of Sokka when he’d been this age, his
mind far smarter than his mouth.
“There’s no one like me here,” The Duke continued quietly, lower lip protruding. “I miss
Pipsqueak.”

“I know everyone’s a lot older than you here,” Hakoda conceded, taking a careful step closer.
“But you get on well with Teo, don’t you? Where is he right now?”
The Duke huffed. “He’s always tinkering with any bits of metal he finds, which is sometimes
cool, but sometimes it’s so boring! I want to play but all he wants to do is sit downstairs with
his tools.”
Hakoda made a point of humming exaggeratedly. “That is frustrating.”
“It is!” The Duke said, scooting a little closer along the bowsprit, feet now dangling above
the deck. Hakoda relaxed fractionally, no longer concerned about the little boy falling into the
water, but he still wanted to get that bone saw far out of his hands.
“Okay, how’s this sound?” Hakoda said. “If you come down and give me that saw, I’ll find
you a different blade, and we can spar for a bit?”
The Duke looked sceptical. “Spar? Like, you’ll teach me some moves?”
“Sure will, kid. Truth be told,” Hakoda lowered his voice like he was telling a secret, “that
bone saw you’ve got now belongs to Kanut, and it means a lot to him. He’ll be really sad if
he doesn’t get it back.”
The Duke looked a little guilty then, and finally, he shuffled the rest of the way along the
bowsprit, hopping down onto the deck. He gave the bone saw one last admiring look, before
huffing, and handing it over to Hakoda. Hakoda kept his relief hidden, but he was quick to
get the blade out of the eight-year-old's hands, giving him a happy grin at his decision.
“Thank you, The Duke,” he said. “Now, let’s go find you a blade of your own, how does that
sound?”
“Okay!” The Duke grinned, any regrets he had about losing his bone saw immediately being
forgotten upon being offered a new blade that could be all his, and if Hakoda purposely gave
the kid a dagger that hadn’t been sharpened in years, blunt enough that it took a lot of
pressure directly against the blade to even cut skin, then The Duke didn’t seem any the wiser,
laughing brightly on deck as Hakoda taught him some basic manoeuvres with it.
-----“Three silver pieces says the brat accidentally stabs Hakoda and we have to go get Kanut,”
Aput said, watching the chief spar with purposely slow, delicate movements against the eightyear-old who had caused them so much stress earlier in the day.
Bato huffed out a laugh beside him. “You have a gambling addiction. Seriously, you need
help.”
“So you’re not taking the bet?” Aput gave him a wolfish smile, knocking their shoulders
together. Bato seemed to stutter a moment, like a bright light had caught his eye and he was
trying to regather his bearings.

“Fuck it,” he eventually grumbled, “fine. It's a stupid bet, Hakoda’s not gonna get caught out
by an eight-year-old. You're on.”
Later, with the sun setting on their port side, the conversation Bato and Aput had been having
was interrupted by a surprised yell, and they looked over to see their chief with a knee to the
deck and blood slowly spreading from his thigh. The Duke stood guiltily in front of him, the
dagger in his hand now stained red.
For a moment, it was silent, Bato and Aput sharing a disbelieving stare, before chaos broke
out. Hakoda immediately shoved to his feet, a little unsteady, trying to cover the wound with
a large hand and forcing a reassuring smile, but The Duke had already burst into tears,
throwing his dagger to the floor like it had burned him and profusely apologising through his
loud sobs.
“I’ll get Kanut,” Bato sighed.
Aput cackled. “He’s gonna be so pissed.”
